lomekwi-3-stone-tools-3298000bce.summary: Excavation at Lomekwi 3 in Kenya's West Turkana recovered 149 stone artefacts, cores, flakes and anvils struck from lava cobbles with passive-hammer and bipolar techniques, from sediments dated to 3.3 million years ago by magnetostratigraphy and tephra correlation. These tools predate the earliest known Homo fossils by about 500,000 years and Gona's by 700,000. No fossil ties them to a maker; Kenyanthropus platyops and Australopithecus afarensis lived nearby. Cut-marked bones from Dikika in Ethiopia, dated past 3.39 million years, would push carcass processing earlier still, a reading other researchers dispute as trampling damage.

sources.title: Harmand, S. et al., '3.3-million-year-old stone tools from Lomekwi 3, West Turkana, Kenya', Nature 521 (2015), 310-315
sources.author: Harmand, Sonia; Lewis, Jason E.; Feibel, Craig S.; Lepre, Christopher J.; Prat, Sandrine; Lenoble, Arnaud
sources.confirms: Reports 149 artefacts from Lomekwi 3 dated to 3.3 million years and describes knapping techniques.

sources.title: McPherron, S. P. et al., 'Evidence for stone-tool-assisted consumption of animal tissues before 3.39 million years ago at Dikika, Ethiopia', Nature 466 (2010), 857-860
sources.author: McPherron, Shannon P.; Alemseged, Zeresenay; Marean, Curtis W.; Wynn, Jonathan G.; Reed, Denné; Geraads, Denis
sources.confirms: Reports stone-tool-inflicted marks on bones older than 3.39 million years at Dikika.
sources.qualifies: Dikika marks remain disputed as evidence of butchery; the record treats them as a contested hint.

lomekwi-3-stone-tools-3298000bce.detail: Lomekwi knapping is cruder than later Oldowan work: cores are heavy, flakes show little control of platform angle, and many pieces came from battering on anvils. Critics, including some who accept Dikika as trampling damage rather than butchery, asked whether Lomekwi material could be derived from younger layers; excavators answered with in situ refits and sediment analysis. Lomekwi gives a starting point for a 3.3-million-year record of extracting edges from rock.

picture.alt: Map of Lomekwi locality west of Lake Turkana, Kenya, where 3.3 million year old stone tools were found
picture.credit: Chartep, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

lomekwi-3-stone-tools-3298000bce.dating_note: Age of 3.3 million years rests on palaeomagnetic stratigraphy and tephra correlation of the host sediments, not on direct dating of artefacts.

oldowan-flake-and-core-tools-2598000bce.summary: Oldowan assemblages mark a long span of flake and core tools across East Africa, from about 2.6 million years ago at Gona in Ethiopia to around 1.7 million years ago when Acheulean handaxes spread. Gona artefacts date to 2.6 to 2.5 million years ago by argon dating and magnetostratigraphy. Bokol Dora 1 in the Ledi-Geraru area adds a securely dated assemblage older than 2.58 million years. At Nyayanga, Kenya, 330 artefacts dated 3.03 to 2.58 million years ago lie alongside butchered hippopotamus bones and Paranthropus teeth, showing Oldowan tools used to cut large carcasses and pound plant foods well before Homo erectus.

sources.title: Semaw, S. et al., '2.5-million-year-old stone tools from Gona, Ethiopia', Nature 385 (1997), 333-336
sources.author: Semaw, S.; Renne, P.; Harris, J. W. K.; Feibel, C. S.; Bernor, R. L.; Fesseha, N.
sources.confirms: Dates Gona stone tools to 2.6 to 2.5 million years by argon dating and magnetostratigraphy.

sources.title: Braun, D. R. et al., 'Earliest known Oldowan artifacts at >2.58 Ma from Ledi-Geraru, Ethiopia, highlight early technological diversity', Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences 116 (2019), 11712-11717
sources.author: Braun, David R.; Aldeias, Vera; Archer, Will; Arrowsmith, J Ramon; Baraki, Niguss; Campisano, Christopher J.
sources.venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
sources.confirms: Reports an Oldowan assemblage older than 2.58 million years at Bokol Dora 1, Ethiopia.

sources.title: Plummer, T. W. et al., 'Expanded geographic distribution and dietary strategies of the earliest Oldowan hominins and Paranthropus', Science 379 (2023), 561-566
sources.author: Plummer, Thomas W.; Oliver, James S.; Finestone, Emma M.; Ditchfield, Peter W.; Bishop, Laura C.; Blumenthal, Scott A.
sources.confirms: Reports 330 Oldowan artefacts at Nyayanga dated 3.03 to 2.58 million years with butchered hippo bones and Paranthropus teeth.

oldowan-flake-and-core-tools-2598000bce.detail: Oldowan knappers selected fine-grained cobbles and struck flakes with hard hammers, controlling platform angles far better than Lomekwi workers. Sharp flakes slice hide and sinew; cores and hammerstones crush bone for marrow and pound tubers. Nyayanga's association of tools with Paranthropus teeth revives questions about which hominins made and used Oldowan kits. Gona's dating combines argon ages on tuffs with palaeomagnetic reversals; the era's end is gradual as handaxes appear in some regions while flake industries persist elsewhere.

picture.alt: Oldowan chopper from Olduvai Gorge, about 1.8 million years old, British Museum
picture.credit: Archaeomoonwalker, CC BY 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

oldowan-flake-and-core-tools-2598000bce.dating_note: Start date of 2.6 million years follows argon dating and magnetostratigraphy at Gona; Nyayanga's wide 3.03 to 2.58 million year bracket could push Oldowan beginnings earlier.

kokiselei-acheulean-handaxes-1758000bce.summary: At Kokiselei 4 in West Turkana, Kenya, large bifacially flaked handaxes and picks date to 1.76 million years ago by magnetostratigraphy tied to Olduvai Subchron. That makes it one of two oldest known Acheulean sites, with Konso in Ethiopia (about 1.75 million years ago) chronologically indistinguishable, co-occurring with Oldowan tools in same stratigraphic interval. Acheulean handaxes are shaped on both faces to a planned form, beyond simple flake removal. Handaxe makers spread across Africa and into Eurasia over following million years, reaching Attirampakkam in India by 1.5 million years ago.

sources.title: Lepre, C. J. et al., 'An earlier origin for the Acheulian', Nature 477 (2011), 82-85
sources.author: Lepre, Christopher J.; Roche, Hélène; Kent, Dennis V.; Harmand, Sonia; Quinn, Rhonda L.; Brugal, Jean-Philippe
sources.confirms: Dates Kokiselei 4 handaxes to 1.76 million years and names it oldest Acheulean.

sources.title: Beyene, Y. et al., 'The characteristics and chronology of the earliest Acheulean at Konso, Ethiopia', Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences 110 (2013), 1584-1591
sources.author: Beyene, Yonas; Katoh, Shigehiro; WoldeGabriel, Giday; Hart, William K.; Uto, Kozo; Sudo, Masafumi; Suwa, Gen; Asfaw, Berhane
sources.venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
sources.confirms: Dates the earliest Konso Acheulean to about 1.75 million years and states it is chronologically indistinguishable from Kokiselei 4, reported at 1.72 to 1.76 million years.
sources.qualifies: Frames Konso and Kokiselei as equally old rather than Kokiselei as uniquely oldest.

kokiselei-acheulean-handaxes-1758000bce.verification_note: Beyene and colleagues (PNAS 2013) date Konso's earliest Acheulean to about 1.75 million years, chronologically indistinguishable from Kokiselei 4, so both sites share oldest Acheulean status.
kokiselei-acheulean-handaxes-1758000bce.detail: Kokiselei's age came from palaeomagnetic sampling of sediments bracketing its artefacts, which fall just below Olduvai Subchron top at 1.78 million years ago. Large cutting tools served for butchery and woodworking; their persistence for over a million years makes Acheulean among longest-lived technologies known. Kokiselei lies in Nachukui Formation, where Lomekwi 3 was later found a few kilometres away.

picture.alt: Acheulean flint handaxe from Saint-Acheul, France (type site, not Kokiselei), Museum de Toulouse
picture.credit: Didier Descouens, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

kokiselei-acheulean-handaxes-1758000bce.dating_note: Age rests on magnetostratigraphy of host sediments relative to Olduvai Subchron.

nihewan-majuangou-stone-tools-1658000bce.summary: Majuangou in Nihewan Basin, Hebei, preserves four stone-tool layers in lake sediments dated by magnetostratigraphy, oldest at 1.66 million years ago. These are among earliest secure records of hominins outside Africa and in high northern latitudes, where winters were cold and seasonal. Flakes and cores resemble Oldowan work. Later Nihewan sites such as Cenjiawan, about 1.1 million years old, show refitting sequences and improved knapping, which Shi-Xia Yang links to Mid-Pleistocene climate shifts.

sources.title: Zhu, R. X. et al., 'New evidence on the earliest human presence at high northern latitudes in northeast Asia', Nature 431 (2004), 559-562
sources.author: Zhu, R. X.; Potts, R.; Xie, F.; Hoffman, K. A.; Deng, C. L.; Shi, C. D.
sources.confirms: Dates Majuangou stone-tool layers to 1.66 million years by magnetostratigraphy.

sources.title: Yang, S. X. et al., 'Technological innovations at the onset of the Mid-Pleistocene Climate Transition in high-latitude East Asia', National Science Review 8 (2020)
sources.author: Yang, Shi-Xia; Wang, Fa-Gang; Xie, Fei; Yue, Jian-Ping; Deng, Cheng-Long; Zhu, Ri-Xiang
sources.confirms: Describes Nihewan Basin sites 1.4 to 1.0 million years old and refitting at Cenjiawan around 1.1 million years.

nihewan-majuangou-stone-tools-1658000bce.detail: Nihewan Basin lacks volcanic ash, so dating depends on palaeomagnetic reversals within lacustrine sediments; this yields brackets rather than pinpoint ages. Majuangou tools occur with cut-marked and percussion-marked bones of elephants and other large mammals. Occupation at 40 degrees north by 1.66 million years implies tolerance of temperate climates long before fire use is securely documented anywhere. Later sites such as Xiaochangliang and Donggutuo extend Nihewan's hominin sequence across hundreds of thousands of years.

picture.alt: Stone cores from Xiaochangliang in Nihewan Basin, China, Smithsonian National Museum of Natural History
picture.credit: Jonathan Chen, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

nihewan-majuangou-stone-tools-1658000bce.dating_note: Age rests on magnetostratigraphy; no radiometric dating is available at Majuangou.

attirampakkam-acheulean-tools-1508000bce.summary: Attirampakkam, near Chennai, yields Acheulean handaxes and cleavers in layers dated by cosmogenic aluminium-26 and beryllium-10 burial dating to about 1.51 million years ago, with magnetostratigraphy in support. Robin Dennell takes at least 1 million years as secure and about 1.5 million as probable. This is earliest Acheulean dated outside Africa and shows handaxe makers crossing into South Asia far earlier than previously held. Attirampakkam later records a Middle Palaeolithic industry with Levallois cores 385,000 years ago, suggesting long continuous occupation and local technological change.

sources.title: Pappu, S. et al., 'Early Pleistocene Presence of Acheulian Hominins in South India', Science 331 (2011), 1596-1599
sources.author: Pappu, Shanti; Gunnell, Yanni; Akhilesh, Kumar; Braucher, Régis; Taieb, Maurice; Demory, François
sources.confirms: Dates Acheulean at Attirampakkam to 1.51 million years by cosmogenic burial dating.

sources.title: Dennell, Robin, 'An Earlier Acheulian Arrival in South Asia', Science 331 (2011), 1532-1533
sources.author: Dennell, Robin
sources.confirms: Independent Perspective on Pappu et al.: the Attirampakkam Acheulian is dated to at least 1 million years and perhaps about 1.5 million years, demonstrating a South Asian Acheulian in the Early Pleistocene, older than 0.78 million years.
sources.qualifies: Dennell states the secure finding as at least 1 million years, with 1.5 million years as the probable upper estimate.

attirampakkam-acheulean-tools-1508000bce.verification_note: Dennell (Science 2011) frames this age as at least 1 million and perhaps about 1.5 million years; 1.51 million is Pappu's central estimate, not a minimum.
attirampakkam-acheulean-tools-1508000bce.detail: Burial dating measures time since quartz grains were shielded from cosmic rays; Attirampakkam's artefact-bearing clays gave a mean 1.51 million years with large uncertainty. Earlier India dates for Acheulean were under 500,000 years. Finds include large cutting tools of quartzite with both faces flaked. Attirampakkam sits in Kortallayar river basin and was excavated by Sharma Centre for Heritage Education. Excavations ran from 1999 under Shanti Pappu and Kumar Akhilesh.

picture.alt: Stone tools from Attirampakkam, Tamil Nadu, India
picture.credit: Ophelia S, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

attirampakkam-acheulean-tools-1508000bce.dating_note: Age is cosmogenic nuclide burial dating of 1.51 plus or minus 0.07 million years, with magnetostratigraphic support.

olduvai-bone-tools-1498000bce.summary: T69 Complex at Olduvai Gorge, Tanzania, yielded 27 bone tools dated to 1.5 million years ago. Knappers selected thick limb bones of elephants and hippopotamuses and flaked them with stone-knapping methods to make elongated, pointed tools up to 38 centimetres long. This is earliest known systematic bone-tool production, a million years before comparable assemblages. Technique transfer from stone to bone shows planning and understanding of material properties among early Acheulean toolmakers.

sources.title: de la Torre, I. et al., 'Systematic bone tool production at 1.5 million years ago', Nature 640 (2025), 130-134
sources.author: de la Torre, Ignacio; Doyon, Luc; Benito-Calvo, Alfonso; Mora, Rafael; Mwakyoma, Ipyana; Njau, Jackson K.
sources.confirms: Reports 27 knapped bone tools from Olduvai Gorge dated to 1.5 million years.

sources.title: Kreier, Freda, 'Ancient humans used bone tools one million years earlier than thought', Nature news, 5 March 2025
sources.author: Kreier, Freda
sources.confirms: Independent Nature news report that objects from Tanzania dated to 1.5 million years ago show hominins used carved bone tools a million years earlier than previously known.

olduvai-bone-tools-1498000bce.detail: Bone tools came from Bed II at Olduvai, in deposits with Acheulean stone artefacts. Workers removed flakes along bone shafts to form tips and edges, producing shapes analogous to stone handaxes. Earlier isolated bone tools from Swartkrans and Olduvai were digging implements with wear rather than deliberately knapped pieces. Tools were recognised during renewed excavation of Olduvai Bed II since 2010, with specimens compared against experimentally knapped elephant bone. Choice of very large mammal bones suggests makers sought thick cortical bone able to hold an edge.

picture.alt: Olduvai Gorge, Tanzania, from the air
picture.credit: Pi3.124, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

olduvai-bone-tools-1498000bce.dating_note: Age derives from Olduvai Bed II stratigraphy and argon dating of tuffs.

flores-wolo-sege-crossing-1018000bce.summary: Flores island in Indonesia lies beyond Wallace Line and was never joined to mainland Asia by land, so any hominin arrival required a sea crossing. Stone tools at Wolo Sege in Soa Basin date by argon-argon to 1.02 million years ago, older than Mata Menge. Tool-making hominins stood on Flores by one million years ago, ancestors of later Homo floresiensis; no evidence shows whether they crossed deliberately or rafted by accident on debris.

sources.title: Brumm, A. et al., 'Hominins on Flores, Indonesia, by one million years ago', Nature 464 (2010), 748-752
sources.author: Brumm, Adam; Jensen, Gitte M.; van den Bergh, Gert D.; Morwood, Michael J.; Kurniawan, Iwan; Aziz, Fachroel
sources.confirms: Dates stone tools at Wolo Sege, Flores, to 1.02 million years by argon-argon.

sources.title: Brumm, A. et al., 'Age and context of the oldest known hominin fossils from Flores', Nature 534 (2016), 249-253
sources.author: Brumm, Adam; van den Bergh, Gerrit D.; Storey, Michael; Kurniawan, Iwan; Alloway, Brent V.; Setiawan, Ruly
sources.confirms: Places hominin fossils at Mata Menge at about 700,000 years and sets them against stone tools at Wolo Sege dated to about 1.0 million years ago in the Soa Basin.

flores-wolo-sege-crossing-1018000bce.detail: Wolo Sege tools lie beneath an ignimbrite dated to 1.02 million years. Earlier claims from Mata Menge were around 880,000 years. Sea gaps between Sunda shelf and Flores were tens of kilometres even at lowest sea levels. One view has tsunami-driven rafts of vegetation carrying hominins across; another has purposeful seafaring. Flores evidence sits with Luzon and Sulawesi as early island records in Wallacea.

picture.alt: Map of Soa Basin, Flores, Indonesia, with Mata Menge and Wolo Sege localities
picture.credit: Meagan J. Powley, Indra Sutisna, Katarina M. Mikac, Unggul Prasetyo Wibowo, Gerr, CC BY 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

flores-wolo-sege-crossing-1018000bce.dating_note: Age is argon-argon on overlying ignimbrite; tools are at least this old.

wonderwerk-cave-fire-998000bce.summary: Burned bone and ashed plant remains lie in Acheulean layers 30 metres inside Wonderwerk Cave, Northern Cape, dated to about 1.0 million years ago. Micromorphology and infrared spectroscopy show bone heated above 500 degrees Celsius and intact ash in place, far from cave mouth where lightning or wildfire could not reach. This is earliest secure evidence of fire use in a controlled setting. Hominins here either made fire or maintained natural fire; either way, heat for cooking, warmth and light was available to Homo erectus.

sources.title: Berna, F. et al., 'Microstratigraphic evidence of in situ fire in the Acheulean strata of Wonderwerk Cave, Northern Cape province, South Africa', Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences 109 (2012)
sources.author: Berna, Francesco; Goldberg, Paul; Horwitz, Liora Kolska; Brink, James; Holt, Sharon; Bamford, Marion
sources.venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
sources.confirms: Reports microstratigraphic evidence of burned bone and ash inside Wonderwerk Cave at about one million years.

sources.title: Shaar, R. et al., 'Magnetostratigraphy and cosmogenic dating of Wonderwerk Cave: New constraints for the chronology of the South African Earlier Stone Age', Quaternary Science Reviews 259 (2021), 106907
sources.author: Shaar, Ron; Matmon, Ari; Horwitz, Liora Kolska; Ebert, Yael; Chazan, Michael; Arnold, Maurice
sources.confirms: Provides an independent magnetostratigraphic and cosmogenic chronology for the Wonderwerk Earlier Stone Age strata that hold the Acheulean fire evidence.

wonderwerk-cave-fire-998000bce.detail: Dating combines palaeomagnetism and cosmogenic nuclide burial ages for Wonderwerk's deep stratigraphy. Earlier claims of fire at Koobi Fora and Swartkrans around 1.5 million years rest on reddened sediment or burned bone in open-air contexts, open to natural explanations. Wonderwerk's deep interior position and microscopic ash fabric remove most of those doubts. Habitual fire use, with hearths across many sites, is not documented until around 400,000 years ago.
wonderwerk-cave-fire-998000bce.dating_note: Age of about one million years uses magnetostratigraphy and cosmogenic burial dating of cave sediments.

gesher-benot-yaaqov-fire-788000bce.summary: At Gesher Benot Ya'aqov on Jordan River in Israel, clustered burned flint microartefacts, along with charred plant remains, run through Acheulean layers dated to about 790,000 years ago by magnetostratigraphy around Brunhes-Matuyama boundary. Burned pieces concentrate in small patches interpreted as hearths, recurring across 100,000 years of occupation. This waterlogged site preserves wood, bark, fruits and nuts, giving fine detail on diet and fire. Fire control here precedes other Eurasian evidence by hundreds of thousands of years; Wonderwerk Cave in South Africa holds older evidence, near 1 million years.

sources.title: Goren-Inbar, N. et al., 'Evidence of Hominin Control of Fire at Gesher Benot Ya`aqov, Israel', Science 304 (2004), 725-727
sources.author: Goren-Inbar, Naama; Alperson, Nira; Kislev, Mordechai E.; Simchoni, Orit; Melamed, Yoel; Ben-Nun, Adi
sources.confirms: Reports clustered burned flint and plant remains as hearths at Gesher Benot Ya'aqov around 790,000 years.

sources.title: Alperson-Afil, Nira, 'Continual fire-making by Hominins at Gesher Benot Ya'aqov, Israel', Quaternary Science Reviews 27 (2008), 1733-1739
sources.author: Alperson-Afil, Nira
sources.confirms: Spatial analysis of burnt flint microartefacts identifies phantom hearths through the Gesher Benot Ya'aqov sequence, dated by the 0.79 million year Brunhes-Matuyama boundary, showing fire-making repeated across roughly 100,000 years of occupation.

gesher-benot-yaaqov-fire-788000bce.verification_note: Wonderwerk Cave lies in South Africa, with fire evidence near 1 million years ago, so it stands as an African comparison rather than Eurasian cave evidence.
gesher-benot-yaaqov-fire-788000bce.detail: Burned flint was identified by thermal damage and potlids; its spatial clustering, absent for unburned flint, argues for in-place fires. Site lies on Dead Sea Rift, where lake-margin sediments buried occupation surfaces rapidly. Acheulean tools include basalt handaxes and cleavers; edible plant remains include acorns, water chestnut, pistachio and wild grape. Later work at same site documents cooking of fish. Excavations ran from 1989 under Naama Goren-Inbar for Hebrew University.

picture.alt: Jordan River at Bnot Yaakov Bridge, Israel, beside Gesher Benot Yaaqov site
picture.credit: Bukvoed, CC BY 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

gesher-benot-yaaqov-fire-788000bce.dating_note: Age of about 790,000 years rests on magnetostratigraphy around Brunhes-Matuyama boundary.

gesher-benot-yaaqov-fish-cooking-778000b.summary: More than 40,000 fish remains from Gesher Benot Ya'aqov, Israel, date to about 780,000 years ago. Pharyngeal teeth of large carp dominate, while bones are nearly absent, and crystal structure of tooth enamel shows exposure to temperatures below 500 degrees Celsius, consistent with controlled cooking rather than burning. Remains cluster near hearths. This is earliest evidence of cooking any food, pushing heat processing of diet far before Homo sapiens. Cooked fish deliver protein and fats with lower chewing and digestion costs.

sources.title: Zohar, I. et al., 'Evidence for the cooking of fish 780,000 years ago at Gesher Benot Ya’aqov, Israel', Nature Ecology & Evolution 6 (2022), 2016-2028
sources.author: Zohar, Irit; Alperson-Afil, Nira; Goren-Inbar, Naama; Prévost, Marion; Tütken, Thomas; Sisma-Ventura, Guy
sources.confirms: Reports over 40,000 fish remains with enamel heated below 500 degrees as evidence of cooking at 780,000 years.

sources.title: Goren-Inbar, N. et al., 'Evidence of Hominin Control of Fire at Gesher Benot Ya'aqov, Israel', Science 304 (2004), 725-727
sources.author: Goren-Inbar, Naama; Alperson, Nira; Kislev, Mordechai E.; Simchoni, Orit; Melamed, Yoel; Ben-Nun, Adi; Werker, Ella
sources.confirms: Burned seeds, wood and flint clustered in hearth-like spots at Gesher Benot Ya'aqov show hominin control of fire nearly 790,000 years ago, the hearths the fish remains cluster around.

gesher-benot-yaaqov-fish-cooking-778000b.detail: Carp species identified include extinct giant barbs over two metres long from palaeo-Lake Hula. X-ray diffraction measured tooth enamel apatite crystals, which coarsen under moderate heat. Absence of bones suggests selective processing. Fish exploitation at this scale implies knowledge of seasonal spawning and lake ecology. Irit Zohar of Oranim College and Steinhardt Museum led this analysis with Naama Goren-Inbar. Lake Hula's fish could be taken from shore during spawning seasons, giving a reliable protein source alongside hunted deer and elephant.

picture.alt: Hula Valley, northern Israel, seen from Golan Heights; former Lake Hula shores held Gesher Benot Yaaqov
picture.credit: Grauesel, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

gesher-benot-yaaqov-fish-cooking-778000b.dating_note: Age follows site magnetostratigraphy around 780,000 years.

zhoukoudian-fire-claims-768000bce.summary: Zhoukoudian Locality 1 outside Beijing yielded Homo erectus fossils whose lower cultural layers date by aluminium-26 and beryllium-10 burial dating to 0.77 million years ago. Excavators in 1930s reported thick ash layers as evidence of fire use. Steve Weiner found no in situ hearths or ash in 1998; dark layers were organic sediments and burned bone could have washed in. Maohua Zhong later reanalysed Layers 4 and 6 and found siliceous aggregates, elemental carbon and potassium-rich residues, read as in situ controlled fire.

sources.title: Shen, G. et al., 'Age of Zhoukoudian Homo erectus determined with 26Al/10Be burial dating', Nature 458 (2009), 198-200
sources.author: Shen, Guanjun; Gao, Xing; Gao, Bin; Granger, Darryl E.
sources.confirms: Dates Zhoukoudian lower cultural layers 7 to 10 to 0.77 million years by cosmogenic burial dating.

sources.title: Weiner, S. et al., 'Evidence for the Use of Fire at Zhoukoudian, China', Science 281 (1998), 251-253
sources.author: Weiner, Steve; Xu, Qinqi; Goldberg, Paul; Liu, Jinyi; Bar-Yosef, Ofer
sources.confirms: Finds no in situ burning evidence and reinterprets ash layers as non-fire sediments.
sources.qualifies: Weiner and colleagues reject fire use at Zhoukoudian as unproven.

sources.title: Zhong, M. et al., 'On the possible use of fire by Homo erectus at Zhoukoudian, China', Chinese Science Bulletin 59 (2013), 335-343
sources.author: Zhong, Maohua; Shi, Congling; Gao, Xing; Wu, Xinzhi; Chen, Fuyou; Zhang, Shuangquan
sources.confirms: Reports analyses of four samples from Layers 4 and 6 supporting in situ controlled fire use.

zhoukoudian-fire-claims-768000bce.verification_note: Fire use is contested; site age is secure.
zhoukoudian-fire-claims-768000bce.detail: Burial dating gave a weighted mean of 0.77 plus or minus 0.08 million years for Layers 7 to 10; Layers 4 and 6 with fire claims are younger, perhaps 500,000 to 400,000 years. Weiner used mineralogy and micromorphology on remaining deposits. Zhong's analysis of four soil samples reported potassium in insoluble residues between 1.21 and 2.94 percent, taken as ash signature. Interpretation depends on whether ash can survive without visible hearth structure.

picture.alt: Locality 1 at Zhoukoudian, China, where burnt bone and ash layers were reported
picture.credit: myself, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

zhoukoudian-fire-claims-768000bce.dating_note: Year gives burial age of lower layers; fire-claim layers 4 and 6 are younger and undated directly, and fire use is disputed between Weiner et al. (1998) and Zhong et al. (2014).

kathu-pan-hafted-spear-tips-498000bce.summary: Stone points from Kathu Pan 1 in Northern Cape carry impact fractures and basal modifications matching experimentally thrust spear tips. Deposits are dated to about 500,000 years ago by optically stimulated luminescence and uranium-series on tooth enamel. If accepted, this is earliest evidence of hafting, fastening stone onto a shaft, roughly 200,000 years earlier than previous records, and attributable to Homo heidelbergensis. Veerle Rots and Hugues Plisson challenge the use-wear reading, arguing fractures could arise from other causes; Jayne Wilkins replied with further analysis.

sources.title: Wilkins, J. et al., 'Evidence for Early Hafted Hunting Technology', Science 338 (2012), 942-946
sources.author: Wilkins, Jayne; Schoville, Benjamin J.; Brown, Kyle S.; Chazan, Michael
sources.confirms: Reports hafted spear tips at Kathu Pan 1 dated about 500,000 years.

sources.title: Rots, V. and Plisson, H., 'Projectiles and the abuse of the use-wear method in a search for impact', Journal of Archaeological Science 48 (2014), 154-165
sources.author: Rots, Veerle; Plisson, Hugues
sources.confirms: Questions use-wear evidence for hafted spear points at Kathu Pan.
sources.qualifies: Rots and Plisson argue the fracture evidence does not prove spear use.

sources.title: Wilkins, J. et al., 'Kathu Pan 1 points and the assemblage-scale, probabilistic approach: a response to Rots and Plisson, “Projectiles and the abuse of the use-wear method in a search for impact”', Journal of Archaeological Science 54 (2015), 294-299
sources.author: Wilkins, Jayne; Schoville, Benjamin J.; Brown, Kyle S.; Chazan, Michael
sources.confirms: Replies to critique with further analysis supporting spear-tip interpretation.

kathu-pan-hafted-spear-tips-498000bce.verification_note: Site age is secure; hafting function is contested.
kathu-pan-hafted-spear-tips-498000bce.detail: Kathu Pan 1 Stratum 4a contains Fauresmith industry, transitional between Acheulean and Middle Stone Age. Points show edge damage concentrated at tips and thinning at bases. Critics argue that diagnostic impact fractures occur on non-projectile tools and that taphonomic processes were not excluded; proponents counter with distribution of fractures and experimental spear thrusting into springbok carcasses. Debate illustrates difficulty of inferring hafting without preserved shafts or adhesive.
kathu-pan-hafted-spear-tips-498000bce.dating_note: Age of about 500,000 years combines optically stimulated luminescence and uranium-series on enamel; hafting interpretation is disputed by Rots and Plisson (2014).

trinil-shell-engraving-498000bce.summary: Pseudodon mussel shells collected by Eugène Dubois at Trinil in 1890s include one with a deliberately engraved zigzag, plus shells opened with a tool and one shaped as a tool. Argon-argon and luminescence dating of sediment in shells give a maximum age of 540,000 and minimum of 430,000 years ago, far younger than a 2009 estimate of about 1.5 million years for Trinil's main bone bed. Only Homo erectus lived on Java then, so this engraving shows geometric mark-making 300,000 years before anatomically modern humans and earlier than any Neanderthal or Homo sapiens engraving.

sources.title: Joordens, J. C. A. et al., 'Homo erectus at Trinil on Java used shells for tool production and engraving', Nature 518 (2014), 228-231
sources.author: Joordens, Josephine C. A.; d’Errico, Francesco; Wesselingh, Frank P.; Munro, Stephen; de Vos, John; Wallinga, Jakob
sources.confirms: Dates Trinil shell engraving to between 540,000 and 430,000 years and attributes it to Homo erectus.

sources.title: Joordens, J. C. A. et al., 'Relevance of aquatic environments for hominins: a case study from Trinil (Java, Indonesia)', Journal of Human Evolution 57 (2009), 656-671
sources.author: Joordens, Josephine C. A.; Wesselingh, Frank P.; de Vos, John; Vonhof, Hubert B.; Kroon, Dick
sources.confirms: Studies the Pseudodon and Elongaria shell beds in the Trinil Hauptknochenschicht fauna, finds midden-like assemblages pointing to deliberate collection, possibly by Homo erectus, and sets out the aquatic resources at the site.
sources.qualifies: Dates the Trinil bone-bed fauna to about 1.5 million years, far older than the 540,000 to 430,000 years later measured for the engraved shell's sediment fill.

sources.title: Callaway, Ewen, 'Homo erectus made world's oldest doodle 500,000 years ago', Nature News, 3 December 2014
sources.author: Callaway, Ewen
sources.confirms: Reports the Joordens study of a zigzag engraved on a Trinil shell about 500,000 years ago as the oldest abstract marks known.

trinil-shell-engraving-498000bce.verification_note: Joordens and colleagues (JHE 2009) dated Trinil's Hauptknochenschicht fauna to about 1.5 million years, while their 2015 Nature paper dated sediment filling these shells to 540,000 to 430,000 years; this entry follows those 2015 direct dates, with Callaway's Nature News report as supporting coverage.
trinil-shell-engraving-498000bce.detail: Engraving was found under a microscope; experimental work showed a shark tooth produced matching grooves and that lines were made in one session on fresh shell. Shells were opened by drilling at muscle attachment, implying knowledge of mollusc anatomy. No use or meaning for the zigzag has been established. Work was led from Leiden on Naturalis museum collection. Dubois' Trinil collection also produced first Homo erectus skullcap and femur in 1891 and 1892.

picture.alt: Excavation pit at Trinil, Java, 1911 photograph from Selenka expedition
picture.credit: Selenka and Blanckenhorn 1911: Tafel III, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

trinil-shell-engraving-498000bce.dating_note: Age of about 500,000 years is midpoint of 540,000 maximum (argon-argon) and 430,000 minimum (luminescence) given by Joordens et al.

olorgesailie-middle-stone-age-318000bce.summary: A Middle Stone Age transition at Olorgesailie Basin, Kenya, falls between 320,000 and 295,000 years ago, dated by argon-argon and uranium-series. Artefacts include small points and blades made on obsidian carried from sources 25 to 50 kilometres away; red and black pigments show grinding. Long-distance raw material transport implies social networks across groups, and pigment use implies marking or colouring. These behaviours appear alongside earliest Homo sapiens fossils in Africa, such as Jebel Irhoud at about 315,000 years ago.

sources.title: Brooks, A. S. et al., 'Long-distance stone transport and pigment use in the earliest Middle Stone Age', Science 360 (2018), 90-94
sources.author: Brooks, Alison S.; Yellen, John E.; Potts, Richard; Behrensmeyer, Anna K.; Deino, Alan L.; Leslie, David E.
sources.confirms: Dates Middle Stone Age at Olorgesailie to 320,000 to 295,000 years with obsidian transport and pigments.

sources.title: Richter, D. et al., 'The age of the hominin fossils from Jebel Irhoud, Morocco, and the origins of the Middle Stone Age', Nature 546 (2017), 293-296
sources.author: Richter, Daniel; Grün, Rainer; Joannes-Boyau, Renaud; Steele, Teresa E.; Amani, Fethi; Rué, Mathieu
sources.confirms: Dates Jebel Irhoud Homo sapiens fossils and Middle Stone Age tools to 315,000 years.

olorgesailie-middle-stone-age-318000bce.detail: Olorgesailie's Acheulean handaxe record ends around 500,000 years ago, then a gap from erosion, then Middle Stone Age sites at 320,000 years ago. Obsidian sourcing used X-ray fluorescence to match artefacts to outcrops. Pigments include manganese and ochre with use facets. Environmental data from same basin show increased climate variability, which Alison Brooks ties to flexible behaviours. Smithsonian's Human Origins Program has worked at Olorgesailie with National Museums of Kenya since 1985.

picture.alt: Acheulean handaxes from Olorgesailie, Kenya, Smithsonian National Museum of Natural History
picture.credit: Jonathan Chen, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

olorgesailie-middle-stone-age-318000bce.dating_note: Age 320,000 to 295,000 years combines argon-argon on tephra and uranium-series.

qesem-cave-hearth-298000bce.summary: Qesem Cave near Tel Aviv preserves a four-square-metre hearth in sediments dated to about 300,000 years ago. Micromorphology shows it was used repeatedly; burned bones and blades cluster around it. Over 4.5 metres of cave sediment consist mostly of wood ash, evidence of habitual fire use from about 400,000 years ago. Ran Barkai reads this as fire for a reason: roasting meat, central to a domestic space.

sources.title: Shahack-Gross, R. et al., 'Evidence for the repeated use of a central hearth at Middle Pleistocene (300 ky ago) Qesem Cave, Israel', Journal of Archaeological Science 44 (2014), 12-21
sources.author: Shahack-Gross, R.; Berna, F.; Karkanas, P.; Lemorini, C.; Gopher, A.; Barkai, R.
sources.confirms: Describes a repeatedly used central hearth at Qesem Cave dated about 300,000 years.

sources.title: KARKANAS, P. et al., 'Evidence for habitual use of fire at the end of the Lower Paleolithic: Site-formation processes at Qesem Cave, Israel', Journal of Human Evolution 53 (2007), 197-212
sources.author: KARKANAS, P; SHAHACKGROSS, R; AYALON, A; BARMATTHEWS, M; BARKAI, R; FRUMKIN, A
sources.confirms: Shows Qesem Cave upper sediments are dominated by wood ash from habitual fire use.

sources.title: Barkai, R. et al., 'Fire for a Reason', Current Anthropology 58 (2017), S314-S328
sources.author: Barkai, Ran; Rosell, Jordi; Blasco, Ruth; Gopher, Avi
sources.confirms: Interprets Qesem fire as habitual use for cooking from about 400,000 years.

qesem-cave-hearth-298000bce.detail: Cave was found during road construction in 2000. Lithics belong to Acheulo-Yabrudian complex with early blades. Fallow deer dominate fauna; cut marks and burning show butchery near fire. Dating of 300,000 plus or minus 30,000 years uses uranium-series and thermoluminescence on burnt flint. Hearth's repeated use implies spatial organisation of activities akin to later camps. Avi Gopher and Ran Barkai of Tel Aviv University direct excavations.

picture.alt: Burned animal bones from Qesem Cave, Israel
picture.credit: Ruth Blasco, CC BY 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

qesem-cave-hearth-298000bce.dating_note: Hearth sediments dated 300,000 plus or minus 30,000 years by uranium-series and thermoluminescence; habitual fire at site begins about 400,000 years.

schoningen-wooden-spears-298000bce.summary: Complete wooden spears, two metres or more in length, made from spruce and shaped with their centre of gravity forward like javelins, lay alongside butchered remains of more than ten horses at Schöningen opencast mine in Lower Saxony. Hartmut Thieme, who published them, put them at 400,000 years ago. Daniel Richter and Matthias Krbetschek redate the spear horizon by thermoluminescence to 321,000 plus or minus 16,000 years ago. Jarod Hutson argues from amino acid racemisation for about 200,000 years ago. Whatever the final age, these are oldest complete hunting weapons known and show systematic big-game hunting with planned wooden tools. A single yew spear tip from Clacton, England, is older but fragmentary.

sources.title: Thieme, H., 'Lower Palaeolithic hunting spears from Germany', Nature 385 (1997), 807-810
sources.author: Thieme, Hartmut
sources.confirms: Reports Schöningen wooden spears with butchered horses and proposes 400,000 years.

sources.title: Richter, D. and Krbetschek, M., 'The age of the Lower Paleolithic occupation at Schöningen', Journal of Human Evolution 89 (2015), 46-56
sources.author: Richter, Daniel; Krbetschek, Matthias
sources.confirms: Redates spear horizon to 321,000 plus or minus 16,000 years by thermoluminescence.
sources.qualifies: Richter and Krbetschek give about 300,000 years rather than 400,000.

sources.title: Hutson, J. M. et al., 'Revised age for Schöningen hunting spears indicates intensification of Neanderthal cooperative behavior around 200,000 years ago', Science Advances 11 (2025)
sources.author: Hutson, Jarod M.; Bittmann, Felix; Fischer, Peter; García-Moreno, Alejandro; Gaudzinski-Windheuser, Sabine; Nelson, Ellie
sources.confirms: Argues for an age around 200,000 years using amino acid racemisation.
sources.qualifies: Hutson et al. (2025) place the spears at about 200,000 years, far younger than Thieme's estimate.

sources.title: Allington-Jones, L., 'The Clacton Spear: The Last One Hundred Years', Archaeological Journal 172 (2015), 273-296
sources.author: Allington-Jones, Lu
sources.confirms: Reviews Clacton yew spear point and its age of about 400,000 years.

schoningen-wooden-spears-298000bce.verification_note: Spears and horse kill are secure; age spans 400,000 to 200,000 years across studies.
schoningen-wooden-spears-298000bce.detail: Spears survived in waterlogged lakeshore sediments. Wood was from slow-grown spruce trunks worked with stone tools; tips are on hard base wood and shafts thin toward tail. A wooden throwing stick and worked stick were also found. Dating dispute matters for attribution: 300,000 years fits Homo heidelbergensis, 200,000 years fits early Neanderthals. Clacton spear point, dated about 400,000 years, shows yew working in Britain.

picture.alt: Schöningen Spear VII in sediment during excavation, 1997
picture.credit: P. Pfarr NLD, CC BY-SA 3.0 de, via Wikimedia Commons

schoningen-wooden-spears-298000bce.dating_note: Year follows Richter and Krbetschek's thermoluminescence age of about 300,000 years; Thieme proposed 400,000 years and Hutson et al. (2025) argue for about 200,000 years.

border-cave-grass-bedding-198000bce.summary: Border Cave, on South Africa's border with Eswatini, preserves fossilised Panicoideae grass bedding in layers dated to about 200,000 years ago. Bedding lies on ash layers, which repel crawling insects, and includes burned camphor-bush leaves. Phytoliths and micromorphology show grass was laid as sheaves, used, then burned and replaced. This is earliest known bedding and shows camp maintenance: cleaning and pest control around sleeping space, 120,000 years before Sibudu's bedding.

sources.title: Wadley, L. et al., 'Fire and grass-bedding construction 200 thousand years ago at Border Cave, South Africa', Science 369 (2020), 863-866
sources.author: Wadley, Lyn; Esteban, Irene; de la Peña, Paloma; Wojcieszak, Marine; Stratford, Dominic; Lennox, Sandra
sources.confirms: Reports grass bedding on ash at Border Cave dated about 200,000 years.

sources.title: Backwell, L. et al., 'New Excavations at Border Cave, KwaZulu-Natal, South Africa', Journal of Field Archaeology 43 (2018), 417-436
sources.author: Backwell, Lucinda; d'Errico, Francesco; Banks, William E.; de la Peña, Paloma; Sievers, Christine; Stratford, Dominic; Lennox, Sandra J.; Wojcieszak, Marine; Bordy, Emese M.; Bradfield, Justin; Wadley, Lyn
sources.confirms: Reports desiccated grass bedding preserved in multiple layers at Border Cave and lithic-rich deposits older than 100,000 years.

border-cave-grass-bedding-198000bce.detail: Border Cave was excavated from 1930s onwards; Wadley's team reopened it in 2015. Grass identification used silica phytoliths; ash under bedding came from old fires and from burning used bedding. Dating relies on electron spin resonance of tooth enamel and stratigraphic correlation. Same cave later yields notched bones, digging sticks, poison applicators and ostrich eggshell beads. Lyn Wadley of University of the Witwatersrand led analysis with Francesco d'Errico and Lucinda Backwell.

picture.alt: Excavations at Border Cave, KwaZulu-Natal, South Africa
picture.credit: Lucinda Backwell, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

border-cave-grass-bedding-198000bce.dating_note: Age of about 200,000 years rests on electron spin resonance and stratigraphy.

campitello-birch-tar-adhesive-198000bce.summary: Two flint flakes from Campitello Quarry in Tuscany are partly coated in birch-bark tar; they lay with an elephant skeleton in sediments of Marine Isotope Stage 6, around 200,000 years ago. Tar must be made by heating bark without oxygen, so this is earliest manufactured substance. Later Neanderthal tar comes from Königsaue, Germany, and from a 50,000-year-old tar-backed flake at Zandmotor, Netherlands. Experiments show usable tar can be made by simple fire methods, while Königsaue tar was made in an underground, oxygen-restricted process.

sources.title: Mazza, P. P. A. et al., 'A new Palaeolithic discovery: tar-hafted stone tools in a European Mid-Pleistocene bone-bearing bed', Journal of Archaeological Science 33 (2006), 1310-1318
sources.author: Mazza, Paul Peter Anthony; Martini, Fabio; Sala, Benedetto; Magi, Maurizio; Colombini, Maria Perla; Giachi, Gianna
sources.confirms: Describes birch-bark tar on flint flakes from Campitello in Middle Pleistocene deposits.

sources.title: Kozowyk, P. R. B. et al., 'Experimental methods for the Palaeolithic dry distillation of birch bark: implications for the origin and development of Neandertal adhesive technology', Scientific Reports 7 (2017)
sources.author: Kozowyk, P. R. B.; Soressi, M.; Pomstra, D.; Langejans, G. H. J.
sources.confirms: Shows birch tar can be produced with simple Palaeolithic fire methods and compares yields.

sources.title: Schmidt, P. et al., 'Production method of the Königsaue birch tar documents cumulative culture in Neanderthals', Archaeological and Anthropological Sciences 15 (2023)
sources.author: Schmidt, Patrick; Koch, Tabea J.; Blessing, Matthias A.; Karakostis, F. Alexandros; Harvati, Katerina; Dresely, Veit
sources.confirms: Finds Königsaue tar was made with an oxygen-restricted underground method, implying cumulative culture.

sources.title: Niekus, M. J. L. T. et al., 'Middle Paleolithic complex technology and a Neandertal tar-backed tool from the Dutch North Sea', Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences 116 (2019), 22081-22087
sources.author: Niekus, Marcel J. L. Th.; Kozowyk, Paul R. B.; Langejans, Geeske H. J.; Ngan-Tillard, Dominique; van Keulen, Henk; van der Plicht, Johannes
sources.venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
sources.confirms: Reports a 50,000-year-old tar-hafted flake from Zandmotor, Netherlands.

campitello-birch-tar-adhesive-198000bce.verification_note: Campitello age is stratigraphic; tar identification is secure.
campitello-birch-tar-adhesive-198000bce.detail: Campitello tar was identified by gas chromatography as birch-bark pitch with betulin markers. Dating rests on stratigraphy and fauna of Middle Pleistocene river deposits rather than radiometric age. Debate over cognitive implications hinges on method: open-fire condensation on cobbles yields small amounts, while pits sealed with embers yield more. Hafting with adhesive let Neanderthals mount stone on wooden handles without bindings alone.

picture.alt: Flint flake with birch tar found on Dutch coast, about 50,000 years old (not Campitello find), Rijksmuseum van Oudheden
picture.credit: Ellywa, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

campitello-birch-tar-adhesive-198000bce.dating_note: Campitello age of about 200,000 years rests on stratigraphic and faunal correlation to Marine Isotope Stage 6, not on direct dating.

bruniquel-cave-ring-structures-174000bce.summary: Two annular structures and several piles built from about 400 broken stalagmite pieces stand deep inside Bruniquel Cave in southwest France. Uranium-series dating of regrowth calcite gives 176,500 years ago, plus or minus 2,100. Structures sit 336 metres from cave entrance in total darkness, with traces of fire on many pieces. Only Neanderthals lived in Europe then. Bruniquel is among oldest well-dated constructions, showing deliberate use of deep cave space, fire for light, and coordinated work far from daylight.

sources.title: Jaubert, J. et al., 'Early Neanderthal constructions deep in Bruniquel Cave in southwestern France', Nature 534 (2016), 111-114
sources.author: Jaubert, Jacques; Verheyden, Sophie; Genty, Dominique; Soulier, Michel; Cheng, Hai; Blamart, Dominique
sources.confirms: Dates Bruniquel stalagmite structures to 176,500 years by uranium-series.

sources.title: Soressi, Marie, 'Neanderthals built underground', Nature 534 (2016), 43-44
sources.author: Soressi, Marie
sources.confirms: Independent News and Views: 175,000-year-old structures deep inside Bruniquel Cave show Neanderthals ventured underground and made some of the earliest known hominin constructions.

bruniquel-cave-ring-structures-174000bce.detail: Structures total about 112 metres of aligned stalagmite segments weighing roughly two tonnes. Burned bone and reddened calcite indicate fires set on structures. Proposed purposes are shelter, ritual and an exploration marker; no evidence decides among them. Cave was discovered in 1990 and first dated by radiocarbon beyond range; uranium-series on calcite that grew over broken pieces resolved age. Jacques Jaubert of University of Bordeaux led dating with Sophie Verheyden.

picture.alt: Ring structure of broken stalagmites in Bruniquel Cave, France
picture.credit: Luc-Henri Fage/SSAC, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

bruniquel-cave-ring-structures-174000bce.dating_note: Age is uranium-series on calcite regrowth; year rounds 176,500 before present.

border-cave-cooked-rhizomes-168000bce.summary: Border Cave layers dated about 170,000 years ago hold charred whole rhizomes of Hypoxis, a starchy plant still eaten in southern Africa. Rhizomes were carried to cave and roasted in hearths, implying sharing and cooking of carbohydrate staples rather than eating on spot. This is earliest direct evidence for cooked plant foods. Hypoxis grows across Africa, so this knowledge could support movement through varied landscapes with reliable, year-round starch.

sources.title: Wadley, L. et al., 'Cooked starchy rhizomes in Africa 170 thousand years ago', Science 367 (2020), 87-91
sources.author: Wadley, Lyn; Backwell, Lucinda; d’Errico, Francesco; Sievers, Christine
sources.confirms: Reports charred Hypoxis rhizomes at Border Cave dated about 170,000 years as earliest cooked starchy food.

sources.title: Larbey, C. et al., 'Cooked starchy food in hearths ca. 120 kya and 65 kya (MIS 5e and MIS 4) from Klasies River Cave, South Africa', Journal of Human Evolution 131 (2019), 210-227
sources.author: Larbey, Cynthia; Mentzer, Susan M.; Ligouis, Bertrand; Wurz, Sarah; Jones, Martin K.
sources.confirms: Independent team reports charred starchy plant tissue in Klasies River hearths at about 120,000 and 65,000 years, the previous earliest claim, which Border Cave's whole rhizomes at 170,000 years predate.
sources.qualifies: Larbey's fragments are charred parenchyma, not identifiable whole rhizomes, so the Border Cave find remains the earliest identified cooked starchy plant.

border-cave-cooked-rhizomes-168000bce.detail: Fifty-five charred rhizomes were identified by comparing cell structure under scanning electron microscopy with modern Hypoxis angustifolia. Age combines electron spin resonance dating and stratigraphy. Digging sticks for extracting underground storage organs appear later at same site. Finding extends plant-food evidence well beyond rare earlier seed finds. Hypoxis rhizomes are rich in carbohydrates and can be stored in ground until needed, so they offer a dependable fallback food through seasons when fruit and game are scarce. Cooking softens fibres and improves digestibility.

picture.alt: Hypoxis angustifolia in flower, the plant whose rhizomes were roasted at Border Cave
picture.credit: Marco Schmidt [1], CC BY-SA 2.5, via Wikimedia Commons

border-cave-cooked-rhizomes-168000bce.dating_note: Age of about 170,000 years uses electron spin resonance and stratigraphy.

pinnacle-point-shellfish-162000bce.summary: Cave PP13B at Pinnacle Point near Mossel Bay holds shellfish remains, bladelets and 57 pieces of ground red ochre, dated by optically stimulated luminescence and uranium-series to 164,000 plus or minus 12,000 years ago. This is earliest evidence of systematic marine food use, during a glacial period when interior Africa was arid. Shellfish gave a predictable, tide-governed food. Ochre, including pieces with grinding facets, points to pigment processing in same layers.

sources.title: Marean, C. W. et al., 'Early human use of marine resources and pigment in South Africa during the Middle Pleistocene', Nature 449 (2007), 905-908
sources.author: Marean, Curtis W.; Bar-Matthews, Miryam; Bernatchez, Jocelyn; Fisher, Erich; Goldberg, Paul; Herries, Andy I. R.
sources.confirms: Reports shellfish, bladelets and ochre at Pinnacle Point dated 164,000 years.

sources.title: Marean, C. W., 'Pinnacle Point Cave 13B (Western Cape Province, South Africa) in context: The Cape Floral kingdom, shellfish, and modern human origins', Journal of Human Evolution 59 (2010), 425-443
sources.author: Marean, Curtis W.
sources.confirms: Restates the PP13B evidence for marine resource use by about 164,000 years, early pigment use and bladelet technology during glacial stage MIS 6, and models why the Cape coast supported early modern humans.

pinnacle-point-shellfish-162000bce.detail: Shellfish include brown mussels, limpets, whelks and giant periwinkles collected from rocky intertidal zone when coastline lay near cave. Bladelets are small blades suited to composite tools. Pinnacle Point project, led by Curtis Marean from Arizona State University, used high-resolution dating of multiple caves along same cliff, with dated speleothems and sea-level models to reconstruct coastline distance. Marean argues coastal resources helped early Homo sapiens through Marine Isotope Stage 6.

picture.alt: Coastline at Pinnacle Point, Mossel Bay, South Africa
picture.credit: Satdeep Gill, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

pinnacle-point-shellfish-162000bce.dating_note: Age 164,000 plus or minus 12,000 years combines optically stimulated luminescence and uranium-series.

bizmoune-cave-shell-beads-140000bce.summary: Bizmoune Cave near Essaouira, Morocco, yielded 33 perforated Tritia gibbosula shells with wear from stringing and traces of ochre, in layers dated by uranium-series on flowstone to at least 142,000 years ago. These are oldest personal ornaments known, predating Skhul and Qafzeh in Levant and Blombos in South Africa. Beads carry identity across distance and generations, so their appearance in Aterian contexts shows symbolic signalling among North African Homo sapiens before 140,000 years ago.

sources.title: Sehasseh, E. M. et al., 'Early Middle Stone Age personal ornaments from Bizmoune Cave, Essaouira, Morocco', Science Advances 7 (2021)
sources.author: Sehasseh, El Mehdi; Fernandez, Philippe; Kuhn, Steven; Stiner, Mary; Mentzer, Susan; Colarossi, Debra
sources.confirms: Reports 33 Tritia shell beads at Bizmoune Cave dated at least 142,000 years.

sources.title: Campmas, É. et al., 'Aterian shell beads from the coastal site of El Mnasra Cave (Rabat-Témara, Morocco): Specificities of the north African MSA personal ornaments', PLOS ONE 21 (2026), e0338785
sources.author: Campmas, Émilie; Lebon, Matthieu; et al.
sources.confirms: Independent team identifies Bizmoune Cave as the site with the oldest known shell ornaments, 33 specimens dated to MIS 6, more than 147,000 years.
sources.qualifies: Gives more than 147,000 years where the record says at least 142,000.

bizmoune-cave-shell-beads-140000bce.detail: Shells came from Atlantic shore about 50 kilometres away. Perforations show wear facets where cords rubbed. Dating used uranium-series on calcite layers above and below bead-bearing deposits. Similar beads occur at Aterian sites across Morocco and Algeria, suggesting shared ornament tradition across Maghreb. Abdeljalil Bouzouggar of Institut National des Sciences de l'Archéologie et du Patrimoine co-directed work with Steven Kuhn of University of Arizona. Beads were found across several layers, so bead-wearing persisted at site for thousands of years.
bizmoune-cave-shell-beads-140000bce.dating_note: Minimum age of 142,000 years from uranium-series on flowstone above bead layers.

lice-genetics-date-clothing-105000bce.summary: Body lice live only in clothing, so their split from head lice dates when people wore garments habitually. Mitochondrial DNA puts body lice origin at no more than about 72,000 plus or minus 42,000 years ago. Nuclear and mitochondrial sequences under a wider model give 83,000 to 170,000 years ago. Both date clothing well before Homo sapiens left Africa, and before loss of body hair would otherwise demand covering. Clothing extends range into cold latitudes and precedes any surviving needle or textile.

sources.title: Kittler, R. et al., 'Molecular Evolution of Pediculus humanus and the Origin of Clothing', Current Biology 13 (2003), 1414-1417
sources.author: Kittler, Ralf; Kayser, Manfred; Stoneking, Mark
sources.confirms: Estimates body lice origin at no more than 72,000 plus or minus 42,000 years from mitochondrial DNA.

sources.title: Toups, M. A. et al., 'Origin of Clothing Lice Indicates Early Clothing Use by Anatomically Modern Humans in Africa', Molecular Biology and Evolution 28 (2010), 29-32
sources.author: Toups, M. A.; Kitchen, A.; Light, J. E.; Reed, D. L.
sources.confirms: Estimates clothing lice divergence at 83,000 to 170,000 years using nuclear and mitochondrial data.
sources.qualifies: Toups et al. give an older range than Kittler et al.

lice-genetics-date-clothing-105000bce.verification_note: Dates are molecular clock estimates with wide uncertainty.
lice-genetics-date-clothing-105000bce.detail: Molecular clocks depend on assumed mutation rates and generation times, so estimates have wide error. Lice diversity is greater in Africa, supporting African origin. An age of 170,000 years ago fits use of clothing during penultimate glaciation. Physical evidence for clothing comes much later: hide-scraping tools at Neanderthal sites and eyed needles after 50,000 years ago. Lice genetics gives an indirect route to a technology that leaves no artefacts.

picture.alt: Male human body louse, Pediculus humanus corporis, scanning electron micrograph (CDC)
picture.credit: Janice Harney Carr, Center for Disease Control, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

lice-genetics-date-clothing-105000bce.dating_note: Year of about 107,000 years is midpoint of Toups et al.'s 83,000 to 170,000 range; Kittler et al. give 72,000 plus or minus 42,000 years; dating is molecular clock, not archaeological.

ngalue-sorghum-starch-103000bce.summary: Starch granules of wild sorghum occur on 70 stone tools from Ngalue Cave in Niassa, Mozambique, dated to about 105,000 years ago, the oldest end of an occupation running to 42,000 years ago. Grinders and scrapers carry starch, implying grass seed was processed into flour or paste. This is earliest evidence of grass-seed use by Homo sapiens, some 80,000 years before Ohalo II in Levant. Sorghum later became a domesticated African staple; here it shows early Middle Stone Age diets included cereal grains alongside tubers and game.

sources.title: Mercader, J., 'Mozambican Grass Seed Consumption During the Middle Stone Age', Science 326 (2009), 1680-1683
sources.author: Mercader, Julio
sources.confirms: Reports wild sorghum starch on Middle Stone Age tools at Ngalue dated about 105,000 years.

sources.title: Mercader, Julio; Asmerom, Yemane; Bennett, Tim; Raja, Mussa; Skinner, Anne, 'Initial excavation and dating of Ngalue Cave: A Middle Stone Age site along the Niassa Rift, Mozambique', Journal of Human Evolution 57 (2009), 63-74
sources.author: Mercader, Julio; Asmerom, Yemane; Bennett, Tim; Raja, Mussa; Skinner, Anne
sources.confirms: Radiometrically dated cave section at Ngalue records human occupation between 105,000 and 42,000 years, with Middle Stone Age Middle Beds holding points, scrapers and ochre-covered grinders and core-axes.

ngalue-sorghum-starch-103000bce.verification_note: Ngalue's dated occupation spans 105,000 to 42,000 years, so 105,000 marks its oldest end; dating and starch identification come from one excavation team.
ngalue-sorghum-starch-103000bce.detail: Starch identification compared granule size and shape with modern reference collections; sorghum dominated among many taxa. Dating used optically stimulated luminescence on cave sediments. Critics caution that starch can move through sediments or be misidentified, so this result is often cited with reservations. Ngalue lies in Mozambique's northern highlands, a region little studied before Mercader's work. Julio Mercader of University of Calgary led work.

picture.alt: Wild sorghum, Sorghum bicolor verticilliflorum
picture.credit: 葉子, CC0, via Wikimedia Commons

ngalue-sorghum-starch-103000bce.dating_note: Age of about 105,000 years is optically stimulated luminescence on cave sediments.

blombos-ochre-workshop-98000bce.summary: Two Haliotis abalone shells at Blombos Cave hold a red ochre-rich mixture, found with grindstones, hammerstones, bone stirrers and charcoal in a layer dated by optically stimulated luminescence to about 100,000 years ago. Ochre was ground and mixed with heated crushed bone and charcoal, then stored in abalone shells as containers. This toolkit shows multi-step production and storage of a pigment compound, among earliest evidence of containers and recipe-based chemistry.

sources.title: Henshilwood, C. S. et al., 'A 100,000-Year-Old Ochre-Processing Workshop at Blombos Cave, South Africa', Science 334 (2011), 219-222
sources.author: Henshilwood, Christopher S.; d’Errico, Francesco; van Niekerk, Karen L.; Coquinot, Yvan; Jacobs, Zenobia; Lauritzen, Stein-Erik
sources.confirms: Reports a 100,000-year-old ochre-processing toolkit with abalone shell containers at Blombos.

sources.title: Bower, Bruce, 'Stone Age paint shop unearthed', Science News 180 (2011), 16
sources.author: Bower, Bruce
sources.confirms: Independent report that Stone Age humans at Blombos about 100,000 years ago mixed ochre powder, heated crushed bone, charcoal and liquid in a set order and stored it in abalone shells, the oldest known containers.

blombos-ochre-workshop-98000bce.detail: Both shells lay on their backs in sand with pigment adhering to inner surfaces; a bone fragment showed use as a stirrer or applicator. Bone was heated to extract marrow fat as binder. Whether paint decorated bodies, hides or surfaces is unknown. Blombos sits on southern Cape coast; Henshilwood's excavations since 1991 reveal a sequence from 100,000 to 70,000 years rich in ochre, shell beads, bone tools and bifacial points.

picture.alt: General view of Blombos Cave, southern Cape, South Africa
picture.credit: Vincent Mourre / Inrap, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

blombos-ochre-workshop-98000bce.dating_note: Age of about 100,000 years is optically stimulated luminescence on sediments.

skhul-qafzeh-shell-beads-98000bce.summary: Two perforated Nassarius gibbosulus shells from Skhul on Mount Carmel, excavated in 1930s and kept in Natural History Museum London, are beads; sediment adhering to shells matches layers dated 100,000 to 135,000 years ago. A similar shell from Oued Djebbana, Algeria, supports marine shells carried inland as ornaments. Skhul and Qafzeh hold early Homo sapiens burials with grave goods and ochre, so beads here join funerary practice in Levant long before comparable finds in Europe.

sources.title: Vanhaeren, M. et al., 'Middle Paleolithic Shell Beads in Israel and Algeria', Science 312 (2006), 1785-1788
sources.author: Vanhaeren, Marian; d'Errico, Francesco; Stringer, Chris; James, Sarah L.; Todd, Jonathan A.; Mienis, Henk K.
sources.confirms: Identifies Skhul shell beads in layers dated 100,000 to 135,000 years.

sources.title: Bar-Yosef Mayer, D. E., Vandermeersch, B. and Bar-Yosef, O., 'Shells and ochre in Middle Paleolithic Qafzeh Cave, Israel: indications for modern behavior', Journal of Human Evolution 56 (2009), 307-314
sources.author: Bar-Yosef Mayer, Daniella E.; Vandermeersch, Bernard; Bar-Yosef, Ofer
sources.confirms: Reports Glycymeris shells, some perforated and ochre-stained, from the Middle Palaeolithic burial layers at Qafzeh dated to about 92,000 years, carried inland from the Mediterranean.
sources.qualifies: Qafzeh's shells are Glycymeris, not Nassarius; the Nassarius beads belong to Skhul and Oued Djebbana.

skhul-qafzeh-shell-beads-98000bce.verification_note: Bar-Yosef Mayer, Vandermeersch and Bar-Yosef (JHE 2009) report Qafzeh's ornaments as Glycymeris valves, some naturally perforated and ochre-stained, about 92,000 years old; only Skhul yielded Nassarius gibbosulus beads.
skhul-qafzeh-shell-beads-98000bce.detail: Shells were collected from Mediterranean shore some kilometres away. Skhul dating uses electron spin resonance and thermoluminescence from earlier work on burial layers. Qafzeh yields Glycymeris valves, some naturally perforated and ochre-stained, at around 92,000 years. Both caves preserve deliberate burials, including a child with deer antler, giving some of earliest evidence for mortuary ritual among modern humans. Marian Vanhaeren and Francesco d'Errico located Skhul shells in museum collections decades after excavation.

picture.alt: Excavated terrace of Skhul Cave, Mount Carmel, Israel
picture.credit: Hanay, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

skhul-qafzeh-shell-beads-98000bce.dating_note: Year of about 100,000 years is lower end of Skhul's 100,000 to 135,000 bracket from electron spin resonance and thermoluminescence; Qafzeh shells are about 92,000 years.

katanda-barbed-bone-harpoons-88000bce.summary: Finely carved barbed bone points come from Katanda sites on Upper Semliki River in Democratic Republic of Congo, with remains of very large catfish, dated by thermoluminescence, electron spin resonance and uranium-series to about 90,000 years ago. Barbed points of this kind were otherwise known only from after 25,000 years ago in Europe. Catfish bones indicate seasonal spawning runs targeted with harpoons, an early planned fishing economy. Age drew scepticism when published because it was so much earlier than comparable tools.

sources.title: Yellen, J. E. et al., 'A Middle Stone Age Worked Bone Industry from Katanda, Upper Semliki Valley, Zaire', Science 268 (1995), 553-556
sources.author: Yellen, John E.; Brooks, Alison S.; Cornelissen, Els; Mehlman, Michael J.; Stewart, Kathlyn
sources.confirms: Dates barbed bone points and catfish remains at Katanda to about 90,000 years using several methods.

sources.title: Brooks, A. S. et al., 'Dating and Context of Three Middle Stone Age Sites with Bone Points in the Upper Semliki Valley, Zaire', Science 268 (1995), 548-553
sources.author: Brooks, Alison S.; Helgren, David M.; Cramer, Jon S.; Franklin, Alan; Hornyak, William; Keating, Jody M.; Klein, Richard G.; Rink, William J.; Schwarcz, Henry; Smith, J. N. Leith; Stewart, Kathlyn; Todd, Nancy E.; Verniers, Jacques; Yellen, John E.
sources.confirms: Companion dating paper gives ages older than 89,000 years (+22,000/-15,000) for the Katanda bone point sites by electron spin resonance, thermoluminescence, optically stimulated luminescence, uranium series and amino acid racemization.

katanda-barbed-bone-harpoons-88000bce.verification_note: Dating is broadly accepted after reassessment, but early doubts over stratigraphic integrity are noted in literature.
katanda-barbed-bone-harpoons-88000bce.detail: Points were shaped from large mammal ribs by carving rows of barbs along one edge with grooves near base for hafting. Dating methods were applied to sediments and hippopotamus teeth from same layers. Some researchers questioned whether points could be intrusive from younger levels; later luminescence reassessment by Feathers and Migliorini supported antiquity. Katanda helped shift views that African Middle Stone Age lacked complex bone technology.

picture.alt: Semliki River, Albertine Rift, near Katanda, Democratic Republic of Congo
picture.credit: Iwoelbern, CC0, via Wikimedia Commons

katanda-barbed-bone-harpoons-88000bce.dating_note: Age of about 90,000 years combines thermoluminescence, electron spin resonance and uranium-series; early critics questioned association, later luminescence work supported it.

panga-ya-saidi-child-burial-76000bce.summary: Africa's oldest known human burial lies at Panga ya Saidi cave on Kenya's coast: a child about three years old, named Mtoto, placed in a deliberately dug pit in flexed position with head on a perishable support, dated by luminescence to 78,300 plus or minus 4,100 years ago. Sediment analysis shows body decomposed in a covered pit, and bone displacement patterns indicate a wrapped or shrouded burial. Mortuary treatment of a young child indicates care and ritual among Middle Stone Age communities.

sources.title: Martinón-Torres, M. et al., 'Earliest known human burial in Africa', Nature 593 (2021), 95-100
sources.author: Martinón-Torres, María; d’Errico, Francesco; Santos, Elena; Álvaro Gallo, Ana; Amano, Noel; Archer, William
sources.confirms: Reports a child burial at Panga ya Saidi dated 78,300 plus or minus 4,100 years.

sources.title: Humphrey, Louise, 'A child's grave is the earliest known burial site in Africa', Nature 593 (2021), 39-40
sources.author: Humphrey, Louise
sources.confirms: Independent News and Views on the discovery of a child's burial in Kenya around 78,000 years ago, the earliest known in Africa.

panga-ya-saidi-child-burial-76000bce.detail: Remains were lifted in a sediment block and excavated in laboratory at CENIEH in Spain. Child's skeleton shows Homo sapiens features with some archaic traits in teeth. Burial lay in layers with Middle Stone Age tools. Earlier Homo sapiens burials at Skhul and Qafzeh in Levant are older, but none in Africa preceded this one. Nicole Boivin and Michael Petraglia co-directed Panga ya Saidi project with National Museums of Kenya.

picture.alt: Excavations at Panga ya Saidi cave, Kilifi County, Kenya
picture.credit: Ceri Shipton, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

panga-ya-saidi-child-burial-76000bce.dating_note: Age 78,300 plus or minus 4,100 years is luminescence on sediments.

blombos-engraved-ochre-and-beads-75000bc.summary: Blombos Cave's Still Bay layers, dated by thermoluminescence and luminescence to about 77,000 to 73,000 years ago, yield two ochre pieces engraved with cross-hatched lines, 41 perforated Nassarius kraussianus shell beads with wear from stringing, and a silcrete flake bearing a red cross-hatched drawing made with an ochre crayon about 73,000 years ago. Together these show repeated geometric design across media and deliberate ornament, making Blombos a central site for symbolic behaviour before modern humans left Africa.

sources.title: Henshilwood, C. S. et al., 'Emergence of Modern Human Behavior: Middle Stone Age Engravings from South Africa', Science 295 (2002), 1278-1280
sources.author: Henshilwood, Christopher S.; d'Errico, Francesco; Yates, Royden; Jacobs, Zenobia; Tribolo, Chantal; Duller, Geoff A. T.
sources.confirms: Reports engraved ochre pieces at Blombos dated about 77,000 years.

sources.title: Henshilwood, C. et al., 'Middle Stone Age Shell Beads from South Africa', Science 304 (2004), 404-404
sources.author: Henshilwood, Christopher; d'Errico, Francesco; Vanhaeren, Marian; van Niekerk, Karen; Jacobs, Zenobia
sources.confirms: Reports perforated Nassarius beads at Blombos about 75,000 years old.

sources.title: Henshilwood, C. S. et al., 'An abstract drawing from the 73,000-year-old levels at Blombos Cave, South Africa', Nature 562 (2018), 115-118
sources.author: Henshilwood, Christopher S.; d’Errico, Francesco; van Niekerk, Karen L.; Dayet, Laure; Queffelec, Alain; Pollarolo, Luca
sources.confirms: Reports a 73,000-year-old ochre drawing on silcrete at Blombos.

blombos-engraved-ochre-and-beads-75000bc.detail: Engraved ochre pieces were ground flat, then incised with a sharp stone point; patterns match across pieces. Beads show ochre traces and wear facets consistent with threading in groups. Drawing consists of nine lines on a flake once part of a grindstone; microscopy and chemistry identified ochre crayon application. Dating combines thermoluminescence on burnt lithics with optically stimulated luminescence on sand.

picture.alt: Stratified deposits in Blombos Cave, South Africa, including Still Bay layers
picture.credit: Kari Janne Stenersen, CC BY-SA 2.5, via Wikimedia Commons

blombos-engraved-ochre-and-beads-75000bc.dating_note: Year of 77,000 before present follows engraved ochre layer; beads are about 75,000 and drawing about 73,000 years.

sibudu-insecticidal-bedding-75000bce.summary: Compacted layers of sedges, rushes, grasses and aromatic leaves at Sibudu Cave near Durban date by optically stimulated luminescence to 77,000 years ago, with later bedding layers through 38,000 years ago. Upper surface of oldest bedding carries leaves of Cryptocarya woodii, a tree whose foliage contains compounds that kill mosquito larvae and repel insects. Bedding was used for sleeping and working surfaces and was periodically burned, a maintenance practice later seen at Border Cave and in many ethnographic camps.

sources.title: Wadley, L. et al., 'Middle Stone Age Bedding Construction and Settlement Patterns at Sibudu, South Africa', Science 334 (2011), 1388-1391
sources.author: Wadley, Lyn; Sievers, Christine; Bamford, Marion; Goldberg, Paul; Berna, Francesco; Miller, Christopher
sources.confirms: Reports 77,000-year-old plant bedding with insecticidal leaves at Sibudu.

sources.title: Goldberg, P. et al., 'Bedding, hearths, and site maintenance in the Middle Stone Age of Sibudu Cave, KwaZulu-Natal, South Africa', Archaeological and Anthropological Sciences 1 (2009), 95-122
sources.author: Goldberg, Paul; Miller, Christopher E.; Schiegl, Solveig; Ligouis, Bertrand; Berna, Francesco; Conard, Nicholas J.; Wadley, Lyn
sources.confirms: Micromorphology at Sibudu shows laminated layers of sedge, reed or grass brought into the shelter as bedding and repeatedly burned as site maintenance.

sibudu-insecticidal-bedding-75000bce.detail: Bedding layers are centimetre-thick mats identified by phytoliths and plant impressions. Burning of old bedding removed pests and prepared cave floor. Sibudu's sequence also contains compound adhesives and early arrow points. Border Cave's 200,000-year bedding pushed this practice back further. Lyn Wadley identified leaves through phytolith and plant anatomy comparison with modern Cryptocarya specimens. Repeated layers show bedding construction was routine over tens of thousands of years at this site.

picture.alt: Excavation area within Sibudu rock shelter, KwaZulu-Natal, South Africa
picture.credit: M. Ecker, CC BY 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

sibudu-insecticidal-bedding-75000bce.dating_note: Age of 77,000 years is optically stimulated luminescence on sediments.

blombos-pressure-flaking-73000bce.summary: Bifacial Still Bay points at Blombos Cave were finished by pressure flaking: pressing a pointed tool against an edge to detach thin regular flakes. Experiments reproduced scars on heat-treated silcrete. Layer dates to about 75,000 years ago. Pressure flaking was previously thought to appear in Upper Palaeolithic Europe around 20,000 years ago. Technique gives sharper, more symmetrical points and relies on prior heat treatment, so it links two innovations in control of stone.

sources.title: Mourre, V. et al., 'Early Use of Pressure Flaking on Lithic Artifacts at Blombos Cave, South Africa', Science 330 (2010), 659-662
sources.author: Mourre, Vincent; Villa, Paola; Henshilwood, Christopher S.
sources.confirms: Demonstrates pressure flaking on 75,000-year-old Still Bay points at Blombos.

sources.title: Brown, K. S. et al., 'Fire As an Engineering Tool of Early Modern Humans', Science 325 (2009), 859-862
sources.author: Brown, Kyle S.; Marean, Curtis W.; Herries, Andy I. R.; Jacobs, Zenobia; Tribolo, Chantal; Braun, David
sources.confirms: Shows that South African Middle Stone Age knappers heat-treated silcrete to improve its flaking, the prior step the Blombos pressure-flaking study depends on, with heat treatment common by about 72,000 years ago.

blombos-pressure-flaking-73000bce.detail: Pressure flaking leaves small, parallel, narrow scars with flat platforms; researchers compared archaeological points to experimental sets made with bone and wood compressors. Silcrete must be heated to become workable by pressure, tying this to Pinnacle Point's heat-treatment evidence. Still Bay points were likely spear or knife tips hafted with adhesive. Vincent Mourre of INRAP and Paola Villa of University of Colorado conducted experiments.

picture.alt: Bifacial silcrete point from Still Bay layer of Blombos Cave, South Africa, scale bar 5 cm
picture.credit: Vincent Mourre / Inrap, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

blombos-pressure-flaking-73000bce.dating_note: Layer age of about 75,000 years from earlier luminescence dating at Blombos.

jwalapuram-toba-ash-tools-72000bce.summary: Michael Petraglia excavated stone tool assemblages above and below a 2.5-metre layer of Youngest Toba Tuff at Jwalapuram in Jurreru Valley, Andhra Pradesh. Toba in Sumatra erupted about 74,000 years ago, largest volcanic event of past two million years. Tools above and below ash are similar Middle Palaeolithic industries, which Petraglia read as populations persisting locally despite ash fall; redating in 2025 puts first post-ash occupation at about 35,000 to 38,000 years ago, after a gap. Petraglia noted resemblance to African Middle Stone Age, raising possibility these were Homo sapiens. Some hold Toba caused a human population bottleneck, others that people survived it; Jwalapuram's evidence for continuity is now weaker.

sources.title: Petraglia, M. et al., 'Middle Paleolithic Assemblages from the Indian Subcontinent Before and After the Toba Super-Eruption', Science 317 (2007), 114-116
sources.author: Petraglia, Michael; Korisettar, Ravi; Boivin, Nicole; Clarkson, Christopher; Ditchfield, Peter; Jones, Sacha
sources.confirms: Reports Middle Palaeolithic assemblages above and below Toba ash at Jwalapuram around 74,000 years.

sources.title: Tsoupra, A. et al., 'Seasonally resolved stratigraphy at Jwalapuram India shows regional surface warming after the Toba volcanic super-eruption', PNAS Nexus 4 (2025), pgaf109
sources.author: Tsoupra, Anna; Barrocas Dias, Cristina; et al.
sources.confirms: Dates the Youngest Toba Tuff at Jwalapuram to about 74,000 years and reports Middle Palaeolithic occupation before and after the ash.
sources.qualifies: Revises the post-ash occupation to about 35,000 to 38,000 years and notes a disconformity, against the record's picture of local persistence.

sources.title: Haslam, M. et al., 'The 74 ka Toba super-eruption and southern Indian hominins: archaeology, lithic technology and environments at Jwalapuram Locality 3', Journal of Archaeological Science 37 (2010), 3370-3384
sources.author: Haslam, Michael; Clarkson, Chris; Petraglia, Michael D.; Korisettar, Ravi; Jones, Sacha; Shipton, Ceri; Ditchfield, Peter; Ambrose, Stanley H.
sources.confirms: Detailed site report for Jwalapuram Locality 3, the locality with assemblages under and over the Toba ash; metadata confirmed through OpenAlex, Elsevier page did not open.

jwalapuram-toba-ash-tools-72000bce.verification_note: Tsoupra and colleagues (PNAS Nexus 2025) confirm Middle Palaeolithic occupation before Toba ash (about 77,000 and 71,000 plus or minus 8,000 years) but date first post-ash occupation in layer A to about 35,000 to 38,000 years above a sedimentary disconformity.
jwalapuram-toba-ash-tools-72000bce.detail: Ash layer is dated by argon-argon on Toba glass from other sites and by optically stimulated luminescence at Jwalapuram, giving about 77,000 to 74,000 years. Over 1,800 artefacts were recovered. Ash preserved land surfaces and allowed direct comparison of pre- and post-eruption occupations. Critics argue stone tools alone cannot identify species and that continuity may reflect reoccupation after a gap.

picture.alt: Lake Toba caldera, Sumatra, source of ash layer at Jwalapuram
picture.credit: Yudhapohan, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

jwalapuram-toba-ash-tools-72000bce.dating_note: Ash age of about 74,000 years from argon-argon on Toba tephra, with optically stimulated luminescence at site.

pinnacle-point-heat-treated-silcrete-700.summary: Silcrete tools from Pinnacle Point caves were heat-treated, as gloss, colour change, thermoluminescence and archaeomagnetic tests show. Heat treatment appears sporadically at about 164,000 years ago and becomes dominant by 72,000 years ago. Burying stone under a controlled fire for hours alters silica structure so it flakes more predictably and sharper. This is earliest known use of fire to engineer a material, a step from fire as heat and light to fire as transformation of matter.

sources.title: Brown, K. S. et al., 'Fire As an Engineering Tool of Early Modern Humans', Science 325 (2009), 859-862
sources.author: Brown, Kyle S.; Marean, Curtis W.; Herries, Andy I. R.; Jacobs, Zenobia; Tribolo, Chantal; Braun, David
