sources.confirms: Reports heat treatment of silcrete at Pinnacle Point from 164,000 years and dominant by 72,000 years.

sources.title: Webb, John; Domanski, Marian, 'Fire and Stone', Science 325 (2009), 820-821
sources.author: Webb, John; Domanski, Marian
sources.confirms: Independent Perspective: Brown et al. show deliberate heat treatment of stone in coastal South Africa from at least 72,000 years and perhaps 164,000 years, by burying stone under a fire for a day or more, before its use outside Africa.

pinnacle-point-heat-treated-silcrete-700.detail: Researchers compared archaeological silcrete with experimentally heated samples; heated pieces show a lustre on post-heating flake scars and distinct magnetic signatures. Process requires sustaining a fire at 300 to 400 degrees Celsius with gradual heating and cooling. Heat-treated silcrete underpins Still Bay points and Howiesons Poort blades across southern Africa. Kyle Brown of University of Cape Town led experiments, replicating heat treatment in sand-buried fires.

picture.alt: Silcrete rock sample, Otago Museum (illustrative of raw material, not Pinnacle Point find)
picture.credit: Daderot, CC0, via Wikimedia Commons

pinnacle-point-heat-treated-silcrete-700.dating_note: Year gives 72,000 years when heat treatment became dominant; sporadic cases date to about 164,000 years.

sibudu-compound-adhesives-68000bce.summary: Residues on Middle Stone Age stone tools from Sibudu Cave, KwaZulu-Natal, dated about 70,000 years ago, show red ochre mixed with plant gum used to fix tools onto handles. Replication showed ochre loading changes acidity and workability, and that glue needed drying near fire without overheating. Lyn Wadley argues this multi-step recipe demands holding several variables in mind at once, evidence of complex cognition without appeal to symbolism. Compound adhesives let hunters mount small stone points as spear and arrow tips.

sources.title: Wadley, L. et al., 'Implications for complex cognition from the hafting of tools with compound adhesives in the Middle Stone Age, South Africa', Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences 106 (2009), 9590-9594
sources.author: Wadley, Lyn; Hodgskiss, Tamaryn; Grant, Michael
sources.venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
sources.confirms: Reports ochre and plant gum compound adhesives on 70,000-year-old tools at Sibudu.

sources.title: Wadley, Lyn, 'Compound-Adhesive Manufacture as a Behavioral Proxy for Complex Cognition in the Middle Stone Age', Current Anthropology 51, S1 (2010), S111-S119
sources.author: Wadley, Lyn
sources.confirms: Compound adhesives were made in southern Africa at least 70,000 years ago from disparate ingredients in an irreversible process, with Sibudu layers dated 70,000 to 61,000 years.

sibudu-compound-adhesives-68000bce.detail: Residues were examined under microscopes and by chemical tests on segments and points from Howiesons Poort and post-Howiesons Poort layers. Experiments with Acacia gum and various ochres identified mixtures that set hard and resist breaking. Sibudu's sequence also preserves bedding and early arrowheads. Birch tar in Europe serves comparable function with different chemistry. Lyn Wadley led experiments at University of the Witwatersrand.

picture.alt: Stone tools from Sibudu Cave, KwaZulu-Natal, South Africa
picture.credit: F. Brodbeck and G. Porraz, CC BY 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

sibudu-compound-adhesives-68000bce.dating_note: Layer ages of about 70,000 years from optically stimulated luminescence at Sibudu.

sulawesi-muna-hand-stencil-65800bce.summary: Laser-ablation uranium-series dating of calcite over a hand stencil at Liang Metanduno on Muna Island, southeast Sulawesi, gives 71,600 plus or minus 3,800 years, a minimum age of 67,800 years for underlying motif. This exceeds previous Maros-Pangkep minimum ages by about 16,600 years and surpasses a Spanish hand stencil attributed to Neanderthals by about 1,100 years. Adhi Agus Oktaviana's team suggests art this old in Sulawesi implies maritime crossings between Borneo and Papua during initial settlement of Sahul around 65,000 years ago.

sources.title: Oktaviana, A. A. et al., 'Rock art from at least 67,800 years ago in Sulawesi', Nature 650 (2026), 652-656
sources.author: Oktaviana, Adhi Agus; Joannes-Boyau, Renaud; Hakim, Budianto; Burhan, Basran; Sardi, Ratno; Adhityatama, Shinatria
sources.confirms: Reports a minimum age of 67,800 years for a hand stencil at Liang Metanduno, Muna Island.

sources.title: Aubert, M. et al., 'Pleistocene cave art from Sulawesi, Indonesia', Nature 514 (2014), 223-227
sources.author: Aubert, Maxime; Brumm, Adam; Ramli, Muhammad; Sutikna, Thomas; Saptomo, E. Wahyu; Hakim, Budianto
sources.confirms: Gives uranium-series minimum ages of 39,900 years for a Maros hand stencil, the earlier Sulawesi benchmark the 2026 Muna Island date exceeds.

sulawesi-muna-hand-stencil-65800bce.detail: Laser-ablation uranium-series samples thin calcite layers in sequence, letting researchers date crusts that formed over pigment. Muna motifs include hand stencils and possibly later figures. Result pushes Indonesian rock art before earliest European cave art by tens of thousands of years and makes Wallacea a focus for image-making origins. Maxime Aubert of Griffith University led dating with Indonesian colleagues from BRIN and local heritage agencies. Hand stencils are made by blowing pigment over a hand pressed against rock, leaving a negative outline.

picture.alt: Hand stencils in Pettakere Cave, Maros, Sulawesi (Maros-Pangkep karst, not Muna Island)
picture.credit: Cahyo, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

sulawesi-muna-hand-stencil-65800bce.dating_note: Minimum age of 67,800 plus or minus 3,800 years by laser-ablation uranium-series on overlying calcite; motif could be older.

madjedbebe-grinding-stones-63000bce.summary: Madjedbebe holds Australia's largest Pleistocene grinding stone assemblage, spanning 65,000 years ago to recent times. Microscopic wear and residues show seed grinding, plant processing, ochre grinding and shaping of edge-ground hatchets from lowest layers. These are earliest evidence of seed grinding and of ground-edge axes anywhere. A ground-edge axe fragment from Carpenter's Gap in Kimberley dates to 49,000 to 44,000 years ago. Richard Fullagar and Judith Field's claim of 30,000-year-old seed grinding stones at Cuddie Springs is disputed on stratigraphic grounds.

sources.title: Hayes, E. H. et al., '65,000-years of continuous grinding stone use at Madjedbebe, Northern Australia', Scientific Reports 12 (2022)
sources.author: Hayes, Elspeth H.; Fullagar, Richard; Field, Judith H.; Coster, Adelle C.F.; Matheson, Carney; Nango, May
sources.confirms: Documents 65,000 years of grinding stone use at Madjedbebe including seed grinding and edge-ground hatchets.

sources.title: Hiscock, P. et al., 'World’s earliest ground-edge axe production coincides with human colonisation of Australia', Australian Archaeology 82 (2016), 2-11
sources.author: Hiscock, Peter; O’Connor, Sue; Balme, Jane; Maloney, Tim
sources.confirms: Dates a ground-edge axe fragment from Carpenter's Gap to 49,000 to 44,000 years.

sources.title: Fullagar, R. and Field, J., 'Pleistocene seed-grinding implements from the Australian arid zone', Antiquity 71 (1997), 300-307
sources.author: Fullagar, Richard; Field, Judith
sources.confirms: Claims seed grinding stones at Cuddie Springs around 30,000 years.
sources.qualifies: Cuddie Springs dating is contested.

sources.title: Gillespie, R. and Brook, B. W., 'Is there a Pleistocene archaeological site at Cuddie Springs?', Archaeology in Oceania 41 (2006), 1-11
sources.author: Gillespie, Richard; Brook, Barry W.
sources.confirms: Argues Cuddie Springs deposits are mixed and dates unreliable.
sources.qualifies: Gillespie and Brook reject Cuddie Springs as secure evidence.

madjedbebe-grinding-stones-63000bce.verification_note: Earliest Madjedbebe age is debated; Kimberley axe dates are secure.
madjedbebe-grinding-stones-63000bce.detail: Grinding stones are sandstone slabs and handstones; wear types distinguished seed, plant, pigment and stone-on-stone grinding. Seed grinding turns small hard grass seeds into flour, a technology once thought Holocene in Australia. Cuddie Springs critics, including Richard Gillespie and Barry Brook, argue site deposits are mixed; Field and Dodson defend stratigraphy. Madjedbebe's age for grinding shares uncertainties of site's 65,000-year date.
madjedbebe-grinding-stones-63000bce.dating_note: Age of 65,000 years follows Madjedbebe lowest layers and inherits their dispute; secure ground-edge axe evidence from Kimberley is 49,000 to 44,000 years.

madjedbebe-sahul-settlement-63000bce.summary: Chris Clarkson dates lowest occupation at Madjedbebe rockshelter in Arnhem Land, Northern Territory, to about 65,000 years ago by single-grain optically stimulated luminescence, with artefacts including grinding stones, ground ochre, reflective pigment and ground-edge hatchet fragments. Reaching Sahul from Sunda required repeated sea crossings of tens of kilometres, so this date marks earliest known planned ocean voyaging. James O'Connell argues a date before 50,000 years ago is unlikely given genetic and other archaeological evidence. Raja Ampat finds in West Papua at 55,000 to 50,000 years ago support early arrival.

sources.title: Clarkson, C. et al., 'Human occupation of northern Australia by 65,000 years ago', Nature 547 (2017), 306-310
sources.author: Clarkson, Chris; Jacobs, Zenobia; Marwick, Ben; Fullagar, Richard; Wallis, Lynley; Smith, Mike
sources.confirms: Dates Madjedbebe lowest occupation to about 65,000 years with grinding stones and ground-edge hatchets.

sources.title: O’Connell, J. F. et al., 'When did Homo sapiens first reach Southeast Asia and Sahul?', Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences 115 (2018), 8482-8490
sources.author: O’Connell, James F.; Allen, Jim; Williams, Martin A. J.; Williams, Alan N.; Turney, Chris S. M.; Spooner, Nigel A.
sources.venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
sources.confirms: Argues Sahul settlement before 50,000 years is unlikely on genetic and archaeological grounds.
sources.qualifies: O'Connell et al. (2018) favour arrival after 50,000 years.

sources.title: Gaffney, D. et al., 'Human dispersal and plant processing in the Pacific 55 000–50 000 years ago', Antiquity 98 (2024), 885-904
sources.author: Gaffney, Dylan; Tanudirjo, Daud A.; Djami, Erlin Novita Idje; Mas'ud, Zubair; Macap, Abdul Razak; Russell, Tristan
sources.confirms: Reports human dispersal and plant processing at Raja Ampat, West Papua, 55,000 to 50,000 years ago.

madjedbebe-sahul-settlement-63000bce.verification_note: Dating method is well supported; age is disputed against genetic and regional evidence.
madjedbebe-sahul-settlement-63000bce.detail: Over 10,000 artefacts came from dense lowest layers; dating used thousands of individual quartz grains with Bayesian modelling. Critics raise termite and trampling displacement of artefacts into older sand, and conflicts with genomic estimates of 50,000 years for divergence of Aboriginal Australian ancestors. Excavation was agreed with Mirarr traditional owners through Gundjeihmi Aboriginal Corporation. Chris Clarkson of University of Queensland led 2012 and 2015 excavations with Zenobia Jacobs dating.

picture.alt: East Alligator River and Arnhem Land escarpment, Northern Territory, near Madjedbebe
picture.credit: Jamie Qi Zhou, CC BY 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

madjedbebe-sahul-settlement-63000bce.dating_note: Age of 65,000 years is single-grain optically stimulated luminescence; O'Connell et al. (2018) argue for under 50,000 years.

sibudu-bow-and-arrow-62000bce.summary: Quartz backed segments 64,000 years old from Howiesons Poort layers at Sibudu Cave carry impact fractures, hafting traces with ochre-rich adhesive and animal residues consistent with use as arrowheads delivered by bow. Bone points from same layers also fit arrow use, and Sibudu bone tools include a probable arrow point. Earlier claims for archery in Europe date after 20,000 years ago. Bows extend hunting range and let hunters take small prey and birds with less risk.

sources.title: Lombard, M. and Phillipson, L., 'Indications of bow and stone-tipped arrow use 64 000 years ago in KwaZulu-Natal, South Africa', Antiquity 84 (2010), 635-648
sources.author: Lombard, Marlize; Phillipson, Laurel
sources.confirms: Argues 64,000-year-old Sibudu segments were arrowheads indicating bow-and-arrow use.

sources.title: Backwell, L. et al., 'Middle Stone Age bone tools from the Howiesons Poort layers, Sibudu Cave, South Africa', Journal of Archaeological Science 35 (2008), 1566-1580
sources.author: Backwell, Lucinda; d'Errico, Francesco; Wadley, Lyn
sources.confirms: Describes Middle Stone Age bone tools from Sibudu including a probable arrow point and awls.

sibudu-bow-and-arrow-62000bce.verification_note: Dating is secure; archery inference depends on fracture and size analysis.
sibudu-bow-and-arrow-62000bce.detail: Segments are crescent-shaped microliths whose blunt backs were set in adhesive at angles that produce diagnostic breaks on impact. Macrofracture analysis used criteria developed on experimental arrowheads. Critics note that spear-thrower darts can produce similar damage, so bow attribution rests on segment size and weight. Fa-Hien Lena in Sri Lanka later provides bone arrow points at 48,000 years. Marlize Lombard of University of Johannesburg led analysis.

picture.alt: Microscope views of Middle Stone Age stone points from Sibudu Cave with traces of hafting, published in 2014.
picture.credit: Lombard et al., PLOS ONE 2014, CC BY 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

sibudu-bow-and-arrow-62000bce.dating_note: Howiesons Poort layers at Sibudu dated about 64,000 years by optically stimulated luminescence; bow use is inferred, not directly preserved.

diepkloof-engraved-eggshells-58000bce.summary: Howiesons Poort layers at Diepkloof Rock Shelter in Western Cape, dated about 60,000 years ago, hold 270 fragments of engraved ostrich eggshell. Engravings follow a few standard motifs, such as hatched bands and parallel lines, repeated across time with gradual change, which their excavators read as a graphic tradition marking containers. Eggshells were used as water flasks with drilled openings. A 2026 geometric analysis finds systematic use of parallelism and nested elements, evidence of structured visual conventions.

sources.title: Texier, P. J. et al., 'A Howiesons Poort tradition of engraving ostrich eggshell containers dated to 60,000 years ago at Diepkloof Rock Shelter, South Africa', Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences 107 (2010), 6180-6185
sources.author: Texier, Pierre-Jean; Porraz, Guillaume; Parkington, John; Rigaud, Jean-Philippe; Poggenpoel, Cedric; Miller, Christopher
sources.venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
sources.confirms: Reports 270 engraved ostrich eggshell fragments at Diepkloof dated about 60,000 years.

sources.title: Decembrini, V. et al., 'Earliest geometries: A cognitive investigation of Howiesons Poort engraved ostrich eggshells', PLOS One 21 (2026), e0338509
sources.author: Decembrini, Valentina; Ottaviano, Ludovica; Cartolano, Mattia; Spinapolice, Enza Elena; Ferrara, Silvia
sources.confirms: Analyses geometric structure of Howiesons Poort engraved eggshells as systematic visual organisation.

diepkloof-engraved-eggshells-58000bce.detail: Diepkloof's sequence spans about 130,000 to 45,000 years; engraved pieces concentrate in Howiesons Poort levels dated by luminescence and thermoluminescence. Motif repetition across stratigraphy implies transmission over generations rather than individual improvisation. Ostrich eggshell flasks remain in use among Kalahari San, supporting container interpretation. Finds complement Blombos engravings and show pattern-making serving group identity or ownership. Pierre-Jean Texier of CNRS directed excavations with Guillaume Porraz.

picture.alt: Engraved ostrich eggshell from Diepkloof Rock Shelter, Iziko South African Museum
picture.credit: Nkansah Rexford, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

diepkloof-engraved-eggshells-58000bce.dating_note: Age of about 60,000 years from thermoluminescence and optically stimulated luminescence on Howiesons Poort layers.

leang-karampuang-narrative-scene-49000bc.summary: Laser-ablation uranium-series imaging of calcite over a painted scene at Leang Karampuang in Maros-Pangkep karst, South Sulawesi, gives a minimum age of 51,200 years. Scene shows three human-like figures interacting with a Sulawesi warty pig. Same method redated Leang Bulu' Sipong 4 hunting scene to at least 48,000 years. A warty pig painting at Leang Tedongnge has a minimum age of 45,500 years. These are oldest known representational images and oldest composed scenes, showing visual storytelling in Island Southeast Asia before European cave art.

sources.title: Oktaviana, A. A. et al., 'Narrative cave art in Indonesia by 51,200 years ago', Nature 631 (2024), 814-818
sources.author: Oktaviana, Adhi Agus; Joannes-Boyau, Renaud; Hakim, Budianto; Burhan, Basran; Sardi, Ratno; Adhityatama, Shinatria
sources.confirms: Dates Leang Karampuang narrative scene to at least 51,200 years by laser-ablation uranium-series.

sources.title: Brumm, A. et al., 'Oldest cave art found in Sulawesi', Science Advances 7 (2021)
sources.author: Brumm, Adam; Oktaviana, Adhi Agus; Burhan, Basran; Hakim, Budianto; Lebe, Rustan; Zhao, Jian-xin
sources.confirms: Dates a Leang Tedongnge warty pig painting to at least 45,500 years.

leang-karampuang-narrative-scene-49000bc.detail: Laser-ablation sampling resolves calcite layers at micrometre scale, avoiding contamination that affected earlier solution dating. Figures are drawn in red ochre; pig is depicted in profile with bristles. Maros-Pangkep karst has hundreds of painted caves, many threatened by weathering and mining. Dating work was led from Griffith University with Indonesian partners, by Adhi Agus Oktaviana of BRIN with Maxime Aubert and Adam Brumm.

picture.alt: Leang Karampuang cave, Maros-Pangkep karst, Sulawesi
picture.credit: Anhar Karim, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

leang-karampuang-narrative-scene-49000bc.dating_note: Minimum age 51,200 years from laser-ablation uranium-series on calcite over pigment.

abri-du-maras-cord-48000bce.summary: Neanderthals at Abri du Maras in Ardèche left a six-millimetre fragment of three-ply cord adhering to a Levallois flake, dated by luminescence and radiocarbon to between about 52,000 and 41,000 years ago. Fibres come from inner bark of a conifer and were S-twisted into yarn then Z-twisted into cord. Cordage underpins bags, nets, clothing, hafting bindings and watercraft, none of which normally survive. Cord-making requires understanding of fibre seasons and of twisting in sequence, evidence of Neanderthal technical knowledge.

sources.title: Hardy, B. L. et al., 'Direct evidence of Neanderthal fibre technology and its cognitive and behavioral implications', Scientific Reports 10 (2020)
sources.author: Hardy, B. L.; Moncel, M.-H.; Kerfant, C.; Lebon, M.; Bellot-Gurlet, L.; Mélard, N.
sources.confirms: Reports a three-ply bark-fibre cord fragment at Abri du Maras dated 52,000 to 41,000 years.

sources.title: Hardy, B. L. et al., 'Impossible Neanderthals? Making string, throwing projectiles and catching small game during Marine Isotope Stage 4 (Abri du Maras, France)', Quaternary Science Reviews 82 (2013), 23-40
sources.author: Hardy, Bruce L.; Moncel, Marie-Hélène; Daujeard, Camille; Fernandes, Paul; Béarez, Philippe; Desclaux, Emmanuel; Chacon Navarro, Maria Gema; Puaud, Simon; Gallotti, Rosalia
sources.confirms: Earlier report of twisted fibre traces at Abri du Maras in Marine Isotope Stage 4, cited by Conard and Rots (Science Advances 2024) as evidence for Neanderthal string-making; abstract page would not open, metadata confirmed through OpenAlex and the 2024 citing paper.

abri-du-maras-cord-48000bce.detail: Fragment was found under a microscope during residue analysis of lithics; scanning electron microscopy showed plied structure. Earlier twisted-fibre evidence came from Ohalo II at 19,000 years. Bast fibres must be harvested in spring or early summer when bark separates. Abri du Maras also yielded evidence of Neanderthals eating fish and birds. Bruce Hardy of Kenyon College led study with Marie-Hélène Moncel of CNRS.

picture.alt: Levallois flake from Abri du Maras with adhering cord fragment
picture.credit: Hardy, B.L., Moncel, MH., Kerfant, C. et al., CC BY 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

abri-du-maras-cord-48000bce.dating_note: Age bracket 52,000 to 41,000 years combines luminescence and radiocarbon; year gives about 50,000.

neanderthal-fire-making-48000bce.summary: Mineral traces and percussion wear on dozens of Mousterian of Acheulean Tradition bifaces from sites across France dated about 50,000 years ago match experimental strikes of pyrite on flint to produce sparks. This is earliest direct evidence for fire production rather than fire maintenance. Neanderthals at Pech-de-l'Azé I collected manganese dioxide blocks, which lower ignition temperature of tinder. Together these point to Neanderthals making fire on demand.

sources.title: Sorensen, A. C. et al., 'Neandertal fire-making technology inferred from microwear analysis', Scientific Reports 8 (2018)
sources.author: Sorensen, A. C.; Claud, E.; Soressi, M.
sources.confirms: Reports mineral traces on Mousterian bifaces as evidence of fire-making about 50,000 years ago.

sources.title: Heyes, P. J. et al., 'Selection and Use of Manganese Dioxide by Neanderthals', Scientific Reports 6 (2016)
sources.author: Heyes, Peter J.; Anastasakis, Konstantinos; de Jong, Wiebren; van Hoesel, Annelies; Roebroeks, Wil; Soressi, Marie
sources.confirms: Shows manganese dioxide collected by Neanderthals at Pech-de-l'Azé lowers tinder ignition temperature.

neanderthal-fire-making-48000bce.detail: Use-wear traces are C-shaped percussion marks with mineral residue on biface faces, distinct from knapping damage. Experiments compared pyrite striking with other activities to rule out alternatives. Sceptics note pyrite rarely survives in sites, so direct strike-a-lights are missing. Manganese dioxide at Pech-de-l'Azé had previously been read as black pigment; combustion experiments showed it aids fire lighting. Andrew Sorensen of Leiden University led analysis.

picture.alt: Mousterian biface from Muizon, Marne, France, Musée Saint-Remi (tool type that carries pyrite strike marks)
picture.credit: Vassil, CC0, via Wikimedia Commons

neanderthal-fire-making-48000bce.dating_note: Mousterian of Acheulean Tradition sites date about 50,000 years by luminescence and radiocarbon.

warratyi-ochre-and-hafting-47000bce.summary: Radiocarbon and luminescence date occupation of Warratyi rockshelter in Flinders Ranges from about 49,000 years ago. Finds include earliest ochre use in Australia and Southeast Asia at or before 49,000 to 46,000 years ago, gypsum pigment at 40,000 to 33,000, bone tools at 40,000 to 38,000, hafted tools at 38,000 to 35,000 and backed artefacts at 30,000 to 24,000 years ago, each up to 10,000 years older than other known occurrences. People lived in arid interior within a few millennia of reaching Sahul and interacted with megafauna such as Diprotodon.

sources.title: Hamm, G. et al., 'Cultural innovation and megafauna interaction in the early settlement of arid Australia', Nature 539 (2016), 280-283
sources.author: Hamm, Giles; Mitchell, Peter; Arnold, Lee J.; Prideaux, Gavin J.; Questiaux, Daniele; Spooner, Nigel A.
sources.confirms: Dates Warratyi occupation from 49,000 years with early ochre, bone tools and hafted tools.

sources.title: Coulthard, Terrence; Johnson, Margaret; Coulthard, Kristian et al., 'Adnyamathanha and Archaeological Views on Warratyi Rock Shelter (The Rock), a 50,000-Year-Old Site in the Flinders Ranges, South Australia', in The Oxford Handbook of Global Indigenous Archaeologies (Oxford University Press, 2025)
sources.author: Coulthard, Terrence; Johnson, Margaret; Coulthard, Kristian; Coulthard, Vince; Smith, Claire
sources.confirms: Chapter dates Warratyi to about 49,000 years BP after Hamm et al. 2016 and presents it as key evidence for early occupation of Australia's semiarid zone, alongside Adnyamathanha custodians' perspectives.

warratyi-ochre-and-hafting-47000bce.detail: Rockshelter was found by Adnyamathanha elder Clifford Coulthard with Giles Hamm in 2011. Deposits about one metre deep preserve hearths and over 4,300 artefacts. A Diprotodon juvenile bone and giant bird eggshell occur in oldest layers. Dating combines charcoal radiocarbon and optically stimulated luminescence; site shows technologies previously assumed to be late Holocene innovations in Australia. Giles Hamm of La Trobe University led excavation with Adnyamathanha Traditional Lands Association.

picture.alt: Brachina Gorge, Ikara-Flinders Ranges, South Australia; Warratyi rock shelter lies in these ranges
picture.credit: DXR, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

warratyi-ochre-and-hafting-47000bce.dating_note: Occupation from about 49,000 years is radiocarbon plus optically stimulated luminescence.

el-sidron-neanderthal-self-medication-46.summary: DNA survives in dental calculus of Neanderthals at El Sidrón in Asturias, dated about 48,000 years ago. One individual with a dental abscess and a chronic gut pathogen carried DNA of poplar, whose bark contains salicylic acid, and of Penicillium mould, source of penicillin. Laura Weyrich reads this as self-medication. Calculus also yielded a near-complete genome of oral archaeon Methanobrevibacter oralis. Neanderthal diets and health varied by region, and this is earliest evidence of medicinal plant use tied to a diagnosed condition.

sources.title: Weyrich, L. S. et al., 'Neanderthal behaviour, diet, and disease inferred from ancient DNA in dental calculus', Nature 544 (2017), 357-361
sources.author: Weyrich, Laura S.; Duchene, Sebastian; Soubrier, Julien; Arriola, Luis; Llamas, Bastien; Breen, James
sources.confirms: Reports poplar and Penicillium DNA in calculus of an El Sidrón Neanderthal with an abscess, read as self-medication.

sources.title: Hardy, K., 'Paleomedicine and the Evolutionary Context of Medicinal Plant Use', Revista Brasileira de Farmacognosia 31 (2020), 1-15
sources.author: Hardy, Karen
sources.confirms: Reviews evidence for Palaeolithic medicinal plant use and care, including El Sidrón.

el-sidron-neanderthal-self-medication-46.detail: El Sidrón Neanderthals ate mushrooms, pine nuts, moss and tree bark, unlike meat-heavy Spy individuals in Belgium. Ancient DNA from calculus is vulnerable to contamination, and plant DNA could reflect incidental ingestion, so medical interpretation is suggestive. Yarrow and chamomile compounds had earlier been found in El Sidrón calculus. Shanidar Neanderthals show long survival after severe injury, implying care. Laura Weyrich and Alan Cooper of University of Adelaide led sequencing.

picture.alt: Core and Levallois flakes from El Sidron cave, Asturias, Spain
picture.credit: Xuliu Pombar, CC0, via Wikimedia Commons

el-sidron-neanderthal-self-medication-46.dating_note: El Sidrón remains date about 48,000 years by radiocarbon with ultrafiltration.

fa-hien-lena-bow-and-arrow-46000bce.summary: Fa-Hien Lena cave in Sri Lanka's wet-zone rainforest yielded 130 bone points dated by radiocarbon to about 48,000 years ago. Fracture patterns and wear indicate use as arrowheads, earliest evidence for bow-and-arrow hunting outside Africa. Fa-Hien Lena also yields bone tools for working skins or plant fibres and shell beads. Arrows suited hunting monkeys and squirrels in dense forest. Rainforests, long considered barriers, were occupied with specialised toolkits early in Homo sapiens dispersal.

sources.title: Langley, M. C. et al., 'Bows and arrows and complex symbolic displays 48,000 years ago in the South Asian tropics', Science Advances 6 (2020)
sources.author: Langley, Michelle C.; Amano, Noel; Wedage, Oshan; Deraniyagala, Siran; Pathmalal, M.M; Perera, Nimal
sources.confirms: Reports 48,000-year-old bone arrow points at Fa-Hien Lena, Sri Lanka.

sources.title: Wedage, O. et al., 'Specialized rainforest hunting by Homo sapiens ~45,000 years ago', Nature Communications 10 (2019), 739
sources.author: Wedage, Oshan; Amano, Noel; Langley, Michelle C.; Douka, Katerina; Blinkhorn, James; Crowther, Alison; Deraniyagala, Siran; Roberts, Patrick
sources.confirms: Fa-Hien Lena's Late Pleistocene occupation runs from about 48,000 years, with bone points showing high-velocity impact damage used to hunt monkeys and squirrels in rainforest.

fa-hien-lena-bow-and-arrow-46000bce.detail: Points are small and symmetrical, with impact fractures and hafting notches. They were compared with ethnographic arrowheads used by rainforest hunters. Fa-Hien Lena's sequence runs from about 48,000 to 4,000 years with monkey and squirrel bones dominant. Sibudu in South Africa offers earlier but more indirect archery evidence at 64,000 years. Michelle Langley of Griffith University and Patrick Roberts of Max Planck Institute led study with Sri Lankan Department of Archaeology.

picture.alt: Fa-Hien Lena (Pahiyangala) rock cave, Sri Lanka
picture.credit: Freelk, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

fa-hien-lena-bow-and-arrow-46000bce.dating_note: Age of about 48,000 years is radiocarbon on charcoal and bone.

eyed-bone-needles-45000bce.summary: Eyed needles let people sew fitted, layered clothing with sinew thread. An eyed bone needle comes from Initial Upper Palaeolithic layers of Denisova Cave's East Chamber in Altai, around 50,000 to 45,000 years ago. Across 271 sites, needles emerge in Siberia and China between 45,000 and 40,000 years ago, possibly as independent inventions, then spread into Eastern Europe, with Western Europe following in Solutrean. Needle size variation at Shuidonggou 12 shows needles made for different tasks. Sewn clothing opened Arctic latitudes.

sources.title: Shunkov, M. V. et al., 'Initial Upper Palaeolithic ornaments and formal bone tools from the East Chamber of Denisova Cave in the Russian Altai', Quaternary International 559 (2020), 47-67
sources.author: Shunkov, Michael V.; Fedorchenko, Alexander Yu.; Kozlikin, Maxim B.; Derevianko, Anatoly P.
sources.confirms: Describes an eyed bone needle from Initial Upper Palaeolithic layers at Denisova Cave.

sources.title: d’Errico, F. et al., 'The origin and evolution of sewing technologies in Eurasia and North America', Journal of Human Evolution 125 (2018), 71-86
sources.author: d’Errico, Francesco; Doyon, Luc; Zhang, Shuangquan; Baumann, Malvina; Lázničková-Galetová, Martina; Gao, Xing
sources.confirms: Reviews 271 sites and finds eyed needles emerge in Siberia and China 45,000 to 40,000 years ago.

eyed-bone-needles-45000bce.detail: Denisova's needle, about 7.6 centimetres long, was found in 2016 in layer 11 with Initial Upper Palaeolithic blades. Needles were cut from bone splinters, ground to shape, polished and drilled or gouged for eye. Chinese needles from 35,000 to 25,000 years are thick and large; later ones are small and flat. Awls without eyes predate needles widely. Tailored clothing does not survive, so needles serve as proxy.

picture.alt: Flat bone sewing needle from Gourdan cave, France, Magdalenian (not Denisova find), Museum de Toulouse
picture.credit: Didier Descouens, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

eyed-bone-needles-45000bce.dating_note: Denisova Initial Upper Palaeolithic layers date about 50,000 to 45,000 years by radiocarbon and luminescence; d'Errico et al. place earliest needles 45,000 to 40,000 years.

ivane-valley-pandanus-and-yams-45000bce.summary: Sites in Ivane Valley, Papua New Guinea highlands, at about 2,000 metres elevation, date by radiocarbon to 49,000 to 44,000 years ago. Finds include charred Pandanus nutshells and yam starch on stone tools; waisted stone axes were likely used to clear forest. This shows early settlers of Sahul moved into cool montane forests early and processed plant staples that later became highland crops. Waisted axes point to deliberate vegetation management. Niah Cave in Borneo shows comparable plant processing, including detoxification of yams, from about 46,000 years ago.

sources.title: Summerhayes, G. R. et al., 'Human Adaptation and Plant Use in Highland New Guinea 49,000 to 44,000 Years Ago', Science 330 (2010), 78-81
sources.author: Summerhayes, Glenn R.; Leavesley, Matthew; Fairbairn, Andrew; Mandui, Herman; Field, Judith; Ford, Anne
sources.confirms: Dates Ivane Valley highland sites to 49,000 to 44,000 years with Pandanus and yam processing.

sources.title: Barker, G. et al., 'The ‘human revolution’ in lowland tropical Southeast Asia: the antiquity and behavior of anatomically modern humans at Niah Cave (Sarawak, Borneo)', Journal of Human Evolution 52 (2007), 243-261
sources.author: Barker, Graeme; Barton, Huw; Bird, Michael; Daly, Patrick; Datan, Ipoi; Dykes, Alan
sources.confirms: Dates Niah Cave Deep Skull and activity from about 46,000 to 34,000 years with plant processing evidence.

ivane-valley-pandanus-and-yams-45000bce.detail: Ivane dates sit near radiocarbon limit and were produced with careful pretreatment. Pandanus nuts need cracking and roasting; yams need peeling and sometimes leaching. Highlands were cooler by several degrees during Pleistocene. New Guinea later becomes an independent centre of plant domestication at Kuk Swamp. Niah Cave foragers used toxic plants and burned forest. Glenn Summerhayes of University of Otago led work.

picture.alt: Pandanus conoideus fruit, Eastern Highlands, Papua New Guinea
picture.credit: Jialiang Gao (peace-on-earth.org), CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

ivane-valley-pandanus-and-yams-45000bce.dating_note: Age 49,000 to 44,000 years is radiocarbon near method limit.

shanidar-neanderthal-care-45000bce.summary: Shanidar 1, excavated by Ralph Solecki in 1950s in Zagros foothills of Iraqi Kurdistan, was a Neanderthal male who lived to middle age with a withered right arm, blindness in one eye, hearing loss and healed head and leg injuries. Trauma recurs across Shanidar skeletons. His hearing loss would have made him dependent on others. Penny Spikins treats Shanidar as evidence of long-term healthcare in Neanderthal groups, dated around 50,000 to 45,000 years ago. Shanidar 4's famous flower pollen is now partly attributed to bee burrowing.

sources.title: Spikins, P. et al., 'Calculated or caring? Neanderthal healthcare in social context', World Archaeology 50 (2018), 384-403
sources.author: Spikins, Penny; Needham, Andy; Tilley, Lorna; Hitchens, Gail
sources.confirms: Argues Neanderthal healthcare, with Shanidar as key case, was calculated and widespread.

sources.title: Trinkaus, E. and Zimmerman, M. R., 'Trauma among the Shanidar Neandertals', American Journal of Physical Anthropology 57 (1982), 61-76
sources.author: Trinkaus, Erik; Zimmerman, M. R.
sources.confirms: Documents trauma and healing among Shanidar Neanderthals including Shanidar 1.

sources.title: Hunt, C. O. et al., 'Shanidar et ses fleurs? Reflections on the palynology of the Neanderthal ‘Flower Burial’ hypothesis', Journal of Archaeological Science 159 (2023), 105822
sources.author: Hunt, Chris O.; Pomeroy, Emma; Reynolds, Tim; Tilby, Emily; Barker, Graeme
sources.confirms: Finds bee burrowing a likely source of pollen around Shanidar 4, qualifying flower burial.
sources.qualifies: Hunt et al. (2023) weaken the flower-burial interpretation.

shanidar-neanderthal-care-45000bce.verification_note: Care inference is widely accepted; flower burial is now doubted.
shanidar-neanderthal-care-45000bce.detail: Healed fractures and bone remodelling show injuries occurred years before death. Care implies food sharing and tolerance of a non-contributing member. Shanidar burials, including recently excavated Shanidar Z, also show deliberate placement. Solitary bee nests are a probable source of flower pollen around Shanidar 4, which weakens flower-burial hypothesis. Penny Spikins of University of York led healthcare study.

picture.alt: Shanidar Cave, Bradost Mountain, Iraqi Kurdistan
picture.credit: Khoshhat, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

shanidar-neanderthal-care-45000bce.dating_note: Shanidar 1 is placed around 50,000 to 45,000 years on radiocarbon and stratigraphy from renewed excavations; older layers are near radiocarbon limit.

border-cave-notched-bones-42000bce.summary: Redated organic artefacts from Border Cave, South Africa, place notched bones at about 44,000 to 42,000 years ago alongside ostrich eggshell beads, a digging stick, a poison applicator and a beeswax-resin hafting compound. One notched baboon fibula, popularised as Lebombo bone, carries 29 notches. Notches on Border Cave pieces were added with different tools at different times, consistent with recording accumulating information. Francesco d'Errico treats them as plausible numerical notation, short of proof; marks alone cannot separate counts from calendars or decoration.

sources.title: d’Errico, F. et al., 'Early evidence of San material culture represented by organic artifacts from Border Cave, South Africa', Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences 109 (2012), 13214-13219
sources.author: d’Errico, Francesco; Backwell, Lucinda; Villa, Paola; Degano, Ilaria; Lucejko, Jeannette J.; Bamford, Marion K.
sources.venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
sources.confirms: Dates Border Cave notched bones, beads, digging stick and hafting compound to about 44,000 to 40,000 years.

sources.title: d'Errico, F. et al., 'From number sense to number symbols. An archaeological perspective', Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society B: Biological Sciences 373 (2018), 20160518
sources.author: d'Errico, Francesco; Doyon, Luc; Colagé, Ivan; Queffelec, Alain; Le Vraux, Emma; Giacobini, Giacomo
sources.venue: Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society B: Biological Sciences
sources.confirms: Analyses Border Cave and Les Pradelles notched bones as possible numerical notation, noting notches made at different times.
sources.qualifies: Authors frame notation as plausible, not proven.

border-cave-notched-bones-42000bce.verification_note: Dates are secure; tally interpretation is contested.
border-cave-notched-bones-42000bce.detail: Border Cave notched pieces were first described by Beaumont in 1970s. Microscopic analysis distinguishes notch sets by cross-section and tool. Les Pradelles hyena bone from France, dated 72,000 to 60,000 years ago, carries nine notches made in one session, raising possibility of Neanderthal notation. Critics point out that any regular notching can be read as counting without a way to test what was counted. A 24,000-year-old poison applicator from Border Cave retains castor-bean residue.

picture.alt: Sifting deposits at mouth of Border Cave near Ingwavuma, South Africa
picture.credit: Androstachys, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

border-cave-notched-bones-42000bce.dating_note: Age 44,000 to 42,000 years from Bayesian modelling of radiocarbon dates; interpretation as counting is disputed and unresolvable from marks alone.

hoabinhian-cobble-tools-41500bce.summary: Hoabinhian is a technocomplex of unifacially flaked river cobbles, including sumatraliths and short axes, found across mainland Southeast Asia and south China, associated with forest foraging. Its oldest assemblage comes from Xiaodong rockshelter in Yunnan, dated by radiocarbon and luminescence to about 43,500 years ago, far earlier than Vietnamese type sites around 20,000 years ago. Ancient genomes link Hoabinhian hunter-gatherers to a deep genetic lineage in Southeast Asia. Tradition continues until about 10,000 to 4,000 years ago, when farming spreads.

sources.title: Ji, X. et al., 'The oldest Hoabinhian technocomplex in Asia (43.5 ka) at Xiaodong rockshelter, Yunnan Province, southwest China', Quaternary International 400 (2016), 166-174
sources.author: Ji, Xueping; Kuman, Kathleen; Clarke, R.J.; Forestier, Hubert; Li, Yinghua; Ma, Juan
sources.confirms: Reports Xiaodong rockshelter as oldest Hoabinhian site at 43,500 years.

sources.title: McColl, H. et al., 'The prehistoric peopling of Southeast Asia', Science 361 (2018), 88-92
sources.author: McColl, Hugh; Racimo, Fernando; Vinner, Lasse; Demeter, Fabrice; Gakuhari, Takashi; Moreno-Mayar, J. Víctor
sources.confirms: Links Hoabinhian hunter-gatherers to a deep Southeast Asian genetic lineage via ancient genomes.

hoabinhian-cobble-tools-41500bce.detail: Xiaodong lies in Cangyuan County near Myanmar border. Hoabinhian tools are large, made on water-worn cobbles with one face flaked, used for woodworking, plant processing and hunting in tropical forest. Name comes from Hoa Binh province, Vietnam, where Madeleine Colani defined complex in 1920s. Ancient genomes from Pha Faen in Laos and Gua Cha in Malaysia show Hoabinhian ancestry related to present-day Andamanese and Papuans.

picture.alt: Hoabinhian pebble tool (Sumatralith) from Deli Serdang, Sumatra, Museum Daerah Deli Serdang
picture.credit: Museumdaerah.deliserdang, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

hoabinhian-cobble-tools-41500bce.dating_note: Start age of 43,500 years at Xiaodong combines radiocarbon and luminescence; end year of about 10,000 years ago is a conventional close as farming arrives, with Hoabinhian persisting later in places.

hohle-fels-bone-and-ivory-flutes-40000bc.summary: A nearly complete flute made from a griffon vulture radius with five finger holes comes from Hohle Fels, along with fragments of ivory flutes, in Aurignacian layers more than 35,000 calendar years old. Geissenklösterle, 20 kilometres away, yielded swan-bone and ivory flutes; ultrafiltered radiocarbon redates its Aurignacian to about 42,000 to 43,000 years ago. These are oldest musical instruments known. Ivory flutes required splitting a tusk, hollowing two halves, drilling holes and sealing them airtight, a demanding craft.

sources.title: Conard, N. J. et al., 'New flutes document the earliest musical tradition in southwestern Germany', Nature 460 (2009), 737-740
sources.author: Conard, Nicholas J.; Malina, Maria; Münzel, Susanne C.
sources.confirms: Reports vulture-bone and ivory flutes from Hohle Fels in Aurignacian layers over 35,000 years old.

sources.title: Higham, T. et al., 'Τesting models for the beginnings of the Aurignacian and the advent of figurative art and music: The radiocarbon chronology of Geißenklösterle', Journal of Human Evolution 62 (2012), 664-676
sources.author: Higham, Thomas; Basell, Laura; Jacobi, Roger; Wood, Rachel; Ramsey, Christopher Bronk; Conard, Nicholas J.
sources.confirms: Redates Geissenklösterle Aurignacian with ultrafiltration radiocarbon to earlier than other southern sites.
sources.qualifies: Higham et al. place Swabian flutes around 42,000 to 43,000 years.

hohle-fels-bone-and-ivory-flutes-40000bc.detail: Vulture-bone flute is 21.8 centimetres long with V-shaped notches at mouth end and fine incisions marking hole positions. Reconstructions play a pentatonic-like scale. Flutes co-occur with figurines and ornaments, which Conard reads as a regional cultural package. Dating dispute concerns whether earlier dates were contaminated; Thomas Higham argues older ages confirm Danube corridor as early Aurignacian region. Nicholas Conard of University of Tübingen directs Hohle Fels excavations.

picture.alt: Griffon vulture bone flute from Hohle Fels, Urgeschichtliches Museum Blaubeuren
picture.credit: Tomatenpflanze, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

hohle-fels-bone-and-ivory-flutes-40000bc.dating_note: Year of about 42,000 years follows Higham et al.'s redating; Conard's minimum is 35,000 calendar years.

jerimalai-pelagic-fishing-40000bce.summary: Jerimalai shelter on East Timor's eastern tip yielded 38,000 fish bones, dated by radiocarbon to 42,000 years ago. Nearly half of bones in oldest layers belong to pelagic species such as tuna, requiring offshore fishing from boats or with sophisticated gear. Jerimalai also yields a shell fishhook fragment dated between 23,000 and 16,000 years ago, among oldest known hooks. Its fish bones show maritime skills consistent with sea crossings that settled Wallacea and Sahul.

sources.title: O’Connor, S. et al., 'Pelagic Fishing at 42,000 Years Before the Present and the Maritime Skills of Modern Humans', Science 334 (2011), 1117-1121
sources.author: O’Connor, Sue; Ono, Rintaro; Clarkson, Chris
sources.confirms: Reports pelagic fish bones at Jerimalai from 42,000 years and an early shell fishhook.

sources.title: O'Connor, S., 'New evidence from East Timor contributes to our understanding of earliest modern human colonisation east of the Sunda Shelf', Antiquity 81 (2007), 523-535
sources.author: O'Connor, Sue
sources.confirms: Reports the first radiocarbon dates of about 42,000 years for occupation at Jerimalai shelter, East Timor, with marine fish and shellfish in the oldest layers.

jerimalai-pelagic-fishing-40000bce.detail: Fish taxa were identified from vertebrae and jaws; pelagic species include tunas and trevallies, inshore species include parrotfish and groupers. Hook was shaped from Trochus shell. Some researchers suggest juvenile tuna could be caught near shore, tempering inference of deep-sea voyaging. Okinawa's Sakitari Cave later yields complete shell hooks at 23,000 years. Sue O'Connor of Australian National University excavated Jerimalai in 2005.

picture.alt: Lene Hara cave near Tutuala, Timor-Leste, close to Jerimalai shelter
picture.credit: Chan, Kin Onn; Grismer, L. Lee; Santana, Fernando; Pinto, Pedro; Loke, Frances W, CC BY 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

jerimalai-pelagic-fishing-40000bce.dating_note: Age of 42,000 years is radiocarbon on shell and charcoal.

lake-mungo-burials-40000bce.summary: Optically stimulated luminescence on sediments bracketing graves dates Mungo burials in Willandra Lakes, New South Wales, to 40,000 plus or minus 2,000 years ago, with human occupation from 50,000 to 46,000 years ago. Mungo Lady (WLH1) was cremated and her crushed bones buried; Mungo Man (WLH3) was laid out with hands clasped and body covered in red ochre carried from afar. These are among oldest ritual burials known and earliest cremation. Dating replaced earlier claims of 62,000 years and ties burials to deteriorating climate as lakes dried.

sources.title: Bowler, J. M. et al., 'New ages for human occupation and climatic change at Lake Mungo, Australia', Nature 421 (2003), 837-840
sources.author: Bowler, James M.; Johnston, Harvey; Olley, Jon M.; Prescott, John R.; Roberts, Richard G.; Shawcross, Wilfred
sources.confirms: Dates Mungo burials to 40,000 plus or minus 2,000 years and occupation from 50,000 to 46,000 years.

sources.title: Olley, J. M. et al., 'Single-grain optical dating of grave-infill associated with human burials at Lake Mungo, Australia', Quaternary Science Reviews 25 (2006), 2469-2474
sources.author: Olley, Jon M.; Roberts, Richard G.; Yoshida, Hiroyuki; Bowler, James M.
sources.confirms: Single-grain optical dating of the grave infill of the Mungo burials, the follow-up to the 2003 Nature chronology; metadata confirmed through OpenAlex, Elsevier page did not open.

sources.title: Fitzsimmons, K. E. et al., 'The Mungo Mega-Lake Event, Semi-Arid Australia: Non-Linear Descent into the Last Ice Age, Implications for Human Behaviour', PLOS ONE 10 (2015), e0127008
sources.author: Fitzsimmons, Kathryn E.; Stern, Nicola; Murray-Wallace, Colin V.; Truscott, William; Pop, Cornel
sources.confirms: Describes the Mungo remains as Australia's oldest known and places human arrival at the Willandra Lakes around 50,000 years during lake-full conditions.

lake-mungo-burials-40000bce.detail: Site lies on Lake Mungo lunette, a crescent dune; Jim Bowler found WLH1 in 1968 and WLH3 in 1974. Earlier electron spin resonance and uranium-series dates of 62,000 years were rejected after 2003 study. Remains were returned to Willandra traditional owner groups and reburied in 2022. Occupation evidence includes hearths and shell middens along lake shores. Lake Mungo lies within Willandra Lakes World Heritage Area in New South Wales.

picture.alt: Lunette dune at Lake Mungo, New South Wales, Australia
picture.credit: Rueparadis, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

lake-mungo-burials-40000bce.dating_note: Age 40,000 plus or minus 2,000 years by optically stimulated luminescence on bracketing sediments; earlier 62,000-year estimates were withdrawn.

oblazowa-ivory-boomerang-39000bce.summary: A 72-centimetre curved implement of mammoth ivory from Obłazowa Cave in Carpathians is shaped like a non-returning boomerang and was found with a human thumb bone. Bayesian modelling of radiocarbon dates on associated bones places it at about 42,290 to 39,280 years ago. This makes it oldest boomerang known, predating Australian wooden examples by 30,000 years, and shows early Upper Palaeolithic Europeans working ivory into throwing weapons for hunting.

sources.title: Valde-Nowak, P. et al., 'Upper Palaeolithic boomerang made of a mammoth tusk in south Poland', Nature 329 (1987), 436-438
sources.author: Valde-Nowak, Pawel; Nadachowski, Adam; Wolsan, Mieczyslaw
sources.confirms: Describes the Obłazowa mammoth-ivory boomerang and initial dating.
sources.qualifies: Original radiocarbon age of about 23,000 years is now superseded.

sources.title: Talamo, S. et al., 'Boomerang and bones: Refining the chronology of the Early Upper Paleolithic at Obłazowa Cave, Poland', PLOS One 20 (2025), e0324911
sources.author: Talamo, Sahra; Casaccia, Nicole; Richards, Michael P.; Wacker, Lukas; Tassoni, Laura; Nadachowski, Adam
sources.confirms: Redates the boomerang to 42,290 to 39,280 calendar years before present.

oblazowa-ivory-boomerang-39000bce.detail: Object was carved from a tusk's outer curve, flattened on one side, polished and shows wear. Original radiocarbon date around 23,000 years came from a contaminated sample; new dates on associated faunal bones place it with early Aurignacian or transitional industries. Thumb bone and arrangement of finds led excavators to suggest ritual deposit. Boomerang reconstructions fly but do not return.

picture.alt: Mammoth ivory boomerang from Obłazowa Cave, Archaeological Museum in Kraków
picture.credit: Archaeological Museum in Kraków, CC0, via Wikimedia Commons

oblazowa-ivory-boomerang-39000bce.dating_note: Age 42,290 to 39,280 calendar years from Bayesian modelling (Talamo et al. 2025); 1987 estimate of about 23,000 years is superseded.

hohle-fels-venus-figurine-38000bce.summary: A six-centimetre female figurine carved from mammoth ivory was found in 2008 in basal Aurignacian layers of Hohle Fels cave in Swabian Jura, dated by radiocarbon to at least 35,000 years ago. Figure has exaggerated breasts and vulva, with a loop in place of head for suspension. It is oldest known depiction of a human body, predating Gravettian Venus figurines by several thousand years. Hohle Fels also yielded ivory animal figurines and a lion-man figure from nearby Hohlenstein-Stadel belongs to same tradition.

sources.title: Conard, N. J., 'A female figurine from the basal Aurignacian of Hohle Fels Cave in southwestern Germany', Nature 459 (2009), 248-252
sources.author: Conard, Nicholas J.
sources.confirms: Reports mammoth-ivory female figurine from Hohle Fels dated at least 35,000 calendar years.

sources.title: Higham, T. et al., 'Τesting models for the beginnings of the Aurignacian and the advent of figurative art and music: The radiocarbon chronology of Geißenklösterle', Journal of Human Evolution 62 (2012), 664-676
sources.author: Higham, Thomas; Basell, Laura; Jacobi, Roger; Wood, Rachel; Ramsey, Christopher Bronk; Conard, Nicholas J.
sources.confirms: Redates Swabian Aurignacian at Geissenklösterle, implying older ages for early figurative art and music.
sources.qualifies: Higham et al. suggest Swabian Aurignacian begins about 42,000 to 43,000 years ago.

hohle-fels-venus-figurine-38000bce.verification_note: Minimum age is secure; regional redating implies older date.
hohle-fels-venus-figurine-38000bce.detail: Figurine was found in six fragments 20 metres from cave entrance in layer with Aurignacian tools and ornaments. Redating of Geissenklösterle Aurignacian in same region to about 42,000 to 43,000 years ago suggests Swabian figurines may be older than 35,000 years. Mammoth ivory carving requires soaking and working with burins. Figurine is displayed at Urgeschichtliches Museum Blaubeuren. Hohle Fels lies in Ach Valley near Schelklingen in Swabian Jura.

picture.alt: Venus of Hohle Fels, mammoth ivory figurine, Urgeschichtliches Museum Blaubeuren
picture.credit: Catatine, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

hohle-fels-venus-figurine-38000bce.dating_note: Conard gives at least 35,000 calendar years; Higham et al. (2012) redate regional Aurignacian to about 42,000 to 43,000 years; year of 40,000 before present sits between.

chauvet-cave-paintings-34000bce.summary: A model of 259 radiocarbon dates from Chauvet-Pont d'Arc in Ardèche finds two phases of human activity, 37,000 to 33,500 and 31,000 to 28,000 years ago, with cave bears using cave until 33,000 and entrance sealed by rockfall around 21,500 years ago. Chauvet's walls carry over 400 animal images, including lions, rhinoceroses, mammoths, horses and bears, drawn with charcoal, red ochre and engraving, using shading, perspective and wall scraping. Discovered in 1994, Chauvet is oldest securely dated figurative cave art in Europe on this chronology; Paul Pettitt and Paul Bahn argue from style for a later, Gravettian date.

sources.title: Quiles, A. et al., 'A high-precision chronological model for the decorated Upper Paleolithic cave of Chauvet-Pont d’Arc, Ardèche, France', Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences 113 (2016), 4670-4675
sources.author: Quiles, Anita; Valladas, Hélène; Bocherens, Hervé; Delqué-Količ, Emmanuelle; Kaltnecker, Evelyne; van der Plicht, Johannes
sources.venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
sources.confirms: Models 259 radiocarbon dates giving two Chauvet occupation phases, 37,000 to 33,500 and 31,000 to 28,000 years.

sources.title: Pettitt, Paul; Bahn, Paul, 'An alternative chronology for the art of Chauvet cave', Antiquity 89 (2015), 542-553
sources.author: Pettitt, Paul; Bahn, Paul
sources.confirms: Confirms that radiocarbon assays place the black charcoal drawings in the Aurignacian, more than 20,000 years earlier than stylistic models suggest, and that controversy over the art's antiquity continued two decades after discovery.
sources.qualifies: Pettitt and Bahn question the radiometric dating and propose a later chronology from style, fauna and stratigraphy; Quiles et al. 2016 answered with the 259-date model.

chauvet-cave-paintings-34000bce.verification_note: Pettitt and Bahn (Antiquity 2015) dispute the Aurignacian radiocarbon chronology and argue from style for a Gravettian or later date for much of Chauvet's art; Quiles (PNAS 2016) models two phases from 37,000 years.
chauvet-cave-paintings-34000bce.detail: Charcoal from drawings and torch marks were dated directly, alongside bear bones and floor charcoal. Stylistic arguments held that such sophisticated images must be Magdalenian; direct dating and sealed entrance answer them. Cave is closed to public; a replica opened in 2015. Painters favoured dangerous animals rarely hunted, unlike Lascaux's horses and aurochs. Anita Quiles of Institut Français d'Archéologie Orientale led dating synthesis with Hélène Valladas.

picture.alt: Horse panel, Chauvet Cave, Ardèche, France
picture.credit: Thomas T. from somewhere on Earth, CC BY-SA 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons

chauvet-cave-paintings-34000bce.dating_note: Year of about 36,000 years sits in first phase 37,000 to 33,500 years before present.

ryukyu-islands-seafaring-33000bce.summary: Palaeolithic sites appear through 1,200 kilometres of Ryukyu islands between about 35,000 and 30,000 years ago. Some islands lay more than 100 kilometres away, invisible over horizon, across one of world's strongest currents. Yousuke Kaifu's project tested rafts and dugouts experimentally and found bamboo rafts unsuitable; a dugout canoe crossed from Taiwan to Yonaguni in 2019. Archaeology, skeletal remains, genetics, palaeogeography and oceanography together show deliberate open-sea voyaging in western Pacific.

sources.title: Kaifu, Y., 'A synthetic model of Palaeolithic seafaring in the Ryukyu Islands, southwestern Japan', World Archaeology 54 (2022), 187-206
sources.author: Kaifu, Yousuke
sources.confirms: Models Ryukyu Palaeolithic seafaring with sites appearing 35,000 to 30,000 years ago across 1,200 kilometres.

sources.title: Kaifu, Y. et al., 'Palaeolithic seafaring in East Asia: testing the bamboo raft hypothesis', Antiquity 93 (2019), 1424-1441
sources.author: Kaifu, Yousuke; Lin, Chih-hsing; Goto, Akira; Ikeya, Nobuyuki; Yamada, Masahisa; Chiang, Wei-Chuan
sources.confirms: Reports experimental voyages and argues bamboo rafts were unsuitable for Ryukyu crossings.

ryukyu-islands-seafaring-33000bce.detail: Sites include Sakitari Cave and Shiraho-Saonetabaru Cave on Ishigaki, with burials around 27,000 years. Kozushima obsidian carried to Honshu sites about 38,000 years ago shows contemporary crossings in main Japanese islands. Kaifu argues navigation knowledge, not drifting, explains distribution against current. Skeletal remains show people distinct from later Jomon populations. Yousuke Kaifu of University of Tokyo led experimental voyage project from 2016 to 2019 with Taiwanese partners.

picture.alt: Coast of Yonaguni Island, Ryukyu archipelago
picture.credit: sota-k, CC BY-SA 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons

ryukyu-islands-seafaring-33000bce.dating_note: Age bracket 35,000 to 30,000 years comes from radiocarbon at multiple Ryukyu sites; year uses midpoint.

sungir-burials-32000bce.summary: Sungir near Vladimir holds Mid Upper Palaeolithic graves: an adult man (Sungir 1) and a double burial of two children laid head to head (Sungir 2 and 3), each covered in thousands of mammoth-ivory beads once sewn onto clothing, with ivory spears, bracelets, pierced fox canines and carved animals. Hydroxyproline radiocarbon dates on all burials are statistically indistinguishable at roughly 34,000 years ago. Grave goods reveal sewn, decorated clothing and labour invested in dead, earliest elaborate burials in Eurasia.

sources.title: Nalawade-Chavan, S. et al., 'New Hydroxyproline Radiocarbon Dates from Sungir, Russia, Confirm Early Mid Upper Palaeolithic Burials in Eurasia', PLoS ONE 9 (2014), e76896
sources.author: Nalawade-Chavan, Shweta; McCullagh, James; Hedges, Robert
sources.confirms: Reports hydroxyproline radiocarbon dates of about 30,000 radiocarbon years for all Sungir burials.

sources.title: Trinkaus, E. et al., 'The Paleobiology of the Sunghir People', The People of Sunghir (2014)
sources.author: Trinkaus, Erik; Buzhilova, Alexandra P.; Mednikova, Maria B.; Dobrovolskaya, Maria V.
sources.confirms: Oxford University Press chapter on Sunghir people's palaeobiology within monograph on burials.

sungir-burials-32000bce.detail: Sungir was excavated by Otto Bader from 1956. Bead counts exceed 13,000 for children; each bead took an estimated hour to make. Spears straightened from mammoth tusk are up to 2.4 metres long. Earlier radiocarbon dates spanned 19,000 to 29,000 years because of contamination; single-amino-acid dating resolved it. Children's skeletons show pathologies. Dating was done at Oxford Radiocarbon Accelerator Unit.

picture.alt: Model of Sunghir double burial (Sungir 2 and 3), Vladimir museum (replica)
picture.credit: Лапоть, CC0, via Wikimedia Commons

sungir-burials-32000bce.dating_note: About 30,000 radiocarbon years calibrates to roughly 34,000 calendar years; year uses calibrated figure.

kilu-cave-solomon-islands-31000bce.summary: Occupation at Kilu Cave on Buka, northern Solomon Islands, begins about 28,000 radiocarbon years ago, requiring a crossing of over 130 kilometres beyond intervisible islands. Caves on New Ireland date to 33,000 years ago, extending Pleistocene settlement into island Melanesia across two ocean straits. Starch grains and raphides of taro genera Colocasia and Alocasia on Kilu stone tools are earliest direct evidence of root-crop use. These crossings precede any other open-ocean colonisation.

sources.title: Wickler, S. and Spriggs, M., 'Pleistocene human occupation of the Solomon Islands, Melanesia', Antiquity 62 (1988), 703-706
sources.author: Wickler, Stephen; Spriggs, Matthew
sources.confirms: Dates Kilu Cave occupation on Buka to about 28,000 years.

sources.title: Allen, J. et al., 'Pleistocene dates for the human occupation of New Ireland, northern Melanesia', Nature 331 (1988), 707-709
sources.author: Allen, Jim; Gosden, Chris; Jones, Rhys; White, J. Peter
sources.confirms: Dates New Ireland cave occupation to 33,000 years across two ocean straits.

sources.title: Loy, T. H. et al., 'Direct evidence for human use of plants 28,000 years ago: starch residues on stone artefacts from the northern Solomon Islands', Antiquity 66 (1992), 898-912
sources.author: Loy, Thomas H.; Spriggs, Matthew; Wickler, Stephen
sources.confirms: Identifies taro starch residues on 28,000-year-old Kilu stone tools.

kilu-cave-solomon-islands-31000bce.detail: Buka was joined to Bougainville and other Solomons during low sea levels as Greater Bougainville, but gap from New Ireland remained open sea with no land visible from departure. Kilu fauna include fish and shellfish; later layers show introduction of cuscus. Taro starch suggests wild or managed aroids were staple. New Ireland sites Matenkupkum and Buang Merabak exploit coast and lowland forest.

picture.alt: Hanahan Bay, Buka Island, Bougainville, where Kilu Cave lies
picture.credit: Jeremy Weate, CC BY 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons

kilu-cave-solomon-islands-31000bce.dating_note: Kilu's 28,000 and New Ireland's 33,000 are radiocarbon years from 1980s; calibration would add some millennia.

lesotho-ostrich-eggshell-networks-31000b.summary: Ostrich eggshell beads from highland Lesotho rockshelters such as Sehonghong and Melikane span about 33,000 years ago to recent times. Strontium isotopes show that many came from ostriches living over 300 kilometres away in lowlands. Brian Stewart and Peter Mitchell read this as long-distance exchange networks like hxaro gift exchange among Kalahari San, which buffer risk across unpredictable environments. Networks persisted through Last Glacial Maximum, showing durable social ties across biomes rather than isolated groups.

sources.title: Stewart, B. A. et al., 'Ostrich eggshell bead strontium isotopes reveal persistent macroscale social networking across late Quaternary southern Africa', Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences 117 (2020), 6453-6462
sources.author: Stewart, Brian A.; Zhao, Yuchao; Mitchell, Peter J.; Dewar, Genevieve; Gleason, James D.; Blum, Joel D.
sources.venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
sources.confirms: Uses strontium isotopes to show ostrich eggshell beads travelled over 300 kilometres to Lesotho over 33,000 years.

sources.title: Mitchell, Peter J., 'Prehistoric exchange and interaction in southeastern southern Africa: Marine shells and ostrich eggshell', African Archaeological Review 13 (1996), 35-76
sources.author: Mitchell, Peter J.
sources.confirms: Distribution of ostrich eggshell and marine shell in Later Stone Age sites of Lesotho and neighbouring regions is read as evidence of long-distance exchange networks, the frame the 2020 isotope study tests.

lesotho-ostrich-eggshell-networks-31000b.detail: Strontium ratios in eggshell reflect local geology where ostrich fed; Lesotho highlands have distinct basalt signature absent from many beads. Beads are small finished discs, implying they arrived as ornaments. Exchange of beads remains central to San social life. Beads span Middle Stone Age to Later Stone Age and give longest known record of such networks. Brian Stewart of University of Michigan and Peter Mitchell of Oxford led this work.

picture.alt: Ostrich eggshell bead necklace, Botswana, 1935 Schapera collection, Iziko museum (ethnographic comparison)
picture.credit: Nkansah Rexford, CC BY 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

lesotho-ostrich-eggshell-networks-31000b.dating_note: Oldest beads in study date about 33,000 years by radiocarbon on associated material.

dzudzuana-flax-fibres-30000bce.summary: Microscopic wild flax fibres in Dzudzuana Cave sediments in western Georgia date by radiocarbon to between about 32,000 and 26,000 years ago. Some fibres are spun or knotted, and some coloured black, grey, turquoise and pink, suggesting dyeing with plant pigments. Flax fibres made thread for sewing clothing and for cordage. These are oldest known processed plant fibres, pre-dating textile impressions at Pavlov. Fibres occur with fur and skin beetle remains, consistent with hide processing in same space.

sources.title: Kvavadze, E. et al., '30,000-Year-Old Wild Flax Fibers', Science 325 (2009), 1359-1359
sources.author: Kvavadze, Eliso; Bar-Yosef, Ofer; Belfer-Cohen, Anna; Boaretto, Elisabetta; Jakeli, Nino; Matskevich, Zinovi
sources.confirms: Reports spun and dyed wild flax fibres at Dzudzuana dated 32,000 to 26,000 years.

sources.title: Bar-Yosef, O. et al., 'Dzudzuana: an Upper Palaeolithic cave site in the Caucasus foothills (Georgia)', Antiquity 85 (2011), 331-349
sources.author: Bar-Yosef, Ofer; Belfer-Cohen, Anna; Mesheviliani, Tengiz; Jakeli, Nino; Bar-Oz, Guy; Boaretto, Elisabetta
sources.confirms: Gives the radiocarbon sequence for Dzudzuana Cave, with modern human occupation from about 34,500 to 32,200 calibrated years, and lists coloured fibres among the finds.

dzudzuana-flax-fibres-30000bce.detail: Fibres were found during pollen analysis of sediment samples; over 480 fibres were recorded across layers. Colours were identified under microscopes and attributed to natural dyes, though some researchers caution colours may be post-depositional. Wild flax grows in Caucasus; domesticated flax appears in Neolithic. Dzudzuana also records Upper Palaeolithic ornaments and lithics. Eliso Kvavadze of Georgian National Museum identified fibres; Ofer Bar-Yosef and Tengiz Meshveliani directed excavation.
