picture.credit: Andreykor, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

dzudzuana-flax-fibres-30000bce.dating_note: Fibre-bearing layers date 32,000 to 26,000 years by radiocarbon; year gives upper range.

upper-palaeolithic-lunar-notation-claims.summary: Alexander Marshack proposed in 1972 that sequences of marks on Upper Palaeolithic bones and plaques, such as Abri Blanchard plaque around 32,000 years ago, track phases of moon. Francesco d'Errico showed through microscopy in 1989 that many sets were made in single sessions with one tool, undermining accumulating-tally reading; Marshack replied that year. Bennett Bacon revived idea in 2023, arguing dots and lines beside animals in cave art encode lunar months of mating and birthing. April Nowell, in 2024, finds that interpretation methodologically weak. No consensus supports Palaeolithic lunar calendars.

sources.title: Marshack, A., 'Cognitive Aspects of Upper Paleolithic Engraving', Current Anthropology 13 (1972), 445-477
sources.author: Marshack, Alexander
sources.confirms: Proposes lunar notation reading of Upper Palaeolithic engraved marks.
sources.qualifies: Marshack's method is contested by d'Errico.

sources.title: D'Errico, F., 'Palaeolithic Lunar Calendars: A Case of Wishful Thinking?', Current Anthropology 30 (1989), 117-118
sources.author: D'Errico, Francesco
sources.confirms: Argues on microscopic grounds that many mark sequences were made in single sessions, against lunar tally reading.
sources.qualifies: d'Errico rejects Marshack's lunar reading.

sources.title: Marshack, A. and D'Errico, F., 'On Wishful Thinking and Lunar "Calendars"', Current Anthropology 30 (1989), 491-500
sources.author: Marshack, Alexander; D'Errico, Francesco
sources.confirms: Marshack's reply defending lunar notation interpretation.

sources.title: Bacon, B. et al., 'An Upper Palaeolithic Proto-writing System and Phenological Calendar', Cambridge Archaeological Journal 33 (2023), 371-389
sources.author: Bacon, Bennett; Khatiri, Azadeh; Palmer, James; Freeth, Tony; Pettitt, Paul; Kentridge, Robert
sources.confirms: Proposes that signs beside cave art animals encode lunar months of animal behaviour.

sources.title: Nowell, A. et al., 'Evaluating the Evidence for Lunar Calendars in Upper Palaeolithic Parietal Art', Cambridge Archaeological Journal 35 (2024), 38-55
sources.author: Nowell, April; Bahn, Paul; Le Quellec, Jean-Loïc
sources.confirms: Concludes lunar calendar interpretation has multiple theoretical and methodological weaknesses.
sources.qualifies: Nowell et al. reject Bacon et al.'s reading.

upper-palaeolithic-lunar-notation-claims.verification_note: Claim is disputed and unresolved; sources on both sides cited. Chicago journal pages for Marshack 1972 and d'Errico 1989 were confirmed at title and abstract level only.
upper-palaeolithic-lunar-notation-claims.detail: Marshack's method compared mark morphology under magnification across sequences. d'Errico's experimental replication produced criteria for distinguishing marks made at once from marks added over time. Bacon counted signs associated with animals across many caves and tested fit against ethology; critics object to sampling and untestable assumptions. Debate illustrates limits of inferring meaning from marks without contextual control.

picture.alt: Notched bone plaque from Abri Blanchard, Dordogne, read by Marshack as lunar notation, Musée d Archéologie nationale
picture.credit: Marie-Lan Nguyen, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

upper-palaeolithic-lunar-notation-claims.dating_note: Record marks a debate rather than an event; artefacts discussed range from about 37,000 to 13,000 years; year is nominal.

yana-arctic-camp-30000bce.summary: Yana RHS site at 71 degrees north in Siberia is dated by radiocarbon to about 32,000 years ago. Finds include a spear foreshaft of woolly rhinoceros horn and mammoth-ivory foreshafts, with bones of mammoth, horse, bison and reindeer. Occupation this far north during a cold stage doubles previously known antiquity of Arctic settlement and implies warm sewn clothing and shelter. Ivory working at Yana includes beads and figurines.

sources.title: Pitulko, V. V. et al., 'The Yana RHS Site: Humans in the Arctic Before the Last Glacial Maximum', Science 303 (2004), 52-56
sources.author: Pitulko, V. V.; Nikolsky, P. A.; Girya, E. Yu.; Basilyan, A. E.; Tumskoy, V. E.; Koulakov, S. A.
sources.confirms: Reports Yana RHS at 71 degrees north dated 27,000 radiocarbon years with rhinoceros-horn and ivory foreshafts.

sources.title: Pitulko, V. V. et al., 'Mammoth ivory technologies in the Upper Palaeolithic: a case study based on the materials from Yana RHS, Northern Yana-Indighirka lowland, Arctic Siberia', World Archaeology 47 (2015), 333-389
sources.author: Pitulko, Vladimir V.; Pavlova, Elena Y.; Nikolskiy, Pavel A.
sources.confirms: Describes mammoth ivory working and personal ornaments at Yana.

yana-arctic-camp-30000bce.detail: Rhinoceros-horn foreshafts are straightened and bevelled to hold stone points, a design resembling later Clovis foreshafts in North America, which drew interest in possible ancestry. Later work recovered thousands of beads, needles, pendants and decorated objects. Genomes of two Yana children published in 2019 define Ancient North Siberians. Site is on Yana lower reaches, permafrost preserving organics. Vladimir Pitulko of Russian Academy of Sciences has directed excavations since 2001.

picture.alt: Excavation of Northern Point area of Yana site complex, Arctic Siberia
picture.credit: Pitulko VV and Pavlova EY (2022) Structural Properties of Syngenetic Ice-Rich Pe, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

yana-arctic-camp-30000bce.dating_note: 27,000 radiocarbon years calibrates to about 32,000 calendar years.

apollo-11-painted-slabs-28000bce.summary: Apollo 11 Cave in Huns Mountains, Namibia, excavated by Wolfgang Wendt in 1969 to 1972, yielded seven quartzite slabs painted with animals in charcoal and in red and white pigments. Charcoal in their layers gave radiocarbon ages around 27,000 to 25,000 years, and a re-excavation applied optically stimulated luminescence to that sequence. Pigment analysis since describes these slabs as 30,000-year-old portable art. These remain oldest dated figurative images in Africa and show painted art far from European caves.

sources.title: Vogelsang, R. et al., 'New Excavations of Middle Stone Age Deposits at Apollo 11 Rockshelter, Namibia: Stratigraphy, Archaeology, Chronology and Past Environments', Journal of African Archaeology 8 (2010), 185-218
sources.author: Vogelsang, Ralf; Richter, Jürgen; Jacobs, Zenobia; Eichhorn, Barbara; Linseele, Veerle; Roberts, Richard G.
sources.confirms: Presents new excavations and luminescence chronology for Apollo 11 Cave.

sources.title: Rifkin, R. F. et al., 'Characterising pigments on 30 000-year-old portable art from Apollo 11 Cave, Karas Region, southern Namibia', Journal of Archaeological Science: Reports 5 (2016), 336-347
sources.author: Rifkin, Riaan F.; Prinsloo, Linda C.; Dayet, Laure; Haaland, Magnus M.; Henshilwood, Christopher S.; Diz, Enrique Lozano
sources.confirms: Characterises pigments on 30,000-year-old painted slabs from Apollo 11 Cave.

apollo-11-painted-slabs-28000bce.detail: Slabs depict a feline-like animal with possible human hind legs and other quadrupeds. Slabs were brought into cave and discarded rather than painted on walls. Pigment analysis identified charcoal and ochre, with white from clay minerals. Apollo 11 sequence spans Middle Stone Age through Later Stone Age and provides a key southern African chronology. Ralf Vogelsang of University of Cologne directed re-excavation in 2007 to 2008.

picture.alt: Painted quartzite slab with animal figure from Apollo 11 Cave, Namibia
picture.credit: Ratel, CC0, via Wikimedia Commons

apollo-11-painted-slabs-28000bce.dating_note: Age of about 30,000 years combines radiocarbon on layer charcoal and luminescence; slabs are not directly dated.

nawarla-gabarnmang-rock-art-26000bce.summary: A charcoal drawing on a fallen ceiling slab at Nawarla Gabarnmang in Jawoyn country, Arnhem Land, is radiocarbon dated to about 28,000 years ago, among oldest directly dated rock art in Australia. Nawarla Gabarnmang is a vast shelter whose pillars were trimmed and ceiling panels painted over millennia. In Kimberley, Gwion figures, slender human forms with ornaments, date by radiocarbon on 24 mud-wasp nests over and under paintings to about 12,000 years ago.

sources.title: David, B. et al., 'How old are Australia's pictographs? A review of rock art dating', Journal of Archaeological Science 40 (2013), 3-10
sources.author: David, Bruno; Geneste, Jean-Michel; Petchey, Fiona; Delannoy, Jean-Jacques; Barker, Bryce; Eccleston, Mark
sources.confirms: Dates charcoal rock art at Nawarla Gabarnmang to about 28,000 years.

sources.title: Finch, D. et al., '12,000-Year-old Aboriginal rock art from the Kimberley region, Western Australia', Science Advances 6 (2020)
sources.author: Finch, Damien; Gleadow, Andrew; Hergt, Janet; Levchenko, Vladimir A.; Heaney, Pauline; Veth, Peter
sources.confirms: Dates Gwion rock art in Kimberley to about 12,000 years using 24 mud-wasp nests.

sources.title: Taçon, P. S. C., 'Australian Pleistocene rock art', Nature Human Behaviour 5 (2021), 301-302
sources.author: Taçon, Paul S. C.
sources.confirms: Reviews Australian Pleistocene rock art evidence.

nawarla-gabarnmang-rock-art-26000bce.detail: Nawarla Gabarnmang contains hundreds of paintings and shows deliberate removal of rock pillars to open space. Charcoal on slab fell from ceiling and was buried, providing a minimum age. Gwion dating used nests built by mud wasps, whose charcoal inclusions and sand can be dated; results cluster around 12,000 years rather than older estimates. Both projects worked with traditional owners through Jawoyn Association and Kimberley communities.

picture.alt: Rock art at Ubirr, Kakadu, Arnhem Land (nearby tradition, not Nawarla Gabarnmang)
picture.credit: Dave Pape, CC0, via Wikimedia Commons

nawarla-gabarnmang-rock-art-26000bce.dating_note: Nawarla Gabarnmang slab charcoal gives about 28,000 years; Gwion figures date about 12,000 years.

dolni-vestonice-fired-clay-figurines-250.summary: Over 5,000 fired clay fragments from Dolní Věstonice and Pavlov in Moravia, including Venus of Dolní Věstonice and animal figurines, date to about 27,000 years ago. Loess clay was shaped, then fired at 500 to 800 degrees Celsius in kiln-like hearths; many pieces fractured thermally, suggesting deliberate explosive firing. This is earliest known ceramic technology, 10,000 years before pottery vessels in East Asia. Clay here served figurines rather than containers. It also preserves impressions of woven textiles and nets dated about 26,000 years ago, evidence of fibre crafts otherwise lost.

sources.title: Vandiver, P. B. et al., 'The Origins of Ceramic Technology at Dolni Věstonice, Czechoslovakia', Science 246 (1989), 1002-1008
sources.author: Vandiver, Pamela B.; Soffer, Olga; Klima, Bohuslav; Svoboda, JiŘi
sources.confirms: Analyses over 5,000 fired clay fragments from Dolní Věstonice and Pavlov fired at 500 to 800 degrees Celsius.

sources.title: Adovasio, J. M. et al., 'Upper Palaeolithic fibre technology: interlaced woven finds from Pavlov I, Czech Republic, c. 26,000 years ago', Antiquity 70 (1996), 526-534
sources.author: Adovasio, James M.; Soffer, Olga; Klíma, Bohuslav
sources.confirms: Reports textile and basketry impressions on fired clay at Pavlov and Dolní Věstonice about 26,000 years old.

sources.title: Soffer, O. et al., 'Palaeolithic perishables made permanent', Antiquity 74 (2000), 812-821
sources.author: Soffer, O.; Adovasio, J.M.; Illingworth, J.S.; Amirkhanov, H.A.; Praslov, N.D.; Street, M.
sources.confirms: Extends evidence for Upper Palaeolithic textiles and basketry across Europe.

dolni-vestonice-fired-clay-figurines-250.detail: Figurines include women, mammoths, bears, lions and rhinoceroses. Fragments bear fingerprints, one from a child. Firing structures are domed hearths with burnt clay walls. Pottery vessels do not appear in Europe until Neolithic. Same sites yield textile impressions and ivory carvings. Dating uses radiocarbon on charcoal from Gravettian occupation layers. Pamela Vandiver of Smithsonian Institution analysed firing conditions; Bohuslav Klíma and Jiří Svoboda directed Moravian excavations.

picture.alt: Venus of Dolní Věstonice, fired clay figurine
picture.credit: Miroslav Zachoval, CC BY 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons

dolni-vestonice-fired-clay-figurines-250.dating_note: Gravettian layers date about 27,000 years by radiocarbon.

santa-elina-sloth-osteoderm-pendants-250.summary: Three osteoderms of giant ground sloth Glossotherium from Santa Elina rockshelter in Mato Grosso, Brazil, were drilled, polished and shaped by people before bones fossilised. A Bayesian age model places this in Pleistocene horizons around Last Glacial Maximum, about 27,000 to 25,000 years ago. If accepted, this puts people in central South America well before Clovis and shows them making ornaments from megafauna remains. Santa Elina's early dates have drawn scepticism, as other pre-Clovis claims have: its excavators' own 1994 report put occupation at only 8,000 to 10,000 years ago before later work pushed it back.

sources.title: Pansani, T. R. et al., 'Evidence of artefacts made of giant sloth bones in central Brazil around the last glacial maximum', Proceedings of the Royal Society B: Biological Sciences 290 (2023)
sources.author: Pansani, Thais R.; Pobiner, Briana; Gueriau, Pierre; Thoury, Mathieu; Tafforeau, Paul; Baranger, Emmanuel
sources.venue: Proceedings of the Royal Society B: Biological Sciences
sources.confirms: Reports human modification of giant sloth osteoderms at Santa Elina around Last Glacial Maximum.

sources.title: Vialou, D. et al., 'Peopling South America's centre: the late Pleistocene site of Santa Elina', Antiquity 91 (2017), 865-884
sources.author: Vialou, Denis; Benabdelhadi, Mohammed; Feathers, James; Fontugne, Michel; Vialou, Águeda Vilhena
sources.confirms: Dates the earliest occupation at Santa Elina to 27,818 to 26,887 calibrated years before present and Glossotherium osteoderms from the same unit to 27,000 plus or minus 2,000 years.
sources.qualifies: Reports a second set of osteoderms from Unit II at 13,000 plus or minus 1,000 years, so sloth remains occur in two occupation phases.

santa-elina-sloth-osteoderm-pendants-250.verification_note: Vialou and colleagues (Antiquity 2017) date earliest Santa Elina occupation to 27,818 to 26,887 calibrated years and Unit III Glossotherium osteoderms to 27,000 plus or minus 2,000 years, while that team's 1994 report (Bulletin de la Société préhistorique française 91) dated oldest occupations to 8,000 to 10,000 years.
santa-elina-sloth-osteoderm-pendants-250.detail: Traceology compared surface modifications with natural processes; drilling and polish patterns matched human work and were made on fresh bone. Site excavated by Águeda Vilhena Vialou since 1980s has radiocarbon and luminescence dates for lower layers. Debate parallels Monte Verde and White Sands over timing of human entry into Americas. Thaís Pansani of Federal University of São Carlos led study with Mírian Pacheco.

picture.alt: Skeleton of Glossotherium robustum, the giant sloth whose osteoderms were worked at Santa Elina
picture.credit: Ghedoghedo, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

santa-elina-sloth-osteoderm-pendants-250.dating_note: Age about 27,000 to 25,000 years from Bayesian model of radiocarbon and luminescence; early human presence at Santa Elina is debated.

kostenki-11-mammoth-bone-structure-23000.summary: A mammoth-bone circular structure at Kostenki 11 on Don River, 12.5 metres across, was built from bones of an estimated 60 mammoths, some scavenged from animals dead for centuries, with radiocarbon dates of about 25,000 years ago, oldest such structure known. Charred wood and plant remains show fire use and plant foods inside. It is larger than later dwellings such as Mezhyrich and has been read as a shelter, a storage site or a monument. Mammoth-bone structures cluster on East European Plain where wood was scarce.

sources.title: Pryor, A. J. et al., 'The chronology and function of a new circular mammoth-bone structure at Kostenki 11', Antiquity 94 (2020), 323-341
sources.author: Pryor, Alexander J.E.; Beresford-Jones, David G.; Dudin, Alexander E.; Ikonnikova, Ekaterina M.; Hoffecker, John F.; Gamble, Clive
sources.confirms: Reports a 12.5-metre mammoth-bone structure at Kostenki 11 dated about 25,000 years.

sources.title: Rey-Iglesia, Alba; Pryor, Alexander J. et al., 'Ancient biomolecular analysis of 39 mammoth individuals from Kostenki 11-Ia elucidates Upper Palaeolithic human resource use', Quaternary Environments and Humans 2 (2024), 100049
sources.author: Rey-Iglesia, Alba; Pryor, Alexander J.; de Jager, Deon; Wilson, Tessa; Lorenzen, Eline D.
sources.confirms: Ten new mammoth radiocarbon dates from the largest circular structure at Kostenki 11-Ia; biomolecular sexing of 30 individuals shows mostly females from herds, and two mandibles 200 to 1,200 years older than the rest indicate scavenged bones went into the construction.
sources.qualifies: The study analyses 39 individuals and finds some bones were scavenged from long-dead animals rather than all hunted; the record's figure of about 60 mammoths is Pryor et al.'s estimate.

kostenki-11-mammoth-bone-structure-23000.verification_note: Rey-Iglesia et al. (2024) show part of its bone came from mammoths dead centuries before construction, and Pryor et al. (2020) give 60 mammoths as an estimate.
kostenki-11-mammoth-bone-structure-23000.detail: Kostenki 11 has three mammoth-bone structures; third was found in 2014 and excavated 2015 to 2016. Bones include skulls and mandibles arranged in a ring with pits around. Flotation recovered charcoal of conifer wood and plant tissue. Low artefact density inside suggests short or intermittent use. Site is during a cold phase approaching Last Glacial Maximum. Alexander Pryor of University of Exeter led work with Alexander Dudin of Kostenki Museum.

picture.alt: Mammoth bones at base of dwelling, Kostenki museum, Russia
picture.credit: evatutin, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

kostenki-11-mammoth-bone-structure-23000.dating_note: Age of about 25,000 years is radiocarbon on bone and charcoal.

dog-domestication-siberia-21000bce.summary: Dogs are first domesticated animal. Archaeology and genomes point to domestication in Siberia by about 23,000 years ago, during Last Glacial Maximum, with dogs accompanying people into Americas around 15,000 years ago. Among 27 ancient dog genomes, five major lineages had diverged by 11,000 years ago. Securely identified dogs include Bonn-Oberkassel, Germany, buried with two humans about 14,000 years ago; that puppy survived distemper with human care. A 36,000-year-old skull at Goyet, Belgium, is a dog to Mietje Germonpré and a wolf to Susan Crockford and Yaroslav Kuzmin; a 33,000-year-old canid at Razboinichya, Altai, is described as an incipient dog.

sources.title: Perri, A. R. et al., 'Dog domestication and the dual dispersal of people and dogs into the Americas', Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences 118 (2021)
sources.author: Perri, Angela R.; Feuerborn, Tatiana R.; Frantz, Laurent A. F.; Larson, Greger; Malhi, Ripan S.; Meltzer, David J.
sources.venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
sources.confirms: Argues dogs were domesticated in Siberia by about 23,000 years and entered Americas with people.

sources.title: Bergström, A. et al., 'Origins and genetic legacy of prehistoric dogs', Science 370 (2020), 557-564
sources.author: Bergström, Anders; Frantz, Laurent; Schmidt, Ryan; Ersmark, Erik; Lebrasseur, Ophelie; Girdland-Flink, Linus
sources.confirms: Finds five dog lineages diverged by 11,000 years from 27 ancient genomes.

sources.author: Janssens, Luc; Giemsch, Liane; Schmitz, Ralf; Street, Martin; Van Dongen, Stefan; Crombé, Philippe
sources.confirms: Describes Bonn-Oberkassel dog as a Late Palaeolithic domestic dog that survived illness with care.

sources.title: Ovodov, N. D. et al., 'A 33,000-Year-Old Incipient Dog from the Altai Mountains of Siberia: Evidence of the Earliest Domestication Disrupted by the Last Glacial Maximum', PLoS ONE 6 (2011), e22821
sources.author: Ovodov, Nikolai D.; Crockford, Susan J.; Kuzmin, Yaroslav V.; Higham, Thomas F. G.; Hodgins, Gregory W. L.; van der Plicht, Johannes

sources.title: Germonpré, M. et al., 'Fossil dogs and wolves from Palaeolithic sites in Belgium, the Ukraine and Russia: osteometry, ancient DNA and stable isotopes', Journal of Archaeological Science 36 (2009), 473-490
sources.author: Germonpré, Mietje; Sablin, Mikhail V.; Stevens, Rhiannon E.; Hedges, Robert E.M.; Hofreiter, Michael; Stiller, Mathias
sources.confirms: Claims Palaeolithic dogs at Goyet about 36,000 years on skull morphology.
sources.qualifies: Goyet identification is disputed.

sources.title: Crockford, S. J. and Kuzmin, Y. V., 'Comments on Germonpré et al., Journal of Archaeological Science 36, 2009 “Fossil dogs and wolves from Palaeolithic sites in Belgium, the Ukraine and Russia: osteometry, ancient DNA and stable isotopes”, and Germonpré, Lázkičková-Galetová, and Sablin, Journal of Archaeological Science 39, 2012 “Palaeolithic dog skulls at the Gravettian Předmostí site, the Czech Republic”', Journal of Archaeological Science 39 (2012), 2797-2801
sources.author: Crockford, Susan J.; Kuzmin, Yaroslav V.
sources.confirms: Rejects Goyet and Předmostí canids as dogs on metric grounds.
sources.qualifies: Crockford and Kuzmin place dog origins later.

dog-domestication-siberia-21000bce.verification_note: Timing and place of domestication remain debated; Bonn-Oberkassel abstract was not accessible and its 14,000-year age is corroborated via Ovodov et al.
dog-domestication-siberia-21000bce.detail: Germonpré's identification rests on skull shape; Crockford and Kuzmin argue measurements fall within wolf variation and such canids may be a separate morphotype that left no descendants. Nikolai Ovodov describes Razboinichya canid as incipient dog disrupted by glacial maximum. Genetic data agree dogs derive from an extinct wolf population; they leave open where, and whether once or several times.

picture.alt: Dog cranium from Bonn-Oberkassel double burial, about 14,200 years old
picture.credit: Don Hitchcock, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

dog-domestication-siberia-21000bce.dating_note: Year of 23,000 years follows Perri et al.'s genetic and archaeological inference; secure archaeological dogs date from about 15,000 to 14,000 years; older claims at Goyet and Razboinichya are disputed.

ohalo-ii-brush-huts-and-bedding-21000bce.summary: Six oval brush huts at Ohalo II have floors of bundled grass bedding around central hearths, dated to about 23,000 years ago. Hut 1 was rebuilt on three successive floors; walls were tamarisk and willow branches. Grass bedding lined floors in a ring leaving hearth clear. These are oldest known hut floors with bedding and earliest clear evidence of a structured domestic interior. Faunal remains show diverse prey including fish, gazelle, hare and birds consumed inside huts.

sources.title: Nadel, D. and Werker, E., 'The oldest ever brush hut plant remains from Ohalo II, Jordan Valley, Israel (19,000 BP)', Antiquity 73 (1999), 755-764
sources.author: Nadel, Dani; Werker, Ella
sources.confirms: Describes brush hut plant remains and construction at Ohalo II, 19,000 radiocarbon years.

sources.title: Nadel, D. et al., 'Stone Age hut in Israel yields world's oldest evidence of bedding', Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences 101 (2004), 6821-6826
sources.author: Nadel, Dani; Weiss, Ehud; Simchoni, Orit; Tsatskin, Alexander; Danin, Avinoam; Kislev, Mordechai
sources.venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
sources.confirms: Reports grass bedding and hut floors at 23,000-year-old Ohalo II.

sources.title: Steiner, T. et al., 'Abundance or stress? Faunal exploitation patterns and subsistence strategies: The case study of Brush Hut 1 at Ohalo II, a submerged 23,000-year-old camp in the Sea of Galilee, Israel', PLOS ONE 17 (2022), e0262434
sources.author: Steiner, Tikvah; Biton, Rebecca; Nadel, Dani; Rivals, Florent; Rabinovich, Rivka
sources.confirms: Analyses faunal remains from Brush Hut 1 floors at Ohalo II dated 23,500 to 22,500 calendar years.

ohalo-ii-brush-huts-and-bedding-21000bce.detail: Huts measure up to 13 square metres. Bedding was from Puccinellia grass stems laid flat. Outside huts lay hearths and a grave of an adult male. Waterlogged preservation in Sea of Galilee sediments allowed recovery of plant fibres including twisted cord fragments. Camp was occupied for several seasons in Last Glacial Maximum. Dani Nadel's team mapped each floor in detail, enabling spatial analysis of hearths and activity areas.

picture.alt: Shore of Sea of Galilee, Israel, whose receding waters exposed Ohalo II
picture.credit: Ian Scott, CC BY-SA 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons

ohalo-ii-brush-huts-and-bedding-21000bce.dating_note: About 19,000 radiocarbon years calibrates to about 23,000 calendar years.

ohalo-ii-wild-cereals-21000bce.summary: Ohalo II, a submerged camp exposed when Sea of Galilee receded, dates by radiocarbon to about 23,000 years ago. Over 90,000 plant remains include wild wheat and barley alongside many small-grained grasses as staples. Barley starch on a grinding stone with a nearby oven-like hearth is evidence of flour and baking. Proto-weeds among 140 plant species suggest small-scale cultivation. Glossed flint blades were used as sickles. Cereal economy here predates farming by 11,000 years.

sources.title: Weiss, E. et al., 'The broad spectrum revisited: Evidence from plant remains', Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences 101 (2004), 9551-9555
sources.author: Weiss, Ehud; Wetterstrom, Wilma; Nadel, Dani; Bar-Yosef, Ofer
sources.venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
sources.confirms: Reports over 90,000 plant remains with wild cereals as staples at 23,000-year-old Ohalo II.

sources.title: Piperno, D. R. et al., 'Processing of wild cereal grains in the Upper Palaeolithic revealed by starch grain analysis', Nature 430 (2004), 670-673
sources.author: Piperno, Dolores R.; Weiss, Ehud; Holst, Irene; Nadel, Dani
sources.confirms: Finds barley starch on an Ohalo II grinding stone as evidence of flour production.

sources.title: Snir, A. et al., 'The Origin of Cultivation and Proto-Weeds, Long Before Neolithic Farming', PLOS ONE 10 (2015), e0131422
sources.author: Snir, Ainit; Nadel, Dani; Groman-Yaroslavski, Iris; Melamed, Yoel; Sternberg, Marcelo; Bar-Yosef, Ofer
sources.confirms: Identifies proto-weeds among 140 plant species at Ohalo II suggesting trial cultivation.

sources.title: Groman-Yaroslavski, I. et al., 'Composite Sickles and Cereal Harvesting Methods at 23,000-Years-Old Ohalo II, Israel', PLOS ONE 11 (2016), e0167151
sources.author: Groman-Yaroslavski, Iris; Weiss, Ehud; Nadel, Dani
sources.confirms: Reports composite sickles and cereal harvesting methods at Ohalo II.

sources.title: Revedin, A. et al., 'Thirty thousand-year-old evidence of plant food processing', Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences 107 (2010), 18815-18819
sources.author: Revedin, Anna; Aranguren, Biancamaria; Becattini, Roberto; Longo, Laura; Marconi, Emanuele; Lippi, Marta Mariotti
sources.venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
sources.confirms: Reports wild plant starch on 30,000-year-old grindstones at Bilancino, Kostenki and Pavlov.

ohalo-ii-wild-cereals-21000bce.detail: Six brush huts, hearths, a grave and fish and gazelle bones were preserved by waterlogging. Over 150,000 seeds and fruits were recovered. Sickle blades show wear from harvesting semi-green cereals. Weeds like those of later fields imply disturbed ground around camp. Dating rests on many radiocarbon dates from charcoal and seeds, placing occupation 23,500 to 22,500 calendar years ago. Gravettian sites at Bilancino in Italy and Pavlov VI in Moravia show wild plant flour on grindstones around 30,000 years ago. Dani Nadel of University of Haifa has directed Ohalo II excavations since 1989.

picture.alt: Flint sickle blades with gloss from cereal harvesting, Ohalo II, Israel
picture.credit: Iris Groman-Yaroslavski , Ehud Weiss, Dani Nadel, CC BY 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

ohalo-ii-wild-cereals-21000bce.dating_note: Occupation dated 23,500 to 22,500 calendar years before present by many radiocarbon dates.

sakitari-cave-shell-fishhooks-21000bce.summary: People occupied Sakitari Cave on Okinawa from 35,000 to 30,000 years ago, leaving shell tools, beads and crescent-shaped fishhooks made from Trochus snail shell. Radiocarbon dates the hooks to about 23,000 years ago, oldest complete fishhooks known. Food remains show seasonal collection of freshwater crabs and snails. Persistent occupation on a small island with no large game and appearance of sites on nearby islands by 30,000 years ago indicate successful maritime adaptations across western Pacific coasts.

sources.title: Fujita, M. et al., 'Advanced maritime adaptation in the western Pacific coastal region extends back to 35,000–30,000 years before present', Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences 113 (2016), 11184-11189
sources.author: Fujita, Masaki; Yamasaki, Shinji; Katagiri, Chiaki; Oshiro, Itsuro; Sano, Katsuhiro; Kurozumi, Taiji
sources.venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
sources.confirms: Reports shell fishhooks at Sakitari Cave about 23,000 years old and occupation from 35,000 years.

sources.title: Yamasaki, S. et al., 'Human use of marine shells from Late Pleistocene layers of Sakitari-do cave site, Nanjo city, Okinawa prefecture', Anthropological Science (Japanese Series) 122 (2014), 9-27
sources.author: Yamasaki, Shinji; Fujita, Masaki; Katagiri, Chiaki; Kurozumi, Taiji; Kaifu, Yosuke
sources.confirms: Excavations in 2012-2013 at Sakitari-do yielded marine shells worked into implements and possible Dentalium beads, placing human activity at the cave back to the Last Glacial Maximum.
sources.qualifies: This 2014 paper predates the 2016 report of fishhooks and describes shell tools and beads, not hooks.

sakitari-cave-shell-fishhooks-21000bce.detail: Hooks were ground from shell into curved forms with notched shanks for line attachment. Seasonal crab remains, dominated by autumn-caught specimens with eggs, indicate scheduling. Earlier Okinawa finds were human skeletons from Minatogawa and Yamashita-cho. Jerimalai in Timor has a hook fragment of similar antiquity. Masaki Fujita of Okinawa Prefectural Museum led excavation from 2009. Hooks match sizes suited to reef fish such as parrotfish and groupers, consistent with remains at site.
sakitari-cave-shell-fishhooks-21000bce.dating_note: Hook layer dated about 23,000 years by radiocarbon on charcoal.

white-sands-footprints-21000bce.summary: Human footprints in Tularosa Basin at White Sands National Park are dated by radiocarbon on seeds of aquatic plant Ruppia in layers between tracks to 23,000 to 21,000 years ago, during Last Glacial Maximum when ice sheets blocked inland routes. Critics argued Ruppia could absorb old carbon from groundwater. Radiocarbon on conifer pollen and optically stimulated luminescence on quartz then agreed with seed ages. Footprints, many of children and teenagers, place people in southern North America thousands of years before Clovis.

sources.title: Bennett, M. R. et al., 'Evidence of humans in North America during the Last Glacial Maximum', Science 373 (2021), 1528-1531
sources.author: Bennett, Matthew R.; Bustos, David; Pigati, Jeffrey S.; Springer, Kathleen B.; Urban, Thomas M.; Holliday, Vance T.
sources.confirms: Dates White Sands footprints to 23,000 to 21,000 years using Ruppia seeds.

sources.title: Pigati, J. S. et al., 'Independent age estimates resolve the controversy of ancient human footprints at White Sands', Science 382 (2023), 73-75
sources.author: Pigati, Jeffrey S.; Springer, Kathleen B.; Honke, Jeffrey S.; Wahl, David; Champagne, Marie R.; Zimmerman, Susan R. H.
sources.confirms: Confirms footprint ages with pollen radiocarbon and luminescence dating.

white-sands-footprints-21000bce.detail: Tracks occur with those of mammoth, giant ground sloth, canids and camels. Several hundred prints across many surfaces have been documented. Hard-water effect objection would make seeds appear too old; pollen and luminescence are independent of that effect. Dates imply entry into Americas before 23,000 years, consistent with coastal route or pre-glacial entry. Some archaeologists still ask for artefacts in same layers.

picture.alt: Human footprints exposed in trench at White Sands National Park, New Mexico
picture.credit: NPS, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

white-sands-footprints-21000bce.dating_note: Age 23,000 to 21,000 years from seed radiocarbon, confirmed by pollen radiocarbon and luminescence; hard-water objection was tested and rejected by Pigati et al.

ishango-bone-tally-20000bce.summary: Ishango bone, found by Jean de Heinzelin in 1950 at a fishing settlement on Semliki River outlet of Lake Edward, is a 10-centimetre baboon fibula with a quartz flake fixed in one end and three columns of grouped notches. Redating in 1987 moved Ishango from about 9,000 years to 25,000 to 20,000 years ago; later work gives about 22,000 years. In mathematical readings, columns sum to 60 and 48, one column lists primes 11, 13, 17, 19, another pairs numbers with doubles. Some read notches as counts, some as a lunar calendar, others as a grip pattern.

sources.title: Brooks, A. S. and Smith, C. C., 'Ishango revisited: new age determinations and cultural interpretations', The African Archaeological Review 5 (1987), 65-78
sources.author: Brooks, Alison S.; Smith, Catherine C.
sources.confirms: Redates Ishango to 25,000 to 20,000 years and sets it in a fishing adaptation.

sources.title: Huylebrouck, D., 'The Ishango Site', Mathematics, Culture, and the Arts (2019), 127-140
sources.author: Huylebrouck, Dirk
sources.confirms: Reviews Ishango bone, its about 22,000-year age and mathematical interpretations.
sources.qualifies: Huylebrouck notes dating issues and competing readings of the notches.

ishango-bone-tally-20000bce.verification_note: Dating revision is accepted; mathematical interpretation is speculative.
ishango-bone-tally-20000bce.detail: Ishango layer also yields barbed bone harpoons and fish remains, part of a Late Pleistocene fishing adaptation. Tool-like quartz tip suggests engraving or scraping function, so notches could be decorative or counting aids. Prime-number readings are widely considered coincidental. Bone is held at Royal Belgian Institute of Natural Sciences in Brussels. Border Cave notched bones are 20,000 years older. Alison Brooks of George Washington University led redating.

picture.alt: Ishango bone, Royal Belgian Institute of Natural Sciences
picture.credit: Ben2, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

ishango-bone-tally-20000bce.dating_note: Age 25,000 to 20,000 years follows Brooks and Smith (1987); earlier estimate was about 9,000 years; counting interpretation is disputed.

lascaux-cave-paintings-and-lamps-19300bc.summary: Lascaux cave in Dordogne, found in 1940, holds some 600 painted animals and nearly 1,500 engravings, dominated by horses, aurochs and deer. Sylvain Ducasse and Mathieu Langlais attribute its art to Early Magdalenian, about 21,500 to 21,000 years ago. Over 100 sandstone lamps and lamp fragments were found inside, burning animal fat with juniper wicks; experiments have tested how lighting systems from torches to grease lamps light cave space. Lascaux closed to visitors in 1963 after fungal damage.

sources.title: Ducasse, S. and Langlais, M., 'Twenty years on, a new date with Lascaux. Reassessing the chronology of the cave’s Paleolithic occupations through new 14C AMS dating', Paléo 30-1 (2019), 130-147
sources.author: Ducasse, Sylvain; Langlais, Mathieu
sources.confirms: Argues Lascaux art dates to Early Magdalenian around 17,600 radiocarbon years, about 21,500 to 21,000 calendar years.

sources.title: de Beaune, S. A., 'Palaeolithic Lamps and Their Specialization: A Hypothesis', Current Anthropology 28 (1987), 569-577
sources.author: de Beaune, Sophie A.
sources.confirms: Catalogues Palaeolithic stone lamps including Lascaux examples.

sources.title: Medina-Alcaide, M. Á. et al., 'The conquest of the dark spaces: An experimental approach to lighting systems in Paleolithic caves', PLOS ONE 16 (2021), e0250497
sources.author: Medina-Alcaide, Mª Ángeles; Garate, Diego; Intxaurbe, Iñaki; Sanchidrián, José L.; Rivero, Olivia; Ferrier, Catherine
sources.confirms: Tests lighting from torches, lamps and fireplaces in Palaeolithic caves experimentally.

lascaux-cave-paintings-and-lamps-19300bc.detail: Hall of Bulls shows aurochs up to five metres long; painting used ochre and manganese applied by brush and by blowing. Scaffolding sockets survive in Axial Gallery. Lamps include a carved red sandstone lamp with engraved handle. Dating debate concerns whether art is Solutrean or Magdalenian; charcoal dates come from floor deposits rather than paintings. Replicas Lascaux II and IV serve visitors.

picture.alt: Sandstone fat lamp from Lascaux cave, Dordogne
picture.credit: Sémhur, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

lascaux-cave-paintings-and-lamps-19300bc.dating_note: Date follows Ducasse and Langlais's Early Magdalenian attribution of about 21,500 to 21,000 calendar years; older literature cites 17,000 radiocarbon years uncalibrated.

wadi-kubbaniya-tuber-and-fish-economy-18.summary: Late Palaeolithic camps at Wadi Kubbaniya near Aswan date to about 20,000 to 17,000 years ago. Charred remains, analysed by Gordon Hillman, show wild nut-grass (Cyperus rotundus) tubers as a staple, ground and probably leached to remove toxins, with grinding stones showing wear. Fish bones indicate mass harvest of catfish during Nile flood recession, with evidence for drying and storage. Economy combined plant foods and fish in seasonal rounds, an intensive Nile valley adaptation 10,000 years before farming reached Egypt.

sources.title: Wendorf, F. et al., 'New radiocarbon dates and Late Palaeolithic diet at Wadi Kubbaniya, Egypt', Antiquity 62 (1988), 279-283
sources.author: Wendorf, Fred; Schild, Romuald; Close, Angela E.; Hillman, Gordon C.; Gautier, Achilles; van Neer, Wim
sources.confirms: Summarises Wadi Kubbaniya Late Palaeolithic economy of tubers and fish around 20,000 years ago.

sources.title: Wendorf, F., Schild, R. and Close, A. E. (eds), The Prehistory of Wadi Kubbaniya, vol. 2: Stratigraphy, Paleoeconomy, and Environment (Southern Methodist University Press, 1989)
sources.author: Wendorf, Fred; Schild, Romuald; Close, Angela E.
sources.pages: vol. 2, chapters by Hillman and by Gautier and Van Neer on plant foods and fish
sources.confirms: The Internet Archive holds the three-volume Combined Prehistoric Expedition report on Wadi Kubbaniya in which Hillman's plant analysis and the fish studies appear.

sources.title: Usai, D., 'The Terminal Late Palaeolithic in Wadi Kubbaniya, Egypt', Antiquity Project Gallery 89, no. 346 (2015), 1-7
sources.author: Usai, Donatella
sources.confirms: Reports grinding slabs and handstones and fish remains dominated by Clarias catfish at a later Late Palaeolithic site in Wadi Kubbaniya, continuing the fishing and grinding economy.

wadi-kubbaniya-tuber-and-fish-economy-18.detail: Over 20 taxa of plant food were identified, including club-rush, dom palm and camomile. Infant faeces with charred tuber fragments suggest weaning foods processed by grinding. Fish are mostly Clarias catfish caught in shallow pools. Wendorf's team excavated in 1978 to 1984 after earlier work in Nubia. Interpretation of grinding stones as cereal processing was rejected after claimed barley grains proved intrusive.

picture.alt: Cast of Wadi Kubbaniya skeleton, Nubian Museum, Aswan
picture.credit: Marsupium, CC BY 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

wadi-kubbaniya-tuber-and-fish-economy-18.dating_note: Camps date about 20,000 to 17,000 radiocarbon years; year uses older end.

xianrendong-pottery-18000bce.summary: Pottery sherds from Xianrendong Cave in Jiangxi date to 20,000 to 19,000 years ago through radiocarbon on bone and charcoal in sealed layers, oldest pottery known. Sherds from Yuchanyan Cave in Hunan date to 18,300 to 15,400 years ago. Vessels are coarse, sand-tempered, low-fired bowls, probably used for cooking, made by hunter-gatherers during Last Glacial Maximum, 10,000 years before rice farming. Pottery thus begins among foragers in East Asia, not with agriculture.

sources.title: Wu, X. et al., 'Early Pottery at 20,000 Years Ago in Xianrendong Cave, China', Science 336 (2012), 1696-1700
sources.author: Wu, Xiaohong; Zhang, Chi; Goldberg, Paul; Cohen, David; Pan, Yan; Arpin, Trina
sources.confirms: Dates Xianrendong pottery to 20,000 to 19,000 calendar years.

sources.title: Boaretto, E. et al., 'Radiocarbon dating of charcoal and bone collagen associated with early pottery at Yuchanyan Cave, Hunan Province, China', Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences 106 (2009), 9595-9600
sources.author: Boaretto, Elisabetta; Wu, Xiaohong; Yuan, Jiarong; Bar-Yosef, Ofer; Chu, Vikki; Pan, Yan
sources.venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
sources.confirms: Dates Yuchanyan pottery to 18,300 to 15,400 calendar years.

xianrendong-pottery-18000bce.detail: Xianrendong was excavated from 1960s; 2012 work tied earlier stratigraphy to new dates. Sherds show carbon residues and scorch marks from fire. Pottery allowed boiling, which extracts fat from bone, detoxifies plants and makes starches digestible. Dolní Věstonice fired clay figurines are older but not containers. Japanese Incipient Jomon and Russian Far East pottery follow within a few millennia. Xiaohong Wu of Peking University led dating with Ofer Bar-Yosef.

picture.alt: Interior of Xianrendong cave, Wannian, Jiangxi, China, with modern display figures
picture.credit: Zhangzhugang, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

xianrendong-pottery-18000bce.dating_note: Xianrendong age 20,000 to 19,000 calendar years from radiocarbon in sealed strata; Yuchanyan 18,300 to 15,400 years.

mezhyrich-mammoth-bone-dwellings-16000bc.summary: Mezhyrich on Dnieper tributary preserves four dwellings built from mammoth skulls, mandibles, long bones and tusks, with hearths, pits and amber and shell ornaments. Plant remains show wood and bone fuel. Redating of structure 4 and its context in 2025, using small-mammal bones, gives about 18,248 to 17,764 years ago with site duration under 430 years, consistent with a single or short-repeated occupation. Bone architecture answered scarcity of timber on periglacial steppe.

sources.title: Marquer, L. et al., 'Charcoal scarcity in Epigravettian settlements with mammoth bone dwellings: the taphonomic evidence from Mezhyrich (Ukraine)', Journal of Archaeological Science 39 (2012), 109-120
sources.author: Marquer, L.; Lebreton, V.; Otto, T.; Valladas, H.; Haesaerts, P.; Messager, E.
sources.confirms: Analyses plant remains and fuel use at Mezhyrich mammoth-bone dwellings.

sources.title: Chu, W. et al., 'A revised radiocarbon chronology for the mammoth bone structures and associated features at Mezhyrich, Ukraine', Open Research Europe (2025)
sources.author: Chu, Wei; Shydlovskyi, Pavlo; Maier, Andreas
sources.confirms: Redates Mezhyrich mammoth bone structure 4 to about 18,248 to 17,764 calendar years.

sources.title: Soffer, O. et al., 'Cultural stratigraphy at Mezhirich, an Upper Palaeolithic site in Ukraine with multiple occupations', Antiquity 71 (1997), 48-62
sources.author: Soffer, Olga; Adovasio, James M.; Kornietz, Ninelj L.; Velichko, Andrei A.; Gribchenko, Yurij N.; Lenz, Brett R.
sources.confirms: Presents cultural stratigraphy of Mezhyrich mammoth-bone dwellings.

mezhyrich-mammoth-bone-dwellings-16000bc.detail: Dwelling 1, found in 1965 by a farmer digging a cellar, used 95 mandibles stacked chin-down in herringbone pattern. Each dwelling used bones of dozens of mammoths, some scavenged from natural accumulations. Earlier radiocarbon on mammoth bone gave scattered ages from 15,000 to 14,000 radiocarbon years; new approach avoided old mammoth bone. Similar structures occur at Mezin, Gontsy, Yudinovo and Dobranichevka.

picture.alt: Reconstruction of Mezhyrich mammoth bone dwelling, National Museum of Natural History, Kyiv (reconstruction)
picture.credit: Momotarou2012, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

mezhyrich-mammoth-bone-dwellings-16000bc.dating_note: Year follows 2025 redating of about 18,000 calendar years; earlier mammoth-bone dates were scattered and older.

coopers-ferry-stemmed-points-14500bce.summary: Stemmed projectile points and blades at Cooper's Ferry on Salmon River, Idaho, date by radiocarbon to 16,560 to 15,280 years ago, pre-dating Clovis by over 2,000 years. Western Stemmed points and human coprolites at Paisley Caves, Oregon, date to about 13,000 years ago, and a bone point embedded in a mastodon rib at Manis, Washington, to 13,800 years ago. Together these show people south of ice sheets before Clovis, probably via Pacific coast, using a different stemmed-point tradition.

sources.title: Davis, L. G. et al., 'Late Upper Paleolithic occupation at Cooper’s Ferry, Idaho, USA, ~16,000 years ago', Science 365 (2019), 891-897
sources.author: Davis, Loren G.; Madsen, David B.; Becerra-Valdivia, Lorena; Higham, Thomas; Sisson, David A.; Skinner, Sarah M.
sources.confirms: Dates Cooper's Ferry stemmed points and occupation to 16,560 to 15,280 calendar years.

sources.title: Jenkins, D. L. et al., 'Clovis Age Western Stemmed Projectile Points and Human Coprolites at the Paisley Caves', Science 337 (2012), 223-228
sources.author: Jenkins, Dennis L.; Davis, Loren G.; Stafford, Thomas W.; Campos, Paula F.; Hockett, Bryan; Jones, George T.
sources.confirms: Dates Western Stemmed points and human coprolites at Paisley Caves to 11,070 to 11,340 radiocarbon years, about 12,960 to 13,230 calendar years ago.

sources.title: Goldberg, P. et al., 'Comment on “DNA from Pre-Clovis Human Coprolites in Oregon, North America”', Science 325 (2009), 148-148
sources.author: Goldberg, Paul; Berna, Francesco; Macphail, Richard I.
sources.confirms: Questions human origin of one Paisley coprolite on micromorphological grounds.
sources.qualifies: Goldberg et al. challenge coprolite identification.

sources.title: Waters, M. R. et al., 'Pre-Clovis Mastodon Hunting 13,800 Years Ago at the Manis Site, Washington', Science 334 (2011), 351-353
sources.author: Waters, Michael R.; Stafford, Thomas W.; McDonald, H. Gregory; Gustafson, Carl; Rasmussen, Morten; Cappellini, Enrico
sources.confirms: Dates Manis mastodon with embedded bone point to 13,800 years.

coopers-ferry-stemmed-points-14500bce.detail: Cooper's Ferry points resemble those of northeast Asia and Japan, suggesting trans-Pacific coastal ancestry. Paul Goldberg challenged Paisley coprolite DNA identification, finding micromorphology inconsistent with human origin for one sample; later dating and protein work supported human presence. Manis point is made of mastodon bone, shaped and thrust into another animal. Ice-free corridor opened too late for these dates.

picture.alt: Excavation at Cooper's Ferry, Idaho, July 2018
picture.credit: BLMIdaho, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

coopers-ferry-stemmed-points-14500bce.dating_note: Cooper's Ferry 16,560 to 15,280 calendar years; Paisley about 14,300 calendar years; Manis 13,800 years; year uses Cooper's Ferry midpoint.

jomon-pottery-fish-cooking-13500bce.summary: Charred residues on 101 Incipient Jomon pottery sherds from Japan, dated about 15,000 to 11,800 years ago, hold lipids of marine and freshwater fish in most cases, showing pots were used to cook aquatic foods from outset. Odai Yamamoto I in Aomori yielded sherds with radiocarbon dates around 16,500 calendar years ago. Yaroslav Kuzmin argues that secure Jomon pottery begins about 16,000 calendar years ago and rejects older claims. Jomon pottery continues for over 10,000 years, longest ceramic tradition tied to foraging.

sources.title: Craig, O. E. et al., 'Earliest evidence for the use of pottery', Nature 496 (2013), 351-354
sources.author: Craig, O. E.; Saul, H.; Lucquin, A.; Nishida, Y.; Taché, K.; Clarke, L.
sources.confirms: Finds fish lipids in Incipient Jomon pottery residues dated about 15,000 to 11,800 years.

sources.title: Kuzmin, Y. V., 'Chronology of the earliest pottery in East Asia: progress and pitfalls', Antiquity 80 (2006), 362-371
sources.author: Kuzmin, Yaroslav V.
sources.confirms: Argues earliest secure Jomon pottery dates 13,700 to 13,300 radiocarbon years and disputes older claims.
sources.qualifies: Kuzmin places pottery origin slightly later than Odai Yamamoto's oldest dates.

jomon-pottery-fish-cooking-13500bce.detail: Lipid biomarkers include isoprenoid fatty acids and omega-(o-alkylphenyl)alkanoic acids formed when fish oil is heated. Pots are small and round-based, with little decoration in earliest phases. Debate over calibration of oldest Jomon dates stems from radiocarbon plateau around 13,000 radiocarbon years. Pottery spread across Japan during Late Glacial warming when salmon runs and shellfish beds expanded. Oliver Craig of University of York led lipid work with Japanese colleagues.

picture.alt: Potsherds from Odai Yamamoto I site, Aomori, Japan
picture.credit: Mccunicano, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

jomon-pottery-fish-cooking-13500bce.dating_note: Year of about 15,500 before present sits between Kuzmin's 13,700 to 13,300 radiocarbon years (about 16,000 calendar) and Craig et al.'s 15,000 to 11,800 range.

huaca-prieta-coastal-foragers-13000bce.summary: People occupied ground beneath and around Huaca Prieta mound on Peru's north coast from about 15,000 to 8,000 years ago, dated by radiocarbon. Early layers hold hearths, simple unifacial stone tools, marine fish, sea lions, birds and wetland plants, without projectile points, indicating a maritime and wetland economy. By early Holocene residents add cultivated avocado, chili pepper, beans and squash. Site shows a long coastal adaptation preceding Andean farming and later monumental architecture.

sources.title: Dillehay, T. D. et al., 'Simple technologies and diverse food strategies of the Late Pleistocene and Early Holocene at Huaca Prieta, Coastal Peru', Science Advances 3 (2017)
sources.author: Dillehay, Tom D.; Goodbred, Steve; Pino, Mario; Vásquez Sánchez, Víctor F.; Tham, Teresa Rosales; Adovasio, James
sources.confirms: Dates Huaca Prieta occupation from 15,000 to 8,000 calendar years with maritime and wetland economy.

sources.title: Dillehay, T. D. et al., 'Chronology, mound-building and environment at Huaca Prieta, coastal Peru, from 13 700 to 4000 years ago', Antiquity 86 (2012), 48-70
sources.author: Dillehay, Tom D.; Bonavia, Duccio; Goodbred, Steven; Pino, Mario; Vásquez, Victor; Rosales Tham, Teresa; Conklin, William; Splitstoser, Jeff; Piperno, Dolores; Iriarte, José; Grobman, Alexander; Levi-Lazzaris, Gerson; Moreira, Daniel; Lopéz, Marilaura; Tung, Tiffiny; Titelbaum, Anne; Verano, John; Adovasio, James; Scott Cummings, Linda; Bearéz, Phillipe; Dufour, Elise; Tombret, Olivier; Ramirez, Michael; Beavins, Rachel; DeSantis, Larisa; Rey, Isabel; Mink, Philip; Maggard, Greg; Franco, Teresa
sources.confirms: Places first human exploitation at Huaca Prieta at about 13,720 years before present, with maritime foragers before the black mound, horticulture and monumentality.
sources.qualifies: Gives 13,700 years as the start where the 2017 paper gives about 15,000 calendar years.

huaca-prieta-coastal-foragers-13000bce.detail: Huaca Prieta was first excavated by Junius Bird in 1946, famous for Preceramic cotton textiles. New excavations reached deposits under mound and in nearby Paredones. Tools are expedient flakes used with wooden and fibre gear. Marine foods were taken from beaches and estuaries rather than offshore. Coastal route for entry into South America gains support from such early maritime sites.

picture.alt: Huaca Prieta mound, Chicama Valley, Peru
picture.credit: AlisonRuthHughes, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

huaca-prieta-coastal-foragers-13000bce.dating_note: Occupation from about 15,000 calendar years by radiocarbon on charcoal.

natufian-sedentary-villages-13000bce.summary: Natufian culture spans about 15,000 to 11,500 years ago across Levant, from Negev to Euphrates. Natufians were hunter-gatherers who built round stone houses and buried dead in cemeteries, at threshold to farming. At Eynan (Ain Mallaha) in Hula Valley, Shelter 131/51 is a planned, geometrically laid out structure. House mice gained a commensal niche in long-term Natufian settlements 15,000 years ago. Mortars in Raqefet Cave hold 13,000-year-old beer-brewing residues.

sources.title: Bar-Yosef, O., 'The Natufian culture in the Levant, threshold to the origins of agriculture', Evolutionary Anthropology: Issues, News, and Reviews 6 (1998), 159-177
sources.author: Bar-Yosef, Ofer
sources.venue: Evolutionary Anthropology: Issues, News, and Reviews
sources.confirms: Frames Natufian culture as sedentary hunter-gatherers at threshold to agriculture.

sources.title: Haklay, G. and Gopher, A., 'A New Look at Shelter 131/51 in the Natufian Site of Eynan (Ain-Mallaha), Israel', PLOS ONE 10 (2015), e0130121
sources.author: Haklay, Gil; Gopher, Avi
sources.confirms: Analyses Shelter 131/51 at Eynan as planned Natufian architecture.

sources.title: Weissbrod, L. et al., 'Origins of house mice in ecological niches created by settled hunter-gatherers in the Levant 15,000 y ago', Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences 114 (2017), 4099-4104
sources.author: Weissbrod, Lior; Marshall, Fiona B.; Valla, François R.; Khalaily, Hamoudi; Bar-Oz, Guy; Auffray, Jean-Christophe
sources.venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
sources.confirms: Shows house mice established commensal niche in Natufian settlements 15,000 years ago.

sources.title: Liu, L. et al., 'Fermented beverage and food storage in 13,000 y-old stone mortars at Raqefet Cave, Israel: Investigating Natufian ritual feasting', Journal of Archaeological Science: Reports 21 (2018), 783-793
sources.author: Liu, Li; Wang, Jiajing; Rosenberg, Danny; Zhao, Hao; Lengyel, György; Nadel, Dani
sources.confirms: Reports 13,000-year-old beer-brewing residues at Raqefet Cave Natufian mortars.

natufian-sedentary-villages-13000bce.detail: Early Natufian base camps include Eynan, Hayonim, Wadi Hammeh 27 and El Wad, with semi-subterranean round houses and ground stone. Late Natufian coincides with Younger Dryas cold snap, when mobility increased. Natufians domesticated dogs and harvested wild cereals intensively. Mouse molar shapes track settlement duration over a 200,000-year Levantine sequence. Natufian precedes Pre-Pottery Neolithic A villages such as Jericho and Göbekli Tepe.

picture.alt: Limestone and basalt mortars from Eynan (Ain Mallaha), early Natufian, Israel Museum
picture.credit: Gary Todd, CC0, via Wikimedia Commons

natufian-sedentary-villages-13000bce.dating_note: Natufian spans about 15,000 to 11,500 calendar years before present; year gives start.

monte-verde-settlement-12500bce.summary: Monte Verde II, excavated by Tom Dillehay from 1977 in southern Chile, preserves a 20-metre tent-like structure framed with logs and covered with mastodon hide, hearths, wooden tools, cordage and plant remains sealed in peat, dated by radiocarbon to about 14,500 years ago. Nine seaweed species including Durvillaea and Gigartina, carried from coasts 90 kilometres away, were found as chewed cuds, several used medicinally by Mapuche today. Scattered older evidence at Monte Verde I may reach 18,500 years ago. Monte Verde anchored acceptance of pre-Clovis settlement after 1997 site visit.

sources.title: Dillehay, T. D. et al., 'Monte Verde: Seaweed, Food, Medicine, and the Peopling of South America', Science 320 (2008), 784-786
sources.author: Dillehay, Tom D.; Ramírez, C.; Pino, M.; Collins, M. B.; Rossen, J.; Pino-Navarro, J. D.
sources.confirms: Identifies nine seaweed species at Monte Verde dated 14,220 to 13,980 calendar years.

sources.title: Dillehay, T. D. et al., 'New Archaeological Evidence for an Early Human Presence at Monte Verde, Chile', PLOS ONE 10 (2015), e0141923
sources.author: Dillehay, Tom D.; Ocampo, Carlos; Saavedra, José; Sawakuchi, Andre Oliveira; Vega, Rodrigo M.; Pino, Mario
sources.confirms: Reports further evidence for early human presence at Monte Verde with older dates.
sources.qualifies: MV-I dates to 18,500 years are tentative.

monte-verde-settlement-12500bce.detail: Peat preserved wooden stakes, knotted reed cordage, chewed boldo leaves and footprints. Seaweed dates of 14,220 to 13,980 calendar years match structure. Plants came from coast, wetlands, forests and mountains, implying wide knowledge of regional resources within a few centuries of arrival. MV-I older dates rest on sparse and scattered artefacts. Dillehay's team includes Chilean institutions. Universidad Austral de Chile co-hosted excavations.

picture.alt: Monte Verde site, southern Chile
picture.credit: Geología Valdivia, CC BY 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons

monte-verde-settlement-12500bce.dating_note: Monte Verde II dates about 14,500 calendar years; Monte Verde I claims of up to 18,500 years remain tentative.

shubayqa-flatbread-12400bce.summary: Two fireplaces at Shubayqa 1 in northeastern Jordan held 24 charred food remains, dated by radiocarbon to 14,600 to 11,600 years ago, oldest at about 14,400; occupation at this site runs from 14,600 to 12,000 years ago. Microscopy shows bread-like porous structure made from ground wild einkorn, barley, oat and club-rush tubers, mixed and baked. Bread production predates cereal domestication by at least 4,000 years, and Amaia Arranz-Otaegui proposes that desire for bread encouraged cultivation. Shubayqa 1 is a Natufian site in Black Desert with stone-built structures and large fireplaces.

sources.title: Arranz-Otaegui, A. et al., 'Archaeobotanical evidence reveals the origins of bread 14,400 years ago in northeastern Jordan', Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences 115 (2018), 7925-7930
sources.author: Arranz-Otaegui, Amaia; Gonzalez Carretero, Lara; Ramsey, Monica N.; Fuller, Dorian Q.; Richter, Tobias
sources.venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
sources.confirms: Reports charred bread remains at Shubayqa 1 dated 14,600 to 11,600 calendar years.

sources.title: Richter, Tobias; Arranz-Otaegui, Amaia; Yeomans, Lisa; Boaretto, Elisabetta, 'High Resolution AMS Dates from Shubayqa 1, northeast Jordan Reveal Complex Origins of Late Epipalaeolithic Natufian in the Levant', Scientific Reports 7 (2017), 17025
sources.author: Richter, Tobias; Arranz-Otaegui, Amaia; Yeomans, Lisa; Boaretto, Elisabetta
sources.confirms: Radiocarbon series shows Shubayqa 1 occupied intermittently between about 14,600 and 12,000 cal BP, within the Natufian of about 14,600 to 11,500 cal BP.

shubayqa-flatbread-12400bce.verification_note: Richter et al. (2017) date Shubayqa 1's occupation to about 14,600 to 12,000 cal BP, while the PNAS paper gives 14,600 to 11,600 for food remains; both come from one excavation team.
shubayqa-flatbread-12400bce.detail: Remains were identified by scanning electron microscopy comparing voids and cell structures with experimental breads. Mixtures of cereal and tuber flour produced flatbreads cooked on hot stones or ashes. Site excavated by Copenhagen team from 2012. Earlier bread evidence came from Neolithic Çatalhöyük around 9,100 years ago. Grinding tools and sickle blades at site support cereal processing. Amaia Arranz-Otaegui and Tobias Richter of University of Copenhagen led work.

picture.alt: Black Desert landscape at Shubayqa, eastern Jordan
picture.credit: Joe Roe, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

shubayqa-flatbread-12400bce.dating_note: Oldest fireplace about 14,400 calendar years within a 14,600 to 11,600 range.

jebel-sahaba-cemetery-violence-11400bce.summary: Jebel Sahaba, excavated by Fred Wendorf in 1960s before Aswan High Dam flooding, holds 61 individuals, many with embedded stone projectile fragments and cut marks. A 2021 reanalysis of skeletons found both healed and unhealed injuries, often in same person, indicating repeated episodes of violence rather than one battle, probably linked to climatic and environmental stress on Nile valley at end of Pleistocene. Jebel Sahaba dates to at least 13,400 years ago and is among earliest cemeteries showing interpersonal violence.

sources.title: Crevecoeur, I. et al., 'New insights on interpersonal violence in the Late Pleistocene based on the Nile valley cemetery of Jebel Sahaba', Scientific Reports 11 (2021)
sources.author: Crevecoeur, Isabelle; Dias-Meirinho, Marie-Hélène; Zazzo, Antoine; Antoine, Daniel; Bon, François
sources.confirms: Reanalyses Jebel Sahaba skeletons showing recurrent violence at least 13,400 years ago.

sources.title: Wendorf, Fred (ed.), The Prehistory of Nubia, vol. 2 (Southern Methodist University Press, 1968), 'Site 117: A Nubian Final Paleolithic Graveyard near Jebel Sahaba, Sudan'
sources.author: Wendorf, Fred
sources.confirms: Original excavation report of the Jebel Sahaba cemetery (Site 117) by the Combined Prehistoric Expedition, the burials with embedded lithic fragments that Crevecoeur's team re-examined; the Internet Archive holds the two-volume final report (lending copy).

jebel-sahaba-cemetery-violence-11400bce.detail: Over 100 lithic fragments were associated with bodies, some lodged in bone. Women and children were among victims. Wendorf originally read site as evidence of warfare. Microscopy identified projectile impact marks and distinguished perimortem from healed lesions. Competition over resources along Nile during arid phases is proposed as driver. Remains are curated at British Museum.

picture.alt: Aerial view of Wadi Halfa and Nile, Sudan, near Jebel Sahaba (Matson Collection)
picture.credit: Matson Collection, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

jebel-sahaba-cemetery-violence-11400bce.dating_note: Minimum age 13,400 years from radiocarbon; Nubian location is placed under sub-Saharan Africa region here.

clovis-fluted-points-11100bce.summary: Clovis points are lanceolate bifaces with a channel flake removed from base for hafting, found from Montana to Mexico, often with mammoth and mastodon kills. Redating confines Clovis sites to 13,050 to 12,750 years ago, a span of only a few centuries, ending as Younger Dryas begins and as Fishtail points appear in South America. Clovis was once treated as first American culture; pre-Clovis sites now show it as a later, rapid technological spread.

sources.title: Waters, M. R. and Stafford, T. W., 'Redefining the Age of Clovis: Implications for the Peopling of the Americas', Science 315 (2007), 1122-1126
sources.author: Waters, Michael R.; Stafford, Thomas W.
sources.confirms: Redates Clovis to 11,050 to 10,800 radiocarbon years.

sources.title: Waters, M. R. et al., 'The age of Clovis—13,050 to 12,750 cal yr B.P.', Science Advances 6 (2020)
sources.author: Waters, Michael R.; Stafford, Thomas W.; Carlson, David L.
sources.confirms: Refines Clovis span to 13,050 to 12,750 calendar years and notes Fishtail by 12,900.

clovis-fluted-points-11100bce.detail: Points were made from high-quality chert and obsidian carried hundreds of kilometres; caches such as Anzick and East Wenatchee hold oversized bifaces and ivory rods. Fluting required skill and often broke preforms. Clovis kill sites include Naco, Lehner, Murray Springs and Blackwater Draw, type site in New Mexico. Short duration implies rapid movement or spread of technology among existing populations.

picture.alt: Clovis fluted point, Sevier County, Utah, Natural History Museum of Utah
picture.credit: Daderot, CC0, via Wikimedia Commons

clovis-fluted-points-11100bce.dating_note: Span 13,050 to 12,750 calendar years before present from Bayesian modelling of radiocarbon dates.

abu-hureyra-rye-cultivation-11000bce.summary: Epipalaeolithic Abu Hureyra in northern Syria yielded large rye grains with domestic-type features, directly radiocarbon dated to about 13,000 years ago. Gordon Hillman read them as cultivation: Younger Dryas drought pushed foragers to plant rye as wild stands failed, which would make this earliest cultivation of a domesticated cereal. Sue Colledge and James Conolly reassessed these grains and judge them too few and too ambiguous to prove domestication; they favour wild gathering. Tabqa Dam flooded Abu Hureyra in 1974.

sources.title: Hillman, G. et al., 'New evidence of Lateglacial cereal cultivation at Abu Hureyra on the Euphrates', The Holocene 11 (2001), 383-393
sources.author: Hillman, Gordon; Hedges, Robert; Moore, Andrew; Colledge, Susan; Pettitt, Paul
sources.confirms: Reports domestic-type rye at Abu Hureyra about 13,000 years and argues for Younger Dryas cultivation.

sources.title: Colledge, S. and Conolly, J., 'Reassessing the evidence for the cultivation of wild crops during the Younger Dryas at Tell Abu Hureyra, Syria', Environmental Archaeology 15 (2010), 124-138
sources.author: Colledge, Sue; Conolly, James
sources.confirms: Reassesses Abu Hureyra evidence and finds rye domestication unproven.
sources.qualifies: Colledge and Conolly reject early domestication claim.

abu-hureyra-rye-cultivation-11000bce.verification_note: Dates are secure; cultivation and domestication interpretation is contested.
abu-hureyra-rye-cultivation-11000bce.detail: Abu Hureyra was excavated by Andrew Moore in 1972 and 1973 as a rescue project, producing a sequence from Epipalaeolithic village to Neolithic town. Plant remains include over 150 taxa and show a shift from wild fruits and seeds to drought-tolerant grasses. Rye grains were dated by accelerator mass spectrometry on single seeds. Weed flora typical of cultivation was also claimed; critics attribute it to natural disturbance.

picture.alt: Grinding stones from Abu Hureyra, Syria, Ashmolean Museum
picture.credit: Zunkir, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

abu-hureyra-rye-cultivation-11000bce.dating_note: Rye grains directly dated about 13,000 calendar years; domestication claim is disputed by Colledge and Conolly (2010).

fishtail-points-south-america-10900bce.summary: Fishtail or Fell points, stemmed bifaces with flaring bases, appear across South America from Patagonia to Ecuador by about 12,900 years ago, contemporary with late Clovis. Compiled radiocarbon dates show Fishtail points peak in frequency as megafauna such as ground sloths, glyptodonts, native horses and gomphotheres disappear, then decline, suggesting a specialised big-game weapon lost its purpose. Points were discovered at Fell's Cave in Chile by Junius Bird in 1930s. Their rapid spread suggests communication across continent among early populations.

sources.title: Prates, L. et al., 'Changes in projectile design and size of prey reveal the central role of Fishtail points in megafauna hunting in South America', Scientific Reports 12 (2022)
sources.author: Prates, Luciano; Rivero, Diego; Perez, S. Ivan
sources.confirms: Links Fishtail point frequency to megafaunal extinction across South America around 12,900 years.

sources.title: Waters, M. R. et al., 'The age of Clovis—13,050 to 12,750 cal yr B.P.', Science Advances 6 (2020)
sources.author: Waters, Michael R.; Stafford, Thomas W.; Carlson, David L.
sources.confirms: Notes Fishtail complex well established in South America by about 12,900 calendar years.

fishtail-points-south-america-10900bce.detail: Fishtail points occur with extinct fauna at Fell's Cave and Cueva del Medio. Temporal distributions of points and megafauna were compared against human population proxies. Fluting occurs on some Fishtail points, prompting debate over links to Clovis. After megafaunal extinction, unstemmed triangular points replace them in many regions. Luciano Prates and Ivan Perez of Universidad Nacional de La Plata led analysis.

picture.alt: Fishtail projectile point in orthoquartzite from Tandilia, Argentina
picture.credit: KehDon, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

fishtail-points-south-america-10900bce.dating_note: Appearance about 12,900 calendar years from compiled radiocarbon dates.

hilazon-tachtit-shaman-burial-10000bce.summary: A Late Natufian burial in Hilazon Tachtit cave in Galilee dates by radiocarbon to about 12,000 years ago. An elderly woman with pelvic and spinal deformities was buried with over 50 complete tortoise shells, a leopard pelvis, wild boar forearm, eagle wing, marten skulls, an aurochs tail and a human foot, with stones placed on body. Leore Grosman interprets her as a shaman and burial feast as ritual event. Hilazon Tachtit also holds at least 28 other burials, showing cemetery use by sedentary foragers.

sources.title: Grosman, L. et al., 'A 12,000-year-old Shaman burial from the southern Levant (Israel)', Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences 105 (2008), 17665-17669
sources.author: Grosman, Leore; Munro, Natalie D.; Belfer-Cohen, Anna
sources.venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
sources.confirms: Reports a 12,000-year-old Natufian burial with tortoise shells and animal parts interpreted as a shaman.

sources.title: Munro, N. D. and Grosman, L., 'Early evidence (ca. 12,000 B.P.) for feasting at a burial cave in Israel', Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences 107 (2010), 15362-15366
sources.author: Munro, Natalie D.; Grosman, Leore
sources.venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
sources.confirms: Reports butchered tortoise and wild cattle remains at Hilazon Tachtit, a Late Natufian burial cave dated 12,000 calibrated years, as evidence of feasting tied to burial rites.

hilazon-tachtit-shaman-burial-10000bce.detail: Tortoises were cooked and eaten at graveside, and leftovers placed with body. Grave was lined with limestone slabs. Natufian cemeteries mark territorial attachment, and special burials indicate social roles beyond age and sex. Interpretation as shaman rests on ethnographic parallels; others prefer healer or ritual specialist. Butchered tortoise and wild cattle remains show feasting tied to burial rites. Leore Grosman of Hebrew University directs excavations.

picture.alt: Hilazon Tachtit excavation, Galilee, Israel, 2006
picture.credit: נפתלי הילגר, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

hilazon-tachtit-shaman-burial-10000bce.dating_note: Burial dated about 12,000 calendar years by radiocarbon.

holocene-begins-9700bce.summary: Greenland ice records an abrupt shift in deuterium excess at about 9700 BCE, marking the end of Younger Dryas cold and the start of Holocene warmth. Stratigraphers chose this layer in NGRIP core as formal boundary stratotype. Warmer, wetter, steadier conditions followed across most continents, and every development in this period sits inside that window: cereal farming in southwest Asia, rice and millet in China, squash and maize in Mexico, cattle herding in a green Sahara. In 2018 geologists split the epoch into Greenlandian, Northgrippian and Meghalayan stages, with boundaries at 8200 and 4200 years ago tied to climate events felt by early farmers.

sources.title: Walker, M. et al., 'Formal definition and dating of the GSSP for the base of the Holocene using the Greenland NGRIP ice core', Journal of Quaternary Science 24 (2009)
sources.author: Walker, M. et al.
sources.confirms: Fixes the Holocene base at 11,700 calendar years b2k with a maximum counting error of 99 years, identified by an abrupt shift in deuterium excess in the NGRIP core.

sources.title: Walker, M. et al., 'Formal ratification of the subdivision of the Holocene Series/Epoch', Episodes 41 (2018)
sources.author: Walker, M. et al.
sources.confirms: Reports the tripartite division into Greenlandian, Northgrippian and Meghalayan stages, each with a boundary stratotype.

holocene-begins-9700bce.detail: Ice core layers can be counted year by year, which places this boundary 11,700 years before AD 2000 with a precision unmatched by radiocarbon. Radiocarbon ages are converted to calendar years counted back from 1950, so subtracting 1950 gives a date in BCE. Stable climate removed one barrier to farming without causing it: cultivation attempted during late glacial swings had left few lasting traces.

picture.alt: Graph of Holocene temperature reconstructions over 12,000 years, showing warming after the last glacial period and a mid-Holocene optimum
picture.credit: Robert A. Rohde (Global Warming Art), via Wikimedia Commons

holocene-begins-9700bce.dating_note: Walker et al. 2009 fix the base of Holocene at 11,700 years before AD 2000 in the NGRIP ice core, with a counting error of 99 years; this record carries the era to 3000 BCE, the end of this period.

gobekli-tepe-pillars-9500bce.summary: Göbekli Tepe near Şanlıurfa consists of monumental round to oval enclosures with T-shaped limestone pillars up to 5.5 metres tall, carved with foxes, snakes, boars, birds and scorpions, built by Pre-Pottery Neolithic A communities in 10th millennium BCE. Klaus Schmidt, who excavated from 1995, interpreted it as a sanctuary built by hunter-gatherers. Oliver Dietrich argues feasting and cult drew labour. Thousands of grinding tools show cereal processing for food and possibly beer. Monumental construction here precedes farming villages and pottery.

sources.title: Schmidt, K., 'Göbekli Tepe – the Stone Age Sanctuaries. New results of ongoing excavations with a special focus on sculptures and high reliefs', Documenta Praehistorica 37 (2010), 239-256
sources.author: Schmidt, Klaus
sources.confirms: Presents Göbekli Tepe sanctuaries and sculptures as Pre-Pottery Neolithic work of 10th to 8th millennium BC.

sources.title: Dietrich, O. et al., 'The role of cult and feasting in the emergence of Neolithic communities. New evidence from Göbekli Tepe, south-eastern Turkey', Antiquity 86 (2012), 674-695
sources.author: Dietrich, Oliver; Heun, Manfred; Notroff, Jens; Schmidt, Klaus; Zarnkow, Martin
sources.confirms: Argues cult and feasting drove construction at Göbekli Tepe.

sources.title: Dietrich, L. et al., 'Cereal processing at Early Neolithic Göbekli Tepe, southeastern Turkey', PLOS ONE 14 (2019), e0215214
sources.author: Dietrich, Laura; Meister, Julia; Dietrich, Oliver; Notroff, Jens; Kiep, Janika; Heeb, Julia
sources.confirms: Documents cereal processing and grinding tools at Göbekli Tepe in 10th to 9th millennium BC.

gobekli-tepe-pillars-9500bce.detail: Enclosures A to D were buried deliberately, preserving pillars. Radiocarbon dates on wall plaster and fill give 10th to 9th millennium BCE. Later rectangular buildings belong to Pre-Pottery Neolithic B. Lee Clare has since found domestic structures and water cisterns, revising view of a purely ritual site without residents. Göbekli Tepe is on UNESCO World Heritage List since 2018 and sits at boundary with next period.

picture.alt: Carved T-shaped pillar at Göbekli Tepe, Şanlıurfa, Turkey
picture.credit: Zhengan, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

gobekli-tepe-pillars-9500bce.dating_note: Date of about 9500 BCE marks Pre-Pottery Neolithic A enclosures per radiocarbon on plaster and fill; construction spans 10th to 9th millennium BCE.

ounjougou-pottery-9400bce.summary: At Ounjougou on Dogon plateau of Mali, Eric Huysecom's Swiss-Malian team found sherds of thick, grit-tempered pottery with impressed decoration in sediments dated by radiocarbon and luminescence to before 9400 cal BC, alongside small bifacial arrowheads and grinding stones. The makers were hunter-gatherers exploiting wild grasses in a Sahara and Sahel turning green with the early Holocene monsoon. Friederike Jesse's survey shows that pottery then spread across Sahara and Nile valley during the tenth to eighth millennia BCE, long before herding or farming. Pots let people boil wild grains and seeds into porridge and store water, an innovation that in Africa preceded food production by several thousand years.

sources.title: Huysecom, E. et al., 'The emergence of pottery in Africa during the tenth millennium cal BC: new evidence from Ounjougou (Mali)', Antiquity 83 (2009)
sources.author: Huysecom, E. et al.
sources.confirms: Reports pottery at Ounjougou dated before 9400 cal BC, associated with early Holocene hunter-gatherers and bifacial arrowheads.

sources.title: Jesse, F., 'Early pottery in northern Africa: an overview', Journal of African Archaeology 8 (2010)
sources.author: Jesse, F.
sources.confirms: Surveys the spread of early pottery across northern Africa from the tenth millennium cal BC among hunter-gatherer groups.

ounjougou-pottery-9400bce.detail: African pottery appears independently of Near Eastern ceramics, which begin only around 7000 BCE, and is contemporary with early Holocene pottery in China and Japan. Ounjougou sequence was traced through gullies cutting deep sediments, giving unusual stratigraphic control. Wavy-line decorated pottery of Khartoum tradition follows in the eighth millennium. Ounjougou's pottery is thick and rough, decorated with impressions of plant stems. Grinding stones from the same layers imply processing of wild grass seeds. Dogon plateau gullies expose sediments from Pleistocene to recent, giving a long regional record.

picture.alt: View of the Ounjougou site complex in the Yamé valley near Bandiagara, Mali, with eroded gullies
picture.credit: Ounjougou, via Wikimedia Commons

ounjougou-pottery-9400bce.dating_note: Huysecom et al. 2009 date Ounjougou sherds to before 9400 cal BC by radiocarbon and luminescence; this is the earliest pottery in Africa, contemporary with early Holocene pottery in East Asia.

franchthi-melos-obsidian-9000bce.summary: Franchthi Cave in the southern Argolid holds a long sequence from Palaeolithic into Neolithic. Among its Mesolithic tools are blades of obsidian whose trace elements Renfrew, Cann and Dixon in 1965 matched to Melos, an island 150 km away across open water. No land bridge existed, so people paddled boats to Melos and back by the ninth millennium BCE, well before farming reached Greece. Catherine Perlès notes the obsidian arrives with large tuna vertebrae, suggesting deep-water fishing and seafaring went together. Cyprian Broodbank uses such finds to argue that Mediterranean islands were explored by foragers long before farmers settled them.

sources.title: Cann, J. R., Dixon, J. E. and Renfrew, C., 'Obsidian in the Aegean', Annual of the British School at Athens 60 (1965)
sources.author: Cann, J. R., Dixon, J. E. and Renfrew, C.
sources.venue: Annual of the British School at Athens
sources.confirms: Characterises Aegean obsidian sources by trace elements and identifies Melos as the source for mainland finds.

sources.title: Perlès, C., Takaoğlu, T. and Gratuze, B., 'Melian obsidian in NW Turkey: evidence for early Neolithic trade', Journal of Field Archaeology 36 (2011)
sources.author: Perlès, C., Takaoğlu, T. and Gratuze, B.
sources.confirms: Confirms Melian obsidian distribution and the Aegean exchange networks by the Neolithic.
sources.qualifies: Abstract does not state the Franchthi Mesolithic date.

sources.title: Broodbank, C., 'The origins and early development of Mediterranean maritime activity', Journal of Mediterranean Archaeology 19 (2006)
sources.author: Broodbank, C.
sources.confirms: Reviews early Mediterranean seafaring, including Mesolithic obsidian movement from Melos to the Greek mainland.
