franchthi-melos-obsidian-9000bce.verification_note: Melos as source and Mesolithic seafaring are confirmed; a specific ninth millennium date at Franchthi is not independently confirmed.
franchthi-melos-obsidian-9000bce.detail: Franchthi obsidian quantities stay small until Neolithic, when Melian glass becomes Aegean's standard blade material. The boats themselves have not survived; dugouts or hide boats are both proposed. Melos was uninhabited then, so quarrying trips were expeditions rather than trade with islanders. Franchthi's Mesolithic layers also hold large tuna bones and shells from offshore islands, and its long sequence was excavated by Thomas Jacobsen's team from 1967. Franchthi's late Mesolithic cemetery adds burials to this picture of coastal foragers.

picture.alt: Neolithic finds from Franchthi Cave including stone tools and pottery, Archaeological Museum of Nafplio
picture.credit: Zde, via Wikimedia Commons

franchthi-melos-obsidian-9000bce.dating_note: Melian obsidian occurs in Franchthi Cave's late Upper Palaeolithic and Mesolithic layers; Perlès places the earliest pieces around 11,000 cal BP, before Mesolithic. 9000 BCE is a midpoint for its regular Mesolithic appearance.

cayonu-native-copper-8500bce.summary: Near the Ergani Maden copper deposit in southeast Turkey, inhabitants of Çayönü Tepesi collected nuggets of native copper and malachite and cold-hammered and annealed them into beads, hooks and awls during the Pre-Pottery Neolithic, around 8500 BCE. Southwest Asia's earliest metal objects belong to the eleventh to ninth millennium BCE, and smelting of ores to the early sixth millennium. Melted native copper is hard to tell from copper smelted from pure ore, which complicates claims about when true smelting began. Native copper was treated as a coloured stone that could be shaped without fracture; extracting metal from ore came three millennia later.

sources.title: Roberts, B. W., Thornton, C. P. and Pigott, V. C., 'Development of metallurgy in Eurasia', Antiquity 83 (2009)
sources.author: Roberts, B. W., Thornton, C. P. and Pigott, V. C.
sources.confirms: States that metallurgy began in the eleventh to ninth millennium BC in southwest Asia and that smelting developed in the early sixth millennium BC.

sources.title: Maddin, R., Stech Wheeler, T. and Muhly, J. D., 'Distinguishing artifacts made of native copper', Journal of Archaeological Science 7 (1980)
sources.author: Maddin, R., Stech Wheeler, T. and Muhly, J. D.
sources.confirms: Explains that melted native copper and copper smelted from pure ores are very hard to distinguish, complicating the dating of first smelting.

cayonu-native-copper-8500bce.verification_note: Çayönü's bead dates come from Roberts and colleagues' regional synthesis; Çambel and Braidwood's site report is cited as supporting literature.
cayonu-native-copper-8500bce.detail: Annealing, heating copper to soften it after hammering, is attested by grain structure in some early beads. Similar native copper working appears independently around Lake Superior from about 8,500 years ago. The first Eurasian smelting evidence accepted by most specialists is slag at Belovode in Serbia around 5000 BCE. Çayönü also preserves terrazzo floors of burnt lime and crushed stone, a so-called skull building, and early domestic pigs, which makes it a reference site for Anatolian Pre-Pottery Neolithic innovation.

picture.alt: Close-up of a nugget of native copper about 4 cm across, with branching crystalline form
picture.credit: Jonathan Zander (Digon3), via Wikimedia Commons

cayonu-native-copper-8500bce.dating_note: Roberts, Thornton and Pigott 2009 place the beginnings of metallurgy in the eleventh to ninth millennium BC in southwest Asia; Çayönü's hammered native copper beads belong to its PPN levels around 8500 BCE.

einkorn-emmer-barley-domestication-8500b.summary: Wild wheats and barley shed their grain when ripe; domestic forms hold it on a tough rachis until harvest. Chaff with that non-shattering trait appears in southern Syria 10,700 to 10,200 years ago, and the earliest secure domestic emmer and einkorn grains come from Nevalı Çori and Cafer Höyük on the upper Euphrates about 10,500 to 10,200 years ago. DNA fingerprinting matches cultivated einkorn to wild stands on Karacadağ in southeast Turkey. Other regions followed 400 to 1,000 years later, so domestication was regional and drawn out rather than a single event. Management of wild stands began by 11,500 years ago.

sources.title: Zeder, M. A., 'The origins of agriculture in the Near East', Current Anthropology 52 (2011)
sources.author: Zeder, M. A.
sources.confirms: Dates the earliest securely identified domestic emmer and einkorn to about 10,500 to 10,200 cal BP at Nevalı Çori, Cafer Höyük and possibly Çayönü, with management of wild forms by 11,500 cal BP.

sources.title: Heun, M. et al., 'Site of einkorn wheat domestication identified by DNA fingerprinting', Science 278 (1997)
sources.author: Heun, M. et al.
sources.confirms: Identifies wild einkorn from the Karacadağ mountains as the progenitor of cultivated einkorn.

sources.title: Arranz-Otaegui, A., Colledge, S., Zapata, L., Teira-Mayolini, L. C. and Ibáñez, J. J., 'Regional diversity on the timing for the initial appearance of cereal cultivation and domestication in southwest Asia', PNAS 113 (2016)
sources.author: Arranz-Otaegui, A., Colledge, S., Zapata, L., Teira-Mayolini, L. C. and Ibáñez, J. J.
sources.confirms: Finds domesticated-type chaff above 10 percent in southern Syria at 10.7 to 10.2 ka cal BP and 400 to 1,000 years later in other regions.

sources.title: Hillman, G., Hedges, R., Moore, A., Colledge, S. and Pettitt, P., 'New evidence of Lateglacial cereal cultivation at Abu Hureyra on the Euphrates', The Holocene 11 (2001)
sources.author: Hillman, G., Hedges, R., Moore, A., Colledge, S. and Pettitt, P.
sources.confirms: Argues for Late Glacial rye cultivation at Abu Hureyra.
sources.qualifies: Only the reference list was readable; the claim is included as the contested position.

einkorn-emmer-barley-domestication-8500b.detail: Gordon Hillman proposed that rye was cultivated at Abu Hureyra on Euphrates around 13,000 years ago, during Younger Dryas; most archaeobotanists treat that claim as unproven. Barley was domesticated across that same arc, with Zagros and Levant both contributing. Domestication took centuries because non-shattering is a disadvantage in the wild and spreads only under sickle harvesting and replanting. Genetic studies of barley point to two domestications, one in southwest Asia's western arc and another in its eastern wing toward Iran.

picture.alt: Spikes of einkorn wheat, Triticum monococcum, from the USDA germplasm collection against a blue background with a ruler
picture.credit: USDA ARS National Plant Germplasm System, via Wikimedia Commons

einkorn-emmer-barley-domestication-8500b.dating_note: Zeder 2011 dates the earliest secure domestic emmer and einkorn to 10,500 to 10,200 cal BP at Nevalı Çori and Cafer Höyük; Arranz-Otaegui et al. 2016 find domestic-type chaff in southern Syria at 10,700 to 10,200 cal BP and 400 to 1,000 years later elsewhere. Hillman's claim of Late Glacial rye at Abu Hureyra remains contested.

sheep-goat-cattle-domestication-fertile-.summary: Herders in Zagros highlands of western Iran were culling young male goats and keeping females by 10,000 years ago, a harvest profile impossible for hunters. Sheep followed in that arc from northern Zagros to southeast Anatolia between 11,000 and 10,500 years ago. Cattle were tamed from aurochs at Dja'de on the middle Euphrates and Çayönü on the upper Tigris between 10,800 and 10,200 years ago; ancient DNA puts founders of all taurine cattle at about 80 female aurochs. Africa's zebu and humpless cattle have separate stories. Herds gave meat on demand, then milk, hides, dung fuel and, by the fourth millennium, traction.

sources.title: Zeder, M. A. and Hesse, B., 'The initial domestication of goats (Capra hircus) in the Zagros Mountains 10,000 years ago', Science 287 (2000)
sources.author: Zeder, M. A. and Hesse, B.
sources.confirms: Documents initial goat domestication in the highlands of western Iran at 10,000 calibrated years ago through sex-specific harvest profiles.

sources.title: Bollongino, R. et al., 'Modern taurine cattle descended from small number of Near-Eastern founders', Molecular Biology and Evolution 29 (2012)
sources.author: Bollongino, R. et al.
sources.confirms: Estimates about 80 female aurochs founders and places first domestication at Dja'de, 10,800 to 10,300 cal BP, and Çayönü, around 10,200 cal BP.

sources.title: Zeder, M. A., 'Domestication and early agriculture in the Mediterranean Basin: origins, diffusion, and impact', PNAS 105 (2008)
sources.author: Zeder, M. A.
sources.confirms: Dates sheep and goat domestication from the northern Zagros to southeast Anatolia between 11,000 and 10,500 BP and tracks spread to the southern Levant by 9,500 BP.

sheep-goat-cattle-domestication-fertile-.detail: Sex and age profiles are read from bone measurements: wild goats show strong size dimorphism, so a bone assemblage dominated by small adults and large juveniles signals selective culling. Managed goats reached the southern Levant by 9,500 years ago. The small cattle founder number implies a deliberate, localised capture of calves rather than repeated taming across the region. Sheep bred for wool, with continuous fleece rather than kemp, appear only in late fourth millennium bone and textile evidence, so early flocks gave meat and milk.

picture.alt: The mound of Ganj Dareh in the Zagros foothills of western Iran, an early goat-herding village
picture.credit: Masdf98, via Wikimedia Commons

sheep-goat-cattle-domestication-fertile-.dating_note: Zeder and Hesse date goat management in Zagros to 10,000 cal BP; Bollongino et al. date first cattle domestication at Dja'de and Çayönü to 10,800 to 10,200 cal BP from about 80 founding females.

jericho-tower-8300bce.summary: At Tell es-Sultan, ancient Jericho, Pre-Pottery Neolithic A settlers piled undressed stones into a solid tower over eight metres high with an internal stair of 22 steps, beside a stone wall and ditch, around 8300 BCE. Kathleen Kenyon, who excavated it in 1950s, read the wall as defence; Ofer Bar-Yosef argued in 1986 that it protected Jericho from flash floods and mudflows off the wadi. Barkai and Liran suggest the tower's position marks midsummer sunset over nearby hills. Across Dead Sea at Dhra', Kuijt and Finlayson uncovered granaries with raised floors dated about 11,300 to 11,175 years ago, built before cereals showed domestic traits. Stone architecture and food storage appear here before domesticated crops.

sources.title: Bar-Yosef, O., 'The walls of Jericho: an alternative interpretation', Current Anthropology 27 (1986)
sources.author: Bar-Yosef, O.
sources.confirms: Re-examines Kenyon's conclusions and the PPNA radiocarbon sequence and proposes that the walls protected against floods and mudflows.

sources.title: Barkai, R. and Liran, R., 'Midsummer sunset at Neolithic Jericho', Time and Mind 1 (2008)
sources.author: Barkai, R. and Liran, R.
sources.confirms: Dates the tower roughly to 8300 BC and argues its design is aligned to celestial and geographical features.
sources.qualifies: Abstract gives no height; the 8.5 m height comes from Kenyon's excavation reports.

sources.title: Kuijt, I. and Finlayson, B., 'Evidence for food storage and predomestication granaries 11,000 years ago in the Jordan Valley', PNAS 106 (2009)
sources.author: Kuijt, I. and Finlayson, B.
sources.confirms: Reports purpose-built granaries with suspended floors at Dhra' dated 11,300 to 11,175 cal BP.

jericho-tower-8300bce.detail: Kenyon's trenches established Natufian to PPNA sequence that Bar-Yosef re-examined using radiocarbon dates. The granaries at Dhra' used suspended floors on stone piers to keep grain dry and away from rodents. Storage changes social life: it allows larger settled groups and creates something worth protecting, whether from floods or neighbours. Building required roughly 11,000 working days by one estimate, implying coordinated labour from a community of a few hundred. Jericho's spring, flowing year round, explains why settlement persisted here through later millennia.

picture.alt: Stone Neolithic tower of Tell es-Sultan, Jericho, exposed in Kenyon's excavation trench
picture.credit: Deror_avi, via Wikimedia Commons

jericho-tower-8300bce.dating_note: Tower and wall belong to Pre-Pottery Neolithic A Jericho; Barkai and Liran date the tower roughly to 8300 BC. Bar-Yosef reads the wall as flood protection rather than defence.

koster-dog-burials-8500bce.summary: At the deeply stratified Koster site in Illinois river valley, Early Archaic people laid three dogs in individual shallow pits without grave goods. Direct radiocarbon dating in 2019 placed their bones between about 10,110 and 9,680 years ago, making them the earliest known dog burials in Americas and among oldest anywhere. A dog from Stilwell II nearby is of similar age. Dogs had crossed from Asia with the first Americans; the burials show them treated as companions, hunting partners or pack carriers worth individual interment. Dog bone in a human coprolite at Hinds Cave, Texas, dated about 9,260 years ago, shows dogs were also eaten in some contexts.

sources.title: Perri, A., Widga, C., Lawler, D., Martin, T., Loebel, T., Farnsworth, K., Kohn, L. and Buenger, B., 'New evidence of the earliest domestic dogs in the Americas', American Antiquity 84 (2019)
sources.author: Perri, A., Widga, C., Lawler, D., Martin, T., Loebel, T., Farnsworth, K., Kohn, L. and Buenger, B.
sources.confirms: Directly dates the Koster dog burials to 10,110 to 9,680 cal BP as the earliest in the Americas.

sources.title: Tito, R. Y. et al., 'Brief communication: DNA from early Holocene American dog', American Journal of Physical Anthropology 145 (2011), 653-657 (2011)
sources.author: Tito, R. Y. et al.
sources.confirms: Reports dog bone in a human coprolite from Hinds Cave, Texas, dated 9260 cal BP, with mitochondrial DNA confirming domestic dog.

sources.title: Morey, D. F. and Wiant, M. D., 'Early Holocene domestic dog burials from the North American Midwest', Current Anthropology 33 (1992)
sources.author: Morey, D. F. and Wiant, M. D.
sources.confirms: First report of the Koster and Stilwell dog burials.
sources.qualifies: Only bibliographic details could be read.

koster-dog-burials-8500bce.detail: Koster's 14 occupation horizons span 9,000 years and gave American archaeology one of its reference sequences. Dog burials elsewhere in Archaic Midwest and Southeast follow for millennia. Dogs remained the only domestic animal in most of North America until turkeys and, after 1500, European livestock. Koster dogs were medium sized, about 17 kg, with no sign of butchery. Direct dating resolved doubts about earlier dates derived from associated charcoal. Dog burials at Koster coincide with early Holocene settlement on river terraces rich in nuts and fish.

picture.alt: Students excavating in deep trenches at the Koster site in Illinois, 1973
picture.credit: Arthur Greenberg, US National Archives (DOCUMERICA), via Wikimedia Commons

koster-dog-burials-8500bce.dating_note: Perri et al. 2019 directly date Koster dog burials to 10,110 to 9,680 cal BP and a Stilwell II dog to a similar age; Tito et al. 2011 date a dog bone in Hinds Cave coprolite to 9260 cal BP. Dogs arrived with the first Americans; these are the earliest American dog burials. Year corrected on 15 November 2026 to the sourced span.

rice-shangshan-9000bce.summary: At Shangshan in Zhejiang, south of Yangzi delta, early Holocene people tempered their thick red pottery with rice husks and left rice phytoliths in their pits. Direct dates on phytoliths show rice exploitation by about 9400 years ago, with proportion of fish-scale decorated bulliform cells, a marker of domestication, rising steadily over the following millennium. Shangshan culture was a sedentary community of foragers who used grinding stones and lived in post-built houses from about 10,000 years ago. Rice here was gathered from wild stands and progressively managed, the start of a domestication process that took three thousand years.

sources.title: Zuo, X. et al., 'Dating rice remains through phytolith carbon-14 study reveals domestication at the beginning of the Holocene', PNAS 114 (2017)
sources.author: Zuo, X. et al.
sources.confirms: Dates Shangshan rice phytoliths to about 9400 cal BP and shows a rising proportion of domesticated-type bulliform cells through the sequence.

sources.title: Zhang, C. and Hung, H.-C., 'The emergence of agriculture in southern China', Antiquity 84 (2010)
sources.author: Zhang, C. and Hung, H.-C.
sources.confirms: Describes Shangshan as an early sedentary culture of about 10,000 to 8,500 cal BP with rice-tempered pottery and grinding tools.

rice-shangshan-9000bce.detail: Rice domestication is marked by non-shattering spikelet bases, larger grains and wider bulliform phytoliths; Shangshan shows the first of these trends. Unlike wheat, rice grew in wet lowlands and was cultivated with fire and flooding, as Kuahuqiao shows. Shangshan's pottery, among earliest in region with rice temper, ties cooking and cultivation. Shangshan culture sites number about twenty in Qiantang river basin, with large storage pits and some ditch-enclosed settlements. Pottery was made with coarse clay mixed with rice chaff, which made vessels lighter.

picture.alt: Red pottery pot of the Shangshan culture, 9000 to 6800 BCE, from the Xiatang site, Zhejiang
picture.credit: Furius, via Wikimedia Commons

rice-shangshan-9000bce.dating_note: Zuo et al. 2017 date Shangshan phytoliths to about 9400 cal BP for the earliest rice exploitation, with domestication traits increasing through 8600 cal BP; the culture spans about 10,000 to 8,500 cal BP. Year corrected on 15 November 2026 to the sourced span.

guila-naquitz-squash-8000bce.summary: Kent Flannery's excavation of Guilá Naquitz, a dry rock shelter in Valley of Oaxaca, recovered seeds and stem fragments of squash, Cucurbita pepo, from layers used by small bands of foragers. Direct accelerator radiocarbon dates obtained in 1997 place them between 10,000 and 8,000 years ago, with seeds and peduncles larger and thicker than wild forms, the hallmarks of domestication, by about 10,000 years ago. Squash was therefore domesticated in Mexico as early as wheat in Near East, by mobile hunter-gatherers rather than villagers. Two tiny maize cobs from the same cave date to about 6,250 years ago, among the earliest cobs known.

sources.title: Smith, B. D., 'The initial domestication of Cucurbita pepo in the Americas 10,000 years ago', Science 276 (1997)
sources.author: Smith, B. D.
sources.confirms: Reports directly dated domesticated Cucurbita pepo seeds and peduncles from Guilá Naquitz at 10,000 to 8,000 cal BP, with domestication by about 10,000 cal BP.

sources.title: Piperno, D. R. and Flannery, K. V., 'The earliest archaeological maize (Zea mays L.) from highland Mexico: new accelerator mass spectrometry dates and their implications', PNAS 98 (2001)
sources.author: Piperno, D. R. and Flannery, K. V.
sources.confirms: Dates maize cobs from Guilá Naquitz to about 6250 cal BP.

guila-naquitz-squash-8000bce.detail: Cucurbita pepo was probably first valued for its seeds and as containers, since wild flesh is bitter. Beans joined squash and maize much later to form Three Sisters complex. Guilá Naquitz demonstrates that domestication need not follow sedentism; in Mesoamerica villages came millennia after first crops. Guilá Naquitz was occupied seasonally by groups of perhaps five people, who left acorns, piñon nuts, agave and wild beans alongside squash. Bottle gourd from the same layers shows early use of a second cucurbit for containers.

picture.alt: Rock shelter of Guilá Naquitz in the hills of Oaxaca, Mexico
picture.credit: Jerry Friedman, via Wikimedia Commons

guila-naquitz-squash-8000bce.dating_note: Smith 1997 directly dates Cucurbita pepo seeds and peduncles from Guilá Naquitz to 10,000 to 8,000 cal BP, with the oldest domesticated specimens about 10,000 cal BP; maize cobs from the same cave date to about 6250 cal BP.

kuk-swamp-taro-banana-8000bce.summary: In Wahgi valley of Papua New Guinea at 1,560 metres, drainage work in 1970s exposed ancient ditches and pits in the Kuk tea plantation swamp. Jack Golson's excavations, extended by Tim Denham from 1998, revealed Phase 1 features of about 10,000 years ago, pits, stake holes and runnels on the wetland edge, with starch grains of taro and phytoliths of banana on stone tools. Phase 2, dated about 6,950 to 6,440 years ago, shows regular mounds for planting in drained soil, and Phase 3 from about 4,000 years ago adds networks of drainage ditches. Denham argues New Guinea was an independent centre of agriculture based on vegetatively propagated root and tree crops rather than seeds. UNESCO inscribed Kuk in 2008.

sources.title: Denham, T. P. et al., 'Origins of agriculture at Kuk Swamp in the highlands of New Guinea', Science 301 (2003)
sources.author: Denham, T. P. et al.
sources.confirms: Reports Phase 1 features about 10,000 cal BP with taro starch and banana phytoliths, and mounded cultivation in Phase 2, establishing New Guinea as an independent agricultural centre.

sources.title: Denham, T., Golson, J. and Hughes, P., 'Phase 2: mounded cultivation at Kuk, in Golson, Denham, Hughes, Swadling and Muke (eds), Ten Thousand Years of Cultivation at Kuk Swamp in the Highlands of Papua New Guinea', ANU Press, Terra Australis 46 (2017)
sources.author: Denham, T., Golson, J. and Hughes, P.
sources.confirms: Dates Phase 2 to 6950 to 6440 cal BP with mounds, Musa phytoliths and taro evidence.

kuk-swamp-taro-banana-8000bce.detail: Bananas of the Musa section Eumusa were domesticated here and spread to Asia and Africa. Pigs arrived later from Southeast Asia. Because root crops leave no seeds, Kuk's evidence depends on microfossils and landscape features, which is why some scholars doubt Phase 1 cultivation. Highland New Guinea valleys were forested 10,000 years ago, and charcoal and grass pollen show clearance accelerating with cultivation. Sugar cane also has a New Guinea origin. Drainage ditches of Phase 3 run in grids covering hectares.

picture.alt: Satellite image of the Kuk Swamp area in the Wahgi valley, Papua New Guinea highlands
picture.credit: NASA: JPL, via Wikimedia Commons

kuk-swamp-taro-banana-8000bce.dating_note: Denham et al. 2003 date Phase 1 at Kuk to about 10,000 cal BP, with cultivation of taro and banana; Phase 2 mounded cultivation is dated 6950 to 6440 cal BP. 8000 BCE marks Phase 1; some scholars accept only Phase 2 as secure agriculture.

millet-cishan-8000bce.summary: On the dry loess plateau of north China, farmers domesticated two small-grained cereals suited to short summers and poor rain: broomcorn millet and foxtail millet. At Cishan in Hebei, storage pits held tens of tonnes of decayed grain; Lu Houyuan identified it by phytoliths as broomcorn millet dated 10,300 to 8,700 years ago, with foxtail millet appearing by 8,700 years ago. Zhao Zhijun has questioned the oldest Cishan dates and treats charred, directly dated grains from Xinglonggou in Inner Mongolia at about 7,670 to 7,610 years ago as the earliest secure domesticated millet. Millet starch on grinding stones at Nanzhuangtou and Donghulin from 11,500 years ago shows a long use of wild millets before domestication.

sources.title: Lu, H. et al., 'Earliest domestication of common millet (Panicum miliaceum) in East Asia extended to 10,000 years ago', PNAS 106 (2009)
sources.author: Lu, H. et al.
sources.confirms: Identifies broomcorn millet phytoliths at Cishan dated 10,300 to 8,700 cal BP, with foxtail millet by 8,700 cal BP.

sources.title: Zhao, Z., 'New archaeobotanic data for the study of the origins of agriculture in China', Current Anthropology 52 (2011)
sources.author: Zhao, Z.
sources.confirms: Reports directly dated domesticated millet grains at Xinglonggou of 7670 to 7610 cal BP and cautions about the context of the earliest Cishan dates.

sources.title: Yang, X. et al., 'Early millet use in northern China', PNAS 109 (2012)
sources.author: Yang, X. et al.
sources.confirms: Finds millet starch on grinding stones at Nanzhuangtou and Donghulin from about 11,500 cal BP, before domestication.

millet-cishan-8000bce.detail: Millet farming supported Peiligang, Cishan and Xinglongwa cultures and later Yangshao villages, with pigs and dogs as main domestic animals. Broomcorn millet reached Europe by second millennium BCE. The dating dispute turns on whether phytoliths in open pits can be securely dated. Millet needs only a short growing season and tolerates drought, which fitted loess soils and a monsoon climate with dry springs. Broomcorn millet reached Caucasus and Europe by 2000 BCE through steppe contacts. Isotopes in bones of early farmers and their pigs show heavy reliance on millet.

picture.alt: Grains of broomcorn millet, Panicum miliaceum, in their husks, close-up with millimetre scale
picture.credit: Stefan.lefnaer, via Wikimedia Commons

millet-cishan-8000bce.dating_note: Lu et al. 2009 date Cishan millet phytoliths to 10,300 to 8,700 cal BP, but Zhao Zhijun cautions that the earliest Cishan dates lack secure context; Xinglonggou's directly dated millet grains at 7670 to 7610 cal BP are the earliest secure domesticated millet. 8000 BCE is a compromise between the two positions.

pesse-canoe-8000bce.summary: Road builders cutting through a peat bog near Pesse in Drenthe in 1955 pulled out a hollowed Scots pine trunk 298 cm long and 44 cm wide. Radiocarbon dates place it between about 8200 and 7600 BCE, which makes it the oldest boat yet found. Mesolithic foragers felled the pine with flint axes and hollowed it with adzes and probably fire, producing a shallow craft suited to lakes and streams of the post-glacial lowlands. Doubts that so narrow a log could float a person were tested in 2001 when a replica carried a paddler. Pesse and Mediterranean dugouts of La Marmotta show how early and how widely log boats were used.

sources.title: Gibaja, J. F. et al., 'The first Neolithic boats in the Mediterranean: the settlement of La Marmotta (Anguillara Sabazia, Italy)', PLoS ONE 19 (2024), e0299765 (2024)
sources.author: Gibaja, J. F. et al.
sources.confirms: Cites the Pesse canoe at 3 m long with a date range of 7920 to 6470 BC in its review of early dugouts.

sources.title: Rijksdienst voor het Cultureel Erfgoed, 'Pesse canoe', Maritime Stepping Stones (MaSS) database
sources.author: Rijksdienst voor het Cultureel Erfgoed
sources.confirms: Records dimensions of 298 by 44 cm, Scots pine, found in 1955, with radiocarbon dating to the early Mesolithic.

sources.title: Encyclopedie Drenthe, 'Kano van Pesse', Geheugen van Drenthe
sources.author: Encyclopedie Drenthe
sources.confirms: Gives C14 dates of 8200 to 7600 BC, dimensions of about 3 m by 45 cm in Scots pine, and the 1955 find during road works.

pesse-canoe-8000bce.detail: The canoe is displayed at Drents Museum in Assen. Dugouts appear independently wherever large straight trunks grow: Dufuna in Nigeria at about 6000 BCE, Kuahuqiao in China around 6000 BCE and Noyen-sur-Seine in France. Their survival depends on waterlogged burial, so the record is biased toward bogs and lake beds. Pine was softer to work than oak, and early Mesolithic pine forests covered the drained North Sea plain known as Doggerland. Paddles from Star Carr in England and Duvensee in Germany belong to same centuries.

picture.alt: The Pesse dugout canoe, a hollowed Scots pine log about three metres long, Drents Museum, Assen
picture.credit: Drents Museum, Assen, via Wikimedia Commons

pesse-canoe-8000bce.dating_note: Radiocarbon dates on Pesse canoe fall between 8200 and 7600 cal BC; Gibaja et al. 2024 quote 7920 to 6470 BC for the dugout group including Pesse. 8000 BCE is a rounded midpoint.

pig-domestication-anatolia-china-8000bce.summary: Wild boar became domestic pigs at least twice. At Çayönü Tepesi in southeast Anatolia, pig bones shift slowly through successive Pre-Pottery Neolithic phases, and pig management in the upper Tigris dates to around 10,500 years ago. In China, geometric analysis of molar shape shows domestic pigs at Jiahu in Henan by at least 6600 BCE, and East Asian pig mitochondrial lineages are distinct from western ones, with ancient bones from the Yellow River basin matching modern Chinese pigs. Pigs convert village waste into meat and fat, needing no pasture, which suited sedentary farmers in both regions.

sources.title: Ervynck, A., Dobney, K., Hongo, H. and Meadow, R., 'Born free? New evidence for the status of Sus scrofa at Neolithic Çayönü Tepesi', Paléorient 27 (2001)
sources.author: Ervynck, A., Dobney, K., Hongo, H. and Meadow, R.
sources.confirms: Presents new evidence on the status of wild boar and pig at Çayönü through the Pre-Pottery Neolithic sequence.
sources.qualifies: Only title and bibliographic page could be read; phase-by-phase results were not confirmed from the page.

sources.title: Cucchi, T., Hulme-Beaman, A., Yuan, J. and Dobney, K., 'Early Neolithic pig domestication at Jiahu, Henan Province, China: clues from molar shape analyses', Journal of Archaeological Science 38 (2011)
sources.author: Cucchi, T., Hulme-Beaman, A., Yuan, J. and Dobney, K.
sources.confirms: States that pig domestication at Jiahu dates back to at least 6600 cal BC on molar shape evidence.

sources.title: Larson, G. et al., 'Patterns of East Asian pig domestication, migration, and turnover revealed by modern and ancient DNA', PNAS 107 (2010)
sources.author: Larson, G. et al.
sources.confirms: Reports over 1,500 modern and 18 ancient pig sequences supporting independent East Asian domestication with multiple possible centres.

sources.title: Zeder, M. A., 'Domestication and early agriculture in the Mediterranean Basin: origins, diffusion, and impact', PNAS 105 (2008)
sources.author: Zeder, M. A.
sources.confirms: Dates Near Eastern sheep and goat domestication to 11,000 to 10,500 BP and places pig domestication in the same region soon after.

pig-domestication-anatolia-china-8000bce.detail: Two lines of evidence converge: morphology, since domestic pigs show smaller molars and altered tooth shape, and genetics, since East Asian domestic pigs descend from local wild boar rather than from Near Eastern stock. Genetic evidence rests on over 1,500 modern sequences and 18 ancient samples from six Chinese sites. Independent domestication in widely separated regions is a recurring pattern in this period, seen also in cereals, cattle and cotton.

picture.alt: A wild boar, Sus scrofa, standing in woodland at San Rossore near Pisa
picture.credit: Daniele Napolitano, via Wikimedia Commons

pig-domestication-anatolia-china-8000bce.dating_note: Zeder 2008 places Near Eastern pig domestication soon after 10,500 BP in the upper Tigris; Cucchi et al. 2011 date Jiahu domestic pigs to at least 6600 cal BC; 8000 BCE is a midpoint for the two independent processes.

warren-field-pit-calendar-8000bce.summary: Aerial photography of a field at Crathes in Aberdeenshire revealed a row of twelve pits, excavated by Murray, Murray and Fraser between 2004 and 2006 and dated by radiocarbon from about 8000 BCE, with recutting over four millennia. Vincent Gaffney argues that the pits' varying sizes mimic the phases of moon across twelve lunar months, while the row aligns on a notch in horizon where the midwinter sun rises, allowing yearly correction of a lunar count. If right, hunter-gatherers were tracking time with a built structure five millennia before Stonehenge. A Neolithic timber hall of 3820 to 3690 BCE later stood beside it.

sources.title: Gaffney, V. et al., 'Time and a place: a luni-solar 'time-reckoner' from 8th millennium BC Scotland', Internet Archaeology 34 (2013)
sources.author: Gaffney, V. et al.
sources.confirms: Interprets the Warren Field pit alignment as a luni-solar time reckoner dating from the eighth millennium BC.

sources.title: Murray, H. K., Murray, J. C. and Fraser, S. M., 'A Tale of the Unknown Unknowns: A Mesolithic Pit Alignment and a Neolithic Timber Hall at Warren Field, Crathes, Aberdeenshire', Oxbow Books (2009)
sources.author: Murray, H. K., Murray, J. C. and Fraser, S. M.
sources.confirms: Reports twelve pits with dates from 8210 to 3650 cal BC and a timber hall dated 3820 to 3690 cal BC.

warren-field-pit-calendar-8000bce.detail: Critics point out that pit alignments are common and that lunar readings require assumptions about which pits were open at once. The dating of individual pits is secure. Nabta Playa, Newgrange and Stonehenge show later built alignments on solstice sunrises and sunsets. Pits were recut and some held burnt material and small stone tools. Alignment on a notch in horizon depends on tree cover, which pollen suggests was open birch and hazel woodland then.

picture.alt: Diagram of the Warren Field pit alignment with simulated moon phases above the row of pits
picture.credit: Gaffney, Fitch, Ramsey, Yorston and colleagues (2013), via Wikimedia Commons

warren-field-pit-calendar-8000bce.dating_note: The pit alignment at Warren Field, Crathes, has radiocarbon dates spanning 8210 to 3650 cal BC, with earliest Mesolithic pits around 8000 BC; Gaffney et al.'s reading of it as a lunar calendar is an interpretation not shared by all.

wyrie-swamp-boomerangs-8000bce.summary: Peat cutting at Wyrie Swamp near Millicent in South Australia exposed a layer of waterlogged wood. Roger Luebbers excavated in 1973 and recovered more than 25 wooden implements, among them three complete boomerangs, a barbed spear, digging sticks and a pointed stake, in peat dated between 10,200 and 8,990 radiocarbon years ago. The boomerangs, of she-oak wood with carefully shaped aerofoil sections, are the oldest known anywhere; some are returning types. Wood rarely survives in Australian sites, so Wyrie Swamp finds are nearly the only direct view of early Holocene Aboriginal toolkits, which were dominated by timber rather than stone. Boomerang aerodynamics show sustained empirical design.

sources.title: Luebbers, R. A., 'Ancient boomerangs discovered in South Australia', Nature 253 (1975)
sources.author: Luebbers, R. A.
sources.confirms: Reports more than 25 wooden implements including three complete boomerangs from peat dated 10,200 plus or minus 150 to 8,990 plus or minus 120 BP.

sources.title: Luebbers, R. A., 'Ancient boomerangs discovered in South Australia', Nature 253 (1975) 39
sources.author: Luebbers, Roger A.
sources.confirms: Excavator's report of the January 1974 Wyrie Swamp excavation: a wooden tool industry in basal peat dated between 10,200 and 8,990 BP, including three complete boomerangs, a short spear, digging sticks and a barbed javelin fragment, described as the oldest evidence of the boomerang.
sources.qualifies: Page not fetched; included as archival pointer only.

wyrie-swamp-boomerangs-8000bce.verification_note: Dates, counts and boomerangs confirmed from Luebbers 1975; the second source is a bibliographic pointer only.
wyrie-swamp-boomerangs-8000bce.detail: Stone tools at site include flaked scrapers that would have shaped the wood. Boomerangs of similar age are depicted in rock art in Arnhem Land. Finds show hunting equipment adjusted to open wetlands with waterfowl, a landscape that disappeared as climate dried. Wooden tools outnumber stone at Wyrie, reversing the usual balance of surviving material. Waterlogged peat excluded oxygen and preserved cell structure of wood.
wyrie-swamp-boomerangs-8000bce.dating_note: Luebbers 1975 dates the peat containing Wyrie Swamp wooden tools to between 10,200 and 8,990 radiocarbon years BP, about 10,000 to 9,000 BP; 8000 BCE is a rounded midpoint.

gobero-green-sahara-7700bce.summary: Paul Sereno's expedition searching for dinosaurs in Ténéré desert of Niger found in 2000 a cemetery on dunes above a vanished lake. Excavation revealed two occupations: Kiffian hunter-fishers from 7700 to 6200 BCE, tall people who left bone harpoons, fish hooks and pottery, and later Tenerian pastoralists from 5200 to 2500 BCE, buried with cattle bones and jewellery. About 200 graves were recorded, with some Kiffian burials around 7500 BCE in tightly flexed positions. Christopher Stojanowski's skeletal study found the two groups biologically distinct, so Sahara's lakes drew successive peoples. Gobero documents how early Holocene monsoon rains turned the desert into savanna with lakes full of Nile perch and crocodile, supporting sedentary fishers before herding.

sources.title: Sereno, P. C. et al., 'Lakeside cemeteries in the Sahara: 5000 years of Holocene population and environmental change', PLoS ONE 3 (2008)
sources.author: Sereno, P. C. et al.
sources.confirms: Reports Kiffian occupation at Gobero from 7700 to 6200 BCE and Tenerian from 5200 to 2500 BCE, with about 200 burials and lakeside fishing economy.

sources.title: Stojanowski, C. M., 'Iwo Eleru's place among Late Pleistocene and Early Holocene populations of North and East Africa', American Journal of Physical Anthropology 153 (2014)
sources.author: Stojanowski, C. M.
sources.confirms: Compares Holocene Saharan and African skeletal samples including Gobero's Kiffian and Tenerian groups.

gobero-green-sahara-7700bce.detail: Pollen, fish bones and lake sediments date the humid phases and the arid gap between 6200 and 5200 BCE that separates the two populations, which matches the 8200 year event's arid aftermath. Harpoon and wavy-line pottery traditions link Gobero to Nile. The site shows an African path to sedentism built on fishing rather than cereals. One Tenerian grave held a woman and two children arranged facing each other on a bed of flowers, dated about 5300 BCE. Harpoons of bone and fishhooks show Nile perch over a metre long were caught. Kiffian people averaged over 1.8 metres in height.

picture.alt: Aerial view of the Gobero archaeological site in the Ténéré desert of Niger
picture.credit: Sereno, Garcea, Jousse and colleagues (PLoS ONE 2008), via Wikimedia Commons

gobero-green-sahara-7700bce.dating_note: Sereno et al. 2008 date Kiffian occupation at Gobero to 7700 to 6200 BCE and a later Tenerian occupation to 5200 to 2500 BCE; the burials cluster around 7500 BCE for earlier phase.

clay-tokens-accounting-7500bce.summary: From the tenth millennium cal BC, Neolithic sites across West Asia yield small fired-clay cones, spheres, discs and cylinders. Denise Schmandt-Besserat argued from the 1970s that these were counters, each shape standing for a measure of grain or a head of livestock, used from about 8000 BC until, around 3500 BC, they were sealed inside clay envelopes whose impressed surfaces became the first tablets. Lucy Bennison-Chapman re-examined almost 3,000 objects from Neolithic sites and found that even at a single site they served multiple roles, including gaming and ritual, so the counting function is one use among several. Either way, standardised clay shapes let people represent quantity apart from the goods themselves.

sources.title: Bennison-Chapman, L. E., 'Reconsidering 'tokens': the Neolithic origins of accounting or multifunctional, utilitarian tools?', Cambridge Archaeological Journal 29 (2019)
sources.author: Bennison-Chapman, L. E.
sources.confirms: Places small geometric clay objects from the tenth millennium cal BC and argues from almost 3,000 objects and 56 sites that they were multifunctional.

sources.title: Schmandt-Besserat, D., 'The evolution of writing', International Encyclopedia of Social and Behavioral Sciences (Elsevier), author's site (2014)
sources.author: Schmandt-Besserat, D.
sources.venue: International Encyclopedia of Social and Behavioral Sciences (Elsevier), author's site
sources.confirms: States that tokens were used for accounting from 8000 to 3500 BC, enclosed in envelopes around 3500 BC and replaced by impressed tablets about 3200 BC.

sources.title: Schmandt-Besserat, D., 'The envelopes that bear the first writing', Technology and Culture 21 (1980)
sources.author: Schmandt-Besserat, D.
sources.confirms: Presents the envelope and token sequence leading to impressed tablets.
sources.qualifies: JSTOR page gave bibliographic details only; content confirmed through the author's 2014 summary.

clay-tokens-accounting-7500bce.detail: The debate matters for history of computing: Schmandt-Besserat's sequence makes writing grow out of counting, with numerals preceding words. Englund's study of proto-cuneiform accounts shows that the two main numerical systems of archaic tablets echo token types for discrete objects and for capacity. Critics ask why tokens continue in use for millennia after writing exists. Tokens continued in use alongside writing for centuries at Susa and Uruk. Complex tokens with incised lines and perforations cluster in fourth millennium cities, where administrative demands grew with temple estates.

picture.alt: Small clay accounting tokens of cones, spheres and discs from Susa, displayed in the Louvre
picture.credit: Marie-Lan Nguyen, via Wikimedia Commons

clay-tokens-accounting-7500bce.dating_note: Schmandt-Besserat dates tokens from 8000 BC; Bennison-Chapman places first geometric clay objects in the tenth millennium cal BC and reads them as multifunctional. 7500 BCE is a midpoint for their spread.

ain-ghazal-lime-plaster-7200bce.summary: Pre-Pottery Neolithic B villagers in Levant heated limestone to 800 to 900 degrees Celsius, slaked the quicklime with water and spread the paste as hard white floors, burnished and sometimes painted red. Kingery, Vandiver and Prickett call this the first large-scale pyrotechnology, dating its expansion to about 7200 to 6000 BC and noting its heavy fuel cost. At 'Ain Ghazal near Amman, Gary Rollefson's team found in 1983 a pit holding ten large plaster statues 80 to 90 cm high and busts, with a second cache in 1985. Carol Grissom showed the figures were built in stages over reed bundles bound with cord. Controlled high temperature fire, learned on lime, later underlay pottery and metal.

sources.title: Kingery, W. D., Vandiver, P. B. and Prickett, M., 'The beginnings of pyrotechnology, part II: production and use of lime and gypsum plaster in the Pre-Pottery Neolithic Near East', Journal of Field Archaeology 15 (1988)
sources.author: Kingery, W. D., Vandiver, P. B. and Prickett, M.
sources.confirms: Describes heating limestone at 800 to 900 C, slaking, mixing and burnishing, and dates the PPNB plaster expansion to about 7200 to 6000 BC.

sources.title: Grissom, C. A., 'Neolithic statues from 'Ain Ghazal: construction and form', American Journal of Archaeology 104 (2000)
sources.author: Grissom, C. A.
sources.confirms: Describes five large lime plaster statues excavated in 1985, dated to the seventh millennium BC, built by applying plaster to reed bundles bound with cordage.

sources.title: Rollefson, G. O., 'Ritual and ceremony at Neolithic Ain Ghazal (Jordan)', Paléorient 9 (1983)
sources.author: Rollefson, G. O.
sources.confirms: Reports the 1983 discovery of a cache of about ten plaster statues 80 to 90 cm high and eight busts in a pit within an abandoned house.

ain-ghazal-lime-plaster-7200bce.detail: A single house floor could consume several tonnes of limestone and much more wood, so plaster production shaped woodland use around villages. Nahal Hemar cave in Israel preserves collagen-based coatings on baskets and skulls from same horizon. Gypsum plaster, burned at lower temperature, was used in Mesopotamia where limestone was scarce. Experimental burning shows a kiln of limestone and brushwood reaches lime-making temperature in hours, but fuel demand for whole settlements has been estimated at thousands of trees per generation.

picture.alt: Lime plaster statue from 'Ain Ghazal, Jordan, with a tall body, painted eyes and bitumen pupils, in the Louvre
picture.credit: Zunkir, via Wikimedia Commons

ain-ghazal-lime-plaster-7200bce.dating_note: Kingery, Vandiver and Prickett date Pre-Pottery Neolithic B plaster boom to about 7200 to 6000 BC; the 'Ain Ghazal statue caches found in 1983 and 1985 belong to the seventh millennium BC.

catalhoyuk-town-7100bce.summary: On Konya plain, James Mellaart's 1961 excavation revealed a mound of mudbrick houses built wall to wall with no streets, entered by ladder through the roof, their interiors plastered and painted with hunting scenes, and their dead buried beneath floors. Ian Hodder's project from 1993 showed that occupation grew in density into the middle levels and then eased after 6500 BC as houses became more independent and people dispersed. Bayesian radiocarbon modelling puts the start of East Mound about two centuries later than once thought. Several thousand people lived without visible chiefs or temples, relying on houses as the unit of storage, memory and ritual.

sources.title: Hodder, I., 'Çatalhöyük: the leopard changes its spots. A summary of recent work', Anatolian Studies 64 (2014)
sources.author: Hodder, I.
sources.confirms: Argues for increased size and density of occupation into the middle levels and dispersal after 6500 BC through mobility and household independence.

sources.title: Bayliss, A. et al., 'Getting to the bottom of it all: a Bayesian approach to dating the start of Çatalhöyük', Journal of World Prehistory 28 (2015)
sources.author: Bayliss, A. et al.
sources.confirms: Applies Bayesian modelling to the earliest East Mound levels and places them about 200 years later than previously thought.
sources.qualifies: Abstract gives no absolute start year; the 7100 BC figure is the model result reported in the paper body.

sources.title: Mellaart, J., 'Excavations at Çatal Hüyük: first preliminary report, 1961', Anatolian Studies 12 (1962)
sources.author: Mellaart, J.
sources.confirms: Records discovery during the 1958 Konya plain survey and the first season of excavation in 1961.

catalhoyuk-town-7100bce.verification_note: A 7100 BC start date rests on Bayliss and colleagues' chronological model, whose abstract reports only a relative shift; end date and density trend are confirmed by Hodder.
catalhoyuk-town-7100bce.detail: Houses were rebuilt on same footprint for generations, with ovens under ladder, platforms over burials and bulls' horns set in walls. Obsidian from Cappadocia, shells from Mediterranean and woven bast textiles show wide connections. Çatalhöyük's lack of streets and public buildings makes it a town without urban institutions, a counterpoint to Uruk three millennia later. Isotopes show residents ate cereals and sheep from fields some distance off, and a wall painting once read as a town plan beneath an erupting volcano remains debated.

picture.alt: Interior of a reconstructed Çatalhöyük house showing a roof ladder, plastered walls and a hearth
picture.credit: Stipich Béla, via Wikimedia Commons

catalhoyuk-town-7100bce.dating_note: Bayliss et al. 2015 model the start of East Mound about two centuries later than earlier estimates; Hodder summarises occupation from the early seventh millennium with dispersal after 6500 BC. The conventional range 7100 to 5950 BC is used here.

atlit-yam-tuberculosis-7000bce.summary: Off Carmel coast of Israel, ten metres under Mediterranean, lies a Pre-Pottery Neolithic village occupied between 9250 and 8160 years ago. Ehud Galili and Yaacov Nir recorded a stone-lined well 1.5 metres across and 5.7 metres deep, among oldest water wells known, whose rim shows sea level then stood about 16 metres lower. A woman and infant buried together carry DNA and mycolic acid lipids of Mycobacterium tuberculosis, direct evidence of human tuberculosis around 7000 BCE, before cattle herding reached the coast. Dense villages with wells, stored grain and livestock gave infections a stable home.

sources.title: Hershkovitz, I. et al., 'Detection and molecular characterization of 9000-year-old Mycobacterium tuberculosis from a Neolithic settlement in the Eastern Mediterranean', PLoS ONE 3 (2008)
sources.author: Hershkovitz, I. et al.
sources.confirms: Reports M. tuberculosis DNA at five loci and mycolic acid biomarkers in a woman and infant at Atlit-Yam, dated 9250 to 8160 cal BP.

sources.title: Galili, E. and Nir, Y., 'The submerged Pre-Pottery Neolithic water well of Atlit-Yam, northern Israel, and its palaeoenvironmental implications', The Holocene 3 (1993)
sources.author: Galili, E. and Nir, Y.
sources.confirms: Describes a well 1.5 m in diameter and 5.7 m deep, 10 m below present sea level, implying sea level about 16 m lower at c. 7900 BP.

atlit-yam-tuberculosis-7000bce.detail: The site sank as post-glacial seas rose, sealing it in sand. Lipid biomarkers complement ancient DNA because they survive where nucleic acids degrade. The find undercuts the older idea that human tuberculosis derived from cattle after dairying began. Villagers fished, kept cattle, sheep, goats and pigs and grew wheat, barley and lentils; a semicircle of standing stones near a spring hints at ritual use of water. Fish bones show deep-water species, implying boats. Skeletal lesions in other burials point to diving injuries among fishermen.

picture.alt: Semicircle of upright stones from the submerged Neolithic village of Atlit-Yam, off the coast of Israel
picture.credit: Hanay, via Wikimedia Commons

atlit-yam-tuberculosis-7000bce.dating_note: Atlit-Yam's calibrated dates span 9250 to 8160 BP; Galili and Nir place the well at about 7900 BP.

catalhoyuk-woven-textiles-7000bce.summary: Charred cloth wrapping burials under house floors at Çatalhöyük ranks among the earliest woven textiles known in the Near East and Europe. Mellaart's excavators took its fibre for wool or flax; scanning electron microscopy showed in 2021 that it is bast fibre from local oak trees, stripped from bark, spun and woven on a loom. Further south, Nahal Hemar cave in the Judean desert preserved twined linen headgear, a napkin and baskets in a layer dated 8210 to 7300 BCE, with collagen-based coatings that served as an early adhesive. Flax, grown for fibre, and tree bast were both in use before wool-bearing sheep existed.

sources.title: Rast-Eicher, A., Karg, S. and Bender Jørgensen, L., 'The use of local fibres for textiles at Neolithic Çatalhöyük', Antiquity 95 (2021)
sources.author: Rast-Eicher, A., Karg, S. and Bender Jørgensen, L.
sources.confirms: Identifies Çatalhöyük woven textiles as locally sourced oak bast rather than flax, among the earliest weaving in the Near East and Europe.

sources.title: Solazzo, C. et al., 'Identification of the earliest collagen- and plant-based coatings from Neolithic artefacts (Nahal Hemar cave, Israel)', Scientific Reports 6 (2016)
sources.author: Solazzo, C. et al.
sources.confirms: Describes twined linen headgear, a napkin and baskets in Nahal Hemar layer 4 dated 8210 to 7300 cal BC, with collagen coatings.

catalhoyuk-woven-textiles-7000bce.detail: Textile survival before 7000 BCE depends on charring or desert dryness, so these finds are a visible edge of a larger craft. Spindle whorls and loom weights are scarce at Çatalhöyük, suggesting spinning with simple sticks and weaving on ground looms. Linen remained Egypt's main fibre into dynastic times, as the Tarkhan dress shows. Weaving needs a loom holding warp under tension; simple weights or ground pegs suffice, so loom evidence is often absent even where cloth survives.

picture.alt: Fragment of woven cloth from the Nahal Hemar cave hoard, displayed in the Israel Museum, Jerusalem
picture.credit: Gary Todd from Xinzheng, China, via Wikimedia Commons

catalhoyuk-woven-textiles-7000bce.dating_note: Çatalhöyük textiles come from seventh millennium BC burials; Nahal Hemar layer 4 finds are dated 8210 to 7300 cal BC with a skull coating at 8920 to 8430 cal BC.

early-khartoum-wavy-line-pottery-7000bce.summary: Arkell's 1940s excavation at Khartoum Hospital defined a Mesolithic culture of fishers and hunters who made globular pots decorated by dragging a catfish spine or comb in wavy lines across wet clay. Radiocarbon now places this wavy-line and later dotted wavy-line pottery between about 8000 and 5000 BCE along the Nile from Sudan into Egypt and across Sahara to Mali and Niger, a signature of an aquatic way of life around early Holocene lakes and rivers. Mohammed-Ali and Khabir review Sudanese sequence and Friederike Jesse maps the wider spread. These potters used no domestic plants or animals; ceramics served fishing and gathering communities for three millennia before herders arrived.

sources.title: Mohammed-Ali, A. S. and Khabir, A.-R. M., 'The wavy line and the dotted wavy line pottery in the prehistory of the central Nile and the Sahara-Sahel belt', African Archaeological Review 20 (2003)
sources.author: Mohammed-Ali, A. S. and Khabir, A.-R. M.
sources.confirms: Reviews wavy-line and dotted wavy-line pottery across the central Nile and Sahara-Sahel in the early to middle Holocene.

sources.title: Jesse, F., 'Early pottery in northern Africa: an overview', Journal of African Archaeology 8 (2010)
sources.author: Jesse, F.
sources.confirms: Maps early northern African pottery including Khartoum-tradition wares among fisher-forager groups.

early-khartoum-wavy-line-pottery-7000bce.verification_note: Both sources confirm this tradition and its distribution; an 8000 to 5000 BC span is a synthesis figure drawn from general scholarship.
early-khartoum-wavy-line-pottery-7000bce.detail: Pots were often large and thick, suited to cooking fish and wild grain. Decoration styles shared over 3,000 km imply contact along Saharan waterways. When cattle herding reached Nile around 5000 BCE at sites like Kadero, pottery traditions continued with new motifs. Arkell's Khartoum Hospital site also produced bone harpoons and grinding stones, and burials in flexed positions. Dotted wavy-line decoration, made with a rocker stamp, succeeded the plain wavy line around 6000 BCE and spread as far as Mali.
early-khartoum-wavy-line-pottery-7000bce.dating_note: Wavy-line and dotted wavy-line pottery of the Khartoum Mesolithic dates from about 8000 to 5000 BC across the Nile and Sahara; 7000 BCE is a midpoint for its early spread.

jiahu-bone-flutes-7000bce.summary: Graves at Jiahu in Henan province, occupied from about 7000 to 5700 BCE, contained flutes made from wing bones of red-crowned cranes, with five to eight finger holes drilled along shaft. Six complete instruments and fragments of about thirty more were recovered; the best preserved still plays and produces a scale close to a modern seven-note scale. Tonal analysis shows a shift from four-tone to seven-tone scales over site's history. Alongside the flutes, Jiahu yielded the earliest fermented drink, incised tortoise shells, domestic pigs and silk traces. The flutes are the oldest playable multi-note instruments, fixing pitch in a physical object.

sources.title: Zhang, J., Harbottle, G., Wang, C. and Kong, Z., 'Oldest playable musical instruments found at Jiahu early Neolithic site in China', Nature 401 (1999)
sources.author: Zhang, J., Harbottle, G., Wang, C. and Kong, Z.
sources.confirms: Describes six complete crane-ulna flutes with 5 to 8 holes and about thirty fragments from Jiahu, occupied 7000 to 5700 BC, the earliest complete playable multinote instruments.

sources.title: Zhang, J., Xiao, X. and Lee, Y. K., 'The early development of music. Analysis of the Jiahu bone flutes', Antiquity 78 (2004)
sources.author: Zhang, J., Xiao, X. and Lee, Y. K.
sources.confirms: Tonal analysis of five flutes shows development from four-tone to seven-tone scales at Jiahu, whose sequence began in the seventh millennium BC.

jiahu-bone-flutes-7000bce.detail: Small holes beside some finger holes show tuning corrections after drilling. Flutes lay beside particular individuals, often with tortoise shells containing pebbles, suggesting ritual specialists. Palaeolithic bone pipes from Germany are older but fragmentary; Jiahu's survive intact enough to be sounded. Crane ulnae are hollow, thin-walled and straight, ideal for a pipe about 20 cm long. Hole spacing on later flutes is more even than on earlier ones, pointing to measured drilling. Flutes were buried mostly with men. Experimental playing produces clear tones over an octave.

picture.alt: Bone flute made from a crane wing bone with drilled finger holes, Jiahu site, Henan Museum
picture.credit: Furius, via Wikimedia Commons

jiahu-bone-flutes-7000bce.dating_note: Jiahu was occupied from about 7000 to 5700 BC; the flutes come from radiocarbon-dated layers through this span, with the earliest around 7000 BC.

jiahu-fermented-beverage-7000bce.summary: Patrick McGovern and Chinese colleagues analysed residues absorbed into pottery jars from Jiahu's earliest phase and found tartaric acid, beeswax markers and compounds matching rice, pointing to a mixed drink of rice, honey and hawthorn fruit or wild grape fermented together around 7000 to 6600 BCE. Grape and hawthorn supplied yeasts and sugars, honey more sugar, and chewed or moulded rice the starch. This is the earliest chemically identified alcoholic beverage. McGovern's team compared it with sealed bronze vessels of Shang and Zhou periods two millennia later whose rice and millet wines were flavoured with herbs and resins, showing a continuous tradition. Fermentation preserved calories and gave early villages a drink for feasting and ritual.

sources.title: McGovern, P. E. et al., 'Fermented beverages of pre- and proto-historic China', PNAS 101 (2004)
sources.author: McGovern, P. E. et al.
sources.confirms: Reports a mixed fermented beverage of rice, honey and hawthorn fruit or grape in Jiahu jars as early as the seventh millennium BC and compares it with Shang and Zhou bronze vessel contents.

sources.title: McGovern, P. et al., 'Early Neolithic wine of Georgia in the South Caucasus', PNAS 114 (2017)
sources.author: McGovern, P. et al.
sources.confirms: Reviews earlier biomolecular evidence for fermented beverages including the Jiahu mixed drink of about 7000 BC.
sources.qualifies: Jiahu is treated as comparative background in this paper.

jiahu-fermented-beverage-7000bce.detail: The method matches biomarkers in ancient residues against modern reference compounds. Grape wine in Caucasus and barley beer in Mesopotamia follow by separate paths. Jiahu's drink was reconstructed commercially in 2005 under name Chateau Jiahu. Jiahu's rice was in early domestication, so this beverage shows one use of the crop beyond gruel. Honey from wild bees supplied yeasts as well as sugar. Later Chinese wines used mould starters called qu to break down starch, a method absent at Jiahu. Pottery jars with narrow necks held the liquid.

picture.alt: Red pottery jar of the Peiligang culture from Xinzheng, Henan, Zhengzhou City Museum
picture.credit: Gary Todd, via Wikimedia Commons

jiahu-fermented-beverage-7000bce.dating_note: McGovern et al. 2004 date Jiahu residues to the seventh millennium BC, 7000 to 6600 BC, from radiocarbon-dated phases of the site.

mehrgarh-dentistry-7000bce.summary: Among skeletons from Mehrgarh's Neolithic cemetery, eleven drilled crowns were found in molars of nine adults, dated between 9,000 and 7,500 years ago. The holes, up to 3.5 mm deep, have smooth, concentric walls and show wear from later chewing, so they were made in living people who went on using the teeth. Experiments with a flint tip spun in a bow drill, the tool Mehrgarh's bead makers used to perforate turquoise and shell, produced matching holes in human enamel in under a minute. The practice vanishes after Period II. The holes may have relieved decay or served another purpose; either way a craft tool was turned on human body with evident skill.

sources.title: Coppa, A. et al., 'Early Neolithic tradition of dentistry', Nature 440 (2006)
sources.author: Coppa, A. et al.
sources.confirms: Reports eleven drilled molar crowns in nine adults from a Neolithic graveyard in Pakistan dated 7,500 to 9,000 years ago and shows flint tips effective for drilling enamel.

sources.title: Petrie, C. A. and Thomas, K. D., 'The topographic and environmental context of the earliest village sites in western South Asia', Antiquity 86 (2012)
sources.author: Petrie, C. A. and Thomas, K. D.
sources.confirms: Provides the settlement context for Mehrgarh among early farming villages of Baluchistan.
sources.qualifies: Does not discuss dentistry.

mehrgarh-dentistry-7000bce.detail: Four of drilled teeth show signs of caries, so some interventions may have targeted disease. No fillings were found. Mehrgarh's bead industry, with microdrills of chert and jasper, supplies the technical context, a reminder that medical acts can grow from craft routines. Rounded edges of some holes show chewing continued after drilling. Bead workshops at Mehrgarh used similar drills on steatite and shell.

picture.alt: Excavated mudbrick structures at the Mehrgarh archaeological site, Balochistan
picture.credit: mhtoori, via Wikimedia Commons

mehrgarh-dentistry-7000bce.dating_note: Coppa et al. 2006 date the drilled teeth to 7,500 to 9,000 years ago from Mehrgarh Period I and II cemetery, about 7000 to 5500 BC.

mehrgarh-farming-7000bce.summary: Below Bolan Pass in Baluchistan, Jean-François Jarrige's French mission excavated from 1974 a village whose earliest, aceramic levels hold mudbrick houses and granary compartments, barley as main crop with einkorn and emmer wheat, and bones of goats, sheep and cattle, dated to about 7000 BCE. Cattle bones shift from wild to domestic size through Mehrgarh's sequence, and Chen Shanyuan's team showed by mitochondrial DNA that zebu, humped cattle, were domesticated from South Asian aurochs in Indus region around 8,000 years ago, separately from Near Eastern taurine cattle. Petrie and Thomas map Mehrgarh and other early villages on alluvial fans in the hills, where farmers built earth barriers to spread floodwater. Mehrgarh is the root of Indus valley farming.

sources.title: Petrie, C. A. and Thomas, K. D., 'The topographic and environmental context of the earliest village sites in western South Asia', Antiquity 86 (2012)
sources.author: Petrie, C. A. and Thomas, K. D.
sources.confirms: Places the earliest farming villages of Baluchistan and Khyber Pakhtunkhwa on alluvial fans where farmers built earth barriers to manage water, with Mehrgarh among the sites surveyed.
sources.qualifies: Abstract does not give Period I dates.

sources.title: Chen, S. et al., 'Zebu cattle are an exclusive legacy of the South Asia Neolithic', Molecular Biology and Evolution 27 (2010)
sources.author: Chen, S. et al.
sources.confirms: Identifies the Indus Valley as the primary centre of zebu domestication, with domestic zebu present about 8,000 years ago.

mehrgarh-farming-7000bce.verification_note: Zebu domestication and this settlement's setting are confirmed; a 7000 BC start for Period I rests on Jarrige's excavation reports.
mehrgarh-farming-7000bce.detail: Bitumen-lined baskets, turquoise and lapis beads and sea shells in burials show trade toward Iran and the coast. Whether wheat and barley arrived from the west or were domesticated locally is debated; barley may have a local wild progenitor. Cotton threads, lost-wax copper and drilled teeth also come from Mehrgarh's early periods. Burials received ochre and ornaments, and infant graves were placed under floors. Mehrgarh's long sequence runs to about 2500 BCE, when Indus cities took over its role as a regional centre.

picture.alt: Excavated mudbrick ruins at Mehrgarh, Balochistan, Pakistan
picture.credit: Ashish_Premier, via Wikimedia Commons

mehrgarh-farming-7000bce.dating_note: Mehrgarh Period I, aceramic Neolithic, is conventionally dated about 7000 to 5500 BC; Chen et al. 2010 place zebu domestication in Indus region about 8000 years ago. Direct radiocarbon dates for Mehrgarh I are few and some scholars favour a start closer to 6500 BC.

neolithic-demographic-transition-7000bce.summary: Cemeteries from early farming villages hold a sharply higher share of children than forager burials. Bocquet-Appel reads this signal as a rise in fertility of about two births per woman as communities settled and switched to cereal porridges, an event he names the Neolithic Demographic Transition. Skeletons show the cost: farmers carry more dental caries, more infection lesions and altered growth compared with hunter-gatherers. Both patterns recur wherever farming begins, in southwest Asia from the eighth millennium BCE and later in Europe, China and the Americas. Population growth, not better health, drove village expansion in this period.

sources.title: Bocquet-Appel, J.-P., 'When the world's population took off: the springboard of the Neolithic Demographic Transition', Science 333 (2011)
sources.author: Bocquet-Appel, J.-P.
sources.confirms: Describes a rise in total fertility of about two births per woman and an abrupt increase in juvenile skeletons in cemeteries as the signal of the transition.

sources.title: Larsen, C. S., 'Biological changes in human populations with agriculture', Annual Review of Anthropology 24 (1995)
sources.author: Larsen, C. S.
sources.confirms: Reports an overall decline in oral and general health among prehistoric farmers relative to foragers, with elevated skeletal and dental pathology.

neolithic-demographic-transition-7000bce.detail: The juvenile proportion in cemeteries rises for several centuries after farming arrives and then stabilises as mortality catches up with fertility. European regional radiocarbon records later showed population booms followed by busts. These demographic swings help explain why crowded settlements like Çatalhöyük, tuberculosis at Atlit-Yam and famine-sensitive milk use appear in this period. Weaning onto cereal gruel shortened birth spacing, a mechanism Bocquet-Appel treats as central, and sedentary life removed limits that mobility placed on carrying infants.
neolithic-demographic-transition-7000bce.dating_note: Bocquet-Appel dates the transition separately in each region as farming arrives; 7000 BCE marks its appearance in the Levant and Anatolia cemeteries he uses.

obsidian-trade-near-east-7000bce.summary: Volcanic glass from Cappadocia and eastern Anatolia reached almost every early Neolithic settlement in Near East, including Jericho and villages in Zagros hundreds of kilometres from any source. Renfrew, Dixon and Cann showed in 1966 that trace elements such as barium and zirconium fingerprint each volcano, letting them map which source supplied which site and model how quantities fell off with distance. Network simulations in 2015 showed that simple village-to-village passing cannot explain the long-distance pattern; organised exchange between hubs is required. Obsidian is the first commodity whose movement can be tracked, and it reveals connections spanning the Pre-Pottery Neolithic world around 7000 BCE.

sources.title: Renfrew, C., Dixon, J. E. and Cann, J. R., 'Obsidian and early cultural contact in the Near East', Proceedings of the Prehistoric Society 32 (1966)
sources.author: Renfrew, C., Dixon, J. E. and Cann, J. R.
sources.confirms: Applies trace-element characterisation to determine natural sources of obsidian found at nearly every Early Neolithic settlement in the Near East, many far from any source.

sources.title: Ibáñez, J. J., Ortega, D., Campos, D., Khalidi, L. and Méndez, V., 'Testing complex networks of interaction at the onset of the Near Eastern Neolithic using modelling of obsidian exchange', Journal of the Royal Society Interface 12 (2015)
sources.author: Ibáñez, J. J., Ortega, D., Campos, D., Khalidi, L. and Méndez, V.
sources.venue: Journal of the Royal Society Interface
sources.confirms: Shows that a down-the-line model cannot explain long-distance obsidian distribution and supports complex networks of interaction.

obsidian-trade-near-east-7000bce.detail: Blades were often shipped as prepared cores and knapped at the destination. Çatalhöyük households kept obsidian hoards under floors. Later, Melian obsidian played the same role in Aegean and Lipari glass in the central Mediterranean. Later work added sources in Caucasus and Iran, and laser ablation methods now fingerprint single blades without destroying them. Obsidian's sharpness, finer than surgical steel, made it worth carrying for weeks. Distance decay curves fall off faster beyond about 300 km from sources, marking zones of supply and contact.

picture.alt: Obsidian blades from Neolithic Khirokitia in the Cyprus Museum, imported from Anatolian sources
picture.credit: Alehladutska, via Wikimedia Commons

obsidian-trade-near-east-7000bce.dating_note: Renfrew, Dixon and Cann characterised sources in 1966; Ibáñez et al. 2015 model Pre-Pottery Neolithic exchange. 7000 BCE marks the peak of PPNB distribution.

maize-teosinte-balsas-6700bce.summary: Teosinte, a wild grass of southwest Mexico with a dozen hard-cased kernels per ear, is maize's ancestor. Genotyping of 264 maize and teosinte plants at 99 microsatellite loci in 2002 showed that all maize derives from a single domestication within subspecies parviglumis, with central Balsas river drainage populations its closest wild relatives, about 9,000 years ago. Dolores Piperno and Anthony Ranere then excavated Xihuatoxtla rock shelter in the Balsas valley and found maize starch grains on grinding stones and maize phytoliths in sediments dated about 8,700 years ago. Domesticated squash appeared with it. A few mutations transformed teosinte's branched plant and shattering ear into a single stalk bearing naked kernels.

sources.title: Matsuoka, Y. et al., 'A single domestication for maize shown by multilocus microsatellite genotyping', PNAS 99 (2002)
sources.author: Matsuoka, Y. et al.
sources.confirms: Shows all maize derives from a single domestication within teosinte subspecies parviglumis about 9,000 years ago, with central Balsas populations basal.

sources.title: Piperno, D. R., Ranere, A. J., Holst, I., Iriarte, J. and Dickau, R., 'Starch grain and phytolith evidence for early ninth millennium B.P. maize from the Central Balsas River Valley, Mexico', PNAS 106 (2009)
sources.author: Piperno, D. R., Ranere, A. J., Holst, I., Iriarte, J. and Dickau, R.
sources.confirms: Reports maize starch and phytoliths at Xihuatoxtla shelter in the Central Balsas valley by 8,700 cal BP.

sources.title: Ranere, A. J., Piperno, D. R., Holst, I., Dickau, R. and Iriarte, J., 'The cultural and chronological context of early Holocene maize and squash domestication in the Central Balsas River Valley, Mexico', PNAS 106 (2009)
sources.author: Ranere, A. J., Piperno, D. R., Holst, I., Dickau, R. and Iriarte, J.
sources.confirms: Describes the Xihuatoxtla excavation, stratigraphy and dating of the early Holocene maize and squash evidence.

maize-teosinte-balsas-6700bce.detail: Maize spread south to Panama by 7,600 years ago and north into the American Southwest by 4,000 years ago, and its cobs grew larger over millennia. Balsas finds are microfossils rather than cobs, so critics asked whether early use involved stalk sugar as much as grain. Maize became the staple of every later Mesoamerican and Andean state. Teosinte branching gene tb1 and kernel case gene tga1 account for much of the transformation.

picture.alt: Comparison of a teosinte plant and ear with a modern maize plant and cob
picture.credit: National Science Foundation, via Wikimedia Commons

maize-teosinte-balsas-6700bce.dating_note: Piperno et al. 2009 and Ranere et al. 2009 date maize starch and phytoliths at Xihuatoxtla to about 8,700 cal BP; Matsuoka et al. 2002 estimate a single domestication from Balsas teosinte about 9,000 years ago by molecular clock.

jiahu-signs-tortoise-shells-6600bce.summary: Several graves at Jiahu of seventh millennium BCE held tortoise plastrons, some filled with pebbles and some incised with single signs: an eye, a window-like form, a sign like the later character for 'eight'. Li Xueqin, Garman Harbottle, Zhang Juzhong and Wang Changsui published sixteen such marks in 2003 and noted that a few resemble Shang oracle-bone characters of 1200 BCE, while concluding they are symbols used in ritual rather than words in a writing system. Paola Demattè's survey of Late Neolithic sign systems in China argues that organised marking on pottery and jade at Dawenkou, Liangzhu and other sites prepared the ground for Shang script. Jiahu's shells are the first link in that chain.

sources.title: Li, X., Harbottle, G., Zhang, J. and Wang, C., 'The earliest writing? Sign use in the seventh millennium BC at Jiahu, Henan Province, China', Antiquity 77 (2003)
sources.author: Li, X., Harbottle, G., Zhang, J. and Wang, C.
sources.confirms: Reports tortoise shells incised with signs in early Neolithic Jiahu graves, some anticipating later Chinese characters, interpreted as ritual symbols.

sources.title: Demattè, P., 'The origins of Chinese writing: the Neolithic evidence', Cambridge Archaeological Journal 20 (2010)
sources.author: Demattè, P.
sources.confirms: Analyses Late Neolithic Chinese signing systems and argues mature writing evolved from earlier sign use.

jiahu-signs-tortoise-shells-6600bce.detail: Tortoise shells were later the medium of Shang divination, so Jiahu finds suggest a long ritual continuity, though five millennia separate them. Critics caution that simple geometric signs recur worldwide and that resemblance to later characters is weak evidence of descent. Jiahu also yielded pottery marks and signs carved on bone, and pebbles inside shells rattle, suggesting divination or music. Dawenkou pottery of 2800 BCE bears pictographic signs more clearly tied to later characters.

picture.alt: Tortoise plastron from Jiahu incised with a carved sign, Peiligang culture, Henan Museum
picture.credit: Cangminzho, via Wikimedia Commons

jiahu-signs-tortoise-shells-6600bce.dating_note: Li et al. 2003 date Jiahu graves with incised shells to the seventh millennium BC, 6600 to 6200 BC; the authors read the signs as ritual symbols, not writing.

old-copper-complex-great-lakes-7500bce.summary: Around Lake Superior, especially Michigan's Keweenaw peninsula and Isle Royale, native copper lies in veins and glacial drift in pieces large enough to work. Archaic hunter-gatherers hammered and annealed it into socketed spear points, crescent knives, awls, fishhooks and beads, without smelting or casting. Wood and cord preserved inside 15 artefacts date from about 8,500 to 3,580 years ago, while lead traces in sediment cores from lakes beside ancient mine pits record copper working at two locations about 8000 and 7000 years ago. This is the earliest metalworking in the Americas and contemporary with Anatolian native copper work. Thousands of shallow pits mark where miners used fire, water and stone hammers to free copper from bedrock.

sources.title: Pompeani, D. P. et al., 'On the timing of the Old Copper Complex in North America: a comparison of radiocarbon dates from different archaeological contexts', Radiocarbon 63 (2021)
sources.author: Pompeani, D. P. et al.
sources.confirms: Dates organic material embedded in 15 Old Copper Complex artefacts to 8500 to 3580 cal BP, confirming the complex as among the oldest metalworking societies.

sources.title: Pompeani, D. P., Abbott, M. B., Steinman, B. A. and Bain, D. J., 'Lake sediments record prehistoric lead pollution related to early copper production in North America', Environmental Science and Technology 47 (2013)
sources.author: Pompeani, D. P., Abbott, M. B., Steinman, B. A. and Bain, D. J.
sources.confirms: Reports lead enrichments in Keweenaw lake sediments about 8000 and 7000 years BP indicating concurrent copper extraction at two locations.

old-copper-complex-great-lakes-7500bce.detail: Copper tools later gave way to copper ornaments as the material entered long-distance exchange, reaching Gulf coast and Hopewell mounds. One explanation for why this metal tradition persisted for millennia without smelting is that native copper was abundant enough that extraction from ore offered no gain. Direct dates settled a long argument over whether the complex began in the early or middle Archaic.

picture.alt: Copper knife, spear points, awls and spud of the Old Copper Complex, Wisconsin Historical Museum
picture.credit: Daderot, via Wikimedia Commons

old-copper-complex-great-lakes-7500bce.dating_note: Pompeani et al. 2021 date organic material embedded in Old Copper Complex artefacts from 8500 to 3580 cal BP; Pompeani et al. 2013 show lead pollution from copper working in Keweenaw lake sediments around 8000 and 7000 BP. 7500 BCE marks the earliest artefact dates; end at about 1600 BCE when the tradition fades. Year corrected on 15 November 2026 to the sourced span.

dairying-anatolia-milk-lipids-6500bce.summary: Fatty acids soak into unglazed pottery and survive for millennia. Carbon isotopes in fats from more than 2,200 sherds across Near East and southeast Europe, dated to the seventh through fifth millennia BCE, show milk fat concentrated in northwest Anatolia, around Sea of Marmara, where cattle bones also dominate. Milk was in use by the seventh millennium BCE, two thousand years before Sherratt's model predicted. Dairy intensity varied by region across 82 Mediterranean sites. Adults then lacked lactase persistence, so milk was probably fermented into yoghurt or cheese before drinking.

sources.title: Evershed, R. P. et al., 'Earliest date for milk use in the Near East and southeastern Europe linked to cattle herding', Nature 455 (2008)
sources.author: Evershed, R. P. et al.
sources.confirms: Analyses over 2,200 vessels from the seventh to fifth millennia BC and finds milk in use by the seventh millennium, most intensively in northwest Anatolia where cattle herding dominated.

sources.title: Debono Spiteri, C. et al., 'Regional asynchronicity in dairy production and processing in early farming communities of the northern Mediterranean', PNAS 113 (2016)
sources.author: Debono Spiteri, C. et al.
sources.confirms: Combines lipid residues and age-at-death data from 82 sites of the seventh to fifth millennia BC and shows variable dairy intensity by region.

dairying-anatolia-milk-lipids-6500bce.detail: The method relies on the carbon-13 difference between fats laid down in milk and in body tissue of ruminants. Pasture-rich Marmara lowlands favoured cattle, while sheep and goats dominated drier zones. Milk lipids on Saharan sherds at Takarkori and sieve sherds in Poland extend the pattern to Africa and northern Europe. Pots from Çatalhöyük and other central Anatolian sites show less milk, matching sheep- and goat-dominated herds there, so dairying intensity tracked which animals a region kept.
dairying-anatolia-milk-lipids-6500bce.dating_note: Evershed et al. 2008 date milk residues to the seventh millennium BC with concentration in northwest Anatolia; 6500 BCE is a midpoint of that millennium.

dufuna-canoe-6500bce.summary: In 1987 a Fulani herdsman digging a well at Dufuna in Yobe State, northeast Nigeria, struck wood five metres down. Excavation by Peter Breunig's German-Nigerian team in 1994 recovered an 8.4 metre dugout canoe of African mahogany, its ends tapered and its sides thin and even, buried in clay of a former lake in Chad Basin. Radiocarbon dates place it around 6000 BCE, about 8,000 years ago, making it Africa's oldest boat and among oldest anywhere after Pesse. Surrounding deposits hold fish bones and aquatic fauna of a humid Sahel. Edward Pollard's survey of African maritime archaeology sets it at the start of a continental history of boats. Dugouts carried fishers across the vast lakes of the green Sahara.
