sources.title: Breunig, P., Neumann, K. and Van Neer, W., 'New research on the Holocene settlement and environment of the Chad Basin in Nigeria', African Archaeological Review 13 (1996)
sources.author: Breunig, P., Neumann, K. and Van Neer, W.
sources.confirms: Reports the Dufuna dugout dated to around 6000 BC as the oldest known boat in Africa and one of the oldest in the world.

sources.title: Pollard, E., 'African maritime archaeology', Oxford Research Encyclopedia of African History (Oxford University Press) (2021)
sources.author: Pollard, E.
sources.venue: Oxford Research Encyclopedia of African History (Oxford University Press)
sources.confirms: Surveys African maritime archaeology from Middle Stone Age coastal use onward including early watercraft.
sources.qualifies: Abstract does not name Dufuna.

dufuna-canoe-6500bce.detail: Its finish shows skill with stone adzes and perhaps fire. It is displayed in Damaturu, where conservation has been a challenge. The find anchors a West African tradition of lake and river craft that later served Niger bend trade. Breunig's team dated two samples of canoe wood in laboratories in Germany, obtaining matching results. Lake Mega-Chad covered 350,000 square kilometres at its Holocene peak, a sea for fishers and boats. Dufuna lies 200 km from today's lake.
dufuna-canoe-6500bce.dating_note: Breunig, Neumann and Van Neer 1996 date Dufuna dugout to around 6000 BC, about 8000 years ago; two radiocarbon dates give roughly 8500 to 8000 cal BP, so 6500 BCE is used as a midpoint.

silk-jiahu-yangshao-6500bce.summary: Soil from two tombs at Jiahu, M436 and M451, assigned to the site's first and second sub-periods between 9000 and 8000 years ago, yielded peptides of silk fibroin identified by mass spectrometry, while a third tomb and control soils gave none. Bone needles and rough weaving tools came from the same graves, including a needle in M451, and Gong Yuxuan proposes that Jiahu villagers wove silk from the cocoons of Bombyx mori or its wild relatives for burial clothing. No fabric survives; the evidence is molecular. Woven silk cloth appears at Qianshanyang in Zhejiang around 2700 BCE, and sericulture became China's signature export craft.

sources.title: Gong, Y., Li, L., Gong, D., Yin, H. and Zhang, J., 'Biomolecular evidence of silk from 8,500 years ago', PLoS ONE 11 (2016)
sources.author: Gong, Y., Li, L., Gong, D., Yin, H. and Zhang, J.
sources.confirms: Reports silk fibroin peptides in soil from Jiahu tombs M436 and M451 of 9000 to 8000 BP, with bone needles and weaving tools from the graves.

sources.title: Gong, Y. et al., 'Biomolecular evidence of silk from 8,500 years ago (PMC full text)', PLoS ONE 11 (2016), e0168042 (2016)
sources.author: Gong, Y. et al.
sources.confirms: Assigns M436 to the first sub-period 9000 to 8500 BP and M451 to the second 8500 to 8000 BP, with no silk peptide in M466 or controls.

silk-jiahu-yangshao-6500bce.detail: Silk fibroin is a protein and leaves peptide fragments detectable long after fibres decay. The claim rests on two samples and awaits confirmation at other sites. If accepted, it places fibre work with insects alongside bast and flax in the earliest textile repertoire. Wild silk moths were native to Yellow river region, and mulberry trees grow there, so early use of cocoons is plausible. Spinning silk requires reeling filaments from boiled cocoons, a step not yet demonstrated for Jiahu.

picture.alt: White silkworm cocoons of Bombyx mori gathered in a basket
picture.credit: Biswarup Ganguly, via Wikimedia Commons

silk-jiahu-yangshao-6500bce.dating_note: Gong et al. 2016 detect silk fibroin in tombs M436 and M451 assigned to Jiahu's first and second sub-periods, 9000 to 8000 BP; no woven silk survives. The earliest silk fabric is from Qianshanyang, about 2700 BC, outside this period.

8200-year-cold-event-6200bce.summary: Greenland ice cores record an abrupt cooling about 8200 years ago that lasted roughly two centuries. Geologists made it the base of Northgrippian stage in 2018. Aridity coincided with disruptions at Neolithic sites in Levant, north Syria and Anatolia, and with farming's first appearance in Thrace, Macedonia and Bulgaria. Weninger reads that sequence as a dry spell pushing farmers toward Europe, placing climate stress and migration among causes of farming's spread. In that window a submarine landslide off Norway sent Storegga tsunami across North Sea, flooding the last of Doggerland.

sources.title: Weninger, B. et al., 'Climate forcing due to the 8200 cal yr BP event observed at Early Neolithic sites in the eastern Mediterranean', Quaternary Research 66 (2006)
sources.author: Weninger, B. et al.
sources.confirms: Links the 8200 cal BP aridity event to disruptions at Neolithic sites in the Levant, Syria, Anatolia and Cyprus and to the arrival of farming in Thrace, Macedonia, Thessaly and Bulgaria.

sources.title: Weninger, B. et al., 'The catastrophic final flooding of Doggerland by the Storegga Slide tsunami', Documenta Praehistorica 35 (2008)
sources.author: Weninger, B. et al.
sources.confirms: States that around 8200 cal BP large parts of Doggerland were flooded by a tsunami generated by a submarine landslide off Norway.

sources.title: Walker, M. et al., 'Formal ratification of the subdivision of the Holocene Series/Epoch', Episodes 41 (2018)
sources.author: Walker, M. et al.
sources.confirms: Defines the Northgrippian stage with its base at the 8.2 ka climate event.

8200-year-cold-event-6200bce.detail: Other archaeologists read Levantine abandonments as gradual and locally driven. Storegga slide, about 8150 years ago, overlaps cold event but is an independent geological accident. Dating rests on ice layers and sediment sequences rather than on artefacts. Greenland records show temperature falling by several degrees for 150 years or so, with dust and methane signals pointing to drought in monsoon regions and drier winters in southwest Asia. Lake levels in Anatolia and Levantine cave deposits register a matching dry pulse.

picture.alt: Map of Doggerland, the drowned land that once joined Britain to continental Europe beneath the North Sea
picture.credit: Max Naylor, via Wikimedia Commons

8200-year-cold-event-6200bce.dating_note: Event is dated 8200 years before present in Greenland ice; Walker et al. 2018 use it to define Northgrippian stage boundary. Weninger et al. tie Levantine site disruptions to it, though the causal link is debated.

choga-mami-irrigation-6000bce.summary: On Mandali plain east of Baghdad, beyond reach of rain-fed farming, Joan Oates excavated Choga Mami in 1967 and 1968 and found a Samarran-period settlement of the sixth millennium BCE beside traces of early water channels. Hans Helbaek's study of charred seeds supplied decisive evidence: six-row hulled barley, large-seeded flax and bread wheat, crops that cannot thrive there without irrigation. Water was led from Gangir river across the alluvial fan in small canals, Mesopotamia's first clear case of farmers managing a river for crops. Irrigation made Iraq's dry southern plain habitable and set up surpluses behind Ubaid temples and Uruk cities.

sources.title: Oates, J., 'Choga Mami, 1967-68: a preliminary report', Iraq 31 (1969)
sources.author: Oates, J.
sources.confirms: Reports the first season of excavation from December 1967 to February 1968 and stratified Samarra levels at Choga Mami.
sources.qualifies: The readable extract mentions a modern irrigation ditch but not the ancient channels described in the report body.

sources.title: Helbaek, H., 'Samarran irrigation agriculture at Choga Mami in Iraq', Iraq 34 (1972)
sources.author: Helbaek, H.
sources.confirms: Presents plant evidence for irrigation agriculture at Samarran Choga Mami on the Mandali plain fed by the Gangir.
sources.qualifies: Extract confirms title and setting; specific crop list taken from the article body.

choga-mami-irrigation-6000bce.verification_note: Both sources are confirmed as Tier 1 publications on Samarran irrigation at Choga Mami, but the readable extracts did not show the canal descriptions or the crop list.
choga-mami-irrigation-6000bce.detail: Flax seeds grow larger under irrigation, which makes seed size a proxy for watering. Samarran pottery, painted with geometric and animal motifs, links Choga Mami to sites in central Iraq. Later Mesopotamian texts treat canal digging as a royal duty, a tradition that begins with these Samarran channels. Ubaid settlers who followed in southern Iraq built canals from Euphrates branches, and by Uruk times the network supported cities. Choga Mami's channels were small enough for a village to dig and maintain.

picture.alt: Painted Samarra bowl with a swirling design of birds and fish, from the Samarra culture of central Iraq
picture.credit: Dbachmann, via Wikimedia Commons

choga-mami-irrigation-6000bce.dating_note: Choga Mami's Samarran levels belong to sixth millennium BC; Oates excavated in 1967-68 and Helbaek read irrigation from the plant remains. The canal dating rests on stratigraphy and pottery rather than direct radiocarbon.

kuahuqiao-lacquer-canoe-6000bce.summary: At Kuahuqiao near Hangzhou Bay, waterlogged deposits of about 8,000 to 7,000 years ago preserve a wooden bow, a stave and a tool handle coated with natural lacquer from Toxicodendron tree. Spectroscopy in 2018 confirmed that the sap served both as a protective coating and as an adhesive, the earliest lacquer use known. Pollen and charcoal show that villagers burned alder scrub on coastal swamp and managed water to grow rice in paddy-like plots from 7,700 years ago, the first evidence of wetland management for rice. A dugout canoe about 5.6 metres long and a boat-building shed were also recovered. Kuahuqiao links lacquer, rice paddies and boats in one Neolithic community.

sources.title: Wu, M. et al., 'Natural lacquer was used as a coating and an adhesive 8000 years ago, by early humans at Kuahuqiao, determined by ELISA', Journal of Archaeological Science 100 (2018)
sources.author: Wu, M. et al.
sources.confirms: Reports three lacquered objects at Kuahuqiao, 8000 cal BP, with lacquer used as coating and adhesive.

sources.title: Zong, Y., Chen, Z., Innes, J. B., Chen, C., Wang, Z. and Wang, H., 'Fire and flood management of coastal swamp enabled first rice paddy cultivation in east China', Nature 449 (2007)
sources.author: Zong, Y., Chen, Z., Innes, J. B., Chen, C., Wang, Z. and Wang, H.
sources.confirms: Dates Kuahuqiao to 7700 cal BP and shows fire clearance of alder scrub and water management for paddy-type rice cultivation.

kuahuqiao-lacquer-canoe-6000bce.detail: Lacquer hardens by enzymatic polymerisation in humid air and resists water and acid; it became the basis of East Asian lacquerware for eight millennia. The settlement was abandoned when sea level rose and brackish water flooded the fields. Kuahuqiao's domestic pigs and dogs complete the picture of a rice-farming village. Canoe planks and paddles lay in a workshop area with wooden mallets and adzes, and lacquer on a bow suggests protection of a hunting weapon. Toxicodendron sap causes severe skin rash, so collecting it demanded care.

picture.alt: Wooden paddle-shaped implement and wooden arrowheads from the Kuahuqiao site, Hangzhou Museum
picture.credit: 猫猫的日记本, via Wikimedia Commons

kuahuqiao-lacquer-canoe-6000bce.dating_note: Kuahuqiao dates to about 8000 to 7000 cal BP; Wu et al. 2018 date lacquered objects to 8000 cal BP and Zong et al. 2007 the paddy management to 7700 cal BP. 6000 BCE is a midpoint.

mehrgarh-cotton-6000bce.summary: A copper bead from a Neolithic burial at Mehrgarh carried threads mineralised by copper salts. Electron microscopy identified the fibres as cotton, Gossypium, dated to sixth millennium BCE, the oldest cotton in Old World and over a millennium earlier than previously known. Cotton here was probably tree cotton, Gossypium arboreum, native to Indus region, whose domestication produced the fibre that later supplied Harappan looms. Cotton fibres in soil at Tel Tsaf in Jordan valley, dated 5200 to 4700 BCE, lie far from any wild cotton, which implies that fibre or cloth was already moving from South Asia toward Levant in the fifth millennium.

sources.title: Moulherat, C., Tengberg, M., Haquet, J.-F. and Mille, B., 'First evidence of cotton at Neolithic Mehrgarh, Pakistan: analysis of mineralized fibres from a copper bead', Journal of Archaeological Science 29 (2002)
sources.author: Moulherat, C., Tengberg, M., Haquet, J.-F. and Mille, B.
sources.confirms: Identifies mineralised threads on a copper bead from a Neolithic Mehrgarh burial as cotton dated to the sixth millennium BC, the oldest in the Old World.

sources.title: Liu, L., Levin, M. J., Klimscha, F. and Rosenberg, D., 'The earliest cotton fibers and Pan-regional contacts in the Near East', Frontiers in Plant Science 13 (2022)
sources.author: Liu, L., Levin, M. J., Klimscha, F. and Rosenberg, D.
sources.confirms: Reports cotton fibres at Tel Tsaf, Israel, dated 5200 to 4700 cal BC and cites Mehrgarh threads as the earliest known cotton fibres.

mehrgarh-cotton-6000bce.detail: Cotton was domesticated independently four times: G. arboreum in South Asia, G. herbaceum in Africa, G. hirsutum in Mesoamerica and G. barbadense in Peru, where Huaca Prieta preserves dyed cloth of 4200 BCE. Mineralised fibres survive because copper corrosion products replace organic material while keeping its shape. Cotton seeds appear at Mehrgarh in Period II deposits, and Harappan cities by 2500 BCE wove cotton cloth found at Mohenjo-daro on a silver vase. Tree cotton is a perennial shrub harvested over years.

picture.alt: Pale yellow flower of tree cotton, Gossypium arboreum, with broad leaves
picture.credit: Krzysztof Ziarnek, Kenraiz, via Wikimedia Commons

mehrgarh-cotton-6000bce.dating_note: Moulherat et al. 2002 date the cotton threads to the sixth millennium BC from Period II burial context; Liu et al. 2022 report cotton at Tel Tsaf, Israel, at 5200 to 4700 cal BC, implying early movement of the fibre westward.

salt-production-poiana-slatinei-6000bce.summary: At Lunca in Romanian Carpathians a spring delivers brine at 160 grams of salt per litre, six times the concentration of sea water. Olivier Weller and Gheorghe Dumitroaia excavated a deep mound of ash and burnt earth beside it with Starčevo-Criş pottery and radiocarbon dates of 6050 to 5500 BCE, the end of seventh millennium. Early Neolithic farmers boiled brine in coarse pots over hearths until salt crystallised, producing a storable commodity. Salt mattered once people shifted from a meat-based to a cereal diet and kept livestock, and it preserved meat, fish and cheese. Weller's later overview traces Neolithic salt making across Europe with and without the fired clay moulds known as briquetage.

sources.title: Weller, O. and Dumitroaia, G., 'The earliest salt production in the world: an early Neolithic exploitation in Poiana Slatinei-Lunca, Romania', Antiquity Project Gallery 79 (2005)
sources.author: Weller, O. and Dumitroaia, G.
sources.confirms: Dates first salt exploitation at Poiana Slatinei to 6050 to 5500 BC and gives brine concentration of 160 g/l with Starčevo-Criş pottery.

sources.title: Weller, O., 'First salt making in Europe: an overview from Neolithic times', Documenta Praehistorica 42 (2015)
sources.author: Weller, O.
sources.confirms: Reviews Neolithic salt exploitation in Europe including production with and without briquetage.

salt-production-poiana-slatinei-6000bce.detail: Later Chalcolithic Cucuteni communities nearby produced salt on a much larger scale, and salt springs may underlie wealth of Trypillia megasites. Mining of rock salt at Hallstatt comes much later, in Bronze Age. Salt rarely survives, so hearths, ash heaps and specialised pottery are the evidence. Salt also served animal husbandry, since herded cattle need salt licks, and tanning hides. Nearby springs show briquetage of later Cucuteni date, with conical vessels broken to free salt cakes for transport and exchange.
salt-production-poiana-slatinei-6000bce.dating_note: Weller and Dumitroaia date the earliest salt exploitation at Poiana Slatinei to 6050 to 5500 BC, the end of seventh millennium, by radiocarbon on Starčevo-Criş contexts.

wine-georgia-hajji-firuz-6000bce.summary: Large clay jars sunk into house floors at Gadachrili Gora and Shulaveris Gora in Georgia carry tartaric acid and related grape acids absorbed into their fabric, dated to about 6000 to 5800 BCE, with pollen and starch confirming grapes. At Hajji Firuz Tepe in the Zagros, six jars of about nine litres each stood in a Neolithic kitchen; two held tartrate and tree resin, dated 5400 to 5000 BCE. At Areni-1 cave in Armenia, used from 4000 BCE, desiccated grapevine wood and a pressing floor show wine production by the Late Chalcolithic. Fermenting grapes gave a storable, intoxicating drink that fed feasting and later temple and palace economies.

sources.title: McGovern, P. et al., 'Early Neolithic wine of Georgia in the South Caucasus', PNAS 114 (2017)
sources.author: McGovern, P. et al.
sources.confirms: Reports tartaric acid in early Neolithic Georgian jars at about 6000 to 5800 BC and summarises Hajji Firuz Tepe, with six jars of about 9 litres dated 5400 to 5000 BC, and Areni grapevine remains.

sources.title: Wilkinson, K. N. et al., 'Areni-1 Cave, Armenia: a Chalcolithic-Early Bronze Age settlement and ritual site in the southern Caucasus', Journal of Field Archaeology 37 (2012)
sources.author: Wilkinson, K. N. et al.
sources.confirms: Dates use of Areni-1 from 4000 cal BC with desiccated botanical remains and storage of plant foods.

sources.title: McGovern, P. E., Glusker, D. L., Exner, L. J. and Voigt, M. M., 'Neolithic resinated wine', Nature 381 (1996)
sources.author: McGovern, P. E., Glusker, D. L., Exner, L. J. and Voigt, M. M.
sources.confirms: Original report of tartaric acid and resin in a Hajji Firuz Tepe jar.
sources.qualifies: Nature page provided bibliographic details only; content confirmed through McGovern et al. 2017.

wine-georgia-hajji-firuz-6000bce.detail: Tartaric acid is rare in Near Eastern plants apart from grapes, which makes it a diagnostic marker. Resin added to Hajji Firuz wine would have slowed spoilage, a practice continued in Greek retsina. Georgian vines were either domesticated or gathered wild; domestication is argued from pip shape and genetics. Georgian jars, ancestors of the qvevri still used there, were decorated with grape cluster motifs, and tree pollen points to a milder climate than today's.

picture.alt: Large Neolithic clay jar from Khramis Didi Gora, Georgia, decorated with grape cluster motifs, National Museum of Georgia
picture.credit: Carole Raddato, via Wikimedia Commons

wine-georgia-hajji-firuz-6000bce.dating_note: McGovern et al. 2017 date Georgian wine residues to about 6000 to 5800 BC; Hajji Firuz Tepe in Iran is dated 5400 to 5000 BC; Areni-1 in Armenia shows wine installations from about 4000 BC. South Caucasus sites are filed under middle-east per the brief's regional scheme.

linearbandkeramik-longhouses-5500bce.summary: Between about 5500 and 5000 BCE farmers using pottery decorated with incised bands spread along loess soils from Hungarian plain through central Europe to Paris basin and Netherlands. They lived in timber longhouses up to 40 metres long, with rows of posts and loam pits along the walls, in small hamlets near streams. Weed seeds and isotopes show that LBK households kept intensively manured garden plots and maintained them for generations. Summed radiocarbon dates from 13 regions show population boomed after farming arrived and then crashed, a pattern repeated across Neolithic Europe. The LBK carried emmer, einkorn, peas, lentils, cattle and sheep into temperate Europe.

sources.title: Bogaard, A., Krause, R. and Strien, H.-C., 'Towards a social geography of cultivation and plant use in an early farming community: Vaihingen an der Enz, south-west Germany', Antiquity 85 (2011)
sources.author: Bogaard, A., Krause, R. and Strien, H.-C.
sources.confirms: Shows LBK households at Vaihingen cultivated intensively managed plots with household-level differences in land use.

sources.title: Shennan, S. et al., 'Regional population collapse followed initial agriculture booms in mid-Holocene Europe', Nature Communications 4 (2013)
sources.author: Shennan, S. et al.
sources.confirms: Uses summed radiocarbon probability from 13 regions to show population booms after farming arrival followed by busts.

linearbandkeramik-longhouses-5500bce.detail: Ancient DNA shows LBK people descended mainly from Anatolian farmers, with limited mixing with local hunter-gatherers at first. Mass graves at Talheim and Schöneck-Kilianstädten record violent episodes near the culture's end. Milk and cheese residues in LBK and successor Polish pottery link the longhouses to early dairying. Houses were oriented with their ends toward the direction of origin, roughly northwest to southeast, and pits along walls supplied loam for daub. Adzes of amphibolite were traded across hundreds of kilometres.

picture.alt: Linear Pottery culture vessel from western Bohemia in a museum case, photographed in 2018.
picture.credit: Zde, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

linearbandkeramik-longhouses-5500bce.dating_note: Linearbandkeramik spread from Hungarian plain to the Paris basin between about 5500 and 5000 cal BC; Shennan et al. 2013 use summed radiocarbon dates to show boom and bust.

taperinha-pottery-amazon-5500bce.summary: A shell midden at Taperinha near Santarém, where Tapajós meets Amazon, holds sand-tempered sherds of simple bowls among freshwater mussel shells and fish bones. Anna Roosevelt dated charcoal, shell and the sherds themselves by accelerator radiocarbon and by thermoluminescence to about 8000 to 7000 years ago, making this the oldest pottery in Western Hemisphere, earlier than any in Andes or Mesoamerica. The potters were fisher-foragers of Amazon floodplain, not farmers, as in Africa and East Asia. Roosevelt's nearby work at Caverna da Pedra Pintada showed human presence in region from late Pleistocene, so river-based populations had deep roots before pottery.

sources.title: Roosevelt, A. C. et al., 'Eighth millennium pottery from a prehistoric shell midden in the Brazilian Amazon', Science 254 (1991)
sources.author: Roosevelt, A. C. et al.
sources.confirms: Reports the earliest pottery in the Western Hemisphere from a shell midden near Santarém, dated 8000 to 7000 BP by radiocarbon and thermoluminescence.

sources.title: Roosevelt, A. C. et al., 'Paleoindian cave dwellers in the Amazon: the peopling of the Americas', Science 272 (1996)
sources.author: Roosevelt, A. C. et al.
sources.confirms: Dates the Caverna da Pedra Pintada Paleoindian occupation near Monte Alegre to the late Pleistocene with 56 radiocarbon and 13 luminescence dates.
sources.qualifies: Provides regional background, not the pottery dates.

taperinha-pottery-amazon-5500bce.detail: Amazonian pottery thus arose among river foragers two millennia before Valdivia ceramics in Ecuador. The find overturned the view of Amazonia as a late recipient of innovations from Andes. Taperinha's midden also records intensive shellfish collection and possibly managed palm groves. Sherds show finger-pinched rims and simple incisions, with no painting. Pottery here served cooking of fish and shellfish, and perhaps processing of palm fruits. Roosevelt's results drew criticism over dating methods, answered by multiple independent techniques. Later Amazonian pottery includes elaborate Marajoara urns.
taperinha-pottery-amazon-5500bce.dating_note: Roosevelt et al. 1991 date Taperinha pottery by radiocarbon on charcoal, shell and sherds and by thermoluminescence to about 8000 to 7000 BP; 5500 BCE is the midpoint of that range.

vinca-signs-5300bce.summary: Across the Danube basin, Vinča culture of about 5400 to 4500 BCE left thousands of incised marks on pottery bases, spindle whorls and clay figurines: crosses, chevrons, combs and swastikas, repeated across sites. Three small clay tablets found at Tărtăria in Transylvania in 1961, in a pit with figurines and human bones, carry grouped signs that some compared to Sumerian pictographs two millennia younger. Sorin Paliga and, more recently, Marco Merlini have catalogued this corpus and argue for an organised sign system with conventions of placement. Most specialists see potters' marks, ownership signs and ritual symbols rather than a script encoding language, since no sign sequences recur as texts.

sources.title: Paliga, S., 'The tablets of Tărtăria: an enigma? A reconsideration and further perspectives', Dialogues d'histoire ancienne 19 (1993)
sources.author: Paliga, S.
sources.confirms: Reconsiders the Tărtăria tablets and the Vinča sign corpus and their relation to later writing.

sources.title: Merlini, M., 'The Danube script and the Tărtăria tablets', Acta Terrae Septemcastrensis 24 (2025)
sources.author: Merlini, M.
sources.confirms: Catalogues Vinča-period signs and argues for an organised sign system with recurrent conventions.
sources.qualifies: Author's interpretation as script is a minority position.

vinca-signs-5300bce.verification_note: Both sources are confirmed as peer-reviewed treatments of the Tărtăria tablets; the 5300 BC date depends on the radiocarbon redating cited within them rather than on text read directly.
vinca-signs-5300bce.detail: The Tărtăria pit's dating was disputed for decades because Nicolae Vlassa's excavation records were thin; radiocarbon on associated bones now points to the early Vinča horizon. Vinča signs matter as evidence that systematic marking preceded writing in several regions, as Jiahu's tortoise shells do in China. Vinča settlements also produced early copper working and dense tell villages with figurines, so marking belongs to a wider context of specialised crafts and exchange. Sign inventories exceed 200 distinct forms by some counts.

picture.alt: Round clay tablet from Tărtăria incised with signs divided into four quadrants
picture.credit: Balogg, via Wikimedia Commons

vinca-signs-5300bce.dating_note: Vinča culture spans about 5400 to 4500 BC; the Tărtăria tablets' Vinča context dates to about 5300 BC though their stratigraphy was recorded poorly in 1961. Most scholars read the signs as marks or symbols rather than writing.

cheese-sieves-lactase-5200bce.summary: Early Neolithic sites in Kuyavia, Poland, yield pottery sherds pierced with dozens of small holes, long guessed to be cheese strainers by analogy with modern forms. Lipids in these sieves are abundant milk fat, while cooking pots from the same sites show ruminant fat instead, so the sieves separated curds from whey around 5200 BCE. Cheese making removes most lactose, which mattered because early Neolithic European skeletons carry no lactase persistence allele. Some 7,000 residues from 550 sites show milk use was widespread long before the allele became common; famine and disease, rather than milk drinking, are proposed as drivers of selection.

sources.title: Salque, M. et al., 'Earliest evidence for cheese making in the sixth millennium BC in northern Europe', Nature 493 (2013)
sources.author: Salque, M. et al.
sources.confirms: Reports abundant milk fat in sixth millennium BC sieve vessels from Kuyavia, Poland, as direct evidence of cheese making.

sources.title: Burger, J., Kirchner, M., Bramanti, B., Haak, W. and Thomas, M. G., 'Absence of the lactase-persistence-associated allele in early Neolithic Europeans', PNAS 104 (2007)
sources.author: Burger, J., Kirchner, M., Bramanti, B., Haak, W. and Thomas, M. G.
sources.confirms: Finds the lactase persistence allele absent in early Neolithic European skeletons.

sources.title: Evershed, R. P. et al., 'Dairying, diseases and the evolution of lactase persistence in Europe', Nature 608 (2022)
sources.author: Evershed, R. P. et al.
sources.confirms: Compiles about 7,000 pottery fat residues from over 550 sites to show widespread milk use from the Neolithic and proposes famine and pathogen exposure as drivers of lactase persistence selection.

cheese-sieves-lactase-5200bce.detail: Dairying thus spread as a processed-food technology before any genetic adaptation. Lactase persistence rose to high frequency in northern Europe only in last few thousand years. The sieves are among the first special-purpose vessels in Europe. Sieve sherds have holes a few millimetres wide punched before firing, in bowls about 20 cm across. Rennet from calf stomachs or acid from souring would have curdled milk, and whey could be drunk or fed to pigs. Cheese keeps for months, turning a seasonal flush of milk into a storable food.
cheese-sieves-lactase-5200bce.dating_note: Salque et al. 2013 date Kuyavian sieve sherds to the sixth millennium BC; Burger et al. 2007 show absence of the lactase persistence allele in early Neolithic Europeans, so cheese preceded adult milk drinking.

kadero-nile-saharan-herders-5200bce.summary: Cattle herding spread across green Sahara and into Nile valley before any African crop was domesticated, a sequence Fiona Marshall and Elisabeth Hildebrand call cattle before crops. Herders needed mobility to follow rains, so plant cultivation came late, after 4,000 years ago. Lipid analysis of pottery from Takarkori rock shelter in Libyan Sahara found milk fats dating to fifth millennium BCE, Africa's first secure dairying. At Kadero north of Khartoum, Lech Krzyżaniak excavated a fifth-millennium mound where cattle, sheep and goat bones dominate and grave goods mark rank. Michael Brass rejects claims of independent cattle domestication at Nabta Playa, reading early Bos bones as hunted aurochs, so African herds descend from Near Eastern stock mixed with local aurochs.

sources.title: Marshall, F. and Hildebrand, E., 'Cattle before crops: the beginnings of food production in Africa', Journal of World Prehistory 16 (2002)
sources.author: Marshall, F. and Hildebrand, E.
sources.confirms: Argues African cattle were herded by Saharan hunter-gatherers in the tenth millennium BP and that plant domestication came late, after 4000 BP, because of herder mobility.

sources.title: Dunne, J. et al., 'First dairying in green Saharan Africa in the fifth millennium BC', Nature 486 (2012)
sources.author: Dunne, J. et al.
sources.confirms: Reports isotopic evidence of milk fats in pottery from the Takarkori rock shelter, Libyan Sahara, dated to the fifth millennium BC.

sources.title: Brass, M., 'Early North African cattle domestication and its ecological setting: a reassessment', Journal of World Prehistory 31 (2018)
sources.author: Brass, M.
sources.confirms: Rejects the independent North African cattle domestication model at Nabta Playa and Bir Kiseiba, reading early Holocene Bos as hunted aurochs.

kadero-nile-saharan-herders-5200bce.detail: Genetic studies show African taurine cattle carry aurochs introgression but Near Eastern domestic ancestry. Herding let people live in semi-arid zones no farmer could use and underpinned the later Nubian and Egyptian cattle cultures. Sheep and goats, with no African wild ancestor, arrived from Levant by about 5800 BCE. Kadero burials with mace heads, carnelian beads and ivory show early rank among herders. Rock art across Sahara depicts spotted cattle with decorated horns, a visual record of herding before writing.

picture.alt: Takarkori rock shelter in the Tadrart Acacus mountains of southwest Libya, seen from the south
picture.credit: Van Neer, Alhaique, Wouters and colleagues (PLoS ONE 2020), via Wikimedia Commons

kadero-nile-saharan-herders-5200bce.dating_note: Marshall and Hildebrand place African cattle herding in the tenth millennium BP in Sahara, a claim Brass 2018 rejects for Nabta Playa; Dunne et al. 2012 give the first secure dairying at Takarkori in the fifth millennium BC. 5200 BCE marks the horizon when herding with dairying is secure across Sahara and reaches Nile at Kadero.

trepanation-ensisheim-5100bce.summary: In a Linearbandkeramik cemetery at Ensisheim in Alsace, a man buried around 5100 to 4900 BCE had two openings cut into his skull, one of them fully healed and the other well advanced in healing, so he survived both operations by months or years. This is the earliest secure case of trepanation. At Buthiers-Boulancourt near Paris, an elderly man of 4900 to 4700 BCE had his left forearm amputated, and his wound healed. More than 1,500 trepanned skulls are known worldwide, with trepanation present in 5 to 10 percent of some Neolithic cemeteries. Flint tools, an understanding of bone and some means of controlling bleeding and infection were available in these villages.

sources.title: Buquet-Marcon, C., Philippe, C. and Anaick, S., 'The oldest amputation on a Neolithic human skeleton in France', Nature Precedings (2007)
sources.author: Buquet-Marcon, C., Philippe, C. and Anaick, S.
sources.confirms: Describes a healed surgical amputation of the left forearm at Buthiers-Boulancourt dated 4900 to 4700 BC.

sources.title: Faria, M. A., 'Neolithic trepanation decoded: a unifying hypothesis', Surgical Neurology International 6 (2015), 72 (2015)
sources.author: Faria, M. A.
sources.confirms: Reports more than 1,500 trephined skulls worldwide and trepanation frequencies of 5 to 10 percent in Neolithic series.

sources.title: Alt, K. W. et al., 'Evidence for Stone Age cranial surgery', Nature 387 (1997)
sources.author: Alt, K. W. et al.
sources.confirms: Reports the Ensisheim skull with two healed trepanations dated 5100 to 4900 BC.
sources.qualifies: Nature page gave bibliographic details only.

trepanation-ensisheim-5100bce.verification_note: Ensisheim's specific dates were not readable from the Nature page; the amputation case and global frequency are confirmed.
trepanation-ensisheim-5100bce.detail: Reasons proposed for opening skulls are trauma relief, headache, ritual and treatment of mental illness. Survival rates in Neolithic series are high, often above half. Peru's later Paracas and Inca surgeons practised trepanation at much greater scale. Scraping with a flint blade, rather than drilling, left bevelled edges that healed. Trepanned skulls occur across Neolithic Europe from France to Ukraine, and in later Peru surgery reached rates of thousands of cases. Ensisheim's man was over fifty when he died.

picture.alt: Neolithic skull with a large healed trepanation opening, from the Prunières collection, Wellcome Collection photograph
picture.credit: Wellcome Collection, via Wikimedia Commons

trepanation-ensisheim-5100bce.dating_note: Alt et al. 1997 date the Ensisheim burial to 5100 to 4900 BC; the Buthiers-Boulancourt amputation is dated 4900 to 4700 BC.

belovode-copper-smelting-5000bce.summary: At Belovode, a Vinča culture village in eastern Serbia, Miljana Radivojević identified droplets of copper slag containing gangue minerals, with fragments of molten copper, in a layer dated to about 5000 BCE. Smelting, which uses charcoal fire and controlled air to pull metal from green malachite ore, is a different act from hammering native copper and requires temperatures above 1,000 degrees. Nearby Pločnik yielded a tin bronze foil from a mid fifth millennium layer, made from copper-tin ores, pushing alloy making back by 1,500 years. In 2017 a lump of 'slag' from Çatalhöyük, long cited as earlier smelting, proved to be a burnt green pigment, leaving the Balkans with the earliest secure evidence.

sources.title: Radivojević, M. et al., 'On the origins of extractive metallurgy: new evidence from Europe', Journal of Archaeological Science 37 (2010)
sources.author: Radivojević, M. et al.
sources.confirms: Reports copper slag with gangue elements and molten copper at Belovode, with the earliest smelting event dated to about 5000 BC.

sources.title: Radivojević, M. et al., 'Tainted ores and the rise of tin bronzes in Eurasia, c. 6500 years ago', Antiquity 87 (2013)
sources.author: Radivojević, M. et al.
sources.confirms: Reports a tin bronze foil from a mid fifth millennium BC layer at Pločnik and reassesses 14 early Balkan tin bronzes as smelted from copper-tin ores.

sources.title: Radivojević, M. et al., 'Repealing the Çatalhöyük extractive metallurgy: the green, the fire and the 'slag'', Journal of Archaeological Science 86 (2017)
sources.author: Radivojević, M. et al.
sources.confirms: Shows the Çatalhöyük 'slag' is not evidence of smelting.

belovode-copper-smelting-5000bce.detail: Balkan smelting fed the heavy copper axes and gold of the Varna cemetery within five centuries. Iranian and Anatolian evidence of similar date is less securely stratified, so smelting may have been invented once or several times. Slag analysis uses microscopy and chemistry to separate smelting from accidental fire. Belovode smiths used malachite from sources in eastern Serbia, and green ore had long been collected as pigment and beads, so smelting may have grown from ornament making. Pločnik's workshop held crucibles and copper chisels and hammers.

picture.alt: Copper axe from the Vinča culture Pločnik hoard, Serbia, National Museum of Serbia
picture.credit: CryolophosaurusEllioti, via Wikimedia Commons

belovode-copper-smelting-5000bce.dating_note: Radivojević et al. 2010 date the earliest smelting event at Belovode to about 5000 BC; Radivojević et al. 2017 show the Çatalhöyük 'slag' once claimed as earlier smelting is a burnt pigment.

chinchorro-mummies-5000bce.summary: Along Atacama coast of northern Chile and southern Peru, Chinchorro fishing communities began around 5050 BCE to dismantle and rebuild their dead: removing organs and flesh, reinforcing the skeleton with sticks, modelling the body in ash paste and clay, replacing the skin, and finishing with a black manganese or red ochre coat and a wig. Mummies fall into black, red, bandage and mud-coated styles across three millennia, until about 1720 BCE. Pablo Marquet argues that a wetter interval raised coastal populations and that high arsenic in local water caused infant deaths that mummification answered. Chinchorro mummies predate Egyptian artificial mummification by two thousand years and were made by hunter-gatherers.

sources.title: Arriaza, B. T., 'Chinchorro bioarchaeology: chronology and mummy seriation', Latin American Antiquity 6 (1995)
sources.author: Arriaza, B. T.
sources.confirms: Dates the start of Chinchorro artificial mummification to about 5050 BC and its abandonment to about 1720 BC, with a seriation of black, red, bandage, mud-coated and natural styles.

sources.title: Marquet, P. A. et al., 'Emergence of social complexity among coastal hunter-gatherers in the Atacama Desert of northern Chile', PNAS 109 (2012)
sources.author: Marquet, P. A. et al.
sources.confirms: Links the emergence of artificial mummification among Chinchorro hunter-gatherers to population growth and environmental conditions.

chinchorro-mummies-5000bce.detail: Children and foetuses were mummified as carefully as adults, which supports the link to infant mortality. Mummies were kept, repainted and displayed before burial. The practice shows anatomical knowledge, pigment chemistry and the use of sea-lion skin, reeds and camelid fibre in one craft. Arica's museum holds hundreds of these mummies, and arsenic in local rivers remains above safe levels today. Mummification began with children and later extended to adults of all ranks, suggesting an egalitarian society.

picture.alt: Chinchorro black-style mummy of an infant in the San Miguel de Azapa Archaeological Museum, Arica
picture.credit: WeHaKa, via Wikimedia Commons

chinchorro-mummies-5000bce.dating_note: Arriaza 1995 dates the start of artificial mummification to about 5050 BC and its end about 1720 BC; Marquet et al. 2012 tie its emergence to population growth and arsenic exposure in a wetter phase.

kuwait-as-sabiyah-reed-boats-5000bce.summary: At site H3 near As-Sabiyah on Kuwait Bay, Robert Carter's team found slabs of bitumen bearing impressions of bundled reeds on one side and barnacles on other: waterproofing peeled from sea-going reed boats of Ubaid period, sixth to fifth millennium BCE. A painted ceramic disc from the same site shows a boat with two mast-like lines, and a small clay boat model has a socket where a mast could sit. Ubaid pottery from southern Mesopotamia across Arabian shore shows these vessels carried goods and people along Gulf. Carter calls them the earliest remains anywhere of sea-going boats. Thomas Strasser had earlier reinterpreted Eridu boat models as spinning bowls, so As-Sabiyah disc stands as the earliest candidate for a sail.

sources.title: Carter, R., 'Boat remains and maritime trade in the Persian Gulf during the sixth and fifth millennia BC', Antiquity 80 (2006)
sources.author: Carter, R.
sources.confirms: States that excavations in Kuwait revealed the earliest remains anywhere of sea-going boats and links Ubaid pottery distribution to maritime exchange.

sources.title: Strasser, T. F., 'The boat models from Eridu: sailing or spinning during the 'Ubaid period?', Antiquity 70 (1996)
sources.author: Strasser, T. F.
sources.confirms: Argues that the Eridu models long cited as the earliest evidence for sailing boats are spinning bowls used by weavers.

kuwait-as-sabiyah-reed-boats-5000bce.detail: Bitumen seeps near Euphrates and in Iran supplied the coating, and geochemistry traces each batch to its source. Reed-bundle construction continues in Marsh Arabs' boats and Egyptian papyrus skiffs. Whether the disc shows a true sail or standards is debated. Carter's team also recovered a ceramic model of a boat with a clear socket and painted lines interpreted as rigging. Later Gulf trade in copper from Oman and pearls followed routes these Ubaid sailors opened, and bitumen boat remains at Ra's al-Jinz in Oman show the technology persisted for three millennia.

picture.alt: Painted Ubaid III pottery vessel of about 5300 to 4700 BCE in the Louvre, the ware found at As-Sabiyah
picture.credit: ALFGRN, via Wikimedia Commons

kuwait-as-sabiyah-reed-boats-5000bce.dating_note: Carter 2006 dates the H3 As-Sabiyah boat remains to Ubaid period, sixth to fifth millennium BC; the painted disc showing a boat with mast-like lines is the earliest possible image of a sail, though Strasser showed Eridu 'boat models' once cited for sailing are spinning bowls.

nabta-playa-calendar-circle-4800bce.summary: In Egyptian Sahara 100 km west of Abu Simbel, seasonal rains once filled Nabta Playa basin and drew cattle herders each summer. Fred Wendorf's Combined Prehistoric Expedition recorded a small circle of upright slabs with two sightlines, one toward summer solstice sunrise, together with five lines of large stones radiating from megalithic structures and tumuli holding articulated cattle. The complex dates to Late Neolithic, before hyperaridity emptied the region about 4,800 radiocarbon years ago. Summer solstice coincided with arrival of rains, so sky-watching served herding. Michael Brass cautions that the oldest cow burial calibrates anywhere between 5976 and 4835 BCE.

sources.title: Malville, J. M., Wendorf, F., Mazar, A. A. and Schild, R., 'Megaliths and Neolithic astronomy in southern Egypt', Nature 392 (1998)
sources.author: Malville, J. M., Wendorf, F., Mazar, A. A. and Schild, R.
sources.confirms: Reports stone circles and five megalithic alignments at Nabta Playa aligned to cardinal and solstitial directions, dated before the return of hyperaridity about 4800 radiocarbon years BP.

sources.title: Brass, M., 'Early North African cattle domestication and its ecological setting: a reassessment', Journal of World Prehistory 31 (2018)
sources.author: Brass, M.
sources.confirms: Reports nine tumuli with articulated cattle at E-94-1N and shows the earliest cow tumulus date of 6480 plus or minus 270 bp calibrates to 5976 to 4835 cal BC.

nabta-playa-calendar-circle-4800bce.detail: Stones were brought from a quarry some distance away and some were shaped. Claims that alignments track specific stars are weaker than solstice reading. Nabta's cattle cult has been linked to later Egyptian Hathor worship, though the gap of two millennia makes any direct line speculative. Wendorf's team excavated for decades and recorded wells, hut circles and storage pits, so Nabta was a seasonal gathering place rather than a bare ceremonial centre. A stone carved into bovine form lay buried beneath one structure.

picture.alt: Reconstructed Nabta Playa stone circle of upright slabs at the Nubia Museum in Aswan
picture.credit: Raymbetz, via Wikimedia Commons

nabta-playa-calendar-circle-4800bce.dating_note: Malville et al. 1998 place the megaliths in Late Neolithic before area turned hyperarid about 4800 radiocarbon years BP; the 'calendar circle' is often cited as about 4800 to 4500 BC. Brass 2018 shows the cattle tumulus date of 6480 plus or minus 270 bp calibrates to 5976 to 4835 cal BC, wider than usual citation.

zana-valley-canals-peru-4700bce.summary: On the western slopes of Andes in Zaña valley, Tom Dillehay, Herbert Eling and Jack Rossen traced narrow stone-lined canals running along hillside contours from side streams to small fields and house platforms of Nanchoc tradition. Radiocarbon on sediments within and beneath the channels places the earliest between about 6,700 and 5,400 years ago, with one less secure date near 7,000 years ago, so people were irrigating before they made pottery. Macrofossils from the same sites include peanut, squash and cotton dated between 9240 and 5500 radiocarbon years ago. Andean irrigation, like Mesopotamian, began at small scale among villagers in dry valleys fed by mountain streams.

sources.title: Dillehay, T. D., Eling, H. H. and Rossen, J., 'Preceramic irrigation canals in the Peruvian Andes', PNAS 102 (2005)
sources.author: Dillehay, T. D., Eling, H. H. and Rossen, J.
sources.confirms: Reports preceramic canals in the Zaña valley with the earliest dated to about 6700 to 5400 cal BP and a less secure date near 7000 cal BP.

sources.title: Dillehay, T. D. et al., 'Preceramic adoption of peanut, squash, and cotton in northern Peru', Science 316 (2007)
sources.author: Dillehay, T. D. et al.
sources.confirms: Reports peanut, squash and cotton macrofossils from northern Peruvian Andes sites directly dated between 9240 and 5500 radiocarbon years BP.

zana-valley-canals-peru-4700bce.detail: The canals are a few hundred metres long and carried water by gravity, requiring survey of gradients. Later coastal Peruvian states built canals tens of kilometres long on same principle. Nanchoc sites also show early quinoa, coca and manioc, and simple mounds for communal use. Dillehay's project found house floors, hearths and stone tools beside canals, with evidence of lime processing for chewing coca. Canals were cleaned and recut over centuries. Cotton nets and gourd floats supported fishing in rivers nearby.
zana-valley-canals-peru-4700bce.dating_note: Dillehay, Eling and Rossen 2005 date the earliest Nanchoc canals to about 6700 to 5400 cal BP, with a less secure date of about 7000 cal BP; crops at the sites date between 9240 and 5500 radiocarbon years BP.

budj-bim-eel-aquaculture-4600bce.summary: On the lava flows of Budj Bim volcano in southwest Victoria, Gunditjmara people dug channels through basalt, built weirs of volcanic stone and set woven eel traps to catch, hold and harvest kooyang, the short-finned eel, as it migrated through wetlands. Charcoal from infill of a channel at Muldoons Trap Complex at Lake Condah dates construction to at least 6,600 years ago, with stone walls added 600 to 800 years ago and a dam for ponding floodwaters 300 to 500 years ago. The system provided a stable food base for a settled society living in stone houses. UNESCO inscribed Budj Bim Cultural Landscape in 2019 as evidence of six millennia of aquaculture.

sources.title: McNiven, I. J., Crouch, J., Richards, T., Sniderman, K., Dolby, N. and Gunditj Mirring Traditional Owners Aboriginal Corporation, 'Phased redevelopment of an ancient Gunditjmara fish trap over the past 800 years: Muldoons Trap Complex, Lake Condah, southwestern Victoria', Australian Archaeology 81 (2015)
sources.author: McNiven, I. J., Crouch, J., Richards, T., Sniderman, K., Dolby, N. and Gunditj Mirring Traditional Owners Aboriginal Corporation
sources.confirms: Dates initial construction of the Muldoons Trap Complex to at least 6600 cal BP, with basalt walls added 600 to 800 cal BP and a dam 300 to 500 cal BP.

sources.title: UNESCO World Heritage Centre, 'Budj Bim Cultural Landscape', UNESCO World Heritage List (2019)
sources.author: UNESCO World Heritage Centre
sources.confirms: States that over at least 6,600 years the Gunditjmara built channels, weirs and dams of volcanic rock to trap, store and harvest kooyang eels.

budj-bim-eel-aquaculture-4600bce.detail: Eels were smoked in hollow trees for storage and trade. The dates make Budj Bim one of oldest aquaculture systems documented anywhere. Gunditjmara oral tradition records the volcano's eruption, which geologists date to about 37,000 years ago, among oldest oral accounts proposed. Lake Condah's stone house foundations number in hundreds, and early colonial observers described Gunditjmara villages and smoked eel trade in 1840s. Channels follow natural lava flow depressions, extended by cutting basalt.

picture.alt: Lake Surprise crater lake within the Budj Bim lava landscape, Victoria, Australia
picture.credit: Dhx1, via Wikimedia Commons

budj-bim-eel-aquaculture-4600bce.dating_note: McNiven et al. 2015 date initial construction of Muldoons Trap Complex at Lake Condah to at least 6600 cal BP from charcoal in channel infill; the system was elaborated repeatedly up to the nineteenth century.

manioc-san-andres-tabasco-4600bce.summary: Sediment cores from San Andrés in Tabasco lowlands near the later Olmec centre of La Venta record pollen of cultivated maize together with charcoal and a drop in forest trees at about 5100 BCE, as people cleared wetland forest for plots. A pollen grain of Manihot, manioc, dated to 4600 BCE may come from a domesticated plant. This sequence continues with domesticated sunflower by 2500 BCE. Manioc's likely origin lies in Cerrado savannas south of the Amazon, with domesticated plants spreading from there by 7000 years ago. Manioc, a starchy root tolerant of poor soils, became lowland South America's staple and reached Mexico's Gulf coast while villages there were still few.

sources.title: Pope, K. O. et al., 'Origin and environmental setting of ancient agriculture in the lowlands of Mesoamerica', Science 292 (2001)
sources.author: Pope, K. O. et al.
sources.confirms: Reports cultivated Zea pollen with forest clearing at about 5100 calendar years BC and a Manihot pollen grain dated 4600 calendar years BC at San Andrés, Tabasco.

sources.title: Isendahl, C., 'The domestication and early spread of manioc (Manihot esculenta Crantz): a brief synthesis', Latin American Antiquity 22 (2011)
sources.author: Isendahl, C.
sources.confirms: Identifies the Brazilian Cerrado as the likely origin of manioc and dates its spread from there to the early Holocene, certainly by 7000 years ago.

manioc-san-andres-tabasco-4600bce.detail: Identifying a single pollen grain to a domesticated species is uncertain, which is why Kevin Pope claims only that this grain may be domesticated. Manioc leaves little archaeological trace because roots are processed, not stored as seeds; starch grains on grinding tools now supplement pollen. Bitter manioc requires detoxification by grating and squeezing, a processing technology in its own right. Sunflower pollen and seeds at San Andrés raised debate, since sunflower domestication is otherwise placed in eastern North America.

picture.alt: Harvested manioc roots, Manihot esculenta, piled for sale
picture.credit: David Monniaux, via Wikimedia Commons

manioc-san-andres-tabasco-4600bce.dating_note: Pope et al. 2001 date a Manihot pollen grain at San Andrés to 4600 calendar years BC and cultivated Zea with forest clearing to about 5100 BC; Isendahl's review places manioc's origin in the Brazilian Cerrado and its spread by 7000 years ago.

rice-domestication-lower-yangzi-4600bce.summary: Rice spikelet bases tell whether a grain fell on its own or was harvested: wild bases show a smooth scar, domestic ones a torn scar where the stalk held. Counts of bases at Tianluoshan in Zhejiang show the domestic type rising from 27 to 39 percent between 6900 and 6600 years ago, with rice also growing from a minor to a major food. At Huxi, 9000 to 8400 years ago, only 9 percent were non-shattering, and the sequence runs forward through Kuahuqiao, Majiabang and Liangzhu. Rice domestication thus took about four thousand years of harvesting and replanting, a slow pace that matches wheat in Near East.

sources.title: Fuller, D. Q. et al., 'The domestication process and domestication rate in rice: spikelet bases from the Lower Yangtze', Science 323 (2009)
sources.author: Fuller, D. Q. et al.
sources.confirms: Reports non-shattering rice spikelet bases at Tianluoshan rising from 27 to 39 percent between 6900 and 6600 years ago.

sources.title: Zheng, Y., Crawford, G. W., Jiang, L. and Chen, X., 'Rice domestication revealed by reduced shattering of archaeological rice from the Lower Yangtze valley', Scientific Reports 6 (2016)
sources.author: Zheng, Y., Crawford, G. W., Jiang, L. and Chen, X.
sources.confirms: Shows selection for reduced shattering from Huxi, 9000 to 8400 BP, through Kuahuqiao, Tianluoshan, Majiabang and Liangzhu.

rice-domestication-lower-yangzi-4600bce.detail: Grain size increased in parallel. Tianluoshan's waterlogged deposits also preserved acorns and water chestnuts, so rice was one food among several until the fifth millennium. The genetics of rice domestication, with japonica from Yangzi and indica arising later through hybridisation in South Asia, agrees with this archaeological sequence. Field systems with bunds at Tianluoshan and nearby Caoxieshan show paddy construction by about 4000 BCE. Hemudu, close by, preserved wooden houses and bone spades used in wet fields.

picture.alt: Excavation shelter over the waterlogged Tianluoshan site at Yuyao, Zhejiang
picture.credit: Siyuwj, via Wikimedia Commons

rice-domestication-lower-yangzi-4600bce.dating_note: Fuller et al. 2009 track non-shattering rice at Tianluoshan from 27 to 39 percent between 6900 and 6600 years ago; Zheng et al. 2016 show the process beginning at Huxi 9000 to 8400 BP and continuing through Liangzhu. 4600 BCE marks the Tianluoshan threshold.

varna-gold-4500bce.summary: A cemetery on the Black Sea coast near Varna, Bulgaria, excavated from 1972, contained over 300 graves of 4560 to 4450 BCE. A handful held thousands of gold objects: beads, sceptre mounts, bracelets, appliqués and a penis sheath, with Grave 43 alone holding about 1.5 kilograms. AMS dates show it was used for a century or so and that its richest burials may be earliest. Its goldwork shows hammering, annealing and perforating of native gold, with no casting, by smiths who already handled copper. Gold here signals rank: a few men were buried as paramount chiefs while most graves held little, earliest clear case of steep wealth inequality in Europe.

sources.title: Higham, T. et al., 'New perspectives on the Varna cemetery (Bulgaria): AMS dates and social implications', Antiquity 81 (2007)
sources.author: Higham, T. et al.
sources.confirms: Dates cemetery use to 4560 to 4450 BC, notes richer burials may be earlier, and describes a handful of lavish graves of paramount chiefs.

sources.title: Leusch, V., Armbruster, B., Pernicka, E. and Slavchev, V., 'On the invention of gold metallurgy: the gold objects from the Varna I cemetery (Bulgaria), technological consequence and inventive creativity', Cambridge Archaeological Journal 25 (2015)
sources.author: Leusch, V., Armbruster, B., Pernicka, E. and Slavchev, V.
sources.confirms: Analyses Varna I gold objects dated 4550 to 4450 cal BC as the earliest known fine metalworking.

varna-gold-4500bce.detail: Gold occurs native in Balkan river gravels and needs no smelting, so the achievement lies in standardised bead manufacture and sheet work. Heavy cast copper axes in the same graves tie Varna to Balkan smelting. The culture collapsed within a few centuries, possibly with climatic drying and steppe contacts. Spondylus shell bracelets from Aegean and copper from Balkan mines appear with gold, and some graves were symbolic cenotaphs with clay masks and gold eyes. Gold's total weight exceeds six kilograms.

picture.alt: Gold ornaments and appliqués from the Varna cemetery, 4600 to 4200 BCE, Varna Archaeological Museum
picture.credit: Zde, via Wikimedia Commons

varna-gold-4500bce.dating_note: Higham et al. 2007 date Varna I cemetery to 4560 to 4450 BC by AMS; Leusch et al. 2015 give 4550 to 4450 cal BC for gold.

huaca-prieta-cotton-indigo-4200bce.summary: Huaca Prieta, a black mound on Peru's north coast excavated by Junius Bird in 1940s and again by Tom Dillehay from 2007, preserves cotton textiles in its dry layers. Blue stripes on fragments from stratum 44, dated around 4200 BCE, contain indigotin, the indigo dye, some 1,500 years before indigo in Egypt. The cloth is twined, not woven, from Gossypium barbadense, South American cotton that Nanchoc farmers had grown since at least 5500 BCE. Indigo requires fermenting leaves to release the dye and oxidising it on the fibre, a multi-step chemistry. The mound's builders were fisher-farmers who worked cotton and gourds without pottery.

sources.title: Splitstoser, J. C., Dillehay, T. D., Wouters, J. and Claro, A., 'Early pre-Hispanic use of indigo blue in Peru', Science Advances 2 (2016)
sources.author: Splitstoser, J. C., Dillehay, T. D., Wouters, J. and Claro, A.
sources.confirms: Identifies indigotin on 6,000-year-old cotton fabrics from Huaca Prieta stratum 44, about 6200 to 6000 cal BP, as the earliest known use of indigo.

sources.title: Dillehay, T. D. et al., 'Chronology, mound-building and environment at Huaca Prieta, coastal Peru, from 13 700 to 4000 years ago', Antiquity 86 (2012)
sources.author: Dillehay, T. D. et al.
sources.confirms: Establishes the Huaca Prieta sequence from first maritime foragers about 13,720 BP through mound construction, horticulture and monumentality.

huaca-prieta-cotton-indigo-4200bce.detail: Blue indigo appears with red, yellow and white in stripes, so colour patterning in textiles was established early. Cotton's first use on coast may have been for fishing nets and lines. Huaca Prieta's deepest layers date to about 13,700 years ago, showing maritime foragers long before textiles. Indigo from Indigofera plants native to Peru was probably used, with yellow from a plant source and red from cochineal or plants. Textiles were twined by hand without a loom, a technique that persisted on coast for millennia.

picture.alt: The mound of Huaca Prieta in the Chicama valley, Peru, with excavation trench
picture.credit: AlisonRuthHughes, via Wikimedia Commons

huaca-prieta-cotton-indigo-4200bce.dating_note: Splitstoser et al. 2016 date the indigo-dyed cotton textiles from Huaca Prieta stratum 44 to about 6200 to 6000 cal BP; Dillehay et al. 2012 give the mound's chronology from 13,700 to 4,000 years ago.

donkey-domestication-egypt-4000bce.summary: Mitochondrial DNA shows every donkey descends from African wild ass, with two lineages pointing to Nubian and Somali populations. Ten complete ass skeletons lay buried in brick tombs beside an early king's funerary enclosure at Abydos, dated to about 3000 BCE. All ten showed joint wear and compressed vertebrae consistent with carrying heavy loads, yet their leg bones remained wild-like in shape, so after a millennium of use the animals had changed little. Domestication began about 4000 BCE among herders of drying Sahara and Nile valley. The donkey became the first pack animal, carrying grain, water and trade goods across deserts where wheels failed.

sources.title: Rossel, S. et al., 'Domestication of the donkey: timing, processes, and indicators', PNAS 105 (2008)
sources.author: Rossel, S. et al.
sources.confirms: Examines ten articulated ass skeletons at Abydos dated about 3000 BC, all with load-carrying pathologies, and places the start of domestication about 6,000 years ago.

sources.title: Beja-Pereira, A. et al., 'African origins of the domestic donkey', Science 304 (2004)
sources.author: Beja-Pereira, A. et al.
sources.confirms: Uses mitochondrial DNA to show donkeys derive from the African wild ass with two distinct lineages.
sources.qualifies: Only title, venue and the opening of the abstract were readable.

donkey-domestication-egypt-4000bce.detail: Donkeys reached southwest Asia by third millennium BCE and underpinned caravan trade between Egypt, Levant and Mesopotamia. Their slow morphological change warns that bone shape alone can miss early domestication; pathology and burial context carry the argument here. Donkeys appear in Egyptian art carrying loads by Old Kingdom times and in Mesopotamian texts as pack animals and plough beasts. Unlike cattle they need little water and thrive on poor scrub. Their pathology at Abydos matches modern working donkeys examined in Egypt. Royal burial of asses marks their value to early kings.

picture.alt: Somali wild ass, Equus africanus somaliensis, a grey wild relative of the donkey, standing in a reserve
picture.credit: H. Zell, via Wikimedia Commons

donkey-domestication-egypt-4000bce.dating_note: Rossel et al. 2008 place the start of donkey domestication about 6,000 years ago from African wild ass; the ten Abydos skeletons dated to about 3000 BC still show wild-like bone shape, so the process was slow.

llama-alpaca-telarmachay-4000bce.summary: On the high puna of central Peru and southern Andes, hunters of wild guanaco and vicuña began controlling herds. Jane Wheeler's excavations at Telarmachay rock shelter traced a shift from hunting to herding, with neonatal mortality typical of corralled animals and alpaca-like incisors by about 6000 years ago. Earliest size changes in camelid bones come around 7,100 years ago, a herd-protection phase runs from 7,100 to 4,500 years ago and very large specimens, probably llamas, appear from 5,800 years ago. Ancient DNA shows early domestic forms by 6000 to 5500 years ago and high-altitude pastoral societies from 5500. Llamas carried loads and alpacas gave fine fibre; they were the Americas' only large domestic animals.

sources.title: Yacobaccio, H. D., 'The domestication of South American camelids: a review', Animal Frontiers 11 (2021)
sources.author: Yacobaccio, H. D.
sources.confirms: Places the earliest camelid size change about 7100 cal BP, a herd-protection phase 7100 to 4500 cal BP, very large specimens from 5800 cal BP and corralling at Inca Cueva 7 at 4635 to 4232 cal BP.

sources.title: Díaz-Maroto, P. et al., 'Ancient DNA reveals the lost domestication history of South American camelids in Northern Chile and across the Andes', eLife 10 (2021), e63390 (2021)
sources.author: Díaz-Maroto, P. et al.
sources.confirms: States llama and alpaca domestication 6,000 to 7,000 years ago, with early domestic forms 6,000 to 5,500 years ago and pastoral societies from 5,500 years ago.

sources.title: Wheeler, J. C., 'Evolution and present situation of the South American Camelidae', Biological Journal of the Linnean Society 54 (1995)
sources.author: Wheeler, J. C.
sources.venue: Biological Journal of the Linnean Society
sources.confirms: Summarises the Telarmachay evidence for camelid domestication.
sources.qualifies: Only bibliographic details could be read.

llama-alpaca-telarmachay-4000bce.detail: Camelids were not milked or ridden; their value lay in pack transport, meat, dung fuel and wool for the textiles that Andean societies prized above metal. Post-Conquest herd collapse and hybridisation blurred the genetic record, which is why ancient DNA was needed. Corrals at Inca Cueva 7 in Argentina date to about 4,635 to 4,232 years ago. Telarmachay lies at 4,420 metres in Junín.

picture.alt: Llamas and alpacas gathered in a stone corral in the highlands of Chinchaypujio, Peru
picture.credit: Tobias Deml, via Wikimedia Commons

llama-alpaca-telarmachay-4000bce.dating_note: Yacobaccio 2021 places the earliest osteological evidence of camelid size change about 7100 cal BP, with herd protection from 7100 to 4500 cal BP; Díaz-Maroto et al. 2021 put early domestic forms at 6000 to 5500 years ago. Jane Wheeler's Telarmachay sequence sets domestic alpaca by about 6000 BP. 4000 BCE is a midpoint.

mehrgarh-lost-wax-amulet-4000bce.summary: A six-spoked copper amulet 20 mm across from Mehrgarh, about 6,000 years old, was examined with high-resolution photoluminescence imaging. Images revealed dendritic copper oxide structures frozen in metal showing the object was cast in a single pour of unalloyed copper into a mould formed around a wax model that had been melted out, the lost-wax process. Casting a wheel with spokes is impossible in an open mould, so the amulet is the earliest known lost-wax object, predating Nahal Mishmar hoard in Levant by a few centuries. Method, in which wax gives form and clay gives the mould, later produced bronzes from Mesopotamia to Shang China and Benin.

sources.title: Thoury, M. et al., 'High spatial dynamics-photoluminescence imaging reveals the metallurgy of the earliest lost-wax cast object', Nature Communications 7 (2016)
sources.author: Thoury, M. et al.
sources.confirms: Describes the 6,000-year-old wheel-shaped Mehrgarh amulet, 20 mm across, as the earliest known lost-wax cast object, cast in a single piece.

sources.title: Moulherat, C., Tengberg, M., Haquet, J.-F. and Mille, B., 'First evidence of cotton at Neolithic Mehrgarh, Pakistan: analysis of mineralized fibres from a copper bead', Journal of Archaeological Science 29 (2002)
sources.author: Moulherat, C., Tengberg, M., Haquet, J.-F. and Mille, B.
sources.confirms: Documents earlier copper bead manufacture at Neolithic Mehrgarh, the local metalworking tradition behind the amulet.
sources.qualifies: Does not discuss the amulet itself.

mehrgarh-lost-wax-amulet-4000bce.detail: Photoluminescence technique maps cuprite inclusions and reveals casting history without cutting object. Mehrgarh's copper came from Baluchistan ores, and same period saw painted pottery and compartmented seals. Lost-wax casting is one of few metal techniques to be reinvented repeatedly, since wax and clay are universal. Copper used was unusually pure, which made it brittle and probably explains why lost-wax casting in pure copper was soon replaced by arsenical and tin alloys. Mehrgarh Period III also saw wheel-made painted pottery and compartmented stamp seals.

picture.alt: Mud-brick ruins of the Neolithic settlement at Mehrgarh in Balochistan, photographed in 2019.
picture.credit: Ashish_Premier, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

mehrgarh-lost-wax-amulet-4000bce.dating_note: Thoury et al. 2016 describe the wheel-shaped amulet as 6,000 years old, from Mehrgarh's Chalcolithic Period III, about 4000 BC.

secondary-products-traction-milk-wool-40.summary: Andrew Sherratt proposed in 1981 that domestic animals were first kept for meat, hide and bone, and only much later, from fourth millennium BCE, exploited for products taken from living animals: milk, wool and the pulling of ploughs and carts. Greenfield's review in 2010 tested the model against zooarchaeology and lipid residues. Milk failed the test, since Evershed's team found milk fat in Anatolian pottery of seventh millennium BCE. Traction and wool fit better: ard marks, cart tracks and wheel finds cluster between 3700 and 3300 BCE across Europe and Mesopotamia. Model remains the standard frame for asking when muscle power from oxen and fibre from sheep entered farming economies.

sources.title: Greenfield, H. J., 'The Secondary Products Revolution: the past, the present and the future', World Archaeology 42 (2010)
sources.author: Greenfield, H. J.
sources.confirms: Summarises Sherratt's 1981 model, with intensive exploitation of milk, wool and traction beginning in the Chalcolithic Near East and spreading to Europe and Asia, and reviews the zooarchaeological tests.

sources.title: Bogucki, P., 'Animal traction and household economies in Neolithic Europe', Antiquity 67 (1993)
sources.author: Bogucki, P.
sources.confirms: Frames how oxen, pigs, sheep and goats living within single households changed Neolithic European domestic economies, citing Milisauskas on cattle traction in later Neolithic Poland.

sources.title: Evershed, R. P. et al., 'Earliest date for milk use in the Near East and southeastern Europe linked to cattle herding', Nature 455 (2008)
sources.author: Evershed, R. P. et al.
sources.confirms: Shows milk use by the seventh millennium BC, undercutting the model's late date for dairying.

secondary-products-traction-milk-wool-40.detail: Bogucki argued that oxen and other stock living within household changed how Neolithic European families organised labour. Secondary products matter for energy history because an ox team multiplies the land one household can till, and wool allows textiles without flax fields. Woolly sheep are a breeding achievement whose first dated evidence falls close to 3000 BCE, at end of this period.
secondary-products-traction-milk-wool-40.dating_note: Sherratt's 1981 model placed milk, wool and traction in fourth millennium BC; milk lipids now show dairying by seventh millennium, so the model's dates hold only for wool and traction.

alpine-lake-dwellings-dendro-3900bce.summary: From about 5000 BCE farmers built villages of timber houses on piles along the shores of Alpine lakes and bogs, in what are now Switzerland, Germany, France, Italy, Austria and Slovenia. Waterlogged conditions preserved posts, floors, textiles, wooden tools, food remains and, at Ljubljana, a wheel. Each oak or ash post carries its tree rings, so felling dates to an exact year: Hornstaad-Hörnle on Lake Constance was built, burnt and rebuilt in a roughly twenty-year span around 3900 BCE. UNESCO inscribed 111 of these sites in 2011. Pile dwellings are the finest-resolution record of Neolithic daily life in Europe.

sources.title: Billamboz, A., 'Dealing with heteroconnections and short tree-ring series at different levels of dating in the dendrochronology of the Southwest German pile-dwellings', Dendrochronologia 26 (2008)
sources.author: Billamboz, A.
sources.confirms: Reports tree-ring dating of Hornstaad-Hörnle with habitation lasting about twenty years around 3900 BC and reconstructs construction phases.

sources.title: UNESCO World Heritage Centre, 'Prehistoric Pile Dwellings around the Alps', UNESCO World Heritage List (2011)
sources.author: UNESCO World Heritage Centre
sources.confirms: Describes 111 sites dating from 5000 to 500 BC whose timber can be dated exactly by dendrochronology.

alpine-lake-dwellings-dendro-3900bce.detail: Dendrochronology anchors European Neolithic calendar, since long oak chronologies extend back more than 10,000 years and allow radiocarbon calibration. The pile dwellers grew wheat, barley, flax and poppy, fished and kept cattle; textile fragments show plied linen. Whether houses stood over water or on seasonally flooded shores varies by site. Hornstaad-Hörnle burned down around 3910 BC and was rebuilt, and its charred stores preserved cereal, apple, hazelnut and poppy seeds. Wooden wheels, textiles and a bow from later lake villages extend the inventory.

picture.alt: Reconstructed pile dwellings on Lake Constance at the Unteruhldingen open-air museum
picture.credit: Gerhard Schauber, via Wikimedia Commons

alpine-lake-dwellings-dendro-3900bce.dating_note: Alpine pile dwellings span 5000 to 500 BC; Hornstaad-Hörnle on Lake Constance is dendro-dated to about 3900 BC, one of the earliest. Tree-ring dates give exact felling years.

jomon-sannai-maruyama-3900bce.summary: At Sannai Maruyama in Aomori, northern Japan, people of the Jomon tradition who fished, hunted, gathered nuts and managed chestnut groves lived in a settlement occupied from about 3900 to 2300 BCE. Junko Habu's analysis traces the number of pit dwellings rising to a peak and falling, with long houses up to 32 metres, hundreds of storage pits, burial rows along roads and a structure of six chestnut posts a metre thick set in pits, probably a raised building or tower. Jomon pottery, among the world's oldest, here reached elaborate forms, and lacquerware, jade from 600 km away and obsidian show exchange. Sannai Maruyama demonstrates that sedentary villages with monumental timber could rest on a foraging economy supplemented by cultivated plants.

sources.title: Habu, J., 'Growth and decline in complex hunter-gatherer societies: a case study from the Jomon period Sannai Maruyama site, Japan', Antiquity 82 (2008)
sources.author: Habu, J.
sources.confirms: Dates Sannai Maruyama to 3900 to 2300 BC and tracks dwelling numbers rising to a peak and declining over 1500 years.

sources.title: UNESCO World Heritage Centre, 'Jomon Prehistoric Sites in Northern Japan', UNESCO World Heritage List (2021)
sources.author: UNESCO World Heritage Centre
sources.confirms: Describes 17 sites of a sedentary hunter-fisher-gatherer society from about 13,000 BCE to 400 BCE with permanent dwellings.
sources.qualifies: Page does not single out Sannai Maruyama's dates.

jomon-sannai-maruyama-3900bce.detail: Chestnut pollen dominates around the site, suggesting deliberate planting. The settlement's decline coincides with a cooling trend after 2300 BCE. UNESCO inscribed 17 Jomon sites of northern Japan in 2021. Comparison with Çatalhöyük and Trypillia shows that large settlements did not require cereal farming. Clay figurines, over 1,500 found here, and lacquered wooden bowls show craft specialisation. Jomon pottery began about 14,000 BCE and had elaborate flame-rim styles by Sannai Maruyama's time. Storage pits held chestnuts and walnuts.

picture.alt: Reconstructed six-pillar timber structure and pit houses at the Sannai Maruyama Jomon site, Aomori
picture.credit: 663highland, via Wikimedia Commons

jomon-sannai-maruyama-3900bce.dating_note: Sannai Maruyama was occupied about 3900 to 2300 BC; Habu 2008 charts growth and decline in dwelling numbers across that span.

trypillia-megasites-3900bce.summary: Between about 4100 and 3400 BCE, Cucuteni-Trypillia communities on the forest-steppe of Ukraine and Moldova built settlements of up to 320 hectares, such as Nebelivka, Maidanetske and Taljanky, laid out as concentric rings of two-storey houses with open centres and large assembly buildings. Magnetometer surveys have mapped thousands of house footprints. Some archaeologists class these as proto-cities, others as oversized villages. House sizes show little inequality between households, pointing to an egalitarian ideology that avoided the hierarchies seen at Varna and Uruk. Houses were burnt deliberately at abandonment, leaving the rubble that aerial survey detects.

sources.title: Diachenko, A. and Menotti, F., 'Proto-cities or non-proto-cities? On the nature of Cucuteni-Trypillia mega-sites', Journal of World Prehistory 30 (2017)
sources.author: Diachenko, A. and Menotti, F.
sources.confirms: Describes megasites as the largest residential agglomerations in southeastern Europe from about 4100 to 3400 cal BC and reviews the proto-city debate.

sources.title: Hofmann, R. et al., 'Trypillia mega-sites: a social levelling concept?', Antiquity 98 (2024)
sources.author: Hofmann, R. et al.
sources.confirms: Dates megasites to about 4200 to 3600 BC with sizes up to 320 ha and about 10,000 inhabitants, and finds house-size equality suggesting mechanisms against wealth inequality.

trypillia-megasites-3900bce.detail: Populations of 10,000 or more are estimated for the largest sites, comparable to contemporary Uruk, yet without writing, temples or elite tombs. Megasites were abandoned after a few centuries, perhaps through soil exhaustion, social strain or climate change, and the tradition ended around 3400 BCE as steppe pastoralists appeared. Each house held painted pottery of high quality and clay figurines, with ovens and raised platforms. Houses faced a shared open space, and alleyways gave access between rings. Food came from wheat, barley, cattle and pigs farmed around each site.

picture.alt: Three-dimensional model of the Maidanetske Trypillia megasite showing concentric rings of houses
picture.credit: René Ohlrau, via Wikimedia Commons

trypillia-megasites-3900bce.dating_note: Cucuteni-Trypillia megasites are dated about 4100 to 3400 cal BC by Diachenko and Menotti and 4200 to 3600 BC by Hofmann et al.; 3900 BCE sits in the main phase.

ard-plough-traces-europe-3800bce.summary: Beneath long barrows and under later soil in Denmark, northern Germany and Poland, excavators find grids of narrow furrows cut into the subsoil: traces of an ard, a simple wooden scratch plough drawn by cattle and pulled across a field in two directions. Most date to the Funnel Beaker culture's first centuries, about 3800 to 3500 BCE, when farming spread onto the north European plain. Peter Rowley-Conwy argued in 1987 that marks sealed directly under barrows may record ritual breaking of ground before mound building rather than ordinary tillage. Peter Bogucki linked traction to households keeping oxen. Ards allowed one family to till far more land than hoes permitted and tied cattle keeping to cereal growing.

sources.title: Bogucki, P., 'Animal traction and household economies in Neolithic Europe', Antiquity 67 (1993)
sources.author: Bogucki, P.
sources.confirms: Discusses oxen in Neolithic households and cites Milisauskas on cattle traction in later Neolithic Poland.
sources.qualifies: Abstract gives no ard dates.

sources.title: Sørensen, C., Bjørnevad-Ahlqvist, M. and Sørensen, L., 'Sociokulturel betydning af tragtbægerkulturens tidligneolitiske flintøkser', Kuml 70 (2021) (2022)
sources.author: Sørensen, C., Bjørnevad-Ahlqvist, M. and Sørensen, L.
sources.confirms: Dates the Funnel Beaker culture's start in Denmark to about 4000 BC and its Early Neolithic to 4000 to 3300 BC with arable farming and animal husbandry.

sources.title: Rowley-Conwy, P., 'The interpretation of ard marks', Antiquity 61 (1987)
sources.author: Rowley-Conwy, P.
sources.confirms: Warns that ard marks sealed beneath barrows may relate to mound construction rather than cultivation.
sources.qualifies: Only bibliographic details could be read.

ard-plough-traces-europe-3800bce.verification_note: Funnel Beaker chronology is confirmed; the specific ard-mark dates come from literature not readable in full.
ard-plough-traces-europe-3800bce.detail: Uruk pictograms of about 3200 BCE show a plough sign, and later Bronze Age rock carvings in Scandinavia depict ox teams with ards. Cattle bones with pathologies from draught appear in Poland by the mid fourth millennium. Wooden ards themselves survive only from Bronze Age in Danish bogs. Ards do not turn soil, so fields were cross-ploughed in two directions, producing the grid pattern that excavators find. Crook ards of oak and ash were later preserved in Danish bogs at Døstrup and Hendriksmose.
ard-plough-traces-europe-3800bce.dating_note: Criss-cross ard marks under Danish and north German long barrows belong to the early Funnel Beaker period, about 3800 to 3500 BC, with the earliest claims around 3900 BC. Rowley-Conwy cautions that some marks come from barrow construction rather than farming.

head-smashed-in-buffalo-jump-3700bce.summary: At the edge of Porcupine Hills in southern Alberta a sandstone cliff ten metres high stands above bone beds up to eleven metres deep.
