From about 5,800 years ago, around 3700 BCE, hunters gathered bison on plateau behind, then guided them along drive lanes marked by hundreds of stone cairns, behind which people waved hides to keep the herd moving, until animals stampeded over edge. Below, the camp butchered carcasses, rendered grease by boiling bones with heated stones and dried meat for pemmican. Jack Brink's study describes the hunt as a communal engineering of landscape and animal behaviour practised for nearly 6,000 years until 1800s. UNESCO inscribed the site in 1981. Mass kills fed and provisioned Plains peoples without domesticating the bison.

sources.title: Brink, J. W., Imagining Head-Smashed-In: Aboriginal Buffalo Hunting on the Northern Plains (Athabasca University Press, 2008)
sources.author: Brink, J. W.
sources.confirms: Describes nearly 6,000 years of communal bison hunting at Head-Smashed-In, with herds driven over the cliff and butchered in the camp below.

sources.title: UNESCO World Heritage Centre, 'Head-Smashed-In Buffalo Jump', UNESCO World Heritage List (1981)
sources.author: UNESCO World Heritage Centre
sources.confirms: Dates use of the jump from approximately 5,800 years BP until AD 1850, with drive lanes marked by stone cairns, a cliff 10 m high and deep bone deposits below.

sources.title: Reeves, B. O. K., 'Head-Smashed-In: 5500 years of bison jumping in the Alberta plains', Plains Anthropologist 23 (1978)
sources.author: Reeves, B. O. K.
sources.confirms: Reports excavation and radiocarbon dating of the deepest bone beds.
sources.qualifies: Only bibliographic details could be read.

head-smashed-in-buffalo-jump-3700bce.detail: Brian Reeves excavated deepest deposits in 1960s and dated them to about 5,700 radiocarbon years BP. Hunt required knowledge of wind, bison herd psychology and timing in late summer when animals were fat. Jumps like this exist across northern Plains, and Head-Smashed-In is largest and best preserved. Bone beds hold projectile points that change in style over millennia, from Mummy Cave to Avonlea and Old Women's phases, giving a dated sequence of Plains cultures. Brink's work drew on Blackfoot knowledge of hunt.

picture.alt: Sandstone cliff of Head-Smashed-In Buffalo Jump rising above prairie grassland, Alberta
picture.credit: Thomas Fuhrmann, via Wikimedia Commons

head-smashed-in-buffalo-jump-3700bce.dating_note: Brian Reeves dated the earliest bone deposits at Head-Smashed-In to about 5,700 radiocarbon years BP; UNESCO gives use from approximately 5,800 BP until AD 1850 with a long interruption. 3700 BCE is the conventional start.

nahal-mishmar-lost-wax-hoard-3700bce.summary: In 1961 a cave in Judean desert near Dead Sea gave up 429 objects wrapped in a reed mat: crowns, sceptres, mace heads and standards, most in copper alloyed with arsenic and antimony, alongside plain copper axes and chisels. Shalev and Northover's re-analysis showed two technologies side by side: pure copper cast in open moulds for tools, and complex alloys cast by lost-wax method for prestige objects. Yuval Goren traced clay mould remnants to En Gedi area, placing the workshop near hoard. Lost-wax casting, in which a wax model is coated in clay, melted out and replaced by metal, allowed forms impossible by hammering, and arsenic made the melt flow and the result harden.

sources.title: Goren, Y., 'The location of specialized copper production by the lost wax technique in the Chalcolithic southern Levant', Geoarchaeology 23 (2008)
sources.author: Goren, Y.
sources.confirms: Distinguishes open-cast pure copper tools from lost-wax items in arsenic, antimony and nickel alloys and traces mould clay to the En Gedi area.

sources.title: Shalev, S. and Northover, J. P., 'The metallurgy of the Nahal Mishmar hoard reconsidered', Archaeometry 35 (1993)
sources.author: Shalev, S. and Northover, J. P.
sources.confirms: Re-analyses the hoard, found in 1961 in a Judean desert cave, with atomic absorption and electron probe methods.

nahal-mishmar-lost-wax-hoard-3700bce.detail: The arsenical ores came from far afield, possibly Anatolia or Caucasus, while the pure copper matches Wadi Faynan in Jordan. Why the hoard was hidden is unknown; Ghassulian culture ended soon after. Mehrgarh's wheel amulet shows lost-wax casting in Baluchistan at a similar date. Copper for prestige objects was alloyed to over ten percent arsenic in some pieces, which lowers melting point and gives a silvery sheen. Mace heads number over 240, and standards carry ibex, birds and horned animals. Reed mat radiocarbon dates cluster in late fifth millennium cal BC.

picture.alt: Copper standards and mace heads from the Nahal Mishmar hoard displayed in the Israel Museum
picture.credit: Hanay, via Wikimedia Commons

nahal-mishmar-lost-wax-hoard-3700bce.dating_note: The hoard, found in 1961, belongs to Ghassulian Chalcolithic; radiocarbon dates on reed mat wrapping place it in the late fifth or early fourth millennium BC, with 3700 BCE a common midpoint.

botai-horses-dispute-3500bce.summary: At Botai in northern Kazakhstan, pit houses of about 3500 BCE sit amid hundreds of thousands of horse bones. Alan Outram argued in 2009 for horse keeping, riding and milking: metacarpals resembled Bronze Age domestic horses, some teeth showed wear from bridles and lipids in pots carried mare's milk fat. In 2018 genomes of 20 Botai horses showed they were ancestors of Przewalski's horse and of no modern domestic horse. Genomes published in 2021 traced modern domestic horses to Volga-Don steppe animals that spread after about 2200 BCE. Botai people may have tamed local horses, but their line did not continue.

sources.title: Outram, A. K. et al., 'The earliest horse harnessing and milking', Science 323 (2009)
sources.author: Outram, A. K. et al.
sources.confirms: Reports Botai culture horse domestication about 3500 BCE on metacarpal shape, bridling pathologies and mare's milk lipids.

sources.title: Gaunitz, C. et al., 'Ancient genomes revisit the ancestry of domestic and Przewalski's horses', Science 360 (2018)
sources.author: Gaunitz, C. et al.
sources.confirms: Shows Botai horses are ancestors of Przewalski's horses rather than modern domestic horses, with Botai as the earliest evidence of horse husbandry about 5500 years ago.

sources.title: Librado, P. et al., 'The origins and spread of domestic horses from the Western Eurasian steppes', Nature 598 (2021)
sources.author: Librado, P. et al.
sources.confirms: Places the ancestors of modern domestic horses in the lower Volga-Don region in the late fourth and early third millennia BC, with their expansion around 2200 to 2000 BC.

botai-horses-dispute-3500bce.detail: Many specialists accept bit wear on premolars as evidence of bridling; others reject it as a marker because wild horses show similar abrasion. Mare's milk residues remain the strongest Botai evidence of management. Horse riding transformed steppe mobility and later warfare, so the question of who first rode carries weight far beyond Kazakhstan. Botai people built large permanent villages, unusual for steppe hunters, and horse remains include whole skeletons in pits. Taming local horses to hunt wild ones is one proposed explanation of such intensive use.

picture.alt: A Przewalski's horse standing in grassland, a living descendant of horses of the Botai culture
picture.credit: Jeff Kubina from Columbia, Maryland, via Wikimedia Commons

botai-horses-dispute-3500bce.dating_note: Outram et al. 2009 date Botai to about 3500 BC with bit wear and mare's milk lipids; Gaunitz et al. 2018 show Botai horses are ancestors of Przewalski's horse, not modern domestic horses, and Librado et al. 2021 place modern horse origins in the Volga-Don steppe about 2200 BC. The Botai horse claim is disputed. Botai is in northern Kazakhstan; filed under europe following the scheme's steppe placement.

bronocice-wagon-pot-3500bce.summary: A Funnel Beaker pot from Bronocice in southern Poland carries an incised design read as a four-wheeled wagon with a pole, seen from above, repeated five times; cattle bone from the same pit dates it to about 3500 to 3350 BCE. Under a long barrow at Flintbek in Schleswig-Holstein, Doris Mischka recorded parallel ruts left by cart wheels and modelled them by Bayesian radiocarbon analysis to 3420 to 3385 cal BC. Bakker, Kruk, Lanting and Milisauskas compared these with Late Uruk pictograms of sledges on wheels and concluded that wheeled vehicles appeared within a century or two in both regions. Wagons let oxen move harvests, manure, timber and people, and wheel finds at Ljubljana and Maykop graves follow within decades.

sources.title: Bakker, J. A., Kruk, J., Lanting, A. E. and Milisauskas, S., 'The earliest evidence of wheeled vehicles in Europe and the Near East', Antiquity 73 (1999)
sources.author: Bakker, J. A., Kruk, J., Lanting, A. E. and Milisauskas, S.
sources.confirms: States that wheeled vehicles appeared contemporaneously in Funnel Beaker Europe and the Late Uruk Near East, with the Bronocice wagon depiction among the evidence.

sources.title: Mischka, D., 'The Neolithic burial sequence at Flintbek LA 3, north Germany, and its cart tracks: a precise chronology', Antiquity 85 (2011)
sources.author: Mischka, D.
sources.confirms: Dates cart tracks beneath the Flintbek long barrow to 3420 to 3385 cal BC using Bayesian modelling of 32 samples.

bronocice-wagon-pot-3500bce.detail: Whether the wheel spread from a single origin or arose twice remains open; near simultaneity across 3,000 km argues for rapid transmission along Carpathian and Pontic routes. Early wheels were solid discs of wood turning with or on a fixed axle. Horses did not pull vehicles until the second millennium BCE. Bronocice's drawing shows a vehicle with four wheels, a shaft and what may be a yoke, drawn in repeated panels around its shoulder. Cattle bone from that pit gave radiocarbon ages used for dating.

picture.alt: Funnel Beaker pot from Bronocice incised with a wagon motif, Archaeological Museum, Kraków
picture.credit: Silar, via Wikimedia Commons

bronocice-wagon-pot-3500bce.dating_note: Bronocice pot is dated by associated bone to about 3500 to 3350 BC; Flintbek cart tracks are modelled to 3420 to 3385 cal BC. Bakker et al. 1999 argue wheeled vehicles appeared almost simultaneously in Europe and the Near East.

cylinder-seals-bullae-susa-uruk-3500bce.summary: Around 3500 BCE administrators at Susa in Elam and Uruk in Sumer began sealing tokens inside hollow clay balls, rolling a carved stone cylinder over the wet surface so that a continuous frieze identified the responsible official. Some envelopes carry impressions of the tokens inside, so contents could be checked without breaking the seal. Cylinder seals, rolled rather than stamped, covered jar stoppers, door pegs and bale ties as well as envelopes and tablets. Pittman and Blackman's neutron activation analysis of 33 Late Uruk sealings from Tell Brak found most made of local clay, with one outlier resembling Susa clay, showing that sealing happened at the point of storage and occasionally travelled. Seals turned ownership and authority into a repeatable mark.

sources.title: Pittman, H. and Blackman, M. J., 'Mobile or stationary? Chemical analysis of clay administrative devices from Tell Brak in the Late Uruk period', Journal of Archaeological Science: Reports 7 (2016)
sources.author: Pittman, H. and Blackman, M. J.
sources.confirms: Analyses 33 Late Uruk clay sealings by neutron activation, finds 25 local and 8 outliers including one resembling Susa clay, and describes cylinder-seal impressions securing packages and authenticating documents.

sources.title: Schmandt-Besserat, D., 'The evolution of writing', International Encyclopedia of Social and Behavioral Sciences (Elsevier), author's site (2014)
sources.author: Schmandt-Besserat, D.
sources.venue: International Encyclopedia of Social and Behavioral Sciences (Elsevier), author's site
sources.confirms: States that around 3500 BC in Sumer and Elam tokens were stored in clay envelopes, some impressed on the surface so contents could be checked.

cylinder-seals-bullae-susa-uruk-3500bce.detail: Seal imagery of period includes rows of animals, boats, temple facades and a 'priest-king' figure. Impressed envelopes gave way about 3200 BCE to flat tablets, with seal rolled across tablet face. Stamp seals had existed in Halaf period from sixth millennium; the cylinder added length and narrative. Seals were carved in limestone, marble, lapis and shell with copper drills and gravers. Owners wore them on pins or cords, and broken sealings discarded in rubbish are what archaeologists usually find.

picture.alt: Uruk and Jemdet Nasr period cylinder seal with its rolled-out impression, Louvre Museum
picture.credit: Gary Todd from Xinzheng, China, via Wikimedia Commons

cylinder-seals-bullae-susa-uruk-3500bce.dating_note: Clay envelopes with impressed tokens and seal impressions appear at Susa and Uruk around 3500 BC in Schmandt-Besserat's sequence; cylinder seals belong to the same Middle to Late Uruk horizon.

godin-tepe-beer-3500bce.summary: At Godin Tepe in the Zagros, a trading post of Late Uruk type, a large jar with internal grooves held a pale yellow residue identified in 1992 as calcium oxalate, the beerstone that precipitates when barley is brewed. Dated by stratigraphy to the late fourth millennium BCE, it is the earliest chemical evidence for beer. Administrative texts from Uruk onward record barley, malt and beer rations in detail yet say little about technique. At Raqefet Cave in Israel, 13,000-year-old mortars hold traces of fermented cereal, suggesting that brewing-like practices preceded farming, but beer as a staple belongs to Mesopotamian cities.

sources.title: Damerow, P., 'Sumerian beer: the origins of brewing technology in ancient Mesopotamia', Cuneiform Digital Library Journal 2012:2 (2012)
sources.author: Damerow, P.
sources.confirms: Identifies the Godin Tepe residue from a late fourth millennium vessel as an oxalate and reviews administrative texts recording brewing ingredients.

sources.title: Liu, L. et al., 'Fermented beverage and food storage in 13,000 y-old stone mortars at Raqefet Cave, Israel', Journal of Archaeological Science: Reports 21 (2018)
sources.author: Liu, L. et al.
sources.confirms: Reports evidence of fermented cereal beverages in Natufian mortars around 13,000 years ago.

sources.title: Michel, R. H., McGovern, P. E. and Badler, V. R., 'Chemical evidence for ancient beer', Nature 360 (1992)
sources.author: Michel, R. H., McGovern, P. E. and Badler, V. R.
sources.confirms: Original identification of calcium oxalate in the Godin Tepe jar.
sources.qualifies: Nature page gave bibliographic details only; content confirmed through Damerow 2012.

godin-tepe-beer-3500bce.detail: Beer converted stored barley into a safe, calorie-rich drink and served as wages for labourers, which is why ration bowls and beer signs dominate early accounts. Godin jar's grooves may have trapped sediment as beer was decanted. Jiahu in China shows an unrelated rice-based ferment two and a half millennia earlier. Beer was drunk through long straws from shared jars, a scene depicted on seals. Barley malting leaves no clear trace, so chemistry rather than botany identifies brewing.

picture.alt: Painted pottery vessel excavated at Godin Tepe in Iran, shown in an exhibition in 2019.
picture.credit: Dorieo, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

godin-tepe-beer-3500bce.dating_note: The Godin Tepe jar belongs to the Late Uruk occupation of the late fourth millennium BC, about 3500 to 3100 BC. Liu et al. 2018 report fermented cereal residues at Raqefet Cave around 13,000 years ago, far earlier but not brewing in the later sense.

naqada-sail-boats-3500bce.summary: A red-slipped pottery jar in the British Museum, EA35324, painted with a boat beneath a chequerboard pattern and a square upright that reads as a sail, belongs to Egypt's Naqada II culture, about 3500 to 3300 BCE by pottery seriation. Steve Vinson catalogued Egypt's earliest sail representations and argued that this and related images show rigging that caught prevailing north winds to push boats upstream while the current carried them down, which made the Nile a two-way highway. Cheryl Ward places the ship's rise as a major technical and ceremonial force by mid fourth millennium BC, leading to sewn plank hulls buried at Abydos around 3000 BCE. Sail is humanity's first harnessing of wind for work.

sources.title: Ward, C., 'Boat-building and its social context in early Egypt: interpretations from the First Dynasty boat-grave cemetery at Abydos', Antiquity 80 (2006)
sources.author: Ward, C.
sources.confirms: Describes the world's oldest sewn planked hulls at Abydos and dates the ship's emergence as a major technical and ceremonial force to the mid fourth millennium BC.

sources.title: British Museum, 'Pottery jar EA35324, Naqada II, with ship under sail', British Museum collection online
sources.author: British Museum
sources.confirms: Describes EA35324 as a red ware jar showing a ship under sail beneath a chequerboard pattern, assigned to Naqada II.

sources.title: Vinson, S., 'The earliest representations of brailed sails', Journal of the American Research Center in Egypt 30 (1993)
sources.author: Vinson, S.
sources.venue: Journal of the American Research Center in Egypt
sources.confirms: Catalogues the earliest Egyptian sail depictions.
sources.qualifies: JSTOR page gave bibliographic details only.

naqada-sail-boats-3500bce.verification_note: Vinson's text could not be read; the sail identification rests on the British Museum catalogue entry and Ward's dating of early Egyptian shipping.
naqada-sail-boats-3500bce.detail: Most Naqada boat images show many oars and cabins and no sail, so sailing was initially rare. Later hieroglyphs for 'travel south' show a boat with sail and 'travel north' a boat with oars. Doubts about the EA35324 upright persist; Huyge and Darnell revisited this vessel in 2010. Painted boats on Naqada jars often carry two cabins and standards with emblems, read as marks of lineage or district. Rock drawings in Egypt's Eastern Desert show similar hulls, suggesting boats were hauled or depicted far from water.

picture.alt: Buff pottery jar painted with many-oared boats and figures, late Naqada II, Metropolitan Museum of Art
picture.credit: Metropolitan Museum of Art, via Wikimedia Commons

naqada-sail-boats-3500bce.dating_note: British Museum jar EA35324 is Naqada II, about 3500 to 3300 BC by pottery seriation; Ward dates the ship's emergence as a technical and ceremonial force to mid fourth millennium BC. Whether the painted upright is a sail or a standard is debated.

sorghum-kg23-sudan-3500bce.summary: Potters of Butana Group near Kassala in eastern Sudan tempered their clay with threshing waste, and the impressions left in sherds from site KG23, excavated by Southern Methodist University in 1980s, preserve sorghum spikelets in detail. They hold both wild-type and domesticated-type chaff with non-shattering trait, dated to the fourth millennium BCE. Sorghum, a drought-tolerant grass of the savanna, was therefore being cultivated and changed by harvest around 3500 BCE, two millennia earlier than previous evidence. Pearl millet in Tilemsi valley of Mali followed by about 2500 BCE. African cereal farming grew out of herding societies that had used wild grains for millennia.

sources.title: Winchell, F., Stevens, C. J., Murphy, C., Champion, L. and Fuller, D. Q., 'Evidence for sorghum domestication in fourth millennium BC eastern Sudan: spikelet morphology from ceramic impressions of the Butana Group', Current Anthropology 58 (2017)
sources.author: Winchell, F., Stevens, C. J., Murphy, C., Champion, L. and Fuller, D. Q.
sources.confirms: Reports domesticated and wild sorghum chaff impressions in KG23 Butana Group pottery near Kassala, excavated by SMU in the 1980s, showing domestication under way.

sources.title: Manning, K., Pelling, R., Higham, T., Schwenniger, J.-L. and Fuller, D. Q., '4500-year old domesticated pearl millet (Pennisetum glaucum) from the Tilemsi Valley, Mali: new insights into an alternative cereal domestication pathway', Journal of Archaeological Science 38 (2011)
sources.author: Manning, K., Pelling, R., Higham, T., Schwenniger, J.-L. and Fuller, D. Q.
sources.confirms: Dates the earliest domesticated pearl millet in the Lower Tilemsi Valley to the mid third millennium BC.

sorghum-kg23-sudan-3500bce.detail: Sorghum later reached India by 2000 BCE and became a staple from Sudan to Deccan. The KG23 evidence is impressions, not grains, so the method depends on silicone casts and microscopy. Full domestication of sorghum, with large grains, is documented only in second millennium BCE. Butana Group people also herded cattle and gathered wild grasses, and their pottery shows links to Nile valley. Sorghum's wild ancestor grows across Sahel, so domestication may have occurred in more than one place.

picture.alt: Sorghum bicolor plants with ripening seed heads in a botanical garden
picture.credit: Pethan, via Wikimedia Commons

sorghum-kg23-sudan-3500bce.dating_note: Winchell et al. 2017 date the KG23 sherds with domesticated-type sorghum chaff to the fourth millennium BC, about 3500 to 3000 BC; Manning et al. 2011 date the earliest domesticated pearl millet in Mali to about 2500 BC, after this period.

uruk-city-3500bce.summary: On a Euphrates channel in southern Iraq, Uruk expanded through the fourth millennium BCE into a settlement of roughly 250 hectares with tens of thousands of people, monumental terraces and temples in Eanna and Anu precincts, and workshops turning out millions of crude bevelled-rim bowls, probably ration containers. Guillermo Algaze argues that record keeping and new forms of labour organisation explain why city-states formed here first, and that Uruk colonies and trading posts spread north along the rivers. Jason Ur reads urbanism as an extension of the household, with temple estates run like giant families. Cylinder seals, tokens and then proto-cuneiform tablets all appear in Uruk's administrative levels.

sources.title: Algaze, G., Ancient Mesopotamia at the Dawn of Civilization: The Evolution of an Urban Landscape (University of Chicago Press, 2008)
sources.author: Algaze, G.
sources.confirms: Argues that southern polities grew in scale through the fourth millennium and that labour organisation and record keeping explain why city-states emerged first in southern Mesopotamia.

sources.title: Ur, J., 'Households and the emergence of cities in ancient Mesopotamia', Cambridge Archaeological Journal 24 (2014)
sources.author: Ur, J.
sources.confirms: States that the world's first cities emerged on the Mesopotamian plains in the fourth millennium BC and models urbanism as an extension of the household.

uruk-city-3500bce.detail: The city's scale required irrigation canals, boat transport of stone and timber from distant uplands, and specialised crafts. Later Sumerian tradition remembered Uruk as city of Gilgamesh and credited its walls to him. Rival centres such as Tell Brak in Syria grew in parallel, so southern primacy is debated. Eanna's temples stood on terraces faced with cone mosaics of baked clay, and a stone-built structure used limestone hauled from 50 km away. Uruk's walls, nine kilometres long, are attributed to Early Dynastic times.

picture.alt: Cone mosaic facade from the Eanna temple precinct at Uruk, coloured clay cones set in geometric patterns, Pergamon Museum, Berlin
picture.credit: Dosseman, via Wikimedia Commons

uruk-city-3500bce.dating_note: Uruk's growth to about 250 hectares with Eanna precinct spans Middle and Late Uruk periods, roughly 3800 to 3100 BC; 3500 BCE marks the city's emergence as the largest settlement in Mesopotamia.

watson-brake-mounds-3500bce.summary: On a terrace above Ouachita river in northeast Louisiana, eleven earthen mounds up to 7.5 metres high connected by a low ridge form an oval 280 metres across. Radiocarbon, luminescence and soil development date minor earthworks from about 3500 BCE and substantial mound raising from about 3350 BCE, continuing in stages until after 3000 BCE when the site was abandoned. The builders were hunter-gatherers who fished, collected mussels and gathered plants that later became domesticates, with no pottery and no farming. Watson Brake predates Stonehenge and Egyptian pyramids and shows that seasonal foragers could organise labour over centuries without chiefs or crops.

sources.title: Saunders, J. W. et al., 'A mound complex in Louisiana at 5400-5000 years before the present', Science 277 (1997)
sources.author: Saunders, J. W. et al.
sources.confirms: Dates the 11-mound complex to over 5000 calendar years BP by radiometric, luminescence, artefactual, geomorphic and pedogenic data, built by hunter-gatherers.

sources.title: Saunders, J. W. et al., 'Watson Brake, a Middle Archaic mound complex in northeast Louisiana', American Antiquity 70 (2005)
sources.author: Saunders, J. W. et al.
sources.confirms: Reports minor earthworks from about 3500 BC, substantial mound raising from about 3350 BC continuing until after 3000 BC.

watson-brake-mounds-3500bce.detail: Fired earthen cubes found in middens may have been cooking stones. No burials have been found, and no evidence shows what the mounds were for. Watson Brake precedes Poverty Point earthworks by two millennia and sits in a cluster of Middle Archaic mound sites along the lower Mississippi. Soil studies show mounds were built in stages separated by periods when surfaces weathered. Microliths and drilled stone beads indicate craft work on site. Mound sites of similar age include Frenchman's Bend and Hedgepeth.

picture.alt: Artist's impression of the Watson Brake mound complex in Louisiana, an oval ring of earthen mounds seen from the south
picture.credit: Martin Pate, National Park Service Southeast Archeological Center, via Wikimedia Commons

watson-brake-mounds-3500bce.dating_note: Saunders et al. 1997 and 2005 date the first earthworks at Watson Brake to about 3500 BC, with major mound building from about 3350 BC until after 3000 BC.

potato-quinoa-titicaca-3400bce.summary: Potatoes were domesticated once, from wild species of Solanum brevicaule complex in southern Peru, a single origin shown by amplified fragment length polymorphism. Direct archaeological evidence is scarce because tubers rot, but Claudia Rumold and Mark Aldenderfer recovered potato starch grains from groundstone tools at Jiskairumoko, an early village west of Lake Titicaca dated about 3400 to 1600 BCE, during the shift from mobile foraging to settled life. Together with quinoa, a chenopod grain domesticated on the altiplano in that span, and llamas and alpacas, potatoes allowed farming at 3,800 metres where maize fails. Freeze-drying tubers into chuño later let Andean states store food for years.

sources.title: Rumold, C. U. and Aldenderfer, M. S., 'Late Archaic-Early Formative period microbotanical evidence for potato at Jiskairumoko in the Titicaca Basin of southern Peru', PNAS 113 (2016)
sources.author: Rumold, C. U. and Aldenderfer, M. S.
sources.confirms: Reports potato starch on groundstone from Jiskairumoko, an early village in the western Titicaca basin dated about 3400 to 1600 cal BC.

sources.title: Spooner, D. M., McLean, K., Ramsay, G., Waugh, R. and Bryan, G. J., 'A single domestication for potato based on multilocus amplified fragment length polymorphism genotyping', PNAS 102 (2005)
sources.author: Spooner, D. M., McLean, K., Ramsay, G., Waugh, R. and Bryan, G. J.
sources.confirms: Shows a monophyletic origin of all potato landraces from the northern Solanum brevicaule complex in southern Peru.

potato-quinoa-titicaca-3400bce.detail: Potatoes carry toxic glycoalkaloids that selection and processing reduced; clay eaten with wild tubers may have bound those toxins. More than 4,000 landraces survive in the Andes. A single origin replaced earlier models of multiple domestications across Peru and Bolivia. Jiskairumoko also yielded gold beads, among the oldest worked gold in the Americas, dated about 2000 BCE. Quinoa seeds with thin coats mark domestication at Chiripa and other altiplano sites by 1500 BCE. Oca and ulluco tubers joined potatoes in highland fields.

picture.alt: Rows of labelled native potato varieties of many colours and shapes from Santa Teresa, Cusco
picture.credit: H.dav.are, via Wikimedia Commons

potato-quinoa-titicaca-3400bce.dating_note: Rumold and Aldenderfer 2016 date Jiskairumoko to about 3400 to 1600 cal BC with potato starch throughout; Spooner et al. 2005 place potato's origin in southern Peru from Solanum brevicaule complex. Quinoa domestication in the altiplano is dated to a similar span.

tarkhan-dress-linen-3400bce.summary: Flinders Petrie's excavations at Tarkhan south of Cairo in 1912 and 1913 brought back a bundle of textiles that lay unexamined until conservators in 1977 found within it a V-necked linen shirt with knife-pleated sleeves and bodice, cut and sewn to fit a slim adult. Radiocarbon dating of a 2.24 mg sample in 2016 gave 3482 to 3102 BCE, confirming it as the oldest woven garment known. Creases at elbows and armpits show it was worn. Flax grown in Nile fields, spun fine and woven on horizontal ground looms, dressed Egyptians from before First Dynasty, and tailoring and pleating were already in the weaver's repertoire.

sources.title: Stevenson, A. and Dee, M., 'Confirmation of the world's oldest woven garment: the Tarkhan Dress', Antiquity Project Gallery 90 (2016)
sources.author: Stevenson, A. and Dee, M.
sources.confirms: Describes the V-neck linen shirt with pleated sleeves, excavated by Petrie in 1912-13 and identified in 1977, and reports the radiocarbon result 4570 plus or minus 36 BP, 3482 to 3102 cal BC.

sources.title: UCL Petrie Museum, 'The Tarkhan Dress', Petrie Museum of Egyptian Archaeology, UCL
sources.author: UCL Petrie Museum
sources.venue: Petrie Museum of Egyptian Archaeology, UCL
sources.confirms: Museum page for the garment's holding collection.
sources.qualifies: Fetched page gave general museum information without the dress description.

tarkhan-dress-linen-3400bce.detail: The dress now hangs in Petrie Museum at University College London. Most ancient textiles survive as scraps; a complete garment this early is a rarity owed to Egypt's dry tombs. Linen production fed a state-level textile economy recorded in later Old Kingdom accounts. Linen was made by retting flax in water, beating out fibre and spinning with a drop spindle. Egyptian spinning twisted yarn in an S direction, matching flax fibre's natural twist, and pleating was set while damp. Petrie's Tarkhan cemetery held over 2,000 graves spanning the first dynasties.

picture.alt: The Tarkhan dress, a pleated linen garment, displayed in the Petrie Museum, London
picture.credit: Nic McPhee, via Wikimedia Commons

tarkhan-dress-linen-3400bce.dating_note: Stevenson and Dee 2016 report a radiocarbon result of 4570 plus or minus 36 BP, calibrated to 3482 to 3102 BC at 95 percent probability; 3400 BCE is near the probability peak.

iceman-kit-3300bce.summary: A body melted out of Tisenjoch glacier on Austrian-Italian border in 1991 with its equipment nearly complete, radiocarbon dated to about 3350 to 3100 BCE. The man carried a copper axe on a yew haft, an unfinished yew longbow, a quiver with two finished and twelve unfinished arrows, a flint dagger with ash handle, a retoucher of lime wood and stag antler, a birch bark container holding embers wrapped in maple leaves, two birch fungus pieces threaded on hide, and clothing of goat, sheep, deer and bear skins with a grass cloak. His six chert tools come from at least three sources in the southern Alps. Lead isotopes show his axe copper came from southern Tuscany, 500 km away.

sources.title: Wierer, U. et al., 'The Iceman's lithic toolkit: raw material, technology, typology and use', PLoS ONE 13 (2018)
sources.author: Wierer, U. et al.
sources.confirms: Traces the six chert artefacts to at least three southern Alpine source areas including the Non Valley and Trento Plateau.

sources.title: Artioli, G. et al., 'Long-distance connections in the Copper Age: new evidence from the Alpine Iceman's copper axe', PLoS ONE 12 (2017)
sources.author: Artioli, G. et al.
sources.confirms: Shows by lead isotopes that the axe copper came from southern Tuscan ores rather than Alpine or Balkan sources.

sources.title: Kutschera, W. and Rom, W., 'Ötzi, the prehistoric Iceman', Nuclear Instruments and Methods in Physics Research B 164 (2000)
sources.author: Kutschera, W. and Rom, W.
sources.venue: Nuclear Instruments and Methods in Physics Research B
sources.confirms: Reports radiocarbon dating of the Iceman and his equipment.
sources.qualifies: Only bibliographic details could be read.

iceman-kit-3300bce.detail: He died from an arrow wound in the shoulder. His gear is the only complete set of a Copper Age European's belongings and shows how metal, stone, wood, fibre and hide coexisted in one toolkit, with the copper axe a rare and valued item. Tattoos on his joints have been read as therapeutic marks. His last meals included ibex meat, einkorn and fat, and pollen in his gut traces a spring journey from valley to pass. Copper in his hair shows exposure to smelting fumes, perhaps as a smith.

picture.alt: The Iceman's copper axe with yew haft and leather binding, South Tyrol Museum of Archaeology
picture.credit: АлександрЛаптев, via Wikimedia Commons

iceman-kit-3300bce.dating_note: Radiocarbon dates on the Iceman's tissue and equipment calibrate to about 3350 to 3100 BC, with Kutschera and Rom giving the equipment dates; 3300 BCE is a conventional midpoint.

liangzhu-city-dams-3300bce.summary: Near Hangzhou, Liangzhu culture built between about 3300 and 2300 BCE a walled town of 300 hectares on an earthen platform, with a palace mound, elite tombs full of carved jade and, in hills above, a system of eleven dams and levees. High dams in mountain valleys and low dams on plain, built of earth wrapped in grass-bound bags of silt, created reservoirs covering about 13 square kilometres, protecting the city from floods, storing water and allowing boat transport of stone and timber. Colin Renfrew and Liu Bin call Liangzhu perhaps the earliest state society in East Asia. Rice paddies fed thousands of labourers; charred rice stores in city ran to tens of tonnes.

sources.title: Liu, B. et al., 'Earliest hydraulic enterprise in China, 5,100 years ago', PNAS 114 (2017)
sources.author: Liu, B. et al.
sources.confirms: Presents the Liangzhu water management system dated 5300 to 4300 cal BP as one of the world's oldest large-scale formalized hydraulic works.

sources.title: Renfrew, C. and Liu, B., 'The emergence of complex society in China: the case of Liangzhu', Antiquity 92 (2018)
sources.author: Renfrew, C. and Liu, B.
sources.confirms: Describes Liangzhu as a fortified town of 3300 to 2300 BC with jade-rich elite burials and large public works, possibly the earliest state society in East Asia.

liangzhu-city-dams-3300bce.detail: The grass-wrapped bags are an early form of sandbag, and the dams predate Mesopotamian large-scale hydraulics. Liangzhu jade cong and bi became emblems reused in later Chinese ritual. The culture ended around 2300 BCE amid flooding and climate change. UNESCO inscribed the site in 2019. Mojiaoshan platform in city centre covered 30 hectares and held large buildings. Jade workshops produced cong tubes with mask motifs cut with sand abrasives, and a single elite tomb could hold hundreds of jades.

picture.alt: Grass-covered remains of the west city wall of the Liangzhu ancient city, Hangzhou
picture.credit: LukeLOU, via Wikimedia Commons

liangzhu-city-dams-3300bce.dating_note: Liu Bin et al. 2017 date Liangzhu hydraulic system to 5300 to 4300 cal BP; Renfrew and Liu 2018 give 3300 to 2300 BC for the fortified town.

proto-cuneiform-uruk-3300bce.summary: Excavations at Uruk between 1928 and 1976 recovered nearly 5,000 clay tablets and fragments inscribed with numerals and pictographic signs pressed and drawn with a reed stylus, from building levels IVa and IIIb, about 3300 to 3000 BCE. Nissen, Damerow and Englund showed that these archaic texts are almost all accounts: grain and beer rations, herds, fields and labour, kept by temple and estate administrators. Englund traces the two main numerical systems back to token types for counting discrete objects and measuring capacity. A smaller group of lexical lists, including a ranked list of professions copied for centuries, trained scribes. Writing began as bookkeeping, not storytelling.

sources.title: Englund, R. K., 'Accounting in proto-cuneiform', The Oxford Handbook of Cuneiform Culture (Oxford University Press) (2011)
sources.author: Englund, R. K.
sources.venue: The Oxford Handbook of Cuneiform Culture (Oxford University Press)
sources.confirms: Describes archaic bookkeeping types and shows that the two most important numerical systems anticipated in tokens counted discrete objects and capacity measures.

sources.title: Cuneiform Digital Library Initiative, 'Proto-cuneiform', CDLI wiki, citing Nissen, Damerow and Englund, Archaic Bookkeeping (Chicago 1993) (2020)
sources.author: Cuneiform Digital Library Initiative
sources.venue: CDLI wiki, citing Nissen, Damerow and Englund, Archaic Bookkeeping (Chicago 1993)
sources.confirms: States that excavations from 1928 to 1976 unearthed nearly 5,000 proto-cuneiform tablets and fragments at Uruk, assigned to script phases IV and III and building levels IVa and IIIb.

proto-cuneiform-uruk-3300bce.detail: Signs of the Uruk IV phase are pictorial and drawn in curves; by Uruk III they are more abstract and wedge-like. Whether these texts encode Sumerian speech or a language-neutral code is debated, since phonetic use of signs is rare until the Early Dynastic period. Egyptian writing at Abydos appears in the same decades, raising unresolved questions about contact. Around 900 distinct signs are known from this phase.

picture.alt: Clay tablet with proto-cuneiform signs and numerals, Uruk III period, Oriental Institute Museum, Chicago
picture.credit: Daderot, derivative by Zunkir, via Wikimedia Commons

proto-cuneiform-uruk-3300bce.dating_note: Uruk IV tablets come from building level IVa, conventionally about 3350 to 3200 BC, and Uruk III from level IIIb, about 3200 to 3000 BC; dating rests on stratigraphy and pottery rather than direct radiocarbon.

abydos-tomb-uj-labels-3250bce.summary: Günter Dreyer's excavation of tomb U-j in Umm el-Qa'ab cemetery at Abydos, a twelve-chambered brick tomb assigned to a ruler nicknamed Scorpion, produced about 160 small bone and ivory labels pierced for attachment, each incised with one or a few signs, together with large painted signs on pottery jars and seal impressions, around 3250 BCE. Ilona Regulski describes the labels as providing the earliest attested two-consonant phonograms, so signs already stood for sounds, not only objects. Dreyer read many labels as names of estates and towns delivering goods, and reconstructed a line of predynastic kings; Francis Breyer and others argue these readings go beyond the evidence. Writing here served to tag deliveries to a royal tomb.

sources.title: Regulski, I., 'The origins and early development of writing in Egypt', Oxford Handbooks Online (Oxford University Press) (2016)
sources.author: Regulski, I.
sources.confirms: Identifies tomb U-j as the find-spot of the oldest Egyptian writing, about 3250 BC, with painted jar signs, seal impressions and incised ivory labels providing the earliest two-consonantal phonograms.

sources.title: Breyer, F. A. K., 'Die Schriftzeugnisse des prädynastischen Königsgrabes U-j in Umm el-Qaab: Versuch einer Neuinterpretation', Journal of Egyptian Archaeology 88 (2002)
sources.author: Breyer, F. A. K.
sources.confirms: Notes Dreyer's publication of the earliest known Egyptian writing from tomb U-j and argues that many interpretations, including the scheme of predynastic kings, do not bear scrutiny.

abydos-tomb-uj-labels-3250bce.detail: Hundreds of imported wine jars from Levant filled the tomb, linking writing to long-distance exchange. Egyptian script and Mesopotamian proto-cuneiform appear within a century of each other, and scholars disagree whether the idea travelled. By First Dynasty, around 3000 BCE, Egyptian writing recorded names, titles and year events on labels and stelae. Labels measure only a few centimetres and were once tied to goods; numbers on some record quantities of cloth or oil.
abydos-tomb-uj-labels-3250bce.dating_note: Tomb U-j at Abydos belongs to Naqada IIIA, about 3250 BC by pottery seriation supported by radiocarbon; Regulski gives about 3250 BC for the earliest phonetic writing. Dreyer's reading of the labels as place names and royal estates is contested by Breyer and others.

newgrange-winter-solstice-3200bce.summary: In Boyne valley of Ireland a passage tomb covered by a mound 85 metres across was built around 3200 BCE from more than 200,000 tonnes of stone, its kerbstones carved with spirals and lozenges. Above entrance a slot called roof-box lets the rising sun on midwinter morning shine 18 metres down the passage to light the chamber floor for about seventeen minutes. Tom Ray calculated in 1989 that when built, first light bisected the chamber exactly, so the gap's size and orientation were designed for that moment. In 2020 Lara Cassidy's team sequenced 44 Neolithic genomes and found a man in central recess born of a first-degree incestuous union, a pattern found among god-king dynasties, implying a hereditary elite directed the labour.

sources.title: Ray, T. P., 'The winter solstice phenomenon at Newgrange, Ireland: accident or design?', Nature 337 (1989)
sources.author: Ray, T. P.
sources.confirms: Describes the midwinter sunrise beam through the roof-box lighting the chamber 18 m away and argues the gap dimensions were deliberate.

sources.title: Cassidy, L. M. et al., 'A dynastic elite in monumental Neolithic society', Nature 582 (2020)
sources.author: Cassidy, L. M. et al.
sources.confirms: Reports 44 genomes and identifies the son of a first-degree incestuous union buried in the Newgrange chamber recess, indicating a politico-religious elite.

newgrange-winter-solstice-3200bce.detail: Newgrange shares its corbelled chamber and art with Knowth and Dowth nearby and with Orkney's Maeshowe. Alignment ties monument, calendar and dead together, marking sun's return. Stonehenge's first phase, a few centuries later, repeats solstice focus on a different axis. Quartz and granite cobbles for facade came from Wicklow and Mourne mountains, 70 to 80 km away, carried by sea and river. Michael O'Kelly excavated Newgrange from 1962 to 1975 and reconstructed its roof-box and facade. Passage grave art here includes a triple spiral on a chamber stone.

picture.alt: Newgrange passage tomb with its white quartz facade and grass-covered mound, County Meath, Ireland
picture.credit: Shira, via Wikimedia Commons

newgrange-winter-solstice-3200bce.dating_note: Newgrange's construction is radiocarbon dated to about 3200 BC; Ray 1989 analyses the roof-box alignment. Cassidy et al. 2020 identify a dynastic elite among its burials.

ljubljana-marshes-wheel-3150bce.summary: In 2002 archaeologists from the Slovenian Academy of Sciences excavating Stare gmajne pile-dwelling settlement in Ljubljana Marshes found a wooden wheel about 72 cm across, made of two ash planks joined by oak battens, with an oak axle fitted through a square hole so wheel and axle turned together. Radiocarbon dating places it around 3150 BCE, older than any other wheel with axle yet recovered. Anton Velušček's monograph on Stare gmajne records two settlement phases, in the late 34th century and in the latter 32nd century BCE. Maja Andrič's pollen work shows which marsh landscape these pile dwellers farmed. This find turns the Bronocice drawing into an object.

sources.title: Velušček, A. (ed.), Koliščarska naselbina Stare gmajne in njen čas / Stare gmajne Pile-dwelling Settlement and Its Era (Založba ZRC, Opera Instituti Archaeologici Sloveniae 16, 2009)
sources.author: Velušček, A. (ed.)
sources.venue: Založba ZRC, Opera Instituti Archaeologici Sloveniae 16
sources.confirms: Presents a wooden wheel with its axle among the finds and dates occupation to the late 34th century BC and the second half of the 32nd century BC.
sources.qualifies: The publisher page does not give wheel dimensions or the 3150 BC radiocarbon result.

sources.title: Andrič, M., 'Maharski prekop, Stare gmajne and Blatna Brezovica settlements and the vegetation of Ljubljansko barje (Slovenia) in the 4th millennium cal BC', Documenta Praehistorica 47 (2020)
sources.author: Andrič, M.
sources.confirms: Confirms Stare gmajne as a fourth millennium cal BC pile-dwelling settlement in the Ljubljana Marshes.

ljubljana-marshes-wheel-3150bce.verification_note: Settlement phases are confirmed; wheel dimensions and the 3150 BC radiocarbon result come from the excavation monograph's body, not readable online.
ljubljana-marshes-wheel-3150bce.detail: This wheel probably belonged to a two-wheeled pushcart or small wagon used on soft ground. Ash is strong and springy; oak resists wear. Comparable wheels from Swiss and German lake sites and from Maykop and Yamnaya steppe graves fall within a few centuries. Pile dwellings preserve such wood because oxygen is excluded. Wheel and axle together weighed about 20 kg. Ash planks were shaped with stone adzes and joined by oak battens let into grooves, and axle ends were squared to fit square holes, a design still used in farm carts.

picture.alt: Wooden wheel with its axle from the Ljubljana Marshes, two ash planks joined by battens, Ljubljana City Museum
picture.credit: Petar Milošević, via Wikimedia Commons

ljubljana-marshes-wheel-3150bce.dating_note: Velušček's volume places Stare gmajne settlement in late 34th century BC and the second half of 32nd century BC; the wheel and axle, found in 2002, are radiocarbon dated to about 3150 BC in project's publications.

skara-brae-stone-furniture-3100bce.summary: A storm in 1850 stripped dunes at Bay of Skaill in Orkney to reveal a cluster of stone-built houses linked by covered passages. Gordon Childe excavated it from 1928 and described walls still standing 8 to 9 feet high, each house with a central hearth, box beds, a stone dresser facing the door, wall cupboards and stone-lined tanks, all built in flagstone because Orkney had almost no timber. Drains ran beneath floors. Bayesian analysis of 613 radiocarbon dates for Orkney places the first nucleated settlement around 2900 BCE, with a possible earlier phase, and reoccupation in 28th century BCE. The interiors give the fullest picture of domestic arrangement in Neolithic Europe.

sources.title: Childe, V. G., 'Skara Brae: a 'Stone Age' village in Orkney', Antiquity 5 (1931)
sources.author: Childe, V. G.
sources.confirms: Describes stone huts with walls 8 to 9 feet high and furniture, including beds, made in stone because of timber shortage.

sources.title: Bayliss, A., Marshall, P., Richards, C. and Whittle, A., 'Islands of history: the Late Neolithic timescape of Orkney', Antiquity 91 (2017)
sources.author: Bayliss, A., Marshall, P., Richards, C. and Whittle, A.
sources.confirms: Models 613 radiocarbon and 79 luminescence results and places Skara Brae's first nucleated settlement around 2900 cal BC with reoccupation in the 28th century cal BC.

skara-brae-stone-furniture-3100bce.detail: Grooved Ware pottery, bone tools, carved stone balls and beads tie Skara Brae to Ness of Brodgar complex and to Grooved Ware users in Ireland and Wessex. The village was buried by sand after a few centuries. Its furniture shows that Neolithic households partitioned space for sleeping, display and storage. Midden packed around walls insulated houses against Atlantic weather, and roofs were probably driftwood or whalebone covered with turf. Stone tanks may have held limpet bait soaking for fishing.

picture.alt: Interior of a Skara Brae house with stone dresser, box beds and central hearth, Orkney
picture.credit: Anne Burgess, via Wikimedia Commons

skara-brae-stone-furniture-3100bce.dating_note: Bayliss et al. 2017 model the first nucleated settlement at Skara Brae to centuries around 2900 cal BC with reoccupation in the 28th century; Historic Environment Scotland cites occupation from about 3180 BC. 3100 BCE is a compromise midpoint.

austronesian-dispersal-taiwan-3000bce.summary: Around 6,000 years ago farmers with cord-marked pottery, polished adzes, rice and millet settled Taiwan from the south China coast. Linguists trace all Austronesian languages, from Madagascar to Easter Island, to Taiwan, and an 8,000-year-old skeleton from Liangdao island carries a mitochondrial lineage ancestral to Austronesian populations. From Taiwan, voyagers reached Philippines by about 2000 BCE and, as matching pottery shows, crossed 2,300 km of open sea to Marianas around 1500 BCE, carrying plants but apparently no animals. Outrigger and later double-hulled sailing canoes made this the largest maritime expansion before European navigation. Its first step, the settlement of Taiwan, falls at the end of this period.

sources.title: Ko, A. M.-S. et al., 'Early Austronesians: into and out of Taiwan', American Journal of Human Genetics 94 (2014)
sources.author: Ko, A. M.-S. et al.
sources.confirms: Supports a Taiwan origin for the Austronesian expansion and reports an 8,000-year-old Liangdao skeleton ancestral to Austronesian lineages, with the Taiwan Neolithic about 6,000 years ago.

sources.title: Hung, H.-C. et al., 'The first settlement of Remote Oceania: the Philippines to the Marianas', Antiquity 85 (2011)
sources.author: Hung, H.-C. et al.
sources.confirms: Compares pottery from the Marianas and Philippines to support a 2,300 km open-sea crossing around 1500 BC carrying cultivated plants but no animals.

austronesian-dispersal-taiwan-3000bce.detail: Austronesian package later included pigs, dogs, chickens, taro, yams and breadfruit, with Lapita pottery marking the move into Remote Oceania after 1300 BCE. Genetics shows mixing with Papuan populations along way. The sailing technology is inferred from crossings; no boats of this date survive. Dapenkeng pottery marks Taiwan's earliest Neolithic, and jade from Fengtian in Taiwan later circulated across Southeast Asia, tracing sea routes. Austronesian languages number over 1,200 today.

picture.alt: Map of the Austronesian expansion from Taiwan across Island Southeast Asia and the Pacific
picture.credit: Obsidian Soul after Blench (2009), base map Lokal_Profil, via Wikimedia Commons

austronesian-dispersal-taiwan-3000bce.dating_note: Taiwan's Neolithic begins about 6,000 years ago by radiocarbon; Ko et al. 2014 date Liangdao skeleton to about 8,000 years ago; Hung et al. 2011 date Philippines-to-Marianas crossing to about 1500 BC, after this period. 3000 BCE marks Taiwan Neolithic horizon from which the dispersal began.

eastern-north-america-squash-domesticati.summary: River valleys of American Midwest and Southeast became one of world's independent centres of plant domestication. A local squash, Cucurbita pepo ovifera, was domesticated by about 5,000 years ago, followed by sunflower, marsh elder and goosefoot with thinner seed coats and larger seeds by about 4,000 years ago, all from native plants rather than imports from Mexico. At Riverton site in Illinois these crops had coalesced into a complex by about 3,800 years ago. Maize arrived only around 200 CE and became dominant after 900 CE. The region's farmers thus began with oily and starchy seeds suited to floodplain gardens.

sources.title: Smith, B. D., 'Eastern North America as an independent center of plant domestication', PNAS 103 (2006)
sources.author: Smith, B. D.
sources.confirms: Synthesises evidence that eastern North America independently domesticated squash, sunflower, marsh elder and goosefoot rather than receiving Mexican crops.

sources.title: Smith, B. D. and Yarnell, R. A., 'Initial formation of an indigenous crop complex in eastern North America at 3800 B.P.', PNAS 106 (2009)
sources.author: Smith, B. D. and Yarnell, R. A.
sources.confirms: Dates the formation of the indigenous crop complex at Riverton, Illinois, to about 3800 BP.

eastern-north-america-squash-domesticati.detail: Genetic analysis of sunflower confirms a domestication in eastern North America independent of Mexico. Goosefoot and marsh elder are now considered lost crops, abandoned after maize took over. These finds answered claims that the region merely received Mesoamerican domesticates. Floodplain disturbance by rivers favoured weedy annuals with large seeds, which gardeners then selected. Sunflower seeds from Hayes, Tennessee, date to about 4,300 years ago. Erect knotweed and maygrass joined the complex later, and all faded as maize spread after 900 CE.

picture.alt: Small dark seeds of Chenopodium berlandieri, goosefoot, held on a fingertip beside a label
picture.credit: Nwbeeson, via Wikimedia Commons

eastern-north-america-squash-domesticati.dating_note: Smith and Yarnell 2009 date the formation of eastern North American crop complex to about 3800 cal BP at Riverton, Illinois; the earliest domesticated Cucurbita pepo ovifera in region dates to about 5000 cal BP, so 3000 BCE marks the start of independent domestication process.

lothagam-north-pillar-site-3000bce.summary: On a ridge west of Lake Turkana in Kenya, mobile herders who had just arrived with cattle, sheep and goats built a platform 30 metres across ringed with basalt pillars dragged from a kilometre away, and buried at least 580 people in a central cavity over several centuries from about 3000 BCE. Elisabeth Hildebrand and Katherine Grillo found men, women and children placed tightly together with ostrich eggshell beads, stone pendants and ear ornaments, without evident differences of rank. The cemetery was built as lake shrank and rainfall became unpredictable, and Hildebrand argues that monument building helped dispersed herders form a shared identity and manage uncertainty. Eastern Africa's first monuments were raised by egalitarian pastoralists, not by states.

sources.title: Hildebrand, E. A. et al., 'A monumental cemetery built by eastern Africa's first herders near Lake Turkana, Kenya', PNAS 115 (2018)
sources.author: Hildebrand, E. A. et al.
sources.confirms: Describes Lothagam North as a monumental cemetery built by mobile herders during a period of environmental change, with communal burial and little evidence of hierarchy.

sources.title: Hildebrand, E. A. and Grillo, K. M., 'Early herders and monumental sites in eastern Africa: dating and interpretation', Antiquity 86 (2012)
sources.author: Hildebrand, E. A. and Grillo, K. M.
sources.confirms: States that megalithic pillar sites in eastern Africa were built by the fifth millennium BP, contemporary with the earliest herding in the region.

lothagam-north-pillar-site-3000bce.detail: Four other pillar sites around Turkana were in use at same time. Dates come from radiocarbon on human bone and ostrich eggshell. Lothagam North finds extend the record of monumentality beyond farmers and complicate the association of monuments with hierarchy seen at Varna and Newgrange. Burials were later sealed under a capping of stones and pillars; some individuals wore over a thousand beads. Herders reached Turkana as lake fell by tens of metres, exposing new pasture along its shore.

picture.alt: Standing stone pillars of the Lothagam North cemetery on the shore of Lake Turkana, Kenya
picture.credit: Ninafundisha, via Wikimedia Commons

lothagam-north-pillar-site-3000bce.dating_note: Hildebrand et al. 2018 date construction and use of Lothagam North to about 5000 to 4300 cal BP; Hildebrand and Grillo 2012 place the start of pillar-site building by the fifth millennium BP. 3000 BCE marks the start of construction.

stonehenge-first-phase-3000bce.summary: Around 3000 BCE people on Salisbury Plain dug a circular ditch and bank 110 metres across with antler picks, setting a ring of 56 pits now called Aubrey Holes just inside. Mike Parker Pearson's Stonehenge Riverside Project argued in 2009 that these pits held the first bluestones, brought 225 km from Preseli hills of Wales, and that the monument began as a cremation cemetery holding the remains of perhaps 150 people. Entrance faced the midsummer sunrise and midwinter sunset axis. Darvill, Marshall, Parker Pearson and Wainwright's 2012 Bayesian model splits the monument into five stages, with this first stage about 3000 to 2920 cal BC. Great sarsen trilithons came five centuries later.

sources.title: Parker Pearson, M. et al., 'Who was buried at Stonehenge?', Antiquity 83 (2009)
sources.author: Parker Pearson, M. et al.
sources.confirms: States that Stonehenge began in the early third millennium cal BC as a cremation cemetery within a circle of upright bluestones.

sources.title: Darvill, T., Marshall, P., Parker Pearson, M. and Wainwright, G., 'Stonehenge remodelled', Antiquity 86 (2012)
sources.author: Darvill, T., Marshall, P., Parker Pearson, M. and Wainwright, G.
sources.confirms: Proposes five construction stages anchored by Bayesian radiocarbon modelling.
sources.qualifies: Abstract gives no stage dates; 3000 to 2920 cal BC for Stage 1 is from the article body.

stonehenge-first-phase-3000bce.detail: Debate continues over whether Aubrey Holes held stones or timber posts. Isotopes in cremated bone show some of dead grew up in west Wales, linking people and stones. Stonehenge's first phase belongs with Newgrange and Orkney's circles in a late fourth millennium wave of solstice-aligned monuments. Cremated remains from Aubrey Hole 7, reburied in 1935, were re-excavated in 2008 and dated, giving burial sequence. Antler picks left in ditch bottom supplied radiocarbon samples. Bluestones each weigh two to four tonnes.

picture.alt: Stonehenge sarsen circle and trilithons under a blue sky, Wiltshire, England
picture.credit: garethwiscombe, via Wikimedia Commons

stonehenge-first-phase-3000bce.dating_note: Stage 1 at Stonehenge, the ditch, bank and Aubrey Holes, dates to about 3000 to 2920 cal BC in Darvill et al.'s model; the sarsen settings belong to about 2500 BC, outside this period.

egyptian-civil-calendar-decans-2800bce.summary: By the early Old Kingdom Egypt uses a civil calendar of twelve 30-day months plus five added days, 365 days with no leap year, so it drifts against seasons by one day every four years. Parker's 1950 study argued it was introduced around 2800 BCE, averaged from the Nile flood, alongside an older lunar calendar for festivals. From about 2100 BCE coffin lids carry diagonal star tables in which 36 decan stars rising at ten-day intervals mark night hours; Neugebauer and Parker edited these. Twelve decans visible per night gave twelve night hours, which with twelve day hours produced the 24-hour day inherited through Greece.

sources.title: Parker, R. A., The Calendars of Ancient Egypt, Studies in Ancient Oriental Civilization 26 (Chicago: University of Chicago Press, 1950)
sources.author: Parker, Richard A.
sources.venue: University of Chicago Press, Oriental Institute
sources.confirms: Reconstructs lunar and civil calendars and argues for civil calendar introduction c. 2800 BCE.

sources.title: Neugebauer, O. and Parker, R. A., Egyptian Astronomical Texts I: The Early Decans (Providence: Brown University Press, 1960)
sources.author: Neugebauer, Otto; Parker, Richard A.
sources.confirms: Edits diagonal star clocks on Middle Kingdom coffins and explains decanal hours.

sources.title: Clagett, M., Ancient Egyptian Science, vol. 2: Calendars, Clocks, and Astronomy (Philadelphia: American Philosophical Society, 1995)
sources.author: Clagett, Marshall
sources.confirms: Surveys calendar, decans, hours and water clocks with translated sources.

egyptian-civil-calendar-decans-2800bce.verification_note: Calendar structure is secure; its origin date is reconstructed.
egyptian-civil-calendar-decans-2800bce.detail: The calendar's fixed length made it a favourite of Hellenistic astronomers, and Clagett's survey traces its use by Ptolemy and Copernicus. Depuydt and others have revisited Parker's origin date; proposals range from c. 2900 to c. 2600 BCE. Hour lengths varied with season until equal hours were adopted much later. Sothic rising of Sirius after its annual invisibility returned to New Year's Day once every 1,460 years, and a Roman notice of such a coincidence in 139 CE underpins reconstructions of Egyptian chronology.

picture.alt: Facsimile of the astronomical ceiling in the tomb of Senenmut with decan lists, Metropolitan Museum of Art.
picture.credit: Charles Wilkinson, via Wikimedia Commons

egyptian-civil-calendar-decans-2800bce.dating_note: Introduction date inferred, not attested; Parker c. 2800 BCE, others later in Old Kingdom. Decan tables c. 2100 BCE by coffin typology.

sadd-el-kafara-dam-failure-2650bce.summary: In Wadi Garawi south of Cairo, builders of Dynasty 3 or 4 (c. 2650 BCE) raise a dam about 110 metres long at crest level, 98 metres thick at its base and 14 metres high, with two rubble-masonry shells faced in limestone blocks and a core of gravel and silt, to hold flash-flood water for a quarrying settlement. Garbrecht's survey showed no spillway and no silt deposit behind it, indicating that a flood overtopped and breached an unfinished structure, after which Egyptians abandoned large dams for about eight centuries. Fahlbusch's engineering review treats it as our oldest known large dam and its failure as our earliest recorded dam disaster.

sources.title: Garbrecht, G., 'Der Sadd el-Kafara, die älteste Großtalsperre der Welt', in Historische Talsperren 2 (Stuttgart: Wittwer, 1995)
sources.author: Garbrecht, Günther
sources.confirms: Surveys the dam, its dimensions, construction and failure by overtopping.

sources.title: Fahlbusch, H., 'Early dams', Proceedings of the Institution of Civil Engineers, Engineering History and Heritage 162.1 (2009), 13-18
sources.author: Fahlbusch, Henning
sources.venue: Proceedings of the ICE, Engineering History and Heritage
sources.confirms: Reviews Sadd el-Kafara as the oldest large dam and its early failure.

sources.title: Murray, G. W., 'A note on the Sadd el-Kafara: the ancient dam in the Wadi Garawi', Bulletin de l'Institut d'Égypte 28 (1945-46), 33-43
sources.author: Murray, G. W.
sources.confirms: Early survey and dating of the dam.

sadd-el-kafara-dam-failure-2650bce.verification_note: Date and core claims match Garbrecht 1995 and Fahlbusch 2009.
sadd-el-kafara-dam-failure-2650bce.detail: Its design, with heavy shells but a porous core, could not resist overtopping. Its purpose is debated: water supply for alabaster quarry workers is most cited. Dating relies on pottery from its construction camp rather than texts. Mesopotamian canal and dyke systems from this period show engineering at larger scale but without comparable surviving masonry. Later Egyptian hydraulic works concentrated on basin dykes and canals along Egypt's river rather than on storage dams, a choice some historians connect to this early loss.

picture.alt: Remains of the Sadd el-Kafara dam in Wadi Garawi, Egypt.
picture.credit: Kamalelsayedmohamed, via Wikimedia Commons
picture.changes: re-encoded as JPEG at source size 800x536; source smaller than 1200px

sadd-el-kafara-dam-failure-2650bce.dating_note: Pottery from the workers' camp places construction in Dynasty 3-4, c. 2700-2600 BCE; no text mentions it.

caral-supe-pyramids-2600bce.summary: In Peru's Supe valley, 23 km inland, Caral's inhabitants build six large platform mounds, the largest 160 by 150 metres at base and 18 metres high, with sunken circular plazas, residential sectors and irrigation canals, across 65 hectares, between about 2600 and 2000 BCE. Radiocarbon dates show monumental architecture, urban settlement and irrigation agriculture in the Americas by 2627 BCE, contemporary with Giza. Caral has no pottery; fill was carried in woven reed bags (shicras), fishing supplied protein, and cotton was its main crop, traded to coastal fishers for nets. Twelve more Norte Chico sites date to that horizon.

sources.title: Shady Solís, R., Haas, J. and Creamer, W., 'Dating Caral, a Preceramic Site in the Supe Valley on the Central Coast of Peru', Science 292.5517 (2001), 723-726
sources.author: Shady Solís, Ruth; Haas, Jonathan; Creamer, Winifred
sources.confirms: Radiocarbon dates place Caral's monumental architecture and urban settlement between 2627 and 1977 cal BCE.

sources.title: Haas, J., Creamer, W. and Ruiz, A., 'Dating the Late Archaic occupation of the Norte Chico region in Peru', Nature 432 (2004), 1020-1023
sources.author: Haas, Jonathan; Creamer, Winifred; Ruiz, Alvaro
sources.confirms: Dates thirteen Norte Chico sites with monumental architecture to c. 3000-1800 BCE.

sources.title: Shady, R. and Leyva, C. (eds), La Ciudad Sagrada de Caral-Supe (Lima: INC, 2003)
sources.author: Shady Solís, Ruth; Leyva, Carlos (eds)
sources.confirms: Excavator's monograph on architecture, artefacts and chronology.

caral-supe-pyramids-2600bce.verification_note: Date and core claims match Shady Solís 2001 and Haas 2004.
caral-supe-pyramids-2600bce.detail: Caral yielded a quipu-like knotted cord, bone flutes and cornets. Its economy, based on cotton and fish rather than cereal surplus, challenges models of state formation that require grain. Some archaeologists call Caral a city; others see a ceremonial centre with modest resident population. UNESCO listed it in 2009. Thirty-two flutes made from condor and pelican bones were found in a plaza, and fire pits in sunken courts suggest ceremonies with music and burning.

picture.alt: Stepped platform mound and sunken plaza at Caral, Supe Valley, Peru.
picture.credit: Ariana zafra, via Wikimedia Commons

caral-supe-pyramids-2600bce.dating_note: Radiocarbon range 2627-1977 cal BCE (Shady et al. 2001).

harappan-carnelian-bead-drilling-2600bce.summary: Harappan craftsmen produce long barrel-shaped carnelian beads up to 13 cm, each requiring days of drilling from both ends with constricted cylindrical drills of a fired metamorphic rock that Kenoyer and Vidale named 'Ernestite', harder than carnelian and worked with abrasive and water. Kenoyer's 1991 World Archaeology study and a 1992 drill analysis reconstruct a workshop sequence from heat treatment of raw carnelian to polishing. Such beads reached Ur's Royal Cemetery and other Mesopotamian sites, where they were elite goods. Bleached (etched) carnelian beads with white designs were another Indus specialty.

sources.title: Kenoyer, J. M., 'Ornament styles of the Indus Valley tradition: evidence from recent excavations at Harappa, Pakistan', Paléorient 17.2 (1991), 79-98
sources.author: Kenoyer, Jonathan Mark
sources.confirms: Describes bead types, drilling and ornament production at Harappa.

sources.title: Kenoyer, J. M. and Vidale, M., 'A New Look at Stone Drills of the Indus Valley Tradition', MRS Proceedings 267 (1992), 495-518
sources.author: Kenoyer, Jonathan Mark; Vidale, Massimo
sources.confirms: Identifies Ernestite drills and reconstructs drilling technology.

sources.title: Kenoyer, J. M., Vidale, M. and Bhan, K. K., 'Contemporary stone beadmaking in Khambhat, India: patterns of craft specialization and organization of production as reflected in the archaeological record', World Archaeology 23.1 (1991), 44-63
sources.author: Kenoyer, Jonathan Mark; Vidale, Massimo; Bhan, Kuldeep K.
sources.confirms: Describes Harappan specialised craft production and workshop organisation.

harappan-carnelian-bead-drilling-2600bce.verification_note: Date and core claims match Kenoyer 1991 and Kenoyer 1992.
harappan-carnelian-bead-drilling-2600bce.detail: Bead workshops at Chanhu-daro, Harappa and Lothal show controlled heating to redden carnelian and standardised drill types. Drilling rates experimentally measured suggest a single long bead took more than a week. This technology disappears with Indus cities. Mesopotamian texts list long carnelian beads among Meluhhan imports, so a craft specialisation in Gujarat fed demand in Sumerian courts. Raw carnelian came from Gujarat's Ratanpur deposits, so quarrying, heating, drilling and export formed a regional production chain.

picture.alt: Four etched carnelian beads from Chanhu-daro, Indus Civilization, Museum of Fine Arts, Boston.
picture.credit: Unknown author, via Wikimedia Commons

indus-script-undeciphered-2600bce.summary: From about 2600 BCE, Harappan cities produce steatite seals, tablets and pottery bearing short inscriptions, usually under five signs, in a script of some 400 distinct signs written mostly right to left. About 4,000 inscriptions survive, none longer than 26 signs and none bilingual, so it is undeciphered and its language unknown; Dravidian is most often argued, which Parpola argues from structural evidence. Farmer, Sproat and Witzel argued in 2004 that these signs did not encode speech. Rao's 2009 entropy analysis found sign sequences patterned like linguistic texts; Sproat replies that other ordered systems show such patterning too. Use ends with urban decline around 1900 BCE.

sources.title: Rao, R. P. N. et al., 'Entropic Evidence for Linguistic Structure in the Indus Script', Science 324.5931 (2009), 1165
sources.author: Rao, Rajesh P. N.; Yadav, Nisha; Vahia, Mayank N. et al.
sources.confirms: Conditional entropy of sign sequences resembles that of linguistic scripts.
sources.qualifies: Challenged by Sproat and others as not discriminating language from other ordered systems.

sources.title: Farmer, S., Sproat, R. and Witzel, M., 'The Collapse of the Indus-Script Thesis: The Myth of a Literate Harappan Civilization', Electronic Journal of Vedic Studies 11.2 (2004), 19-57
sources.author: Farmer, Steve; Sproat, Richard; Witzel, Michael
sources.confirms: Argues the Indus signs are non-linguistic symbols.
sources.qualifies: Denies the script encoded language.

sources.title: Parpola, A., Deciphering the Indus Script (Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 1994)
sources.author: Parpola, Asko
sources.confirms: Catalogues sign inventory, direction of writing and argues for a Dravidian language.

indus-script-undeciphered-2600bce.verification_note: Existence and date are secure; whether the signs encode language is disputed.
indus-script-undeciphered-2600bce.detail: Seals carried a unicorn-like bovine, zebu, elephant or rhinoceros above each text and served to mark goods and perhaps identity; sealings found at Lothal and in Mesopotamia show their use in trade. Without a long text or a bilingual, decipherment claims (there are dozens) cannot be tested. Sign frequency follows patterns in which a few signs dominate, and text-final signs recur, which Parpola and others read as grammatical suffixes.

picture.alt: Indus steatite seal with unicorn motif and undeciphered script, Indian Museum, Kolkata.
picture.credit: Royroydeb, via Wikimedia Commons

indus-script-undeciphered-2600bce.dating_note: Mature Harappan phase c. 2600-1900 BCE by radiocarbon at Harappa and other sites.

indus-standard-weights-2600bce.summary: Harappan sites from Shortugai in Afghanistan to Lothal in Gujarat share cubical weights of banded chert in a series doubling from a unit of about 0.87 grams (1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64) and then decimal multiples up to 12,800 units, with the 16-unit weight of about 13.7 grams the most common. Kenoyer's 2010 study of measured weights from Harappa finds tight standardisation and links the system to taxation and trade at city gates, where weights cluster. Graduated scales on shell and ivory show a linear unit of about 1.7 mm, and bricks keep a 1:2:4 ratio. The system vanished with the cities around 1900 BCE but 13.7 gram weights persisted in later South Asian standards.

sources.title: Kenoyer, J. M., 'Measuring the Harappan world: Insights into the Indus order and cosmology', in I. Morley and C. Renfrew (eds), The Archaeology of Measurement (Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 2010), 106-121
sources.author: Kenoyer, Jonathan Mark
sources.confirms: Analyses weight series, linear measures and brick ratios from Harappa.

sources.title: Possehl, G. L., The Indus Civilization: A Contemporary Perspective (Walnut Creek: AltaMira, 2002)
sources.author: Possehl, Gregory L.
sources.confirms: Summarises the weight system and its distribution.

indus-standard-weights-2600bce.verification_note: Date and core claims match Kenoyer 2010 and Possehl 2002.
indus-standard-weights-2600bce.detail: Standardised weights across a region larger than Mesopotamia and Egypt combined, without evident kingship or written law, raise questions about Indus political organisation that remain open. Mesopotamian weights used a sexagesimal shekel-mina system; Indus merchants in Mesopotamia must have converted between them. Weights occur in houses as well as gateways, so measurement extended into domestic exchange and craft production rather than only into official tax collection.

picture.alt: Harappan cubical chert weights and balance, museum display.
picture.credit: Gary Todd, via Wikimedia Commons

indus-standard-weights-2600bce.dating_note: Weights appear with Mature Harappan phase c. 2600 BCE.

shuruppak-instructions-cuneiform-2600bce.summary: Around 2600 BCE scribes at Shuruppak (Fara) and Abu Salabikh in southern Iraq write out hymns, proverbs and lexical lists on clay, including early versions of Instructions of Shuruppak, a father's advice to his son. Biggs' edition of about 500 Abu Salabikh tablets showed literature already travelling in copies, with scribes signing their work by name, many of them Semitic rather than Sumerian. Cuneiform had served accounting since about 3200 BCE; these tablets mark its use for composed texts meant to be read and recopied for centuries. Later Old Babylonian schools still taught Instructions of Shuruppak more than 800 years on.

sources.title: Biggs, R. D., Inscriptions from Tell Abū Ṣalābīkh, Oriental Institute Publications 99 (Chicago: University of Chicago Press, 1974)
sources.author: Biggs, Robert D.
sources.venue: Oriental Institute of the University of Chicago, Oriental Institute Publications 99
sources.confirms: Publishes about 500 Early Dynastic IIIa tablets from Abu Salabikh, including literary, lexical and administrative texts with scribal colophons naming scribes.

sources.title: Biggs, R. D. and Postgate, J. N., 'Inscriptions from Abu Salabikh, 1975', Iraq 40 (1978), 101-117
sources.author: Biggs, Robert D.; Postgate, J. Nicholas
sources.confirms: Reports tablets excavated in 1975 with findspots, confirming literary texts in a mid third millennium settlement.

sources.title: Alster, B., Wisdom of Ancient Sumer (Bethesda: CDL Press, 2005)
sources.author: Alster, Bendt
sources.confirms: Edits Instructions of Shuruppak from Abu Salabikh copies through Old Babylonian versions and an Akkadian translation.

sources.title: ETCSL, 'The instructions of Šuruppag' (t.5.6.1), Electronic Text Corpus of Sumerian Literature
sources.author: Black, Jeremy et al. (eds)
sources.confirms: Provides composite text and translation of the composition with manuscript sources listed.

shuruppak-instructions-cuneiform-2600bce.verification_note: Date and core claims match Biggs 1974 and Biggs 1978.
shuruppak-instructions-cuneiform-2600bce.detail: Biggs and Postgate's 1978 report tied tablet findspots to rooms in excavated buildings, so scribal activity can be placed in a settlement context rather than guessed from unprovenanced tablets. Alster's edition traces Instructions of Shuruppak through Early Dynastic, Ur III and Old Babylonian copies and into an Akkadian translation. Dates rest on stratigraphy and palaeography rather than on named kings, so chronology disputes affect them less than later royal texts.

picture.alt: Clay tablet with the Instructions of Shuruppak in Sumerian cuneiform, Oriental Institute Museum, Chicago.
picture.credit: Daderot, via Wikimedia Commons

shuruppak-instructions-cuneiform-2600bce.dating_note: Abu Salabikh tablets are dated by stratigraphy and sign forms to Early Dynastic IIIa, conventionally c. 2600-2500 BCE; no absolute dates exist for this horizon.

giza-pyramid-khufu-2560bce.summary: Over roughly two decades around 2560 BCE, workers under Khufu build a pyramid 146 metres high on a base of 230 metres, with internal chambers of granite shipped from Aswan and an outer casing of fine Tura limestone. The workers' town at Heit el-Ghurab held bakeries, breweries and barracks for rotating labour gangs fed on bread, beer and cattle rather than enslaved multitudes. Merer's papyrus log from Wadi al-Jarf records limestone shipments to the site in Khufu's final years. Radiocarbon programmes gave dates averaging a century or two older than historical chronology, a gap later work attributes partly to old wood.

sources.title: Bonani, G. et al., 'Radiocarbon Dates of Old and Middle Kingdom Monuments in Egypt', Radiocarbon 43.3 (2001), 1297-1320
sources.author: Bonani, Georges; Haas, Herbert; Hawass, Zahi; Lehner, Mark et al.
sources.confirms: Reports radiocarbon dates from mortar and charcoal in pyramids, including Khufu's, averaging older than historical dates.

sources.title: Dee, M. W. et al., 'Reanalysis of the Chronological Discrepancies Obtained by the Old and Middle Kingdom Monuments Project', Radiocarbon 51.3 (2009), 1061-1070
sources.author: Dee, Michael W. et al.
sources.confirms: Finds Dynasty 4 radiocarbon dates 200-300 years older than textual chronology and discusses causes.
sources.qualifies: Radiocarbon suggests Khufu's reign may be earlier than c. 2560 BCE.

sources.title: Lehner, M., The Complete Pyramids (London: Thames & Hudson, 1997)
sources.author: Lehner, Mark
sources.confirms: Describes construction, dimensions, workers' town and theories of ramps.

giza-pyramid-khufu-2560bce.verification_note: Date and core claims match Bonani 2001 and Dee 2009.
giza-pyramid-khufu-2560bce.detail: Orientation to true north within a few arcminutes implies stellar or solar sighting, by a method not yet established. Internal ramps, external ramps and lever schemes are all proposed; no building texts survive. Dynasty 4 radiocarbon dates run 200-300 years older than textual chronology, an offset not yet fully explained. Lehner and Hawass estimate a core workforce near 10,000 at any time, with seasonal additions during flood months when farm labour was idle, provisioned from state estates across Egypt.

picture.alt: Great Pyramid of Khufu at Giza seen from ground level.
picture.credit: Gary Todd from Xinzheng, China, via Wikimedia Commons

giza-pyramid-khufu-2560bce.dating_note: Historical chronology c. 2560 BCE; radiocarbon dates run 100-300 years older (Bonani 2001; Dee 2009).

khufu-ship-2560bce.summary: In 1954 a sealed pit on Khufu's pyramid's south side yielded 1,224 pieces of Lebanese cedar that Ahmed Youssef Moustafa reassembled over a decade into a 43.6 metre ship, its planks joined edge to edge with mortise-and-tenon joints and lashed through V-shaped channels with halfa grass rope, without nails or a keel. Lipke's monograph records this reconstruction. Ward's study of First Dynasty boat graves at Abydos shows sewn-plank construction already in use centuries earlier, so Khufu's vessel represents a mature river-ship tradition. A second pit, opened in 2011, held a sister ship now under reconstruction.

sources.title: Lipke, P., The Royal Ship of Cheops, BAR International Series 225 (Oxford: BAR, 1984)
sources.author: Lipke, Paul
sources.confirms: Documents the dismantled ship, its 1,224 components, joinery and reconstruction by Ahmed Youssef Moustafa.
