sources.title: Ward, C., 'Boat-building and its social context in early Egypt: interpretations from the First Dynasty boat-grave cemetery at Abydos', Antiquity 80 (2006), 118-129
sources.author: Ward, Cheryl
sources.confirms: Shows sewn-plank hull construction at Abydos c. 3000 BCE, placing the Khufu ship in a longer tradition.

sources.title: Ward, C., Sacred and Secular: Ancient Egyptian Ships and Boats (Philadelphia: Archaeological Institute of America, 2000)
sources.author: Ward, Cheryl
sources.confirms: Surveys excavated Egyptian hulls including Khufu's ship and its construction techniques.

khufu-ship-2560bce.verification_note: Date and core claims match Lipke 1984 and Ward 2006.
khufu-ship-2560bce.detail: Its hull shows no sea wear and was probably a ceremonial or funerary vessel, though its construction mirrors working Nile craft. Shell-first building, in which planks define hull shape before internal framing is added, remains the Mediterranean norm for two thousand years. Cedar came by sea from Byblos, which documents maritime trade with Lebanon. Planks up to 23 metres long were carved to curved profiles, and rope lashings tightened as wet wood swelled, sealing seams without caulking.

picture.alt: Reassembled cedar ship of Khufu displayed at the Grand Egyptian Museum, Giza.
picture.credit: Alena Belova for Exhibo, via Wikimedia Commons

khufu-ship-2560bce.dating_note: Pit sealed with blocks bearing Djedefre's name, so burial c. 2560-2550 BCE on Egyptian chronology.

wadi-al-jarf-papyri-hieratic-2560bce.summary: At Wadi al-Jarf on the Red Sea coast, Tallet's team recovered hundreds of papyrus fragments in 2013, sealed in galleries closed late in Khufu's reign, about 2560 BCE. One roll, kept by an inspector named Merer, records his team ferrying limestone blocks from Tura quarries to a Giza construction site called Akhet-Khufu over several months. These are our oldest inscribed papyri, written in cursive hieratic with accounts set out in tables of days and deliveries. They also fix a working harbour with stone anchors and storage galleries on the Red Sea, used for expeditions to Sinai copper and turquoise mines.

sources.title: Tallet, P. and Marouard, G., 'The Harbor of Khufu on the Red Sea Coast at Wadi al-Jarf, Egypt', Near Eastern Archaeology 77.1 (2014), 4-14
sources.author: Tallet, Pierre; Marouard, Gregory
sources.confirms: Describes the harbour, galleries sealed under Khufu, and discovery of the oldest inscribed papyri including Merer's logbook of limestone transport to Giza.

sources.title: Tallet, P. and Marouard, G., 'The Harbor Facilities of King Khufu on the Red Sea Shore: The Wadi al-Jarf/Tell Ras Budran System', Journal of the American Research Center in Egypt 52 (2016), 135-177
sources.author: Tallet, Pierre; Marouard, Gregory
sources.venue: Journal of the American Research Center in Egypt
sources.confirms: Gives detailed stratigraphy and sealings dating the complex to Khufu's reign and its abandonment at his death.

sources.title: Tallet, P., Les papyrus de la mer Rouge II (Cairo: IFAO, 2021)
sources.author: Tallet, Pierre
sources.confirms: Continues full edition of the accounting papyri from the site.

wadi-al-jarf-papyri-hieratic-2560bce.verification_note: Date and core claims match Tallet 2014 and Tallet 2016.
wadi-al-jarf-papyri-hieratic-2560bce.detail: Hieratic, a cursive form of hieroglyphs written with a reed brush, served administration for two thousand years; Merer's log shows a mature bureaucratic hand already in Dynasty 4. Tallet and Marouard date gallery closure by sealings naming Khufu, so the papyri belong to his last years. Publication continues in Tallet's Les papyrus de la mer Rouge series (IFAO, 2017 onward).

picture.alt: Abusir papyrus fragment in hieratic script (c. 2450 BCE), standing in for the Wadi al-Jarf papyri, which are not on Commons; Cleveland Museum of Art loan display.
picture.credit: Tim Evanson from Cleveland Heights, Ohio, USA, via Wikimedia Commons

wadi-al-jarf-papyri-hieratic-2560bce.dating_note: Dated by sealings and the papyri themselves to Khufu's year 26-27; absolute date c. 2560 BCE depends on Egyptian chronology, which radiocarbon work (Dee et al. 2009) suggests may run 50-100 years earlier for Dynasty 4.

kerma-deffufa-nubia-2500bce.summary: South of the Third Cataract in Sudan, Kerma develops from about 2500 BCE into the capital of a Nubian kingdom Egyptians called Kush, with a walled town, a massive mud-brick temple (the Western Deffufa, still 18 metres high), workshops producing fine black-topped red pottery and bronze, and a cemetery of some 30,000 graves. In the Classic Kerma phase (c. 1750-1500 BCE) kings were buried under tumuli up to 90 metres across with hundreds of sacrificed retainers. Honegger's Oxford Handbook chapter and Bonnet's excavations document a state that controlled Nile trade in gold, ivory and ebony and that Egypt conquered under Thutmose I around 1500 BCE.

sources.title: Honegger, M., 'The Pre-Kerma Culture and the Beginning of the Kerma Kingdom', in G. Emberling and B. B. Williams (eds), The Oxford Handbook of Ancient Nubia (Oxford: Oxford University Press, 2021), 179-200
sources.author: Honegger, Matthieu
sources.confirms: Traces Kerma's development from c. 2500 BCE, the town, deffufa and cemetery.

sources.title: Edwards, D. N., The Nubian Past: An Archaeology of the Sudan (London: Routledge, 2004)
sources.author: Edwards, David N.
sources.confirms: Surveys Kerma within Middle Nile history and its conquest by Egypt.

sources.title: Bonnet, C., The Black Kingdom of the Nile (Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 2019)
sources.author: Bonnet, Charles
sources.confirms: Excavator's synthesis of Kerma and Dukki Gel.

kerma-deffufa-nubia-2500bce.verification_note: Date and core claims match Honegger 2021 and Edwards 2004.
kerma-deffufa-nubia-2500bce.detail: Kerma is the earliest urban society in Africa outside Egypt and had no writing of its own; its history is known from archaeology and Egyptian texts that treat it as a rival. Cattle burials and pottery styles connect it with wider Sahelian pastoral traditions. Edwards' synthesis of Nubian history places Kerma within a long sequence of Middle Nile states. Kerma's royal tumuli included Egyptian statues taken as booty, and its archers served as mercenaries in Egypt, showing two-way traffic in people and goods.

picture.alt: Western Deffufa mudbrick temple at Kerma, Sudan.
picture.credit: Lassi, via Wikimedia Commons

kerma-deffufa-nubia-2500bce.dating_note: Early Kerma c. 2500-2050 BCE, Middle c. 2050-1750, Classic c. 1750-1500 BCE by radiocarbon and Egyptian synchronisms.

mohenjo-daro-drains-wells-2500bce.summary: At Mohenjo-daro in Sindh, around 2500 BCE, a city of perhaps 40,000 people is laid out with brick-lined wells, more than 700 by Jansen's estimate, so that most houses had one within reach; bathing platforms and latrines drain through clay pipes into covered brick drains running along streets, with inspection openings and soak pits. The Great Bath, a watertight tank 12 by 7 metres sealed with bitumen, sits on the citadel. Jansen's 1989 study describes this as the most elaborate pre-Roman urban sanitation known. Fired brick of standard proportions (1:2:4) was used throughout.

sources.title: Jansen, M., 'Water supply and sewage disposal at Mohenjo-Daro', World Archaeology 21.2 (1989), 177-192
sources.author: Jansen, Michael
sources.confirms: Describes wells, drains, baths and their social context at Mohenjo-daro.

sources.title: Kenoyer, J. M., Ancient Cities of the Indus Valley Civilization (Karachi: Oxford University Press, 1998)
sources.author: Kenoyer, Jonathan Mark
sources.confirms: Surveys Indus urban planning, drainage and brick standards.

sources.title: Possehl, G. L., The Indus Civilization: A Contemporary Perspective (Walnut Creek: AltaMira, 2002)
sources.author: Possehl, Gregory L.
sources.confirms: Describes Mohenjo-daro's layout, Great Bath and sanitation.

mohenjo-daro-drains-wells-2500bce.verification_note: Date and core claims match Jansen 1989 and Kenoyer 1998.
mohenjo-daro-drains-wells-2500bce.detail: The system's maintenance implies civic organisation, though no palaces or temples are identified and the script is unread. Comparable drainage appears at Harappa, Dholavira and Lothal. Minoan Crete developed similar systems about seven centuries later, apparently independently. Dholavira added large stone-cut reservoirs for rainwater in an arid setting. Wells were rebuilt upward as street levels rose, so some now stand like chimneys several metres above original ground, a visible record of long urban continuity.

picture.alt: Brick-lined well at Mohenjo-daro, Sindh, Pakistan.
picture.credit: Najamuddin Shahwani, via Wikimedia Commons

mohenjo-daro-drains-wells-2500bce.dating_note: Mature Harappan c. 2600-1900 BCE; Mohenjo-daro's main occupation c. 2500-1900 BCE.

paleo-inuit-arctic-migration-2500bce.summary: Around 2500 BCE, small groups carrying a microblade and burin toolkit, called Arctic Small Tool tradition, move from Bering Strait eastward across Arctic Canada and reach Greenland within a few centuries, founding Saqqaq and Independence I cultures and later Dorset. Genomes from ancient remains show these Paleo-Inuit descended from a single Siberian migration distinct from both earlier Native Americans and later Thule Inuit, and that they persisted in isolation for some 4,000 years before being replaced. They hunted seal, musk ox and caribou with toggling harpoons and bows, built skin tents and used soapstone lamps burning sea-mammal oil.

sources.title: Raghavan, M. et al., 'The genetic prehistory of the New World Arctic', Science 345.6200 (2014), 1255832
sources.author: Raghavan, Maanasa; DeGiorgio, Michael; Albrechtsen, Anders et al.
sources.confirms: Ancient genomes show Paleo-Inuit as a single Siberian migration c. 3000 BCE persisting 4,000 years.

sources.title: Friesen, T. M. and Mason, O. K. (eds), The Oxford Handbook of the Prehistoric Arctic (New York: Oxford University Press, 2016)
sources.author: Friesen, T. Max; Mason, Owen K. (eds)
sources.confirms: Chapters on Arctic Small Tool tradition, Saqqaq and Independence I chronology.

paleo-inuit-arctic-migration-2500bce.verification_note: Date and core claims match Raghavan 2014 and Friesen 2016.
paleo-inuit-arctic-migration-2500bce.detail: Independence I sites in northern Greenland are among humanity's most northerly settlements ever occupied, at 82 degrees north. Bow and arrow technology entered North America with this migration. Dating rests on radiocarbon with marine reservoir corrections, which widen error ranges. Saqqaq settlers in west Greenland hunted harp seal and caribou with bows, and permafrost preserved hair from which a complete ancient genome was sequenced in 2010.

picture.alt: Saqqaq culture stone artefacts from Disko Bay, Greenland.
picture.credit: Christian Pingel, 1843, via Wikimedia Commons
picture.changes: re-encoded as JPEG at source size 747x434; source smaller than 1200px

paleo-inuit-arctic-migration-2500bce.dating_note: Arctic Small Tool tradition appears c. 2500 BCE in Alaska and reaches Greenland by c. 2400 BCE; genomic estimate c. 3000 BCE for migration.

pearl-millet-domestication-mali-2500bce.summary: Charred grains and chaff impressions in pottery from Karkarichinkat in Mali's lower Tilemsi valley show domesticated pearl millet (Pennisetum glaucum) with non-shattering, enlarged grains dated about 2500-2000 BCE, our earliest secure evidence for this crop, domesticated from a wild Sahelian grass. It spread across Sahelian grasslands to Tichitt, Chad basin and Nok and south toward the forest, and by about 1700 BCE to India via Indian Ocean routes. Pearl millet tolerates heat and drought beyond any other cereal and remains a Sahelian staple.

sources.title: Manning, K., Pelling, R., Higham, T., Schwenniger, J.-L. and Fuller, D. Q., '4500-Year old domesticated pearl millet (Pennisetum glaucum) from the Tilemsi Valley, Mali: new insights into an alternative cereal domestication pathway', Journal of Archaeological Science 38.2 (2011), 312-322
sources.author: Manning, Katie; Pelling, Ruth; Higham, Tom; Schwenniger, Jean-Luc; Fuller, Dorian Q.
sources.confirms: Reports domesticated pearl millet dated c. 2500-2000 BCE at Karkarichinkat.

sources.title: Fuller, D. Q. et al., 'Transition From Wild to Domesticated Pearl Millet (Pennisetum glaucum) Revealed in Ceramic Temper at Three Middle Holocene Sites in Northern Mali', African Archaeological Review 38 (2021), 211-230
sources.author: Fuller, Dorian Q.; Barron, Aleese; Champion, Louis et al.
sources.confirms: Documents the wild-to-domestic transition in Malian pottery temper and reviews spread.

pearl-millet-domestication-mali-2500bce.verification_note: Date and core claims match Manning 2011 and Fuller 2021.
pearl-millet-domestication-mali-2500bce.detail: Domestication proceeded as desiccation pushed herders south after 3000 BCE; Tilemsi evidence shows a pastoral society adopting cultivation. Sorghum domestication followed in eastern Sahel country. Pearl millet's arrival in India by about 1700 BCE is one of few documented pre-1000 BCE crop transfers out of Africa. Chaff impressions in pottery temper preserve spikelet bases that reveal non-shattering, a key domestication trait otherwise invisible in charred grain.

picture.alt: Field of pearl millet (Pennisetum glaucum); modern photograph for illustration.
picture.credit: Shanmugamp7, via Wikimedia Commons

pearl-millet-domestication-mali-2500bce.dating_note: Direct AMS dates on grains c. 2500-2000 BCE.

stallings-fiber-tempered-pottery-2500bce.summary: Along the Savannah River and Atlantic coast of Georgia and South Carolina, Late Archaic shell-ring and riverside communities make the earliest pottery in North America north of Mexico from about 2500 BCE: thick bowls and basins tempered with Spanish moss and plant fibre, later decorated with punctations and drag-and-jab designs. Sassaman's monograph on Stallings culture traces the sequence, and Gilmore's 2015 direct radiocarbon dating of Spanish moss in sherds confirmed dates around 2500-2200 BCE. Soapstone cooking slabs preceded pots and continued alongside them, suggesting pottery served social gatherings at shell rings rather than replacing existing cooking methods.

sources.title: Sassaman, K. E., Early Pottery in the Southeast: Tradition and Innovation in Cooking Technology (Tuscaloosa: University of Alabama Press, 1993)
sources.author: Sassaman, Kenneth E.
sources.confirms: Analyses Stallings and Orange fibre-tempered pottery, chronology and cooking technology.

sources.title: Gilmore, Z. I., 'Direct radiocarbon dating of Spanish moss (Tillandsia usneoides) from early fiber-tempered pottery in the southeastern U.S.', Journal of Archaeological Science 58 (2015), 1-8
sources.author: Gilmore, Zackary I.
sources.confirms: Direct AMS dates on temper confirm pottery c. 2500-2200 BCE.

stallings-fiber-tempered-pottery-2500bce.verification_note: Date and core claims match Sassaman 1993 and Gilmore 2015.
stallings-fiber-tempered-pottery-2500bce.detail: Fibre-tempered pottery appeared in Florida (Orange) and Georgia (Stallings) centuries before pottery spread north. Whether the idea arrived from South America or arose locally is debated; no connecting sites are known. Shell rings themselves record large-scale feasting on oysters. Fibre temper burned out in firing, leaving porous walls that insulated contents and suited indirect heating with hot stones dropped into stews.

picture.alt: Partially reconstructed fibre-tempered bowl, St. Simons period, Fernbank Museum of Natural History, Atlanta.
picture.credit: Daderot, via Wikimedia Commons

stallings-fiber-tempered-pottery-2500bce.dating_note: Direct dates on Spanish moss temper c. 2500-2200 BCE.

stonehenge-sarsens-2500bce.summary: Around 2500 BCE, in its second major phase, Stonehenge acquires a circle of 30 sarsen uprights with lintels and five inner trilithons, each upright weighing up to 30 tonnes, joined by mortise-and-tenon and tongue-and-groove joints cut in stone. Geochemical analysis of a core from Stone 58 in 2020 matched 50 of 52 sarsens to West Woods, Wiltshire, 25 km north. Smaller bluestones were brought about 225 km from the Preseli Hills in Wales, where Timothy Darvill identified quarrying at Carn Menyn. The axis aligns on midsummer sunrise and midwinter sunset. Radiocarbon modelling dates the sarsen phase to 2620-2480 BCE.

sources.title: Nash, D. J. et al., 'Origins of the sarsen megaliths at Stonehenge', Science Advances 6.31 (2020), eabc0133
sources.author: Nash, David J. et al.
sources.confirms: Geochemical provenance of 50 of 52 sarsens to West Woods, 25 km north of Stonehenge.

sources.title: Darvill, T., Marshall, P., Parker Pearson, M. and Wainwright, G., 'Stonehenge remodelled', Antiquity 86 (2012), 1021-1040
sources.author: Darvill, Timothy; Marshall, Peter; Parker Pearson, Mike; Wainwright, Geoffrey
sources.confirms: Bayesian radiocarbon model dates the sarsen phase to 2620-2480 BCE.

sources.title: Darvill, T. and Wainwright, G., 'Beyond Stonehenge: Carn Menyn Quarry and the origin and date of bluestone extraction in the Preseli Hills of south-west Wales', Antiquity 88 (2014), 1099-1114
sources.author: Darvill, Timothy; Wainwright, Geoffrey
sources.confirms: Identifies bluestone quarrying in Wales in the later third millennium BCE.

stonehenge-sarsens-2500bce.verification_note: Date and core claims match Nash 2020 and Darvill 2012.
stonehenge-sarsens-2500bce.detail: Moving and raising sarsens implies sledges, ropes, timber frames and a labour force drawn from a wide region; isotopes from pigs feasted at nearby Durrington Walls show animals brought from across Britain. Stonehenge has been read as a solar temple, an ancestor monument and a healing centre; construction methods are well documented from tooling marks. In experiments, teams of about 200 could move a 30-tonne sarsen on sledges over timber rails at a few hundred metres a day.

picture.alt: Sarsen trilithons of Stonehenge, Wiltshire, England.
picture.credit: Diego Delso, via Wikimedia Commons

stonehenge-sarsens-2500bce.dating_note: Sarsen phase modelled at 2620-2480 BCE (Darvill et al. 2012).

wheat-reaches-china-2500bce.summary: Directly dated wheat grains show this western Asian cereal reaching China's north-west and Shandong coast by about 2500 BCE, alongside barley a few centuries later. Bayesian analysis of radiocarbon-dated grains finds wheat present in multiple regions by about 2600-2300 BCE, then spreading onto China's Central Plains after 2000 BCE; proposed routes run along Inner Asia's mountain corridor and across steppes. Millet remained China's staple; wheat was a minor crop until milling and noodle-making in Han times. Movement of wheat west to east paralleled movement of millet east to west.

sources.title: Long, T. et al., 'The early history of wheat in China from 14C dating and Bayesian chronological modelling', Nature Plants 4 (2018), 272-279
sources.author: Long, Tengwen; Leipe, Christian; Jin, Guiyun et al.
sources.confirms: Bayesian model of directly dated wheat grains shows arrival c. 2600-2300 BCE and later spread.

sources.title: Betts, A., Jia, P. W. and Dodson, J., 'The origins of wheat in China and potential pathways for its introduction: A review', Quaternary International 348 (2014), 158-168
sources.author: Betts, Alison; Jia, Peter Weiming; Dodson, John
sources.confirms: Reviews routes and dates for wheat's introduction.

wheat-reaches-china-2500bce.verification_note: Date and core claims match Long 2018 and Betts 2014.
wheat-reaches-china-2500bce.detail: Sheep, goats, cattle and bronze metallurgy travelled along similar routes around 3000-2000 BCE, which Liu and Chen call a 'Bronze Age globalisation'. Earlier claims for wheat in China around 3000 BCE rest on indirect dating. Hexaploid bread wheat was what arrived. Winter wheat allowed double cropping with millet in later periods, and its spread changed rotation and storage practices across northern China.

picture.alt: Naked bread wheat kernels (Triticum aestivum); modern photograph for illustration.
picture.credit: Peer Schilperoord, via Wikimedia Commons
picture.changes: re-encoded as JPEG at source size 933x819; source smaller than 1200px

wheat-reaches-china-2500bce.dating_note: Directly dated grains c. 2600-2300 BCE in Gansu-Qinghai and Shandong.

harappan-silk-fibres-2450bce.summary: Good, Kenoyer and Meadow's 2009 microscopy of fibres preserved inside copper-alloy bangles and beads from Harappa and Chanhu-daro, dated about 2450-2000 BCE, identified silk from wild moths of genera Antheraea and Philosamia, native to South Asia, some of it reeled rather than spun. No older silk is known outside China, and these finds are about contemporary with China's earliest. These fibres indicate a South Asian knowledge of silk processing independent of Chinese sericulture, which depended on domesticated Bombyx mori.

sources.title: Good, I. L., Kenoyer, J. M. and Meadow, R. H., 'New Evidence for Early Silk in the Indus Civilization', Archaeometry 51.3 (2009), 457-466
sources.author: Good, Irene L.; Kenoyer, Jonathan Mark; Meadow, Richard H.
sources.confirms: Identifies wild silk fibres in Harappan copper ornaments c. 2450-2000 BCE.

sources.title: Kenoyer, J. M., Ancient Cities of the Indus Valley Civilization (Karachi: Oxford University Press, 1998)
sources.author: Kenoyer, Jonathan Mark
sources.confirms: Context for Harappan ornament and textile crafts.

harappan-silk-fibres-2450bce.verification_note: Date and core claims match Good 2009 and Kenoyer 1998.
harappan-silk-fibres-2450bce.detail: Wild silk continued as tussar and eri silk in India into modern times. Preservation occurred only because copper corrosion products replaced or encased fibres, so scale of Harappan silk use is unknown. This find revised a long assumption of exclusive Chinese origin for silk working. Reeled fibres imply cocoons softened and unwound rather than carded, which indicates processing knowledge beyond opportunistic use of wild cocoons.

picture.alt: Assam silk moth (Antheraea assamensis), a wild silk species; modern photograph for illustration.
picture.credit: Tom Marshall, via Wikimedia Commons

harappan-silk-fibres-2450bce.dating_note: Contexts dated c. 2450-2000 BCE at Harappa.

lothal-dockyard-2400bce.summary: At Lothal, on Gujarat's Gulf of Khambhat, excavator S. R. Rao uncovered a trapezoidal brick-lined basin about 217 by 37 metres and 4 metres deep, with an inlet channel and a spillway, beside a warehouse platform and a town with drains and bead workshops. Rao called it a tidal dockyard for sea-going ships, which would make it our earliest known. Lawrence Leshnik argued in 1968 that it was an irrigation or drinking-water tank, since no ship fittings or harbour equipment were found. A palaeochannel connecting basin and river, identified in 2004, supports its use for boats. Persian Gulf seals and Mesopotamian-style objects show overseas contacts.

sources.title: Leshnik, L. S., 'The Harappan "Port" at Lothal: Another View', American Anthropologist 70.5 (1968), 911-922
sources.author: Leshnik, Lawrence S.
sources.confirms: Argues the basin was a water tank rather than a dock.
sources.qualifies: Rejects the dockyard interpretation.

sources.title: Khadkikar, A. S., Rajshekhar, C. and Kumaran, K. P. N., 'Palaeogeography around the Harappan port of Lothal, Gujarat, western India', Antiquity 78.302 (2004), 896-903
sources.author: Khadkikar, A. S.; Rajshekhar, C.; Kumaran, K. P. N.
sources.confirms: Identifies a palaeochannel linking basin and river, supporting navigation.

sources.title: Rao, S. R., Lothal: A Harappan Port Town (1955-62), Memoirs of the Archaeological Survey of India 78, 2 vols (New Delhi: ASI, 1979-1985)
sources.author: Rao, Shikaripura Ranganatha
sources.confirms: Excavation report presenting the basin as a tidal dockyard.

lothal-dockyard-2400bce.verification_note: Structure is secure; dock versus reservoir function is disputed.
lothal-dockyard-2400bce.detail: Lothal's bead factory produced carnelian and agate beads for export. A dock reading remains majority opinion among Indian archaeologists and is contested by others; its engineering is secure either way. Radiocarbon places occupation c. 2400-1900 BCE. Rao also identified a warehouse with 64 brick blocks where sealings with cloth impressions suggest packaged goods awaiting shipment. Lothal's town plan, with an acropolis, lower town, bead workshop and drains, follows Indus norms at small scale.

picture.alt: Brick-lined basin at Lothal, Gujarat, interpreted as a dockyard or reservoir.
picture.credit: Sanjunath S, via Wikimedia Commons

lothal-dockyard-2400bce.dating_note: Occupation c. 2400-1900 BCE; dock function debated.

mesopotamian-salinization-failure-2400bc.summary: Jacobsen and Adams argued in 1958 that cuneiform crop records from Girsu and Lagash show wheat falling from about one sixth of harvests around 2400 BCE to two percent of it by 2100 BCE and vanishing by 1700 BCE, while barley yields per hectare dropped by more than half between 2400 and 1700 BCE. They attributed this to salt accumulating in irrigated soils with poor drainage and a rising water table, and to administrative notes of 'fields turned white'. Their paper is often cited as history's first documented environmental failure caused by human land use. Powell's 1985 critique questioned the yield statistics and the extent of long-term decline.

sources.title: Jacobsen, T. and Adams, R. M., 'Salt and Silt in Ancient Mesopotamian Agriculture', Science 128.3334 (1958), 1251-1258
sources.author: Jacobsen, Thorkild; Adams, Robert McC.
sources.confirms: Argues from crop records that salinization reduced yields and eliminated wheat in southern Mesopotamia 2400-1700 BCE.

sources.title: Powell, M. A., 'Salt, Seed, and Yields in Sumerian Agriculture: A Critique of the Theory of Progressive Salinization', Zeitschrift für Assyriologie 75 (1985), 7-38
sources.author: Powell, Marvin A.
sources.venue: Zeitschrift für Assyriologie und Vorderasiatische Archäologie
sources.confirms: Challenges the statistical basis of progressive salinization.
sources.qualifies: Argues yield decline is not demonstrated by the texts cited.

mesopotamian-salinization-failure-2400bc.verification_note: Salinization occurred; its scale and the yield statistics are contested by Powell.
mesopotamian-salinization-failure-2400bc.detail: The debate matters for understanding why political power shifted north from Sumer to Babylon. Barley's salt tolerance explains its dominance in later ration texts and in the beer economy. Modern soil surveys confirm severe salinity across southern Iraq, though separating ancient from recent damage is difficult. Mesopotamian farmers knew fallowing and leaching as remedies, and later texts prescribe alternate-year fallow, which suggests awareness of salt even if long-term decline is uncertain.

picture.alt: Inscribed clay cone of Urukagina of Lagash, a near-contemporary of the Girsu field records, Louvre AO 4598.
picture.credit: Unknown artist, via Wikimedia Commons

mesopotamian-salinization-failure-2400bc.dating_note: Crop figures come from administrative texts dated by Ur III and Old Babylonian king lists (middle chronology); that trend is disputed.

ebla-palace-archive-2350bce.summary: In Palace G at Ebla (Tell Mardikh, Syria), Matthiae's excavations from 1974 uncovered an archive room where about 17,000 tablets and fragments had fallen from collapsed wooden shelves when the palace burned around 2300 BCE. Texts in Sumerian and in a local Semitic language now called Eblaite record textile and metal deliveries, treaties, rations, rituals and bilingual word lists. Archi's long study of the archive shows tablets stored by category and retrievable by shape and placement, which makes Ebla one of the earliest known organised archives. Lexical lists pairing Sumerian signs with Eblaite words are among the earliest bilingual dictionaries.

sources.title: Archi, A., Ebla and Its Archives: Texts, History, and Society (Berlin: De Gruyter, 2015)
sources.author: Archi, Alfonso
sources.confirms: Collects studies on the archive's organisation, contents, language and chronology.

sources.title: Matthiae, P., Ebla: Archaeology and History (London: Routledge, 2020)
sources.author: Matthiae, Paolo
sources.confirms: Excavator's account of Palace G, the archive room and its destruction attributed to Akkadian kings.

sources.title: Matthiae, P., 'The Ebla Debate', Biblical Archaeologist 44 (1981), 137
sources.author: Matthiae, Paolo
sources.confirms: Early statement by the excavator on the archive's size and date.

ebla-palace-archive-2350bce.verification_note: Date and core claims match Archi 2015 and Matthiae 2020.
ebla-palace-archive-2350bce.detail: Ebla's destruction is usually attributed to Sargon or Naram-Sin of Akkad, giving a date around 2300 BCE on middle chronology. Archive practice here, with tablets arranged on shelves and dockets, anticipates Hattusa and Nineveh. Most tablets are administrative; the literary share is small but includes incantations and hymns. Tablet shapes signalled content: large square tablets held annual metal accounts, small round ones held monthly textile deliveries, so clerks could locate records by form before reading a line.

picture.alt: Cast (replica) of a cuneiform tablet from the royal palace archive at Ebla, Museo d'Arte Orientale, Rome.
picture.credit: Davide Mauro, via Wikimedia Commons

ebla-palace-archive-2350bce.dating_note: Textual dates for Mesopotamian kings depend on a chosen chronology; middle chronology figures are given here, short chronology runs about 64 years later. Destruction c. 2300 BCE (middle) attributed to Sargon or Naram-Sin; stratigraphic dates are consistent.

kotosh-crossed-hands-2300bce.summary: At Kotosh near Huánuco in Peru's central highlands, Japanese excavators led by Izumi Seiichi uncovered in 1960-63 a sequence of small rectangular temples with central hearths and ventilation ducts, superimposed by ritual burial of each building under its successor. Its Temple of Crossed Hands, Mito phase, around 2300-2000 BCE, has niched walls with two clay reliefs of crossed forearms beneath them. Lathrap's Science review introduced these finds as evidence for Andean ceremonial architecture before pottery. Burger named this pattern of hearth-centred ritual chambers Kotosh Religious Tradition, found from La Galgada to Huaricoto.

sources.title: Lathrap, D. W., 'Origins of Central Andean Civilization: New Evidence (review of Andes 2: Excavations at Kotosh, Peru, 1960)', Science 148.3671 (1965), 796-798
sources.author: Lathrap, Donald W.
sources.confirms: Reviews the Kotosh excavations and their implications for preceramic ceremonial architecture.

sources.title: Burger, R. L., Chavín and the Origins of Andean Civilization (London: Thames & Hudson, 1992)
sources.author: Burger, Richard L.
sources.confirms: Defines the Kotosh Religious Tradition and dates the Mito phase.

sources.title: Izumi, S. and Sono, T., Andes 2: Excavations at Kotosh, Peru, 1960 (Tokyo: Kadokawa, 1963)
sources.author: Izumi, Seiichi; Sono, Toshihiko
sources.confirms: Excavation report for the Temple of the Crossed Hands.

kotosh-crossed-hands-2300bce.verification_note: Date and core claims match Lathrap 1965 and Burger 1992.
kotosh-crossed-hands-2300bce.detail: Hearths burned offerings with air drawn through sub-floor ducts, a shared design across highland sites. Kotosh is preceramic in its early phases and later received Chavín-related pottery. Dating relies on radiocarbon from Japanese expeditions and later work, with some uncertainty. Crossed-arm reliefs may represent paired figures, and their placement below niches implies offerings set above them during rites held in small groups.

picture.alt: Crossed hands relief in the Temple of the Crossed Hands at Kotosh, Huanuco, Peru.
picture.credit: Juan A. Morales C., via Wikimedia Commons

kotosh-crossed-hands-2300bce.dating_note: Mito phase c. 2300-2000 BCE (some estimates 2500-1800 BCE).

meluhha-indus-mesopotamia-trade-2300bce.summary: Sargon of Akkad boasts around 2300 BCE that ships from Meluhha, Magan and Dilmun moor at his capital, and Ur III texts record a 'Meluhha village' of settled traders near Lagash with a Meluhhan interpreter attested on a seal. Meluhha is identified with Indus country on strength of its exports: carnelian, ivory, lapis via Indus middlemen, timber and a 'Meluhha bird'. Indus seals, etched carnelian beads and cubical weights found at Ur, Kish and in the Gulf, and Gulf-type seals at Lothal, confirm this contact. Ratnagar's study and Thornton's review reconstruct routes down the Gulf through Dilmun (Bahrain) and Magan (Oman), where Indus pottery occurs.

sources.title: Thornton, C. P., 'Mesopotamia, Meluhha, and Those in Between', in H. Crawford (ed.), The Sumerian World (London: Routledge, 2013), 600-619
sources.author: Thornton, Christopher P.
sources.confirms: Reviews textual and archaeological evidence for Indus-Mesopotamian exchange.

sources.title: Ratnagar, S., Trading Encounters: From the Euphrates to the Indus in the Bronze Age (New Delhi: Oxford University Press, 2004)
sources.author: Ratnagar, Shereen
sources.confirms: Reconstructs commodities, routes and mechanisms of trade.

sources.title: Possehl, G. L., The Indus Civilization: A Contemporary Perspective (Walnut Creek: AltaMira, 2002)
sources.author: Possehl, Gregory L.
sources.confirms: Lists Indus objects found in Mesopotamia and the Gulf.

meluhha-indus-mesopotamia-trade-2300bce.verification_note: Date and core claims match Thornton 2013 and Ratnagar 2004.
meluhha-indus-mesopotamia-trade-2300bce.detail: Trade was indirect in part, through Gulf intermediaries, and what Mesopotamia sent in return (textiles, oil, silver) left little trace. Contact fades after 1900 BCE with Indus deurbanisation. Possehl's survey collects Mesopotamian finds. A cylinder seal names Shu-ilishu as Meluhhan interpreter, which shows that language difference was managed by professional translators. Round Gulf-type seals found at Lothal and Indus-style seals at Ur show merchants carrying their own marking devices across sea lanes, with Dilmun as a meeting point.

picture.alt: Akkadian cylinder seal of Shu-ilishu, interpreter of the Meluhhan language, Louvre AO 22310 (19th-century catalogue drawing).
picture.credit: Clercq, M. de (Louis), 1836-1901, via Wikimedia Commons

meluhha-indus-mesopotamia-trade-2300bce.dating_note: Sargon's inscription c. 2300 BCE (middle chronology); archaeological finds span c. 2500-1900 BCE.

shimao-stone-city-2300bce.summary: On Loess Plateau of northern Shaanxi, Shimao grew from about 2300 BCE into a 400-hectare settlement enclosed by stone walls with bastions, gates and a 70 metre high stepped platform at its centre, faced with stone and decorated with carved faces and serpents. Jade blades were set into walls, and pits beside the gate held dozens of human skulls. It was abandoned around 1800 BCE. Shimao is largest known walled settlement of its time in China and shows a northern tradition distinct from Central Plains sites of Taosi and Erlitou.

sources.title: Sun, Z. et al., 'The first Neolithic urban center on China's north Loess Plateau: The rise and fall of Shimao', Archaeological Research in Asia 14 (2018), 33-45
sources.author: Sun, Zhouyong; Shao, Jing; Liu, Li et al.
sources.confirms: Reports walls, platform, jade and radiocarbon chronology c. 2300-1800 BCE.

sources.title: Jaang, L., Sun, Z., Shao, J. and Li, M., 'When peripheries were centres: a preliminary study of the Shimao-centred polity in the loess highland, China', Antiquity 92.364 (2018), 1008-1022
sources.author: Jaang, Li; Sun, Zhouyong; Shao, Jing; Li, Min
sources.confirms: Discusses Shimao as a regional centre and its relation to Taosi.

shimao-stone-city-2300bce.verification_note: Date and core claims match Sun 2018 and Jaang 2018.
shimao-stone-city-2300bce.detail: Mouth harps of bone from Shimao are the oldest known examples of that instrument. Shimao's stone architecture had no successor in Chinese tradition, where rammed earth dominated. Climate deterioration around 2000 BCE is proposed for its decline. Stone carvings on Shimao's platform walls include faces and animals in a style later echoed in Shang bronzes, which some scholars read as a northern source for Shang motifs.

picture.alt: Carved stone animal face from the Shimao walled site, Shaanxi.
picture.credit: Bilaterian, via Wikimedia Commons
picture.changes: re-encoded as JPEG at source size 964x1036; source smaller than 1200px
